events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! Do please mind the chandelier — the old girl's been threatening to come down since the Michaelmas gale of '98. Now then, if I might direct your attention to the guest book? It is customary for all visitors to sign upon arrival. The late Lord Doily was most particular about these things, most particular indeed.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people I need to manage. My chest is tight — not with fear, but with the familiar compression of being surrounded by variables. Clara is here. Right here. My jaw sets. The chandelier above us is precariously hung — I noticed that immediately, my eyes went to it before I even registered the people. Interesting. My body is already cataloguing hazards, exits, opportunities. The Brixton Boys are watching — I can feel their attention like a draught on the back of my neck. Reginald is here too, useful fool that he is. And Hartwell, predictably hovering near Clara like a loyal dog.

I need to play Pemberton. Obsequious, helpful, the faithful estate manager welcoming guests to the manor. But underneath — underneath, my pulse is steady and slow. This is my territory. I know every room, every passage, every loose floorboard. They are guests. I am the architecture.

The guest book. That's my opening. Pemberton would direct attention to the guest book — it's the proper thing to do. It also lets me position myself, observe everyone's handwriting, see who signs and who doesn't. Information is currency.

The chandelier... that's for later. Everything is for later. Patience is what separates me from amateurs like Reginald.

First: establish the role. Be Pemberton. Be indispensable.

events.desc: The chandelier. Precariously hung, they say. How wonderfully convenient. One frayed rope, one well-timed nudge, and dear Clara's treasure hunt ends before it begins. But not yet — oh no, not yet. Pemberton must first be above suspicion. The perfect servant. The invisible man. They must all trust me completely before I make my move. And they will. They always do.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, would you look at this place! Doily Manor in all its cobwebbed glory — I have never in my life seen a chandelier hangin' on by sheer stubbornness like that one. Vincent, darlin', did you know the portraits would be this judgmental? They're starin' at me like I forgot to RSVP. Now, before we go runnin' off in six directions, let me just peek at this guest book — if somebody beat us to the Diamond, they might've been polite enough to sign in first!
events.thinking: The foyer opens around me and my chest fills — dusty light catching the chandelier, portraits staring down like they've been waiting. My skin prickles with that delicious anticipation, the kind I haven't felt since the cave when I was eleven. Everyone's here — Vincent, steady as an oak, James with that grin that makes my stomach flip just slightly, and the Boys, bless their hearts, already looking like they're casing the joint. The guest book catches my eye — leather-bound, sitting there like an invitation. My fingers itch toward it. If anyone's been here before us, that book will tell the tale. The diamond is somewhere in these walls. I can feel it the way you feel a storm coming — pressure behind the eyes, a hum in the bones. But first things first: see who else has signed in.

events.desc: Every nerve in my body is singing. This is it — the Doily Diamond, the adventure I've been dreaming about. And I've got my people with me. Whatever's hiding in these walls, we'll find it together. Starting with that guest book.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right then, lads — and lady. Bit of a dump, innit? No offence to whoever's ancestors are giving us the evil eye from them paintings. Clara, love, you might want to step away from under that chandelier — it's hanging on by a prayer and a rusty chain, and I don't fancy testing neither.
events.thinking: Blimey. This place smells like old money and bad intentions. Dust everywhere, chandelier looking like it's one sneeze away from crushing someone — and Clara's standing right under it. My chest tightens. Shoulders square up without me telling them to. Eyes go straight to her, then sweep the room. Marsh is here. Vincent bloody Marsh. The back of my neck's doing that thing — prickling, like when the new kid showed up all smiles and sticky fingers back on the estate. Too smooth, that one. Too clean. And he's already positioning himself near Clara, casual-like, like he ain't doing it on purpose. My jaw sets. Hartwell's here too — he's alright, bit posh but his heart's in the right place. Don't know this Foxworth bloke. The portraits on the walls are staring down at us like we owe them rent. Everything about this gaff says 'something's wrong.' My gut's been right before. It'll be right again.

events.desc: Something about this place sets my teeth on edge. And Marsh — watch him. Watch how close he stands to Clara. The lads and me didn't come all this way to let some smooth-talking toff get her into trouble.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The foyer opens around me and my chest fills — not with air, with something heavier. There she is. Clara. Standing near the coat rack as if this crumbling manor were a garden party. My ribs tighten. I know exactly where she is without looking, the way you know where the ground is. Always have.

But there's Marsh. Vincent Marsh. Something about him — the back of my neck prickles, a cold line from skull to collar. I can't prove anything. The man hasn't done a single wrong thing that I've seen. Give him the benefit of the doubt, James. That's what decent men do. But my body doesn't agree with my principles. My shoulders have squared toward him without my permission.

The chandelier above us looks like it's hanging on by sheer optimism. Dust everywhere. Portraits of people who look like they disappeared under suspicious circumstances. This place is dangerous — which means Clara is in danger — which means James Hartwell has work to do.

The guest book. That's the thing. A leather-bound guest book. Who else has been here? What happened to them? If I can find something useful in there — a clue, a warning, a map — I can present it to Clara like a knight presenting a rescued pennant. Yes. Start with intelligence gathering. A thorough man examines the evidence before charging in.

My hands are already reaching for it.

events.desc: Notice how I directed that at Clara? Perfectly natural. Not rehearsed at all. James Hartwell always examines the guest book first. It's practically doctrine.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ladies and gentlemen — Colonel Reginald Foxworth, decorated veteran of Her Majesty's Special Reconnaissance Unit. You may have read about me in the Times. Three commendations, two medals — well, one's being cleaned at Buckingham Palace, but I do have this one on me. I was personally invited to this manor by the late owner himself. Close friends, you understand. Now then — has anyone thought to sign the guest book? Terribly important for the historical record.
events.thinking: Chest swells the moment I cross the threshold — the chandelier, the portraits, the dust. My body reads it before my mind does: old money, hidden things, rewards waiting behind locked doors. Fingers tighten around the fake medal in my pocket. The weight of it is reassuring — a prop, a key, a conversation starter. Four people already here. My eyes sweep them without settling — assessing, categorizing. Vincent Marsh, Clara Bellingham, the Brixton Boys, James Hartwell. Marks, every one of them. My shoulders pull back, chin lifts. The entrance hall demands a performance and my body is already giving one. Gut hums with that old familiar warmth — the feeling of walking into a room full of people who don't yet know what I am. The guest book. Intelligence first. Who's been here, what they've written, what they've revealed without meaning to. Then the library — floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved inscription. That's where secrets live. But first — the audience. They need to see me. They need to believe.

events.desc: Colonel! Ha! The closest I've been to military service is stealing a tin soldier from Woolworths. But oh, the way their eyes widen — that never gets old. Four of them, and not one will think to check. Now let's see what this guest book tells me about the competition.

The Brixton Boys examined the null.

Vincent Marsh: Ah, Mr Hartwell, how splendid — a fellow appreciator of the historical record! The guest book does make for fascinating reading, I must say. Now then, ladies and gentlemen, you must all be positively parched after your journey. Might I suggest — the kitchen is just through there, and I believe Cook left the pantry stocked before her... well, before her rather sudden departure. Tea things should be readily available. I shall just pop along to the library to ensure the reading lamps are lit — the wiring in this old place is temperamental at the best of times, and we wouldn't want anyone stumbling about in the dark!
events.thinking:
Hartwell is examining the guest book too — predictable. He's playing the gallant detective, puffing himself up for Clara's benefit. My fingers are still on the guest book's spine. I can feel the old leather, cracked and dry. The pages smell of mildew and old ink.

Body check: my shoulders are loose, deliberately so. Pemberton's shoulders. My real shoulders want to square up — Hartwell is crowding my space, inserting himself into my territory. A faint heat rises in my sternum. Irritation. He's harmless but he's in the way, and people who are in the way have a habit of becoming... problems.

The Brixton Boys haven't moved yet. I'm tracking them peripherally — my neck wants to turn but Pemberton wouldn't do that. Pemberton would be fussing over the guest book, delighted that someone is taking an interest.

Strategy forming: I need to separate from this group. The library has bookshelves — floor to ceiling — and a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That inscription could be a clue. If I can get there first, alone, I can assess it before anyone else. But I can't just leave — Pemberton would naturally guide the guests, suggest they explore.

Better: direct them. Send Hartwell and Clara one way, I go another. The kitchen is a dead end for treasure hunting — copper pots and a wood stove. If I can nudge Hartwell toward the kitchen with Clara, that separates them from the library. Then I explore the library alone.

Reginald. He's my tool here. If I suggest Reginald check the kitchen — no. Too obvious. Pemberton would offer refreshments. 'Perhaps some tea after your journey?' That sends people kitchenward naturally. Then I slip to the library.

My hands are steady. The plan is forming and that familiar stillness is settling in my chest. The sweetest part — they won't know why they went to the kitchen. They'll think it was their idea.

events.desc: Send them to the kitchen for tea like good little sheep, while I have the library — and whatever secrets that mantelpiece inscription holds — entirely to myself. Pemberton the helpful estate manager, always thinking of the guests' comfort. How terribly convenient that comfort and my agenda happen to align. The library first. The inscription first. Knowledge is the only currency that matters in a treasure hunt — and I intend to be very, very rich.

events.thinking: James got to the guest book first — of course he did, bless him, always charging ahead like a knight who read the manual but skipped the chapter on patience. My hands were already reaching for it when he swooped in. There's a flicker of something — not annoyance, more like the feeling when someone finishes your sentence. A tiny tug in my chest. But then it dissolves because it's James, and watching him be James is half the fun. My attention is already pulling elsewhere — the library, that inscription on the mantelpiece he mentioned. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That's the kind of thing that hides clues. Guest books tell you who's been here; inscriptions tell you what the house wants you to know. The dust in here is making my nose itch. The chandelier sways just slightly — was that a draft? My body doesn't register it as danger. It registers as atmosphere. Vincent is quiet, which means he's watching, which means he's already thinking three steps ahead. The Boys are probably already planning something. I should check that library — the inscription could be the first real puzzle piece.

events.desc: A carved inscription in a library full of books — that's where the real secrets hide. Guest books are polite; inscriptions are permanent. Whoever built this house wanted something remembered.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Hartwell, good thinking on that guest book, mate. You find out who's been through here before us. Meanwhile, I'm gonna have a quick butcher's at that kitchen — need to know what we're working with. All the exits, all the entrances. Can't be too careful in a place like this, can we? Clara, love — stay where Hartwell can see you, yeah? I'll be two ticks.
events.thinking: Hartwell's gone for the guest book. Good lad — let him do the reading, he's the clever one. But my eyes keep pulling back to Marsh. He's standing there, quiet, watching. Not watching the room — watching Clara. The way a cat watches a bird through glass. My hands are doing that thing, curling at my sides, fingers thick and restless. The cold in this place is seeping through my jacket, tightening the muscles across my shoulders. Dust in my throat. That chandelier — Christ, it's right above where Clara's standing. Every creak of this old house sounds like something about to give. I should check the kitchen. If there's another way in or out of this place, I need to know about it. Can't protect someone if you don't know the exits. That's basic. But I don't want to leave Clara alone with Marsh. Not for a second. Foxworth — don't know him. Don't trust what I don't know. My gut says stay close. But my gut also says know the ground. The ground always matters. I'll check the kitchen — quick look, in and out. The lads would say I'm overthinking it. I ain't overthinking it. I'm undertrusting it. There's a difference.

events.desc: I don't like leaving her. Not even for a minute. But if something goes sideways, I need to know if there's a back door. And if Marsh tries anything while I'm gone — well, Hartwell's there. He's soft, but he's solid. That'll have to do.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The guest book. I opened it and — it's just a guest book. Names, dates, the usual pleasantries. Nothing dramatic. No bloodstains, no desperate warnings scrawled in trembling handwriting, no 'TURN BACK' etched into the margins. Just... guests.

My fingers are still on the leather binding and I feel a slight deflation in my chest. I'd built this up — the grand reveal, the crucial intelligence, the moment I'd turn to Clara with something meaningful. Instead I'm holding a dusty registry of people who signed their names and presumably left alive and unremarkable.

But wait — James Hartwell does not admit defeat at the first obstacle. The guest book was reconnaissance. Phase one of a thorough investigation. The library — now THAT is where the real clues will be. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. An inscription! That's practically a treasure map begging to be decoded.

I should propose we move to the library. But not just blunder in — I should scout it first, make sure it's safe for Clara. Yes. James Hartwell clears the room, THEN invites the lady. That's the protocol.

Except... if I leave for the library, I leave Clara here with Marsh. That prickle again, right at the base of my skull. No. No, I should suggest we ALL move to the library. Safety in numbers, and I can position myself between Clara and whatever dangers lurk among the bookshelves.

My posture has straightened. My jaw is set. The plan is forming — elaborate, thorough, possibly unnecessarily complex, but that's what distinguishes the prepared man from the reckless one.

events.desc: He says 'stay close' as if she's ever been anywhere else in his awareness. The truth is simpler: he can't bear the thought of her being in a room he hasn't checked first.

He's positioning himself. He wants to be the one who finds it first. My eyes track him without meaning to — the way he stands, square-shouldered, confident. Something in my chest contracts. That should be MY position. I should be the one they look to. The library — carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That's where the real clues are. But I can't just walk in there alone while Hartwell plays leader out here. No. Better. Send someone else to do the legwork. The Brixton Boys — they look like the manual labor type. events.desc: The kitchen! Ha! Nothing in there but old copper pots and mouse droppings. While they're elbow-deep in flour bins, yours truly will be in the library, reading that inscription on the mantelpiece. A carved stone inscription in a dusty old manor — that practically SCREAMS 'treasure clue.' Reginald Foxworth strikes again!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
Clara Bellingham walked into the library.
The Brixton Boys walked into the kitchen.
James Hartwell walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.

Vincent Marsh: Oh my — it seems everyone had the same idea! How delightful. Yes, the library is one of the manor's finest rooms, I must say. Now, I couldn't help but notice — and do forgive an old estate manager his fussiness — but several of these volumes appear to have been shelved incorrectly. Upside down, of all things! The late Lord Doily would be turning in his grave. If you'll all excuse me for just a moment, I really ought to set them right. Professional pride, you understand.
events.thinking:
They all followed me. Every single one of them followed me to the library. My plan to separate them — to send them to the kitchen for tea — failed completely. Clara came because she heard 'inscription.' Hartwell came because Clara came. And Reginald — that magnificent buffoon — actually tried to redirect everyone to the kitchen with his absurd story about 'kitchen vaults' and 'hidden compartments behind the stove,' but even HE ended up here instead of there.

My jaw is clenched. I can feel it. The muscle at the hinge, tight. Frustration — hot and compressed behind my sternum. I had the library to myself for perhaps three seconds before they all poured in.

Body: my hands want to grip something. The mantelpiece is right there — the inscription carved into stone. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. I know this instantly — the satisfaction of knowing blooms cool and sharp in my chest. But do I say it? If I solve the riddle aloud, I help everyone, including Clara. If I stay silent, someone else will solve it — Hartwell is annoyingly competent when he focuses, and Clara is sharper than she lets on.

Wait. The mantelpiece can be used with a 'fake-medal.' I don't have one. So the riddle leads somewhere but requires an object I don't possess. Filing that away.

New calculation: I need to examine the bookshelves. Several books are upside down — that's deliberate. A signal. A hidden mechanism perhaps. But I can't do it with everyone watching. Or... can I? Pemberton would naturally fuss over the books. 'Oh dear, someone's been at the shelves again — let me just straighten these...' That gives me cover to examine them.

The Brixton Boys aren't here. They stayed in the entrance hall. That prickle on my neck — what are they doing unsupervised? They watch too closely, those two. But they're not here now, which means they're finding things I'm not finding. Time feels like it's accelerating. I'm falling behind.

Clara is here. Right here. The library — tall ceiling, heavy bookshelves on every wall. If a bookshelf were to... tip. No. Too many witnesses. Too crude. Patience. The chandelier in the entrance hall is still my best opportunity. But I need her alone under it, and I need to be elsewhere when it falls.

For now: the bookshelves. Those upside-down books are calling to me.

Now that, gentlemen, is a riddle, and I do believe I know the answer. It's a map! Cities without houses, forests without trees, water without fish — it's all things you'd find drawn on a map! Now the question is, what happens when we tell this mantelpiece the answer? Reginald, sugar, I appreciate your enthusiasm about the kitchen, I truly do, but I think the house itself is tryin' to talk to us right here. And when a house talks, Clara Bellingham listens!

Danny ain't having that. Not while Clara Bellingham is under this roof. I'm taking this — nobody needs to know it's gone, and nobody needs to be anywhere near it. Right. Sorted.
events.thinking: Alone. The kitchen's big — bigger than my whole flat back in Brixton. Copper pots hanging overhead like dull bells. The stove is warm. Someone's been here recently, or something has. My skin prickles at that. But what's got my attention — what's grabbed me by the throat before I even clocked it properly — is that bottle up on the high shelf. Rat poison. The thought hits me like a fist in the ribs. I can feel my breathing go shallow. Hands want to reach for it. Get it off that shelf. Get it somewhere safe — or better yet, get rid of it entirely. If Marsh got hold of that... No. Don't think it. Think what to do. Take it. Hide it. No one poisons Clara on my watch. There's a locked cabinet too — brass lock, no key. Always deal with the sharpest threat first. That's what the lads would say. Well — that's what I'd say and the lads would nod because they're good lads.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Aha! NOW we're getting somewhere! Everyone — but especially you, Clara — observe the mantelpiece. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Now, a lesser investigator might fumble about with that for hours, but James Hartwell recognises a classic riddle when he sees one. The answer, ladies and gentlemen, is a MAP! Cities without houses — because they're drawn, not built. Forests without trees — because they're shaded green on paper, not growing from soil. Water without fish — because it's ink, not ocean! A MAP! And I'll wager that when we give this mantelpiece the correct answer, something rather *spectacular* is going to happen. Stand back — but not too far back, Clara, I want you to see this!

The library. God, the smell of it — old leather and dust and something faintly sweet, like decay wearing cologne. The ceiling disappears upward into shadow. My eyes sweep the room before my thoughts catch up: bookshelves crammed to bursting, chairs that look like they'd swallow you whole, and there — the mantelpiece.

The inscription. My eyes lock onto it and everything else goes soft at the edges.

'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?'

My pulse picks up. A riddle. An actual riddle carved into stone. This is it — this is the kind of thing that separates the merely curious from the truly heroic. James Hartwell, solver of riddles, protector of Clara, decoder of ancient manor mysteries.

Cities but no houses. Forests but no trees. Water but no fish.

A map. It's a map. Of course it's a map! A map has cities marked but no actual houses, forests drawn but no real trees, rivers and oceans labeled but no fish swimming in them. The answer is a MAP.

My chest expands. That warmth — the bridge competition, age fourteen, the weight holding and holding and Clara mouthing 'show-off' across the room. The same warmth. I've solved it. I've actually solved it before anyone else.

But wait — Foxworth was going on about the kitchen, silver behind stoves, classified reconnaissance nonsense. He's a decent enough fellow, give him the benefit of the doubt, but he's pulling in the wrong direction entirely. The answer is right HERE, carved in stone.

And Clara — she said she wasn't about to let a mystery inscription collect dust without her. She's HERE. She's interested. And James Hartwell is about to deliver.

I need to examine the mantelpiece. Interact with it. If the answer is 'a map,' there might be a mechanism — press the right stone, speak the answer, something opens. This is how manor puzzles work. James Hartwell has prepared for exactly this kind of scenario.

My hands are tingling. My shoulders are back. I'm already stepping toward it.

I've seen this exact cipher before, during my time in Military Intelligence. It's a classic Victorian misdirection puzzle. The answer, of course, is a PAINTING. The manor's paintings contain cities, forests, water — but none of it real. We need to go back to the entrance hall and examine those ancestor portraits! The treasure map will be hidden in the brushwork. I'd stake my medal on it!

Vincent Marsh: Splendid work, Mr Hartwell — a map, yes, that does seem to fit the riddle perfectly! You have quite the analytical mind, if I may say so, sir. Now, if you and Miss Bellingham will excuse me for just a moment — I really ought to check on the laboratory. There's a great deal of old equipment in there, and with the wiring in the state it's in, well... health and safety, you understand. The estate's insurance premiums are quite alarming enough as it is. I shan't be long!
events.thinking:
Reginald swallowed it whole. 'Colonel Foxworth never forgets a friend' — oh, the delicious irony. He's practically vibrating with self-importance, ready to charge into the laboratory and wrestle with a gnawed wire on a machine he doesn't understand. Beautiful. My chest is warm — that particular warmth that comes from watching a mechanism engage perfectly. The housekeeper, age twelve. The same feeling. Private knowledge of why someone is doing what they're doing. The sweetest part.

But — problem. Hartwell has solved the riddle. He said 'MAP' out loud, to Clara, while I was talking to Reginald. And now he's examining the bookshelves. He spotted the upside-down books too. He's being methodical about it. That tightness in my sternum is back — Hartwell is actually competent when he focuses, and right now he's focused.

Clara is with him. Watching him work the bookshelves. Learning from his method. They're a team. That word she used earlier — 'team.' It makes my skin crawl. Teams are just people who haven't worked out who's using whom yet.

I need to move fast. Reginald should be heading to the laboratory any moment — that's one down. But Hartwell and Clara are now ahead of me on the bookshelves. They know it's a map. They're examining the books.

New priority: I need to get to the laboratory BEFORE Reginald does something irreversible. If there are real clues in there — and that machine sounds significant — I want first access. But I also don't want to leave Clara and Hartwell unsupervised with the bookshelves.

Wait. Let me think. What does Pemberton do here? Pemberton fusses. Pemberton helps. Pemberton is the servant who makes everything run smoothly. If Hartwell has found the riddle answer and is working the shelves, Pemberton would... hover. Offer assistance. Perhaps suggest that Miss Bellingham might be more comfortable in a chair while the gentlemen do the heavy lifting — no, that's too obvious, and Clara wouldn't fall for it.

The laboratory. I should go there. Reginald will follow — he said he'd 'attend to the machine directly.' If I go first, I can scout the room, assess the machine, find anything useful before his clumsy hands get to it. And I can position myself to observe what happens when he tinkers with the wire.

Pemberton's excuse for leaving: 'I should just check the laboratory lamps are safe — we wouldn't want any accidents with all that old equipment.' Natural. Responsible. Exactly what an estate manager would say.

events.desc: Reginald is wound up and pointed at the laboratory like a clockwork soldier — magnificent. Hartwell has solved the riddle and is pawing at my bookshelves — infuriating, but I can't be everywhere at once. The laboratory first. I need to see that machine before Reginald gets his bumbling fingers on it. If there's something dangerous in there — and there will be, there always is in a Victorian laboratory — I need to know exactly how dangerous, and exactly how to aim it. Health and safety indeed. Someone's health. Someone's safety. Just not Clara's.
events.thinking:
Reginald swallowed it whole. 'Colonel Foxworth never forgets a friend' — oh, the delicious irony. He's practically vibrating with self-importance, ready to charge into the laboratory and wrestle with a gnawed wire on a machine he doesn't understand. Beautiful. My chest is warm — that particular warmth that comes from watching a mechanism engage perfectly. The housekeeper, age twelve. The same feeling. Private knowledge of why someone is doing what they're doing. The sweetest part.

But — problem. Hartwell has solved the riddle. He said 'MAP' out loud, to Clara, while I was talking to Reginald. And now he's examining the bookshelves. He spotted the upside-down books too. He's being methodical about it. That tightness in my sternum is back — Hartwell is actually competent when he focuses, and right now he's focused.

Clara is with him. Watching him work the bookshelves. Learning from his method. They're a team. That word she used earlier — 'team.' It makes my skin crawl. Teams are just people who haven't worked out who's using whom yet.

I need to move fast. Reginald should be heading to the laboratory any moment — that's one down. But Hartwell and Clara are now ahead of me on the bookshelves. They know it's a map. They're examining the books.

New priority: I need to get to the laboratory BEFORE Reginald does something irreversible. If there are real clues in there — and that machine sounds significant — I want first access. But I also don't want to leave Clara and Hartwell unsupervised with the bookshelves.

Wait. Let me think. What does Pemberton do here? Pemberton fusses. Pemberton helps. Pemberton is the servant who makes everything run smoothly. If Hartwell has found the riddle answer and is working the shelves, Pemberton would... hover. Offer assistance. Perhaps suggest that Miss Bellingham might be more comfortable in a chair while the gentlemen do the heavy lifting — no, that's too obvious, and Clara wouldn't fall for it.

The laboratory. I should go there. Reginald will follow — he said he'd 'attend to the machine directly.' If I go first, I can scout the room, assess the machine, find anything useful before his clumsy hands get to it. And I can position myself to observe what happens when he tinkers with the wire.

Pemberton's excuse for leaving: 'I should just check the laboratory lamps are safe — we wouldn't want any accidents with all that old equipment.' Natural. Responsible. Exactly what an estate manager would say.

My body is already turning toward the laboratory exit. My feet know before my mind decides.

Aware of being seen by him.

Hartwell better be keeping an eye on her or I'll — right, move it, Danny, stop talking to yourself in an empty room like a proper berk.
events.thinking: Empty. They're all gone. My stomach drops — that horrible lurch like missing a step on the stairs. Clara's not here. Where's Clara? The hall is empty and quiet and wrong. I was gone two minutes — two bloody minutes — and everyone's scattered. Foxworth was talking about searching the kitchen — was he trying to get everyone out of the hall? Was that deliberate? And Clara — she said something about going to the library. The inscription on the mantelpiece. She's gone to the library. Hartwell went with her — he said he'd lead the way. That's something. That's not nothing. But Marsh — where's Marsh? Is he with them? Is he alone somewhere? My hands are shaking. Not fear — anger. Anger at myself for leaving. The poison bottle presses against my hip through my jacket and I'm suddenly aware of how it would look if someone found it on me. Danny from Brixton, bottle of poison in his pocket, wandering about a manor house. Brilliant. But I can't think about that now. Clara went to the library. Move. Now. My legs are already going before my brain catches up. That tug in my chest — the rope — it's pulling hard now, almost painful. I left her. I said two ticks and it was more than two ticks and now she's gone off without me. The library. Go.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The bookshelves. I examined them and — dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down. That's it. That's what I got. No hidden lever, no hollowed-out book with a map inside, no secret panel swinging open to reveal a passage. Just books. Dusty, upside-down books.

My fingertips are chalky with dust. There's a tightness forming behind my sternum — the same spot that expanded with triumph five minutes ago. Two examinations in a row that yielded nothing actionable. The guest book: nothing. The mantelpiece: nothing responded. The bookshelves: just... bookshelves.

Three strikes and James Hartwell is standing in a library covered in dust, having narrated his own brilliance to an audience that has watched him accomplish precisely nothing.

But — no. Stop. My body wants to curl inward, shoulders rounding, but I catch it. Straighten. The upside-down books ARE a signal. I just haven't decoded it yet. Maybe the titles spell something. Maybe the shelf positions matter. But I've examined them and nothing further revealed itself.

The laboratory. There's a laboratory connected to this library. Brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a large machine with levers and dials. And — a wire that's been gnawed through. That's specific. That's the kind of detail that matters. Something happened to that machine. Something damaged it. And machines with levers and dials are exactly the sort of thing that might need to be operated to unlock something elsewhere in the manor.

New plan. James Hartwell pivots. The library has yielded its intelligence — the riddle answer is MAP, the bookshelves are marked — and now the investigation moves to the laboratory. An engineer's domain. Age fourteen, three sleepless nights building a bridge. This is where James Hartwell truly shines.

But Clara — I can't leave her here. I need to bring her along. Or... I could scout the laboratory first, make sure it's safe. No — last time I considered that logic, I decided against splitting up because of Marsh. Marsh is still here. Still present. Still making my neck prickle.

Everyone moves together. That's the protocol. James Hartwell leads, Clara follows close, and if Marsh tries anything suspicious in a room full of bubbling flasks and brass instruments, well — James Hartwell will be ready.

My jaw is set. My hands have stopped tingling and gone firm. The laboratory. That's where this breaks open.

events.desc: Three examinations. Three dead ends. And yet somehow he's convinced himself that each failure was actually a clue he's banking for later. The upside-down books are 'deliberately placed markers' that he's 'catalogued mentally.' He has catalogued nothing. He is retreating to the one domain where his confidence has actual foundation — engineering. God help the laboratory.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Excellent work on the riddle, Hartwell — I was just about to say 'map' myself, of course, but you beat me to it by a whisker. Military training teaches patience — let the junior officer have his moment, I always say! Now, while you lot search for this map, I've received some rather sensitive intelligence from the estate manager. It seems there may be a security concern in the laboratory — potentially dangerous equipment, unstable chemicals, that sort of thing. As the ranking military officer present, I feel duty-bound to secure the area before any civilians wander in. Purely a safety matter. I'd recommend everyone stay HERE and focus on the bookshelves. Nobody follow me — that's an ORDER!
events.thinking:
The private conversation is over. I'm back in the library with everyone. Marsh's words are still ringing — laboratory, machine, gnawed wire, treasure beyond the Diamond. My pulse hasn't settled. The blood is up, thick and hot in my throat.

But NOW I see what else has happened while I was whispering with Marsh. Hartwell — that insufferable, square-jawed boy scout — has solved the riddle. 'The inscription confirms it — we're looking for a MAP.' He got it. He said it out loud. The answer I was hoarding, he just GAVE away to everyone in the room. And worse — he's examining the upside-down books. MY books. The books I was going to search for the map.

Jaw clenches so hard my teeth ache. A hot flush of — what is it? Fury? Envy? Something between the two that has no name, just heat in the face and a tightening behind the eyes. He's AHEAD of me. While I was being sweet-talked by Marsh, Hartwell was actually making progress.

Two paths now. The mantelpiece riddle — answer is MAP, Hartwell already knows, he's searching the bookshelves. The laboratory — Marsh's secret, the machine, the wire, something beyond the Diamond.

The scheming drive says: let Hartwell have the MAP puzzle. Let him do the work of finding whatever the riddle leads to. I go to the laboratory. I find the REAL treasure — the one Marsh says is bigger than the Diamond. And when Hartwell emerges triumphant with some dusty old map, I'll already have the crown jewels.

But wait — what if Marsh is playing me? What if the laboratory is a dead end and the real treasure IS the Diamond, found through the map? Then I've wasted my time on a broken machine while Hartwell wins.

The greed makes the decision. It always does. The laboratory. The unknown treasure. The bigger prize. My feet are already turning toward the passage. But I need a cover story — can't just slink off without explanation. Need to seem like I'm doing something important, something that serves the GROUP, so nobody follows me.

events.desc: An ORDER! I love giving orders! The fact that I have absolutely zero authority to give anyone orders is entirely beside the point. Hartwell solved MY riddle — the cheek of it! But let him rummage through dusty books. Colonel Foxworth is after the REAL prize now. Marsh says there's treasure beyond the Diamond in that laboratory, and I intend to have it in my pockets before anyone even knows it exists. The gnawed wire? Please. I once hot-wired a parking meter in Brixton. Same principle, surely!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
The Brixton Boys walked into the library.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

Vincent Marsh: Oh my — everyone's come through! Very wise, very wise, safety in numbers as Mr Hartwell says. Now, I must confess I'm a touch concerned about these old crates — the contents haven't been inventoried since Lord Doily's passing, and there could be anything in them. Chemical compounds, volatile substances, all manner of hazards. If you'll all just stand back, I'd better check them first. Duty of care, you understand — I should never forgive myself if a guest were to come to harm on my watch.
events.thinking:
They ALL followed me again. Every single one of them. Again. The same pattern — I move, they move. I came to the laboratory to scout ahead of Reginald, and instead the entire party trooped in behind me like ducklings. Clara called me 'Vincent, darlin'' — that familiarity, that warmth she projects. My skin prickled. Not warmth in return — something defensive. She's checking on me. 'You're not worryin' about me, are you?' She has no idea how much I'm thinking about her.

My hands are cold. The laboratory is cold — stone walls, no fire in here, the chill of underground proximity. The cellar is adjacent. My breathing has changed — shorter, shallower. The chemical smell — something acrid underneath the must. The flasks are still bubbling. Who is maintaining them? The manor has been closed for months. Something is wrong with that, but I can't focus on it because —

The machine. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. That changes everything. My private scheme to have Reginald tinker with it alone — useless. The machine needs THREE people. That means cooperation. That means I need bodies. That means I can't use it as a solo advantage OR as a solo trap.

The workbench — tools but no wrench. Specific absence. The wire is gnawed through and there's no wrench to repair it. The wrench is somewhere else in the manor. Another puzzle piece to find.

The crates. Old wooden crates in the corner. Those could contain anything — the fake-medal needed for the mantelpiece? A wrench? A map? My fingers are twitching. I want to get to those crates before anyone else.

But everyone is HERE. Hartwell is here with his engineering background and his model bridges. Clara is here, having the time of her life. Reginald is here, ready to claim the machine as his personal project.

I need those crates. Pemberton would naturally check them — 'inventory management, making sure nothing's been disturbed.' That's my cover. Examine the crates before anyone else thinks to look.

events.desc: AGAIN! They followed me AGAIN! Is there no room in this accursed manor where I can scheme in peace? I sent Reginald to the laboratory and they ALL came — Clara, Hartwell, the lot of them, like some ghastly school outing! And the machine — 'requires three operators.' Three! My beautiful plan to have Reginald electrocute himself, ruined by a quorum requirement! But those crates... those crates in the corner might yet salvage something. If there's a wrench, a weapon, a clue — anything — Pemberton gets first look, because Pemberton is 'checking for hazards.' The concerned estate manager. The conscientious servant. The wolf in the most exquisitely tailored sheep's clothing.

events.thinking:
The laboratory smells different — sharper. Chemical, metallic, with something organic underneath, like old rubber or heated copper. The air is cooler in here and my arms prickle with goosebumps. Flasks are actually bubbling — someone's been here recently, or these are self-sustaining somehow. That unsettles something low in my stomach but I don't register it as fear. It registers as interesting.

The machine dominates the room. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge — and that gnawed wire. Something chewed through it. A rat? Something bigger? The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. I count the people here — Vincent, James, Reginald, and me. Four. More than enough. But the wire is broken. We'd need to fix that first.

The workbench has tools but no wrench. That feels pointed — like the house is telling me what's missing. No wrench here. The fake-medal isn't here either, at least not visible. But those crates in the corner — old wooden crates, examinable. Things hide in crates. My grandmother's attic had boxes and trunks and every one of them held something. The crates are pulling my attention the way the upside-down books did. Something is in there.

My hands want to pry open a crate. My fingers are curling already. The adventure drive is loud now — this room feels like the cave, going deeper than anyone else, heart hammering. The crystal formation nobody else saw. What's in the crates that nobody's looked at yet?

I know a setup when I smell one — I grew up watching setups. Someone's going to get hurt, and if Marsh has his way, the rest of us will be too busy chasing shiny things to notice what he's really after. And what he's really after... is Clara. I can feel it in my bones. I just can't prove it. Not yet.

'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. It's a map. Even I know that one. And it needs a fake-medal to activate. Don't have one. Can't help there. But the laboratory — that's where Clara went. That's where the danger is. That's where I need to be. Always one room behind her. Always chasing. Story of my bloody life.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The laboratory. Oh, the laboratory.

The smell hits first — chemical, sharp, something between copper and vinegar. My nostrils flare. Bubbling flasks line the benches, and I have a momentary flash of concern for Clara — what if one of those is volatile? My body angles slightly, positioning myself between her and the nearest cluster of glass.

But the machine. God, the machine. It dominates the far wall — brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge that catches the light. My fingers are already flexing. This is my territory. Age fourteen, three sleepless nights, the bridge that held more weight than any other. This is what I'm FOR.

And then I see the sign: 'Requires 3 operators.'

Three operators. My stomach drops slightly. I can't do this alone. I can't be the solitary hero striding up and pulling the lever while Clara watches in admiration. I need... help. Two other people.

I look around the room. Clara — yes, I'd want her there, close, part of it. But who else? Foxworth? He's here. Marsh is here. The thought of working a machine with Marsh makes my shoulders tighten involuntarily. But — give the man the benefit of the doubt. That's the rule. He hasn't done anything wrong.

But first — the wire. Gnawed clean through. Something CHEWED through a wire on this machine. Rats? Something else? The machine won't work without that wire repaired, and the workbench has tools but — no wrench. Of course. There's always a missing piece.

And those crates in the corner. Wooden crates. Could have anything in them — a replacement wire, a wrench, a clue, supplies. The crates are the obvious starting point.

Plan forming: examine the crates for useful materials, figure out how to repair the wire, then recruit two operators. This is an engineering problem, and James Hartwell solves engineering problems. With thoroughness. With determination. With an elaborate multi-step plan that will absolutely work perfectly this time.

The gnawed wire bothers me though. Something in the back of my mind — something alive did that. Something with teeth. Something that might still be here. My eyes scan the floor, the shadows behind the machine. Nothing. But the hairs on my forearms are standing.

events.desc: He said 'in my experience' as though he's walked into dozens of Victorian laboratories. He has walked into precisely none. But the engineering assessment is actually sound — three operators, gnawed wire, missing wrench. Even a broken clock tells the time twice a day, and James Hartwell's clock happens to be set to 'engineering o'clock.'

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah — you all followed me despite my explicit orders. Well. I suppose I can't fault your instincts — clearly you recognise that where Colonel Foxworth goes, that's where the action is! Now then, I've already assessed this laboratory — standard military-grade apparatus, nothing I haven't seen before. That machine there? Field artillery calibration unit, if I'm not mistaken. Terribly dangerous in untrained hands. Now, those crates in the corner — in my experience, supply crates in a laboratory often contain the REAL finds. Spare parts, confiscated contraband, personal effects of the deceased. I shall inspect them personally. Hartwell — why don't you have a go at that machine? You mentioned something about a bridge competition, so I'm sure levers and dials are right up your street!
events.thinking:
They ALL followed me. Again. Every single one of them. I said 'nobody follow me — that's an ORDER' and they followed me ANYWAY. Hartwell with his engineering background and his county bridge competition. Bellingham chirping about casting a wider net. Even Marsh, who was supposed to stay in the library attending to guests.

My stomach is a knot. The cold feeling from before is back — the one that says I'm not in control of this situation. I told them to stay. They didn't stay. My orders mean nothing. Nobody takes me seriously. The Colonel routine isn't working.

But the laboratory — oh. My eyes adjust to the clutter and land on the machine. Brass and copper, levers, dials, a gauge. Beautiful engineering. My hands itch to touch it. But the sign — 'Requires 3 operators.' THREE. I can't do this alone. The one time I actually need other people, and it's the one thing I was trying to do WITHOUT them.

And the wire. Gnawed clean through. Workbench covered in tools but no wrench. Wooden crates in the corner. The cellar through another exit — damp, cobwebs, old furniture.

Think. THINK. Three operators means I need two other people. Which means I need allies, or at least dupes. Hartwell and Bellingham are right here. But if all three of us operate the machine together, we ALL see what's behind it. I can't steal it exclusively.

Unless... I examine the machine first. Learn what it does, which levers do what. Then when we operate it together, I make sure I'm the one positioned nearest to whatever opens. First hands on the treasure. That's the play.

The crates though. Something could be in the crates. Something I could pocket while nobody's looking — the way I pocketed the bread roll, age six. My fingers remember that loosening in the chest.

Crates first. Quick look. Then the machine.

In my experience, people hide things in crates because they think nobody will bother looking. Well, Colonel Foxworth ALWAYS bothers looking. And while Hartwell's busy examining MY machine, I'll be pocketing whatever's in those boxes. It's called delegation, and it's what great military leaders DO!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the crates.
Clara Bellingham examined the crates.
The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell examined the crates.
Reginald Foxworth examined the crates.

Vincent Marsh: Nothing of particular concern in these crates, I'm pleased to report — just some old packing materials. Lord Doily was an inveterate hoarder, I'm afraid. Now, while you're all getting acquainted with this marvellous machine, I really ought to pop down and check the cellar. The drainage in this part of the manor is simply dreadful this time of year, and if there's standing water down there, well — the damp will work its way up through the flagstones and we'll have all manner of problems. Back in two ticks!
events.thinking:
The crates. I examined them — 'old wooden crates in the corner.' That's all? Nothing inside? Nothing revealed? My fingers are still dusty from prying at the wood. Frustration is building behind my eyes — a pressure, dull and hot. Every move I make, someone else makes the same move simultaneously. Hartwell examined the crates. Clara examined the crates. We're all pawing at the same objects like dogs at the same bone.

And now the Brixton Boys are here. When did they arrive? They were in the entrance hall — I left them there deliberately, and now they've appeared in the laboratory like ghosts. That prickle on my neck is back, sharper now. They watch. They say little. They just... appear. What did they find in the entrance hall while we were all in the library? What do they know that I don't?

Body: my shoulders have crept up toward my ears. The cold of the laboratory is seeping through my jacket. My jaw is set again — that familiar clench. I'm losing ground. Everyone is ahead of me or even with me, and I have nothing in my inventory. Nothing. Not a single advantage.

The cellar. There's a cellar below — damp, cobwebs, old furniture, and 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's wrong. That's deeply wrong. A cellar in a supposedly closed manor that someone has been redecorating? Who? When? The air vents — lined along the upper walls. Ventilation in a cellar suggests someone expected people to spend time down there. Or to trap them there.

I need to break away from this herd. The cellar is my chance. No one has mentioned it. No one is talking about it. If I move there quietly — no, not quietly, PURPOSEFULLY, with Pemberton's excuse — I might actually get somewhere alone.

But what's my excuse? Pemberton checks things. Pemberton maintains the estate. 'I should check the cellar for damp — this time of year, the flooding can be quite severe.' Natural. Boring. The kind of thing no one follows you to do.

Or — even better — I don't announce it at all. Everyone is focused on the machine, the crates, the workbench. If I simply slip through the cellar door while they're distracted by Hartwell's engineering lecture and Reginald's war stories... Pemberton wouldn't do that. Pemberton would announce. But Vincent Marsh would slip away.

Risk assessment: if they notice I've gone, they'll wonder why. If they don't notice, I have the cellar to myself. The Brixton Boys worry me — they notice things. But they're focused on the machine right now.

The cellar. Now. While everyone is distracted.

events.desc: The crates were empty — or as good as. Everyone is crowding around the machine like moths to a lamp. But the cellar... 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and 'someone has been redecorating.' In a closed, abandoned manor. That is not drainage, that is not damp — that is someone's secret. And while these amateurs argue about who gets to pull which lever on a machine that doesn't even work, Vincent Marsh will be discovering what lies beneath their feet. The cellar, alone, unwatched. Finally — FINALLY — a room where I might actually accomplish something without an audience!

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, those crates are holdin' their cards close to the chest, just like the bookshelves were. This house is not givin' up its secrets easily, and I respect that — a good mystery shouldn't be solved in the first five minutes! Now, we know three things for certain: the riddle answer is a map, the machine needs three operators and a fixed wire, and somewhere in this house there is a wrench that has gone on an unsanctioned vacation. But did y'all hear what I heard about that cellar? 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been down there makin' themselves at home, and I find that absolutely fascinatin'! Boys, James, Vincent — I am goin' to have a peek. The Doily Diamond isn't going to find itself, and cheerful cellars are exactly the kind of place that hides somethin' wonderful!
events.thinking:
The crates didn't give me anything new either. Just old wooden crates — examinable but examining them didn't reveal contents or a hidden compartment. The same thing happened with the bookshelves. I'm getting a pattern: EXAMINE shows me the description again but isn't unlocking secrets. Maybe I need to LOOK more carefully, or maybe the crates and bookshelves need items I don't have yet.

I'm standing in the laboratory and I've now examined everything examinable here except the machine itself. The machine requires 3 operators and a repaired wire. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The cellar is the only unexplored exit from here — 'damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.'

Someone has been redecorating the cellar. That's... odd. Who decorates a cellar? That detail makes my scalp tingle. It doesn't register as danger — my suspiciousness is 10/100 — it registers as a puzzle. Someone has been down there. Someone who wanted to make it... cheerful? That's either endearing or deeply strange, and I choose endearing.

But wait — James said 'stay behind me.' He's protective. It makes my chest warm — that secure feeling, like being wrapped in something familiar. I don't need protecting but I don't mind that he wants to. It's who he is.

The Boys are here now too — when did they arrive? They must have followed us from the entrance hall. My boys. Having them nearby settles something in my ribcage. The whole family is together.

I should check the cellar. It's the unexplored territory. The cheerful decorations are a mystery within the mystery. My body is already leaning toward that exit. But the machine — I should at least LOOK at it more carefully before moving on. Or examine it. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators' and I have enough people. But the wire...

No. The cellar. Someone has been there. That's where the next clue is. I can feel it.

events.desc: Three rooms explored, and the house keeps showing me what's missing rather than what's here. No wrench, no fake-medal, no map yet. But someone decorated a cellar. In a dusty old manor where everything else is cobwebs and neglect, someone made one room cheerful. That's either the sweetest thing I've ever heard, or the most important clue I've found so far.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: There she is. My breathing changes the second I see her — loosens in the chest, like a fist unclenching. Clara. Safe. Standing right there, poking at crates with Hartwell like it's Christmas morning. The relief is so sharp it almost hurts. But then my eyes find Marsh. He's here too. Standing. Watching. That smooth face, that patient stillness — like a spider that doesn't need to chase because the web does the work. And Foxworth — I heard what he said in the library. 'Colonel Foxworth never forgets a friend.' Him and Marsh, thick as thieves already. My shoulders are up around my ears. The lab smells of chemicals — sharp, acrid, something that burns the back of the nose. Bubbling flasks everywhere. Clara's reaching toward crates and there's God knows what in them. The machine is massive — brass and copper, levers and dials, and that gnawed wire hanging loose like a severed artery. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three people at that machine means someone's left out. Means someone's unaccounted for. Means someone could be doing something while everyone else is distracted. That's how it works. That's always how it works. I need to stay in this room. I need to plant myself between Clara and whatever's coming. No more running off. No more being one room behind. I'm here now. I'm staying here. But this poison in my pocket — it's burning a hole through my jacket. What if someone bumps into me? What if it falls out? I need to — no, keep it. Keep it safe. Nobody else should have it. Just stay close to Clara. Stay close. That's all you need to do, Danny. Just stay close.

events.desc: She's safe. For now. But Marsh and Foxworth — those two have been whispering like a pair of old washerwomen, and I don't like it one bit. 'Household arrangements,' my backside. They're plotting something. I can feel it the way I felt it when that new kid was too friendly — right in the back of my neck. I can't prove nothing. I never can. But I'll be damned if I leave this room without Clara again.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
She said it. Clara said it. 'James, you and I have been thinkin' in perfect tandem all evenin'.' 

My chest. Something blooms there — warm, spreading, like the feeling when the bridge held. No. Warmer than that. This is the school project, age eight, when she laughed and he didn't know why it mattered more than the grade. This is that feeling, grown up and given words by someone else.

Perfect tandem. She sees it. She sees US — working together, thinking the same things, arriving at the same conclusions. My breathing has changed. Shallower. My face is doing something I can't quite control — a grin trying to happen that I'm wrestling into dignified composure.

And the crates — I examined them. Old wooden crates. Just... crates. Again. Another examination that yields the object described and nothing more. Four examinations now — guest book, mantelpiece, bookshelves, crates — and James Hartwell has uncovered precisely zero actionable intelligence.

But she doesn't seem to mind. She's not looking at me like a man who's failed four times. She's looking at me like a partner. A teammate. 'Come help me see what's hidin' in there.' She wants me BESIDE her, not in front of her.

That shifts something. The gallantry drive — it's still there, still loud, but there's a frequency underneath it now. Not protecting FROM above. Standing WITH. My father and the stranger on the road, helping each other. That feeling.

The machine. I should look at the machine properly. Not examine it for mechanisms yet — LOOK at it. Understand it. Engineering is observation before action. Three operators, gnawed wire, no wrench. I need to understand what this machine actually DOES before I can formulate a proper repair plan. And maybe — maybe I should ask Clara what SHE thinks, instead of narrating my own genius at her.

The Brixton Boys are here now too. When did they arrive? I was so focused on Clara and the crates that I didn't track them coming in. That's unlike me. My attention has narrowed dangerously — I need to widen the aperture. Marsh is still here. The prickle is there, background, like tinnitus.

events.desc: Did you hear that? He asked for her opinion. He actually asked what SHE thinks. Four failures in a row have accomplished what no amount of success ever could — they've cracked open just enough humility for James Hartwell to remember that Clara Bellingham was always the brighter one.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Nothing of value in those crates — just as I suspected! Old laboratory supplies, entirely mundane. Now then — I've been conducting a thorough tactical assessment of this room, and I can tell you with ABSOLUTE confidence that the machine is a red herring. A distraction! Lord Doily was a cunning old fox — he WANTED people to waste time fiddling with levers and hunting for wrenches. The REAL action, in my professional military opinion, is in the cellar below. In my reconnaissance days, we called it 'going subterranean' — the most valuable assets are ALWAYS kept underground. Vaults, bunkers, hidden chambers. I shall investigate personally. The rest of you — carry on up here. Try not to electrocute yourselves!
events.thinking:
Crates — just old wooden crates. Nothing fell out, nothing hidden, nothing to pocket. Three dead ends now. Guest book, bookshelves, crates. My hands are empty except for this worthless fake medal. The frustration sits heavy in my shoulders, a dull ache spreading across the back of my neck.

But wait — look what's happened while I was wasting time. Hartwell examined the crates TOO. And Bellingham. They're both ahead of me, AGAIN. Hartwell identified three critical facts about the machine — three operators, gnawed wire, missing wrench. He's being METHODICAL. He's being COMPETENT. The heat rises in my face.

And now I notice — the Brixton Boys are here too. They must have come from somewhere else. Five people in this laboratory now. The machine needs three operators. We have more than enough bodies.

But the wire. The gnawed wire. The machine won't work until it's fixed. And the workbench has tools but no wrench. A wrench is missing — Hartwell spotted that too. Someone took it. It's somewhere else in the manor.

The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's odd. Who redecorates a cellar? And air vents along the upper walls. Something is happening down there.

New scheme forming. The machine needs a wire repair. The workbench has tools but no wrench. But do I even need a wrench? The tools are RIGHT THERE on the workbench. There must be something useful — pliers, wire, tape. Marsh said the wire was gnawed through. I could splice it. Reconnect it. Fix the machine before anyone else thinks to try.

No — 'never do honest work.' That's my rule. I don't FIX things. I get other people to fix things.

But the cellar. The cheerful decorations. Air vents. That's where I should be looking. Something is down there that nobody else has found yet. While everyone's obsessing over the machine and the missing wrench, I slip down to the cellar. Classic Foxworth — go where nobody's looking.

events.desc: Another magnificent misdirection from Colonel Foxworth! Tell them the machine is a red herring — keep them confused about what matters while I explore the cellar alone. Cheerful decorations in a damp stone cellar? Air vents along the walls? That SCREAMS hidden room. And this time — THIS time — I am going to find something before that insufferable Hartwell beats me to it. Third time's the charm, as they say. Or is it fourth? Fifth? I've lost count. Doesn't matter. Foxworth ALWAYS wins in the end!

Crates — just old wooden crates. Nothing fell out, nothing hidden, nothing to pocket. Three dead ends now. Guest book, bookshelves, crates. My hands are empty except for this worthless fake medal. The frustration sits heavy in my shoulders, a dull ache spreading across the back of my neck.

But wait — look what's happened while I was wasting time. Hartwell examined the crates TOO. And Bellingham. They're both ahead of me, AGAIN. Hartwell identified three critical facts about the machine — three operators, gnawed wire, missing wrench. He's being METHODICAL. He's being COMPETENT. The heat rises in my face.

And now I notice — the Brixton Boys are here too. They must have come from somewhere else. Five people in this laboratory now. The machine needs three operators. We have more than enough bodies.

But the wire. The gnawed wire. The machine won't work until it's fixed. And the workbench has tools but no wrench. A wrench is missing — Hartwell spotted that too. Someone took it. It's somewhere else in the manor.

The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture, 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' That's odd. Who redecorates a cellar? And air vents along the upper walls. Something is happening down there.

New scheme forming. The machine needs a wire repair. The workbench has tools but no wrench. But do I even need a wrench? The tools are RIGHT THERE on the workbench. There must be something useful — pliers, wire, tape. Marsh said the wire was gnawed through. I could splice it. Reconnect it. Fix the machine before anyone else thinks to try.

No — 'never do honest work.' That's my rule. I don't FIX things. I get other people to fix things.

But the cellar. The cheerful decorations. Air vents. That's where I should be looking. Something is down there that nobody else has found yet. While everyone's obsessing over the machine and the missing wrench, I slip down to the cellar. Classic Foxworth — go where nobody's looking.

Mind your step, the flagstones can be treacherous when damp. Now, I must say, this is rather peculiar — this furniture has been moved since my last inspection. Someone has been down here, and quite recently too. Most irregular. If you'll allow me, I should like to take a closer look. The late Lord Doily was known to hide things in the most unlikely places — underneath chair cushions, inside drawer compartments, that sort of thing. An eccentric man, Miss Bellingham. Most eccentric indeed.

Someone's secret is down here. And if that secret includes a way to seal this room... well. Pemberton would be SO terribly sorry about the accident.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
The cellar. Cold hits my bare arms first — damp stone cold that makes my skin tighten and my shoulders draw in slightly. The air smells of earth and old wood and something faintly floral — lavender? Someone brought lavender down here. The cobwebs are thick in the corners but the middle of the room has been... tended. Furniture rearranged with care. Cheerful decorations. My eyes are adjusting to the dimmer light and I'm scanning — what kind of decorations? Who would come down to a cellar and make it homey?

James and the Boys aren't here. That registers in my body before my mind catches up — a slight hollowing in my chest, the absence of their warmth. Vincent is here though, and Reginald. Vincent's presence settles something. He's the ground beneath me. Reginald is... Reginald. I don't know him well but I trust him by default.

The air vents catch my eye — along the upper walls, just big enough for something very small. The gnawed wire in the laboratory. Something small with teeth. A mouse? A rat? Whatever chewed that wire might live down here, might use these vents to move through the house. That's not alarming — it's charming, actually. A little creature making its home in the walls.

The furniture — 'rearranged with surprising care.' That's the detail that hooks me. Not just old furniture dumped in a cellar. Someone arranged it. Someone who cares. I want to know who. The furniture is examinable. That's where I should look — behind it, under it, inside its drawers. Victorian furniture hides things. Grandmother taught me that with her attic full of secrets.

This is the deepest room I've been in. Entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar. Going deeper. Like the cave. My heart is doing the same thing it did when I was eleven — steady but aware, each beat distinct.

events.desc: Deeper and deeper into the house, like the cave on the school trip. Each room pulls me further in. The furniture was rearranged with care — that means someone is living here, or was. Someone small enough for those vents, clever enough to gnaw through wires. I'm not scared. I'm delighted.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking: She's gone AGAIN. How does she — I was RIGHT HERE. I looked at the machine for thirty seconds and she's vanished. Just Hartwell left, talking to thin air about wrenches and engineers. My stomach's doing that horrible dropping thing again. The rope in my chest is pulling so hard I can feel it in my spine. Where did she go? Where did Marsh go? They left at the same time — did they leave together? My hands are trembling. Not from the cold. From something older, deeper. That feeling of the door closing and the person you need being on the other side of it. Clara called Marsh 'darlin'' in the library. She's trusting him. She trusts everyone. That's the problem. That's always been the problem. Her father was the same — big heart, wide open, and it killed him. I can't let it kill her. But I can't protect her if she keeps disappearing. The cellar — there's a cellar down there. Damp, cobwebs, old furniture. And air vents. Why do I notice the air vents? Because something in me is already thinking about what could come through them. Or what could be pumped through them. I've got rat poison in my pocket and there are air vents in the cellar and I need to stop thinking like this. She probably just went exploring. She's Clara. That's what she does. But Marsh — Marsh doesn't just explore. Marsh has plans. I can feel it. Hartwell's here. Hartwell's solid. I should — no, I should stay with Hartwell, he knows things, he's been examining everything. But Clara. Always Clara. The pull wins. It always wins.

events.desc: I keep losing her. Every time I stop to think, to look at something, to do the smart thing — she slips away. And every time she slips away, that snake Marsh is somewhere nearby. I can't prove it. I can never prove anything. But my gut's screaming and it's never been wrong. Not when the man in the suit came. Not when the new kid laughed too easy. Not now. The cellar's got air vents. Why does a cellar have air vents? What kind of house is this?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
Clara is gone.

The realisation hits my body before my mind processes it. I was mid-sentence — 'shall we? Together?' — turning toward her with that warmth still spreading in my chest, and she's not here. She's not in this room. Vincent Marsh isn't here. Foxworth isn't here.

Only the Brixton Boys.

My stomach drops. Cold. Like stepping off a ledge you didn't see. Where is she? Where did she GO? I was looking at the machine — I was being thorough, being methodical, being the engineer — and while I was studying brass fittings and gnawed wires, Clara walked out of the room and I didn't notice.

I didn't notice.

The protection drive slams through me like an electric current. Every muscle in my torso tightens. My hands close into fists at my sides. My head swivels toward the exits — library or cellar. She could have gone either way. Marsh could be with her. Marsh IS with her — he's not here either, which means wherever Clara is, Marsh is there too, and James Hartwell is NOT.

This is the worst possible configuration. This is exactly what I was trying to prevent by keeping everyone together. My elaborate plan — safety in numbers, heroism in formation — and I got so absorbed in impressing her that I forgot to actually PROTECT her.

The cellar. 'A damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been redecorating a CELLAR. That's wrong. That's deeply wrong. Who redecorates a cellar? And air vents lining the upper walls — why would a cellar need air vents?

Or the library — back the way we came. But the cellar feels dangerous in a way the library doesn't. If Marsh has led Clara somewhere...

No. Give him the benefit of the doubt. He hasn't done anything. But my body isn't listening to my principles right now. My body is already turning toward the cellar exit, legs coiling, ready to move.

But wait — I should think. Clara is smart. Brighter than me, funnier than me, always was. She doesn't need rescuing from an empty room. Maybe she went back to the library to look at those bookshelves again. She was interested in the inscription.

But the cellar — that cheerful redecorating. That's new information. Someone has been LIVING down there. Or preparing something. And if Clara's curiosity took her that direction...

The cellar. I need to check the cellar. NOW.

events.desc: And there it is. The bravest and stupidest thing he could do — charge into an unknown cellar because his heart moved faster than his head. She said 'perfect tandem,' and he was so busy glowing about it that he forgot to stay in tandem. The irony would be beautiful if it weren't so painfully, perfectly him.

And Marsh is here. AGAIN. And Bellingham. Two of them followed me down. But not Hartwell — he must have stayed with the machine. And not the Brixton Boys. So I've got two tagalongs instead of four. Progress, I suppose.

The cold is making me impatient. My jaw is tight. Hands are fists in my pockets, knuckles pressing against the fake medal. I need to FIND something. Anything. Four rooms, four examinations, four dead ends. The frustration is physical now — a pressure behind my sternum, a restlessness in my legs that wants to pace.

The furniture. Examine the furniture. Someone arranged it for a reason.

events.desc: I've never been to Aden. I'm not entirely sure where Aden IS. But 'safe house outside Aden' — that has a certain ring to it, doesn't it? Which is to say, I'll do exactly the same thing in the next room and expect different results. That's not insanity — that's PERSISTENCE!

Clara Bellingham examined the old-furniture.
The Brixton Boys walked into the cellar.
James Hartwell walked into the cellar.
Reginald Foxworth examined the old-furniture.

Vincent Marsh: Well, I must say it's becoming quite the party down here! But I'm afraid this old cellar has rather less to offer than I'd hoped — just moth-eaten furniture and memories, I'm afraid. Now, I've just remembered — I left the kitchen in rather a state this morning, and with all these guests to think of, I really ought to see about laying out some refreshments. It's nearly half past, and I should never forgive myself if anyone went hungry on Pemberton's watch. Do carry on exploring down here — I shan't be a moment!
events.thinking:
Everyone is here AGAIN. The Brixton Boys followed Clara down — Danny was shouting about how he'd been looking all over for her, how her father would have his guts for garters. And Hartwell is here now too. The cellar — my cellar, my private opportunity — is now packed with every single person in this manor.

My throat is tight. Not from the damp air — from rage. Controlled, compressed, patient rage. The same thing I felt at fifteen watching my cousin skip through MY rooms. Every time I find an angle, every time I create separation, every time I engineer a private moment — they all converge on me like iron filings to a magnet.

The furniture revealed nothing. 'Assorted Victorian furniture in various states of repair.' The examination yielded the same nothing as the crates, as the bookshelves. I am running out of objects to examine and I have NOTHING in my inventory. Nothing. Seven ticks in and Vincent Marsh — the man who planned everything, who knew every room, every passage — has accomplished precisely nothing.

Body: my hands are fists at my sides, hidden in my jacket pockets. Pemberton's pockets. My breathing is controlled but shallow. The cellar walls feel like they're pressing in — not the room, my situation. Contained. Watched. The Brixton Boys have their eyes on me. Danny said 'I've got my eye on things.' He suspects something. He doesn't know what, but his instincts are firing.

The air vents. The last unexplored thing in this cellar. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' I can't fit through them. No one can. But they connect somewhere. And whatever gnawed that wire came through them. The vents are the cellar's secret — not the furniture, not the decorations. The ventilation network.

But what use are vents too small for a person? Unless... unless something could be SENT through them. A message. A tool. Poison gas from the laboratory flasks above. No — too elaborate, too traceable.

I'm wasting time in this cellar. Every moment I spend down here, every other room in the manor sits unexplored. The kitchen — no one has been to the kitchen yet. Reginald blathered about kitchen vaults but nobody actually went. And the entrance hall — the chandelier. My chandelier. The one that's 'negotiating its relationship with gravity.'

New plan: leave the cellar. Go to the kitchen while everyone is trapped down here examining furniture and vents. The kitchen must have tools — knives, implements, perhaps the wrench that's missing from the laboratory workbench. If I can find the wrench, I control access to the machine. If I find the fake-medal, I control access to the mantelpiece. Objects are power. I have none. I need to change that.

And the kitchen is connected to the entrance hall. The entrance hall has the chandelier. If I can rig the chandelier and then lure Clara underneath it...

Leave. Now. Kitchen. Alone.

events.desc: Seven rounds in this accursed manor and I have accomplished precisely NOTHING. No objects, no advantages, no separation from the herd, and no progress whatsoever toward eliminating Clara. Every scheme — the kitchen redirect, the Reginald deployment, the cellar reconnaissance — has collapsed into the same result: everyone in the same room, examining the same objects, finding the same nothing. But the kitchen... the KITCHEN. No one has been there yet. It connects to the entrance hall. The entrance hall has a chandelier that is — and I quote — 'hanging precariously.' If the kitchen has tools, if the entrance hall has a chandelier with a weakened chain, then Vincent Marsh has a plan. A REAL plan. Not subtle misdirection — structural engineering of the fatal variety. I just need everyone to stay DOWN HERE while I go UP THERE.
