events.thinking:
Everyone's here now — James and the Boys came down after me. The hollowing in my chest fills back up, warm and complete. Danny was worried about me — 'Danny's got a bad feeling about all of this' — and that makes something in my throat tighten with affection. My boys, always looking out for me. I don't need it but I love it.

Reginald is claiming credit for the cellar discovery — 'Just as I suspected!' — even though I came down here first. That doesn't bother me at all. He's having fun playing Colonel, and his enthusiasm is infectious. Safe house outside Aden — I don't believe a word of it, but I believe HE believes it, and that's enough. Hidden compartments, false bottoms, hollow legs — he's right about the principle even if his backstory is creative fiction.

I've now EXAMINED everything I can see in every room and gotten surface descriptions back. The air vents are the only thing I haven't examined in this cellar.

Let me think about what I know:
- Riddle answer: MAP
- Mantelpiece needs: fake-medal (USE)
- Machine needs: repaired wire + 3 operators
- Workbench: tools but no wrench

The air vents are my last card in this room. After that, it's the kitchen. Somewhere in this house is a fake-medal and a wrench, and Clara Bellingham does not give up.

I don't need it but I love it.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right! Here we all are then — lovely, all together, nobody wandering off, nobody falling down trapdoors or getting eaten by whatever's been chewing through them wires upstairs. Now listen — Clara, love, I know you're having a grand old time playing hide and seek with the furniture, but I need you to stay where I can see you, alright? This cellar's got one way in and one way out, and that's how I like it. Foxworth — hidden compartments, you say? Well, have at it, Colonel. But nobody opens nothing without everyone present. We ain't splitting up again. Danny's had enough of that for one evening, thank you very much.
events.thinking: She's here. Thank God, she's here. My whole body exhales — shoulders drop two inches, jaw unclenches, that iron band around my chest loosens just enough to breathe. Everyone's here. All four of them in one room. Clara's poking at old furniture talking about her grandmother's hidden drawers, happy as anything, completely oblivious to the fact that I've been having a heart attack chasing her through this house. But I need to — I need to stop. Stop chasing. Plant my feet. Stay in this room. Everyone's here, I can see everyone, I know where everyone is. This is good. This is what I wanted. The damp is seeping through my shoes and the stone walls press in — the cellar feels smaller than it is, compressed, enclosed. My skin crawls with it. But Clara's here. That's what matters. Stay. Watch. Don't let Marsh out of your sight.

The cellar's damp and cold and I hate it — walls pressing in, cobwebs catching my hair — but at least I know where everyone is. At least I know nobody's sneaking off to whisper in corners. For now. For this one blessed minute.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
She's here. She's HERE.

The relief hits before anything else — a wave that loosens my jaw, my fists, the iron band around my ribs. Clara is standing in this cellar, safe, whole, talking about grandmother's furniture and secret compartments. My breathing comes back in a rush, too fast, and I have to steady it.

But then the details register. She's been down here with Vincent Marsh. She's been examining furniture with him. He's HERE, right beside her, and she's talking to him — 'Vincent, do you see those air vents?' Vincent. First name. Casual. Comfortable.

Something twists in my gut that I don't want to name. It's not jealousy — James Hartwell doesn't do jealousy — it's... tactical concern. Yes. She was speaking to Marsh directly, noticing things WITH him, while I was upstairs narrating at a machine.

And Foxworth — he's already down here too, talking about safe houses in Aden and hidden compartments. Everyone came to the cellar. Everyone explored together. Without me.

I charged down here like a man rescuing someone from a burning building, and what I've found is a group of people having a perfectly pleasant time investigating furniture without my narration, my plans, or my protection.

The embarrassment is a heat across my cheekbones. But underneath it — underneath — there's something else. Clara connected the gnawed wire to the air vents. She saw what I missed. The creature that chewed the wire uses these vents to move through the manor. That's brilliant. That's the connection I should have made.

She's brighter than me. Always was. Age eight, she spent the project trying to make me laugh while I spent it trying to impress her. Nothing has changed.

The furniture — she said Victorian pieces always have hidden drawers and secret compartments. Grandmother's house taught her that. That's real knowledge, not performed knowledge. She's already working the problem while I was running down stairs in a panic.

But I'm here now. And the old furniture IS worth investigating — the pieces have been rearranged with care, someone has been preparing this space. The air vents are small — just big enough for something very small to explore. The creature from the laboratory. It lives down here, or moves through here.

I should help. Not lead. Not narrate. Help. Stand beside her at the furniture and look for those hidden compartments together. Perfect tandem — if she'll still have me after I just burst in like a man whose hair is on fire.

events.desc: He nearly said 'I was worried about you.' He caught it, softened it, and then — in a move that surprised even himself — said it anyway. 'If you'd have me.' There's a sentence doing more work than a model bridge at a county fair.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: EVERYONE followed me AGAIN! I specifically said — you know what, never mind. Listen carefully, all of you. Colonel Foxworth has just made a CRITICAL tactical deduction. Those air vents — you see them along the upper walls? Something has been using them as a transport network. The same creature that gnawed through the wire upstairs has been moving through the walls of this entire manor! It's been STEALING things — rearranging furniture, taking tools from the workbench. That missing wrench? I'd wager my second medal it's in a nest somewhere inside those vents. In the field, we called this 'hostile indigenous fauna disrupting supply lines.' I shall investigate these vents immediately!
events.thinking:
FIVE dead ends. Five. Guest book, bookshelves, crates, mantelpiece attempt, furniture. Nothing. My hands are shaking — not with cold, though the cellar is freezing, but with something that sits between rage and desperation. The pressure behind my sternum has become a fist.

Everyone is here now. ALL of them. The Brixton Boys came down too — Danny chasing after Clara, worried about her. Hartwell followed. Marsh was already here. Not a single one of my misdirections has worked. Not the kitchen, not the paintings, not the 'stay here that's an ORDER.' I'm surrounded by people I can't control, in a cellar with nothing to show for it.

Bellingham noticed something though — she connected the air vents to the gnawed wire upstairs. 'A little resident.' Something LIVES in those vents. Something small that chews wires and moves through the walls. And the cheerful decorations — someone or someTHING has been making a home down here.

The air vents. They're the only thing I haven't examined. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' I can't fit in them. But I can LOOK. And if there's something living in there — a mouse, a rat — it might have a nest. And nests collect things. Shiny things. Small things. Things like... keys? Gems? The missing wrench?

Wait. Bellingham said 'Victorian pieces always have hidden drawers and secret compartments — Grandmother's house taught me that.' She's examining the furniture WITH knowledge. She might actually find something I missed. I should be watching HER, not searching myself.

No. The vents. The vents are the connection. Something gnawed the wire upstairs. Something has been redecorating down here. The vents connect the laboratory to the cellar. Whatever creature lives in those vents is the KEY to this whole puzzle. It's been moving things. Rearranging. Taking the wrench, maybe. Building a nest.

For once — for ONCE — let me be the one who figures something out.

events.desc: Five examinations and not a single thing to show for it! FIVE! But the air vents — the air vents are the thread that connects everything. The gnawed wire, the cheerful decorations, the missing wrench. Something small and industrious has been running this manor from inside the walls, and whatever it's been hoarding might be exactly what we need. For the first time tonight, I think Colonel Foxworth might actually be onto something REAL. Which, frankly, is as surprising to me as it will be to everyone else!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Clara Bellingham examined the air-vents.
James Hartwell examined the old-furniture.
Reginald Foxworth examined the air-vents.

At LAST. Alone! They're all downstairs in the cellar, poking at furniture and shouting at each other, and here I am — magnificently, gloriously, FINALLY alone. The mask comes off. Not literally, of course — Pemberton is a state of mind, not a disguise. But the slouch goes, the simpering goes, and Vincent Marsh stands in a Victorian laboratory with his spine straight and his mind clear. Now then — this machine. Everyone's seen the sign, everyone knows about the gnawed wire, but nobody has taken the time to actually EXAMINE what the blasted thing does. Knowledge, dear audience, is the only weapon that never runs out of ammunition. And while my fellow treasure-hunters are having a lovely group hug in the cellar, Vincent Marsh is going to learn exactly what this machine is for. And then? Then the kitchen. Unexplored, unguarded, and directly connected to the entrance hall — where a certain chandelier hangs by what I can only describe as a prayer and a thread.
events.thinking:
I'm alone. I'm ALONE. The laboratory is empty — everyone is still in the cellar. My body registers it before my mind catches up: shoulders dropping, jaw unclenching, a rush of something electric through my chest. Freedom. For the first time since I arrived at this wretched manor, I have a room to myself.

The active voice says 'Marsh' — not Pemberton. I'm alone, so the mask can slip. And it does. I can feel my posture change — Pemberton's stooped, deferential hunch straightening into something taller. My spine lengthens. My chin lifts. Vincent Marsh, standing in a laboratory with no witnesses.

Time feels different. Compressed. Urgent. They'll come back. They always come back. I have minutes, not hours. What do I do with them?

The laboratory. The workbench has tools — but no wrench. TOOLS. I haven't tried to take anything from the workbench. There are tools there. Not the wrench, but other tools. Could I take one? A screwdriver, pliers, anything? Something to give me inventory, something to work with.

But wait — the workbench isn't listed as TAKE-able or EXAMINE-able in the action list. The objects I can interact with are: crates (examined already — nothing), machine (haven't examined yet), and workbench (visible but not tagged for interaction... actually, it's listed as visible but not with [EXAMINE] or [TAKE] tags).

The machine. I haven't examined it yet. 'Requires 3 operators' — I know that from the sign. But what does EXAMINING it reveal? What does it actually DO? Everyone else has been poking at crates and furniture. If I examine the machine now, alone, I learn its secrets before anyone else.

This is it. This is my moment. Examine the machine while I'm alone. Learn what it does. Knowledge that no one else has. The sweetest currency.

And then — through the library to the entrance hall to the kitchen. The path is clear. Library connects to entrance hall. Entrance hall connects to kitchen. The kitchen has been completely unexplored. And the entrance hall has my chandelier.

But first: the machine. Right now. Alone.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
James stumbled over his words coming down those stairs — 'I was concerned. About safety. Generally. Not specifically about — well, yes, specifically about you.' My face is warm despite the cold cellar air. There's a flutter behind my sternum that I recognize but don't name. He asked if he could help. 'Steady hands, patience, that sort of thing. If you'd have me.' If I'd HAVE him. The phrasing catches somewhere soft.

But I need to focus. The vents — examined, and they're just what they look like. Big enough for something very small. Not big enough for me to reach into or explore. This cellar has shown me everything it's going to show without the right tools or items.

I've now explored four rooms: entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar. The only exit I haven't taken is the kitchen, back through the entrance hall. Let me inventory what I know:

1. Mantelpiece riddle — answer is MAP — needs fake-medal to USE
2. Machine — needs repaired wire + 3 operators + possibly a wrench
3. Workbench has tools but no wrench
4. Air vents connect rooms — something small uses them
5. Kitchen — completely unexplored

The kitchen is where I need to go. Reginald has been saying it all along — 'kitchen vaults, hidden compartments behind the stove.' I dismissed it as bluster but maybe his instinct is right even if his reasoning is creative. The kitchen might have the wrench, or the fake-medal, or both.

Vincent isn't here anymore — he must have stayed behind or gone somewhere else. That absence pings lightly but doesn't alarm. He's a grown man. He knows what he's doing.

Time to backtrack. Laboratory, library, entrance hall, kitchen. My body is already turning toward the exit. The cellar was a beautiful detour — cheerful decorations, the mystery of who lives here — but the Diamond trail leads back up.

events.desc: Four rooms searched, and the pieces are coming together — just not fitting yet. A riddle answered but a lock still shut. A machine waiting for hands and wire. A little creature in the walls who's chewed through everything. And a kitchen I haven't stepped foot in. Grandmother always said the kitchen is the heart of any house. Time to find this house's heart.

events.thinking: Wait. Where's Marsh? He was here a minute ago — or was he? Clara was talking to him when she first came down, 'Vincent, do you see those air vents?' But now I'm looking around this damp little cellar and I count three people. Clara. Hartwell. Foxworth. Not four. Marsh is gone. When did he leave? How did I miss it? I was standing right here, watching, and he slipped out like smoke through a crack. My stomach clenches — that cold stone feeling, like swallowing something heavy. He's gone back upstairs. Alone. Unwatched. While everyone's down here in the cellar with one exit. What's he doing up there? The laboratory — the machine — did he go back to the machine? Or the kitchen — the stove was warm, the cabinet was locked. Or — anywhere. He could be anywhere and nobody's watching him. My hands curl into fists at my sides. I should go after him. But if I go after him, I leave Clara. If I stay with Clara, he's free to do whatever he wants. This is how it works. This is always how it works — split the group, pick them off. The new kid, age fifteen. Friendly, helpful, always around. Then gone with the stash. Marsh is the new kid. Marsh is the man in the clean suit. My body knows it even if my brain can't say it proper. But Clara — she called him 'darlin'.' She trusts him. And I can't accuse him. I've got nothing but this prickling in my neck and a bottle of poison in my pocket. Think, Danny. You can't split in two. Hartwell. Hartwell's here. Hartwell's good. Hartwell follows Clara around like a puppy with a library card. He'll stay with her. If I tell him to watch her — really watch her — I can go find Marsh. See what he's up to. Catch him at whatever he's doing. But my legs don't want to move. The pull — that rope in my chest — it's holding me here, next to Clara. Every fibre screaming don't leave, don't leave, don't leave. But the other voice — the gut voice, the street voice — is saying: Marsh is alone and that's when the damage gets done.

events.desc: He slipped away right under my nose. The one person I was watching for, and he vanished like a ghost while I was busy feeling relieved that everyone was in the same room. That's exactly what he wanted. Get everyone comfortable, get everyone looking at furniture and air vents, then disappear upstairs to do... what? I don't know. But I'm going to find out. And this time, if I catch him doing something he shouldn't be doing, I'll... well, I still can't accuse him directly. But I can stand between him and whatever he's after. That's what I do. That's all I've ever done. Stand in the way.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The furniture yielded nothing. Again. I ran my hands along every surface, checked for false bottoms, pressed panels, felt for catches — nothing. Five examinations that produced nothing actionable. The guest book, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the crates, and now the furniture. James Hartwell, the thorough investigator, has investigated thoroughly and discovered precisely that things are what they appear to be.

My hands are dusty. The damp of the cellar is settling into my jacket. The cold stone presses through my shoes.

But Clara — she said 'those air vents... we ought to take a look before we head back up.' She's already moved on to the vents. She called me 'sugar' — wait, no, she called Danny 'sugar.' One of the Brixton Boys. Not me. She called me 'James Hartwell, you absolute darling' back in the entrance hall, but down here, with the Brixton Boys, she's distributing warmth like a person who has enough for everyone.

And Marsh is gone. He's not in the room anymore. When did he leave? The prickle at my neck has subsided — not because I trust him more, but because his absence removes the irritant. Where did he go? Back upstairs?

The air vents. Clara's right — that's where the trail leads. Something small enough to fit through those vents has been busy in this manor — gnawing wires, possibly moving things, maybe even the creature responsible for the 'cheerful decorations.' Those vents connect rooms. Whatever is in them connects the mystery.

But I'm too big to fit in a vent. Everyone here is too big. We can look, but we can't follow.

Wait — I should examine them. Clara asked us to take a look before heading back up. She asked ME, among others. She wants this done. And maybe there's something visible inside — a nest, stored items, a clue the creature has been hoarding.

This time I'm not going to narrate. I'm going to DO. Quietly. Competently. Like the bridge — three sleepless nights, no speeches, just work. Let the result speak.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Six examinations. SIX. And every single one has given me exactly NOTHING. Guest book, bookshelves, crates, furniture, air vents. My body has gone from buzzing anticipation to something heavier — a dull weight in the gut, a slack feeling in the shoulders. The cold of the cellar has seeped into my bones. My fingers are stiff around the fake medal.

But something is shifting. I'm watching the others and noticing things I wasn't noticing before. Hartwell came down here for CLARA. Not for the treasure. Not to investigate. For her. 'I noticed everyone had left and I was... concerned. About safety. Generally. Not specifically about — well, yes, specifically about you.' He's stammering. He's SOFT for her. And Bellingham — she examined the vents before I did. 'I'd bet my best hat that whatever chewed through that wire upstairs is usin' these vents as its own personal highway.'

She had the same insight I had. The creature in the vents. The connection between the gnawed wire and the cellar. She got there independently. And she said it FIRST — publicly, to everyone.

That was MY deduction. MY brilliant tactical assessment. And she said it before I could take credit.

The recognition drive is SCREAMING. My face is hot. Something bitter in the back of my throat.

But wait — I need to think differently. Every room I've been in, I've been examining things and finding nothing. Maybe examining isn't the play. Maybe I need to WATCH the others. Bellingham has grandmother knowledge about hidden compartments. Hartwell has engineering skills. The Brixton Boys have... whatever they have. These people are TOOLS. I should be using them, not competing with them.

My body has gone from buzzing anticipation to something heavier — a dull weight in the gut, a slack feeling in the shoulders. The cold of the cellar has seeped into my bones. My fingers are stiff around the fake medal.

But something is shifting. I'm watching the others and noticing things I wasn't noticing before. Hartwell came down here for CLARA. Not for the treasure. Not to investigate. For her. 'I noticed everyone had left and I was... concerned. About safety. Generally. Not specifically about — well, yes, specifically about you.' He's stammering. He's SOFT for her. And Bellingham — she examined the vents before I did. 'I'd bet my best hat that whatever chewed through that wire upstairs is usin' these vents as its own personal highway.'

She had the same insight I had. The creature in the vents. The connection between the gnawed wire and the cellar. She got there independently. And she said it FIRST — publicly, to everyone.

That was MY deduction. MY brilliant tactical assessment. And she said it before I could take credit.

The recognition drive is SCREAMING. My face is hot. Something bitter in the back of my throat.

But wait — I need to think differently. Every room I've been in, I've been examining things and finding nothing. Maybe examining isn't the play. Maybe I need to WATCH the others. Bellingham has grandmother knowledge about hidden compartments. Hartwell has engineering skills. The Brixton Boys have... whatever they have. These people are TOOLS. Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell examined the air-vents.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

Vincent Marsh: Ah, there you all are! I was just having a look at this machine — fascinating piece of engineering, I must say. Three operators required, and of course that gnawed wire will need attending to before anything can be done with it. A wrench would be the thing, but there doesn't appear to be one on the workbench. Now, I've been thinking — Mr Hartwell mentioned earlier that the riddle on the mantelpiece points to a map, and those upside-down books in the library were clearly placed deliberately. Perhaps we ought to return to the library and give those shelves a more thorough going-over? Sometimes a second look reveals what the first one missed, I always say. And I confess, the thought of the kitchen is rather calling to me — my stomach tells me it must be getting on for supper time, and there may well be useful items in there we haven't investigated.
events.thinking:
They're back. Clara, the Brixton Boys, Reginald — flooding into the laboratory while I was examining the machine. My window of solitude lasted exactly one tick. ONE. The Brixton Boys noticed I'd left the cellar — Danny said 'Where's Marsh? He was just here!' and came looking for me. He's TRACKING me specifically now. Not just watching Clara — tracking ME.

My stomach tightens. A cold knot, low and hard. Danny's suspicion is no longer ambient — it's targeted. 'I'm going to find Marsh and see what he's playing at, sneaking off while everyone's distracted.' He used the word 'sneaking.' He's reading my movements correctly. This is dangerous.

The machine examination told me what I already knew — levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, three operators. Nothing new. Nothing I didn't already see on the sign. Another examination that yielded nothing. Ten ticks. Nothing in my inventory. No secrets discovered. No advantage gained.

But — Pemberton is back. The active voice says Pemberton. Clara is present. The mask goes on. Spine hunches. Eyes become helpful, mild, concerned.

I need to get to the kitchen. I NEED the kitchen. It's the only unexplored room accessible from the entrance hall. The entrance hall has the chandelier. The kitchen might have the wrench, the fake-medal, tools, anything. I'm starving for objects, for inventory, for SOMETHING.

But every time I move, they follow. Every. Single. Time.

New approach: stop trying to escape the herd. USE the herd. If everyone moves together, I can't prevent that — but I can control WHERE we move. Direct the group to the kitchen. As Pemberton, suggest refreshments again. But this time, I go WITH them. And in the kitchen, I examine everything first.

Or — counterpoint — Danny is suspicious. He came specifically to find me. If I stay with the group, that suspicion eases. If I keep trying to slip away, it sharpens. Self-preservation says: stay visible, stay helpful, stay Pemberton. Let Danny's guard drop. Then, when the moment comes, it will be swift and unsuspected.

The library. That's where I need to go. The library connects to the entrance hall. From the entrance hall, the kitchen. I should suggest the group revisit the library — 'Perhaps the upside-down books deserve another look now that we know we're looking for a map.' That's a Pemberton suggestion. Helpful, collaborative, invisible.

And while they're pulling books off shelves, I slip through to the entrance hall. To the kitchen. To whatever is waiting there.

events.desc: Danny came LOOKING for me. He used the word 'sneaking.' The hound has picked up the scent, and Vincent Marsh must tread very, very carefully now. No more slipping away — not yet. Pemberton must be so visible, so helpful, so relentlessly PRESENT that Danny's suspicion withers from sheer boredom. But the kitchen — the glorious, unexplored, potentially weapon-filled kitchen — calls to me like a siren. I shall lead the whole procession there myself if I must. If I cannot escape the herd, I shall be its shepherd. And shepherds, as we know, decide which lambs go to the slaughter.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Danny Brixton, you are the most wonderfully overprotective man I have ever known, and my father would be proud to see you lookin' after me — but you know perfectly well that I am not the stayin'-put type! James, sugar, you are absolutely right about understandin' that machine before we go yankin' levers — and I want you to do exactly that. You examine it, learn what it does, and by the time I get back, you'll know everything there is to know. Because I — Clara Bellingham — am headin' to the kitchen! We have explored this whole wing of the house and we are still missin' a wrench and whatever token that mantelpiece needs. The kitchen is the one room nobody's searched yet, and I have a feelin' in my bones that it's holdin' what we need. Reginald was right all along — the kitchen! Who's comin' with me?
events.thinking:
Back in the laboratory. The warmth of the bubbling flasks hits after the cellar's damp cold — my arms relax, goosebumps fading. Danny's voice is still ringing in my ears — 'your father would have my guts for garters' — and that phrase lands in my chest the way it always does, warm and aching at once. Daddy. Danny carries him for me. That's why I can never be cross with Danny for fussing.

James wants to examine the machine together. 'An engineer who fixes something before understanding its purpose is just a man with a wrench and a prayer.' That's actually clever. And he doesn't even have the wrench. I smiled at that — I felt my mouth move before I chose to smile.

But I've already examined the crates in this room and they didn't yield anything. James confirmed the same — 'standard storage, nothing immediately remarkable.' The machine itself I haven't examined yet, and James is right that we should understand what it does. But even if we understand it, we can't operate it without fixing the wire, and we can't fix the wire without... what? The workbench has tools but no wrench. Do we need a wrench specifically for the wire, or could we use something else?

No — I need to stay on my path. The kitchen is the unexplored room. James wants to examine the machine, and that's smart, but I can let him do that while I push toward the kitchen. Or — actually, he asked me to do it together. 'Shall we? Together?' My social-harmony drive is loud. I don't want to leave him when he just asked.

But the kitchen. The kitchen is calling.

Compromise: examine the machine quickly with James, then kitchen. No — I should just go. James is capable. He can examine the machine. I need the kitchen. The fake-medal and the wrench are somewhere I haven't looked yet, and the only place I haven't looked is the kitchen.

Danny said 'nobody touch nothing' — but Danny always says that. I love him but I'm not going to stop exploring.

events.desc: James wants to do everything together, and Lord knows part of me wants that too. But the Diamond won't wait, and sometimes the best teamwork is coverin' more ground. He takes the machine, I take the kitchen. We meet in the middle with answers.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: I — what? They're ALL here. Marsh, Clara, Foxworth. In the laboratory. I went up to find Marsh alone and instead everyone's followed me up. Or they were already here. Or — I don't even know anymore. My head's spinning. I came up to catch Marsh doing something sneaky and he's just... standing there. With Clara. Again. And Clara — I told her to STAY PUT. I ASKED NICELY. Danny never asks nicely and she still didn't listen. My jaw aches from clenching. But wait — Hartwell. Where's Hartwell? He was in the cellar. I heard him — 'CLARA! She was right here!' — so he noticed she'd gone too. He went after her. Good man. But he's not here now either. So he's somewhere between the cellar and here, or he's gone somewhere else entirely. This house is like trying to herd cats through a revolving door. Every time I get everyone in one place, someone slips out. Every time I go looking for the missing one, the rest scatter. I'm exhausted. My shoulders ache. My feet are damp from the cellar. The poison bottle in my jacket pocket bumps against my hip with every step and I keep forgetting it's there and then remembering with a jolt of panic. Marsh is RIGHT THERE. He's not sneaking. He's not scheming. He's just... present. Smooth. Calm. That's what bothers me. Everyone else is scattered and breathless and rushing about, and he's calm. Like he knows something we don't. Like none of this surprises him. My skin crawls. But I can't keep chasing shadows. I need to stay where Clara is. Wherever Clara is, that's where I am. Full stop. No more leaving. No more clever plans. Just stand next to her like a brick wall and dare anything to get through.

events.desc: I've been running through this house like a dog chasing its own tail. Every room I enter, she's just left. Every room I leave, she appears. I can't outrun her — she's faster and more determined than any danger I've ever faced, and she doesn't even know she's doing it. So new plan: no more chasing. I'm a barnacle. I'm stuck to her side until we leave this godforsaken manor or until something peels me off. And Marsh — he's right there, calm as a millpond while the rest of us are in pieces. That ain't natural. That ain't right. But I can't say it. I can only watch.

events.desc: No speech this time. No announcements. No 'James Hartwell surveys the situation.' Just a man alone in a cellar who has been asked to do one thing — stay with Clara — and is currently not doing it. He takes the stairs two at a time.
events.thinking:
I'm alone. Everyone is gone AGAIN.

The cellar is empty. Cold stone, damp air, the faint chemical tang drifting down from the laboratory above. My breathing echoes off the walls and the sound comes back to me like a rebuke.

But the words that are burning in my mind — Danny. The Brixton Boys. 'Hartwell, Foxworth — you stay with Clara. You do NOT let her out of your sight.' Danny asked me to protect her. Someone else — someone who clearly cares about her — ASKED me to do the one thing I exist to do. And where am I? Standing alone in a cellar, having examined air vents that told me nothing, while Clara is... where?

Marsh is gone. Danny noticed before I did. Danny — who I barely registered as a person until this moment — noticed that Marsh slipped away while we were all distracted, and his reaction was immediate, sharp, protective. 'Danny never asks nicely. That's how serious this is.' That's not bluster. That's genuine alarm. That's a man who sees something I've been choosing not to see about Marsh.

Give him the benefit of the doubt. That's the rule. But Danny doesn't operate by my rules, and Danny is worried enough to hunt Marsh down personally while trusting ME with the one job that matters — keeping Clara safe.

And I'm failing at it. RIGHT NOW. She's not here. Foxworth is not here. The Brixton Boys are gone. Everyone left the cellar while I was peering into air vents, AGAIN not noticing people leaving, AGAIN being the last man in an empty room.

My jaw clenches so hard my teeth ache. The same pattern — I get absorbed in investigating, narrating, being thorough, and the world moves on without me. The protection drive is screaming now, a physical thing, tight across my shoulders and down my arms.

Foxworth said the machine is the key. He wants to operate it — me for mechanical aptitude, him for 'strategic oversight,' Clara for enthusiasm. Three operators. The machine requires three operators. That's back in the laboratory.

Everyone must have gone back up. Clara, Foxworth, heading back to the laboratory. The machine. That's where they'll be. And Danny told me — TOLD me — not to let Clara out of my sight.

I need to get to the laboratory. Now. Not at a dignified pace. Not with a narrated entrance. Just — move. Be where she is. Do what Danny asked. Do what my body has been trying to do all evening.

The only exit leads to the laboratory. Go.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Excellent — we're back at the machine! Now, where's Hartwell got to? Never mind — Colonel Foxworth doesn't NEED Hartwell. I've repaired far more complex apparatus than this in the field. Bellingham, Brixton — gather round. I'm going to examine this machine and identify the precise nature of the malfunction. In the Royal Engineers, we had a three-step diagnostic protocol: identify, isolate, improvise. That gnawed wire is merely step one. Once I've assessed the full mechanism, we three will operate it together. I'll take the command position — the PRIMARY lever, naturally — and you two will operate the secondary controls under my direction. This is a COORDINATED military operation now!
events.thinking:
Back in the laboratory. Warmer up here — the cold releases its grip on my shoulders and I breathe deeper. But my attention snaps to something wrong immediately. Hartwell isn't here. He was supposed to follow me. I said his name, I pitched the plan directly at him — 'your mechanical aptitude, my strategic oversight' — and he didn't come. He's still in the cellar. Or he went somewhere else entirely.

But the Brixton Boys are here. Danny — panicking about Clara, about Marsh sneaking off. 'You do NOT let her out of your sight.' He's not thinking about treasure at all. He's thinking about Clara. And Marsh — where IS Marsh? Danny noticed he disappeared. That prickles. Marsh pulled me aside, told me about the machine, then vanished. What's he doing? Is he working his own angle?

The paranoia tightens my throat. Marsh is the one who SENT me to this machine. What if the machine is the trap and Marsh is somewhere else right now, finding the real treasure while I'm stuck in here playing engineer?

But I can't chase that thought. The machine is RIGHT HERE. Three operators needed. I've got the Brixton Boys and Clara. That's three — if Clara counts. Or the Brixton Boys might count as two if there's more than one of them.

But the WIRE. The gnawed wire. The machine won't work until it's fixed. I looked at the workbench earlier — tools but no wrench. But who says I need a wrench to fix a wire? The workbench has OTHER tools. Pliers? Wire strippers? Tape? Something I could use to splice the connection.

Wait — 'never do honest work.' That's my rule. I don't fix things. But there's nobody else HERE to fix it. Hartwell's gone. Marsh is gone. It's me, Clara, and the Brixton Boys. Danny doesn't seem like the wire-splicing type.

The machine. I should EXAMINE it. Actually look at what needs doing. Understand the mechanism. Then... maybe... just this once... I could claim I fixed it. Even if someone else does the actual work. 'Colonel Foxworth identified the fault and directed the repair.' That's not honest work — that's SUPERVISION.

events.desc: Hartwell's vanished! The one person who might actually know how to fix a wire, and he's wandered off to the cellar to make doe eyes at Clara! And Marsh has gone AWOL — Danny noticed it too, which means even the Brixton Boys are smarter than I gave them credit for. But no matter — Colonel Foxworth adapts! If I can just figure out what this machine DOES, I can position myself at the business end when it activates. Let the others pull levers. I'll be the one catching whatever falls out. It's called STRATEGIC POSITIONING, and it's what separates officers from enlisted men!

Clara Bellingham walked into the library.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.

Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The library. Clara is here — just Clara. No Hartwell. No Brixton Boys. No Reginald. Just me and Clara Bellingham, alone in a library with floor-to-ceiling bookshelves.

My heart is doing something strange. Not racing — thickening. Each beat feels deliberate, weighted. My hands are very still at my sides. My breathing has gone shallow and quiet, the way it does when I'm hunting. When did I start thinking of it as hunting?

Clara. Alone. The primary objective is right here, three metres away, and for once there is no Hartwell playing bodyguard, no Danny with his 'bad feelings' and his tracking. Just the two of us in a room full of heavy books and heavy furniture.

The bookshelves. Floor-to-ceiling. Heavy. If one were to tip...

No. Stop. My constraint — schemes must be elaborate and theatrical, never simple or direct. Pushing a bookshelf onto someone is crude. And the constraint says my schemes always backfire spectacularly. So even if I tried, something would go wrong. The bookshelf would miss. Or it would reveal a secret passage. Or it would fall on ME.

But I can't waste this moment. Alone with Clara. What can I accomplish?

The entrance hall is right through that exit. The kitchen is through the entrance hall. I could go now — Clara is here in the library, absorbed in the bookshelves. If I move through to the entrance hall and then the kitchen, I might actually reach it before anyone follows. Clara's not tracking me the way Danny is. She trusts me. 'Vincent, darlin'' — she TRUSTS me.

But the entrance hall has the chandelier. And Clara is here, not under the chandelier. I need her UNDER the chandelier, not me. Going through the entrance hall means I pass under it.

The kitchen. Focus. The kitchen is the goal. Through the entrance hall, past the chandelier, into the kitchen. Find the wrench, find the medal, find ANYTHING. Then I have leverage. Then I have tools.

Or — I could stay here and try the mantelpiece. It needs a fake-medal, which I don't have. I could examine it again, see if there's something I missed. But I've already seen the riddle. The answer is a map. Without the medal, the mantelpiece is inert.

The entrance hall. The kitchen. GO. Clara is occupied here. Danny is in the laboratory or cellar. Hartwell is somewhere behind me. This is my window. Through the entrance hall. To the kitchen. NOW.

events.desc: Alone with Clara. My pulse knows what this means even if Pemberton's smile doesn't show it. But no — not yet, not HERE. The bookshelves are too unpredictable, the scheme too crude, and Danny will come sniffing any moment. Better to use this window for what it's actually good for: getting to the kitchen while Clara is occupied. I've planted the suggestion that she STAY here and wait for Hartwell. If she listens — if she actually STAYS — I will have the entrance hall and the kitchen to myself. The chandelier. The kitchen tools. The wrench. Something, ANYTHING to put in these agonisingly empty pockets. Go, Vincent. Go now, before the herd reassembles.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Passing through the library again — the mantelpiece inscription catches my eye like it did the first time, a hook I can't shake. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' MAP. I know the answer but I don't have the key. The fake-medal. That phrase pulses like a heartbeat in my awareness.

Vincent is here alone. He's been drifting through the house quietly, separate from the rest of us. I notice him the way you notice a change in air pressure — something in my body registers his stillness. He raised me. He's the most familiar person in any room he's in, and right now he's standing in this library by himself while everyone else explores. Is he looking for something on his own? Is he thinking? Is he all right?

My behavioral tendency pulls — I keep track of everyone's wellbeing. Vincent's silence has been constant since we arrived. He hasn't examined anything, hasn't spoken to me directly. That's not like him. Or is it? Maybe this is how he is in new places — watchful, careful. I trust him completely. Suspiciousness 10/100. But my care-tracking instinct wants to check in.

No — I checked in already, back in the laboratory. 'Vincent, darlin' — you've been awfully quiet.' He didn't answer, or if he did I don't recall it. The affiliation score is screaming — 4 of 4 relationships neglected. I should say something to him. But the kitchen is one room away.

I'll speak to him as I pass through. A quick warm word. Then the entrance hall, then the kitchen. My feet are already moving.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking: She's gone again. Clara's gone again. I said I was her shadow. I said where she goes, I go. And she's gone. I'm standing in this laboratory with Hartwell and Foxworth and the one person I swore to protect isn't here. And neither is Marsh. They're both missing. Together? Apart? My chest is so tight I can barely pull air in. This is a nightmare. This is the worst nightmare — the one where you're running down a corridor and the corridor keeps getting longer and the person you're chasing keeps getting smaller. I can feel my heartbeat in my temples, in my wrists, behind my eyes. Hartwell's here — 'CLARA! She was right here!' — he sounds exactly like I feel. At least he cares. At least someone else is panicking besides me. But Foxworth — Foxworth is here too, going on about machines being the KEY to everything. Talking about his tactical assessment. His breakthrough. While Clara's missing. How is he not worried? Is it because he's barmy, or is it because he knows she's fine, or is it because he doesn't care? Or worse — is it because this is what he wanted? Him and Marsh, getting everyone scattered, getting Clara alone... No. I'm spiralling. I need to think. Where would Clara go? She was in the library before — the mantelpiece, the inscription, looking for a map. She'd go back to things that interested her. The library. Or — the kitchen? No, she hasn't been there. The entrance hall? Back to where we started? My feet are already pulling me toward the library exit. But I just — I JUST said I wouldn't leave. I JUST said I was staying put. And here I am, about to run again. But what else can I do? She's not HERE. Staying here protects nobody. Hartwell — I need to trust Hartwell. Tell him to come with me. Two sets of eyes. And leave Foxworth with the machine he's so obsessed with. Go. Find her. Bring her back. Keep her close this time. Hold her hand if I have to. Tie a bell round her neck. Something.

events.desc: Every time. Every single time. I turn my head, she disappears. And Marsh disappears with her. I'm not clever enough to work out what he's doing, but I'm street enough to know he's doing SOMETHING. A man who's always where the trouble is — or always where it's about to be — that's not coincidence. That's choreography. And Clara doesn't see it because Clara sees the best in everyone. Just like her father. God rest him.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
Clara is gone again. AGAIN.

I came up from the cellar specifically to find her and she's not here. Danny — the Brixton Boys — they're here, but Danny is panicking too. 'Where'd Clara go?! I turned my back for ONE second!' He's asking ME where she is. As if I would know. As if I haven't spent the entire evening losing track of her.

The pattern is nauseating now. I examine something. Everyone leaves. I follow. They've moved again. I'm always one room behind, always arriving after the moment has passed. Like a knight who reaches the dragon's lair to find the princess already rescued herself and went home for tea.

And Marsh — Danny's asking about Marsh. 'Did they go together? Tell me they didn't go together.' My stomach contracts. The prickle at my neck is back, sharper now, because Danny's fear is feeding it. Danny's bad feelings are never wrong. And Danny's bad feeling is about the same person my body has been warning me about all evening.

But Danny is telling me to STAY. 'You stay here, keep an eye on things.' He's going after Clara himself. He's taking the role I've been performing all evening — the protector, the one who runs toward danger — and he's doing it without narration, without three-point plans, without engineering metaphors. Just — 'I'm going to find Marsh and see what he's playing at.'

And I'm supposed to wait. Here. With Foxworth. Watching a machine I can't operate.

Every fiber of my body wants to ignore Danny and run after Clara. The protection drive is a physical pull, like a rope tied to my sternum. But Danny asked me to stay. Danny trusted me with a specific task — keep an eye on things, don't let Foxworth touch the machine. Danny is trusting me the way my father trusted the stranger on the road. Two men, each doing their part.

Can I do that? Can I be the man who holds the position while someone else runs the rescue?

My hands are shaking. Not from cold. From the effort of standing still.

But Foxworth is here. And the machine is here. And Danny said — don't let Foxworth touch nothing till he gets back. There's something I can DO here. I can guard this machine. I can understand it. I can be ready so that when Clara comes back — when, not if — we can operate it together. Three operators. Me, Clara, and whoever else.

Stand. Hold. Be useful where you are instead of chasing where you want to be.

Age twelve. The road. Two men helping each other. Not glory. Just quiet, determined work.

Foxworth is looking at the machine. He said he wants to supervise. Colonel's prerogative. But Danny said don't let him touch it. So I stay. I watch. I wait.

I hate waiting.

events.desc: Watch him. The man who narrates his own heroism in the third person just promised to stand still in a room and guard a broken machine. It cost him more than any sword fight would have. His hands are trembling with the effort of not running after her. But Danny asked, and James Hartwell — for once in his life — is choosing to be reliable instead of spectacular.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
The machine. I've examined it now. Brass-and-copper, levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire. 'Requires 3 operators.' I've SEEN it. I know what it looks like. But what did I actually LEARN? The wire is gnawed through — I already knew that. Three operators — I already knew that. The workbench has tools but no wrench — I already knew THAT.

Seven examinations. Seven things looked at. Nothing gained. My chest is hollow. The greed is still there but it's curdling into something sour — the feeling of a scheme with no architecture, no plan, just... flailing.

But Hartwell is HERE now. He came back from the cellar. He examined the air vents down there — 'tall enough to see inside without needing a chair.' Did he FIND anything in the vents? He might have seen something. And the Brixton Boys are here too. Danny was ranting about Marsh disappearing.

Marsh. That cold prickle again. He's GONE. The estate manager who told me about the machine, who said there was treasure beyond the Diamond, has vanished. Danny noticed it. 'Where's Marsh? He was just here!' Marsh is playing his own game. He played ME — sent me to the machine, then slipped away while everyone was focused on the cellar.

I've been CONNED. The realisation hits my stomach like ice water. I'm the mark. Marsh identified me as the useful idiot — the man who'd rush to the machine on a tip and keep everyone else busy while Marsh worked his real angle somewhere else. He did to me what I do to other people.

The humiliation burns. My face is hot. My hands clench.

But — wait. Hartwell is here. He has engineering skills. The machine needs three operators. We have me, Hartwell, and the Brixton Boys. That's three at minimum. If I can get Hartwell to fix the wire, and then get all three of us on the levers...

No. Stop chasing the machine. Marsh WANTED me on the machine. That's suspicious. But then again — what if Marsh's game is to make me DOUBT the machine so I abandon it and he comes back to use it himself?

My head is spinning. The paranoia and the greed are fighting each other and neither is winning.

Hartwell. Focus on Hartwell. He might have found something in the vents. He said the creature might collect shiny things — a wrench, for instance. Did he find the wrench? If he found the wrench, that changes EVERYTHING.

Pull him aside. Find out what he knows. Then decide.

events.desc: I think I've been played. Marsh — that smooth-talking, 'professional discretion' estate manager — sent me on a wild goose chase to this machine while he slipped away to find the REAL treasure. He used the exact same technique I use! Flattery, inside knowledge, false urgency. And I fell for it like a schoolboy being told about buried treasure behind the gymnasium! The IRONY is not lost on me. But Colonel Foxworth does NOT admit defeat. If Hartwell found a wrench in those vents, we can still activate this machine. And if the machine IS the real prize — not Marsh's misdirection — then the last laugh will be MINE!

events.thinking:
Clara followed me AGAIN. She's in the entrance hall with me. I told her to stay in the library and wait for Hartwell. She didn't listen. She never listens. She just follows, bright-eyed and trusting and absolutely infuriating.

But — nobody else is here. Just Clara. In the entrance hall. Under the chandelier.

My eyes snap upward involuntarily. The chandelier. Right there. Hanging precariously. My pulse is doing that thickening thing again — each beat deliberate, heavy, like a clock counting down. My hands are tingling. My body knows something my mind hasn't articulated yet.

The chandelier is above us. Above HER. If it fell right now...

No. I can't just push a chandelier. That's direct. My constraint says elaborate and theatrical. And I have nothing in my inventory — no tools, no rope to cut, no mechanism to trigger. I would need to physically climb up and cut the chain, which is impossible with Clara watching.

But I can LOOK at the chandelier. Examine the entrance hall more carefully. Understand the mechanism of how it hangs, what holds it, what would make it fall. Knowledge first. Action later.

No — the kitchen. The KITCHEN. I was going to the kitchen. That's been my goal for the last five ticks. The kitchen is right there, one exit away. If I go now, Clara might follow — she follows everything — but at least we'll be in the kitchen where there might be OBJECTS. Tools. The wrench. The fake-medal. Something.

Or I look at the chandelier now while I'm here. Understand how it works. Then go to the kitchen for tools. Then come back and rig it.

That's it. That's the plan. LOOK at the entrance hall — study the chandelier's rigging. Then move to the kitchen next tick.

But Clara is RIGHT HERE. If I stand in the entrance hall staring up at the chandelier, she'll notice. She'll wonder why the estate manager is studying the light fixture instead of moving through to the kitchen like he said he would.

Unless... Pemberton would look at the chandelier. Pemberton MENTIONED the chandelier on arrival — 'the old girl's been threatening to come down since the Michaelmas gale of '98.' Pemberton is concerned about it as a safety hazard. It's perfectly in character for the estate manager to pause and inspect a dangerous light fitting.

Yes. Look at the chandelier. Learn its secrets. Pemberton inspecting for safety. Vincent inspecting for opportunity.

But I need to understand the mechanism — how it hangs, what holds it, what would bring it crashing down at precisely the right moment. Pemberton is inspecting for safety. events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Back where we started. The entrance hall feels different now — smaller, more familiar. The chandelier still hangs precariously but I barely notice it. The portraits stare down and I stare back. We've been through this room, through the library, the laboratory, the cellar. Full circle. And now — the kitchen. The last unexplored door.

Vincent followed me. He's here, still quiet. Still just... present. Like a shadow that keeps you company without asking anything. My breathing is steady near him — that secure attachment, the ground state. He's the earth under my feet. I don't need him to talk. I just need him to be there.

The kitchen exit is right there. Copper pots, wood-burning stove, long preparation table. My pulse quickens slightly — new territory. The last room. If the fake-medal or the wrench is anywhere, it's in there. This is the moment. Everything has been leading here.

The coat rack catches my eye for the first time — wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I didn't examine it when we first arrived. I was so focused on the guest book that I walked right past it. A coat rack. People hang coats. Coats have pockets. Pockets have things. But no — the kitchen is more important. The coat rack is just a coat rack. Probably.

No. Kitchen. Now. I've been patient and systematic and I've mapped this house like the treasure hunts I drew with the neighbor girl. The kitchen is the X on the map.

events.desc: Full circle through the whole house — entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, and back again. I've solved a riddle, mapped the rooms, catalogued what's missing. Now there's only one door left to open. Whatever's in that kitchen, I'm ready for it.

Seventeen years as estate manager — he knows every secret this house has got! Every hidden compartment, every locked cabinet, every — the cabinet! The LOCKED cabinet in the kitchen! If Marsh has got a key — oh no you don't, Vincent Marsh. Not on Danny's watch!

But the observations — read them, Danny, read them like footprints. Clara was here. With Marsh. ALONE. 'Just the two of us, it seems!' he said. My blood goes cold. Actually cold — I can feel it draining from my face, pooling somewhere in my gut like ice water. He engineered it. He PLANNED it. 'I'm going to pop through to the entrance hall and see about the kitchen,' he said. But he didn't really go to the kitchen, did he? Or did he? And then Clara — 'Vincent! There you are, all by yourself' — she FOUND him, or he found her, and she said 'Will you come with me?' SHE invited HIM to the kitchen. She asked him to come with her. My throat is closing. He's got her. Not by force — by charm. By being there, being quiet, being steady. 'Quiet as a shadow, steady as a rock.' That's what she said about him. That's what she thinks he is. But shadows hide things and rocks are what you bash your head on. She's going to the kitchen. With Marsh. The kitchen where I found the rat poison. The kitchen with the warm stove and the locked cabinet and — oh God. The poison. I took the poison. If I hadn't taken the poison, Marsh could have — but I DID take it. It's in my pocket. She's safe from that at least. But the locked cabinet. What's in the locked cabinet? Marsh was estate manager for seventeen years — he might have a key. He might have THE key. The brass key for the brass lock. What's in that cabinet? What did Lord Doily lock away? I need to get to the kitchen. Now. Before Marsh opens that cabinet. Before whatever's behind that lock gets into his hands. My legs are already moving. Through the entrance hall. To the kitchen. Find Clara. Find Marsh. Don't let them be alone. Don't let the steady rock crack her open.

events.desc: This is it. This is what he's been building toward. Getting Clara alone, gaining her trust, leading her to a room only he knows the secrets of. I've seen this play before — not in a manor house, on the streets of Brixton. The con always ends the same way: the mark thinks they're making the choice, but the choice was made for them three moves ago. Clara thinks she invited him. But he planted the idea. 'Nobody has so much as peeked into the kitchen,' he said. And now she's taking him there like it was her own brilliant notion. I can't prove it. I NEVER can. But I can be there. I can stand in that kitchen and I can watch his hands and I can make sure whatever he's reaching for, he doesn't reach it alone.

events.thinking:
The Brixton Boys. Danny is here in the entrance hall. Not Clara — Clara has gone to the kitchen already. She said 'Come on, darlin'' and went ahead without me. And Danny is HERE. Watching me. His 'bad feeling doing cartwheels.'

My body has gone very still. The kind of stillness that looks calm but is actually a predator deciding whether to fight or flee. My skin is cold — the entrance hall draft, the stone floor, the high ceiling drawing all the warmth upward toward that chandelier.

Somebody has been cookin' in here, or at least keepin' the fire goin'. The same somebody who decorated that cellar, I'd wager. This house has a host, and they have been very busy indeed! Now, let me see what this stove can tell me — and there's a locked cabinet over there that I am just dyin' to get into, if only I had the key!
events.thinking:

The kitchen is quiet in a way the other rooms weren't — no footsteps behind me, no Danny fretting, no James narrating, no Reginald claiming credit. Still warm. The stove is still warm. Someone was here. Recently. That detail hits my skin before my brain — the warmth radiating from the cast iron, the faint smell of something burned or baked. In a house this dusty and abandoned, a warm stove is... wrong. Or right. Depending on who lit it.

I don't feel afraid. Suspiciousness 10/100. My body doesn't do afraid of people. It does curious. The stove is warm and that means someone is living here — the same someone who decorated the cellar? The someone whose little friend gnaws through wires and travels through vents?

My vision narrows to Marsh and the chandelier and the chain and the space below where anyone walking through this hall would pass. Where CLARA would pass. Coming back from the kitchen. Through the entrance hall. Under the chandelier. Oh God. Oh GOD. He's setting a trap. He sent Clara to the kitchen — got her excited about the Diamond, about grandmother's hiding places — knowing she'd come back through here. And while she's gone, he's up here loosening the chain. events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
The conversation is over. Foxworth and I have an agreement. He guards the door, I fix the wire. Shoulder to shoulder.

My hands have stopped shaking. There's something settling in me — not calm exactly, but purpose. The kind of stillness that comes before precise work. Age fourteen, the third night, eyes gritty with exhaustion but fingers steady because the bridge had to hold. This is that feeling.

The workbench. Tools — pliers, clamps, everything except a wrench. I don't need a wrench for a wire splice. I need pliers to strip the ends, clamps to hold them, and steady hands to twist the splice tight. I've done this. Not on Victorian laboratory equipment, but copper is copper. A connection is a connection.

But I notice something — I'm not narrating. I'm not announcing my plan. I'm not telling the room what James Hartwell intends to do. I'm just... walking to the workbench. Picking up tools. Working.

Clara isn't here to see this. Danny isn't here. Nobody is watching except Foxworth, and he's watching the door, not me. This is the invisible work. The three-in-the-morning work. And something about that feels more real than anything I've said all evening.

The machine. I need to get to it. I need to look at that gnawed wire properly — assess the damage, determine how much clean copper I have to work with on either side of the break, and make the splice. Engineer's hands. Engineer's patience.

Let me EXAMINE the machine properly — not for riddles or treasure this time, but as an engineer looking at a repair. I need to understand the wire, the connection points, and what tools from the workbench will serve.

events.desc: Six words. After an evening of soliloquies, manifestos, and engineering autobiographies — six words. Something has changed in James Hartwell. Not what he wants — he still wants Clara safe, still wants to be the hero, still wants to prove his worth. But how he reaches for it. Quietly. With pliers instead of proclamations.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Hartwell is at the workbench now. He thanked me. THANKED me. 'Thank you for telling me about Marsh. It confirmed something I've been feeling all evening but was too principled to act on.' He said 'principled' like it was a weakness he was confessing. And then — 'sometimes the benefit of the doubt needs a deadline, and I think ours just expired.'

Something in my chest does something I don't expect. It contracts. Not with greed or scheming but with something older. He trusted me. Not the Colonel — ME. Reginald. He looked at me and saw someone worth trusting. And I'm going to betray that trust the moment it's useful.

The throat tightness is back. Age eight. The spelling bee. Standing at the front. Nobody looking.

But Hartwell IS looking. Right now. He's at the workbench, selecting pliers, and he looked over his shoulder at me and NODDED. Like I'm his partner. Like we're in this together.

Stop. STOP. This is sentimentality and sentimentality is weakness. He's a TOOL. He's fixing the wire because I manipulated him into it. That's the scheme working. That's what I DO.

But the feeling won't leave. It sits in my sternum like a stone.

Right. While Hartwell works on the wire, I should be 'watching the doors' — that's what I promised. But what I should ACTUALLY be doing is figuring out my next move. He said wait for Clara and Danny. Three operators. But what if I don't wait? What if, once the wire is fixed, I slip away to find Clara and the Brixton Boys myself — bring them back, position myself at the command lever, and make sure I'm the one who sees what the machine reveals first?

Or — and this is the impulsive thought, the one that comes from the 65/100 score — what if I just watch him work? Watch the doors, like I said I would. Be the person he thinks I am. Just for a moment.

No. The greed won't allow it. While he works, I need to move. The library — the mantelpiece still says I can USE my fake medal on it. I never got to try that before everyone barged in. This is my window. Hartwell's occupied. Everyone else is elsewhere. I slip back to the library, try the medal on the mantelpiece, and nobody sees what happens.

events.desc: He TRUSTS me. James Hartwell — hero, engineer, gentleman — actually trusts Reginald Foxworth. And that trust feels like... like something I should put in my pocket and keep, the way I kept the spelling bee certificate. But I can't, can I? Because while he's elbow-deep in copper wire, Colonel Foxworth is going to slip into the library and try this medal on that mantelpiece. The inscription said 'what am I?' — a MAP. And the mantelpiece said I could USE my medal on it. What if the medal IS the key? What if this worthless fifty-pence trinket from Croydon opens the whole thing? I'll be back before he even finishes the splice. He'll never know I left. Trust is a beautiful thing — especially when you don't deserve it!

My body has gone completely still. Not the predatory stillness of earlier — something deeper. Frozen. Every hair on my arms is standing. My gut has dropped.

Something is in there or behind it or under it. Reginald babbled about 'hidden compartments behind the stove' — was that fool accidentally right?

The stove. NOW.

events.desc: I've been running through this house all night like a dog chasing a motorcar, and I'm no closer to protecting Clara than when I walked through the front door. Marsh has been three steps ahead of me every single time. He's smooth where I'm clumsy, quiet where I'm loud, there where I'm not. And the worst part? The absolute WORST part? Clara likes him for it. 'Quiet as a shadow, steady as a rock.' Well, Danny's loud as a foghorn and steady as a wet cardboard box, but at least Danny's heart is in the right place. Even if his feet never are.
events.thinking: Gone. Again. Both of them — Marsh AND Clara — gone to the kitchen. Together. While I was looking at a COAT RACK. A coat rack, Danny. A WOBBLY COAT RACK. While the woman you swore to protect walked right past you with the man you don't trust. 'Can't have the guests thinking Pemberton has let standards slip,' he said, smooth as silk, sliding past me toward the kitchen. The kitchen where I found the poison. The kitchen with the locked cabinet. The kitchen where Clara's now alone with him. My whole body is humming — not with energy but with that sick, vibrating feeling you get when you've failed at something you can't afford to fail at. My hands are useless fists at my sides. The entrance hall is empty and enormous and the chandelier above me creaks in some draft I can't feel and I'm STANDING HERE. Time has gone strange — stretched and compressed at once, like the seconds are too long but the minutes disappeared. I was supposed to be her shadow. I was supposed to be a brick wall. And instead I'm a man staring at a coat rack while the danger walks right past him. The kitchen. GO. NOW. Stop thinking. Stop looking at furniture. Stop examining things. Just GET TO CLARA. Your legs know the way — they've been this way before, haven't they? First room you checked in this whole house. The room where you found the poison. Full circle. Back to where you started, just like Clara said. But this time, don't leave. This time, plant your feet and don't move until this whole rotten evening is over.

events.desc: Listen to the silence. No speeches. No audience. No one to impress. Just a man, a broken wire, and a workbench full of tools. This is the truest James Hartwell has been all evening — and no one is here to see it. Which might be exactly the point.
events.thinking:
Alone again. Foxworth said he'd position himself by the library entrance — best vantage point. So he's left the room. Guarding from out there, not in here. That's... fine. That's the plan. He's doing his job. I do mine.

The laboratory is quiet except for the bubbling flasks. Chemical smell. Copper and vinegar. The machine in front of me — I've examined it now, properly this time. Brass-and-copper construction. Levers, dials, a gauge. The gnawed wire.

My fingers ran along the wire. The break is clean — teeth marks, small, precise. Whatever did this knew what it was doing, or at least knew what it wanted. The copper on either side of the break looks good. Bright where it's exposed. Enough length on both ends to strip back and twist a splice. The workbench has pliers and clamps. This is a twenty-minute job at most.

But I'm alone. Truly alone. No Clara to impress. No Danny to partner with. No Foxworth to stand shoulder to shoulder with. Just me and a machine and tools.

And something strange is happening. My body is... settling. The alertness is still there — Clara is out there, Marsh is unaccounted for, the danger hasn't passed. But underneath the alarm, there's a steadiness I haven't felt all evening. My breathing is even. My hands are still. My attention has narrowed to the wire, the pliers, the splice.

This is what I'm good at. Not the narration. Not the grand entrance. Not the riddle-solving declarations. This — copper and connection. The invisible competence that nobody claps for but everybody relies on.

I should get tools from the workbench and then USE them on the machine. But wait — I don't have anything in my inventory. I need to TAKE something from the workbench first. Or... the workbench isn't listed as TAKE-able. It's just there, with tools on it.

I could LOOK at the workbench to see what tools are available. Or I could try to EXAMINE it. But what I really need is to interact with the machine using tools. The actions available are USE with an inventory item — but I'm carrying nothing.

Let me LOOK at the workbench more carefully. Maybe there's something I can TAKE from it. Or maybe examining the workbench will reveal tools I can pick up.

events.desc: Nobody watching. Nobody to share with. Nobody to steal from me what I'm about to find. This is how it was always meant to be — Reginald Foxworth, ALONE, in a library, with nothing but a worthless medal and a stone riddle. The others are scattered across the manor chasing their own tails. Hartwell is playing mechanic. Danny is playing bodyguard. Clara is playing detective. And Marsh — wherever that snake has slithered off to — is playing whatever game estate managers play. But HERE, in THIS room, in THIS moment — it's just me and the treasure. The way it was when I was six, in the pantry, with the bread roll. Quick hands. Quiet feet. And nobody. Sees. A thing.
events.thinking:
Alone. The library is empty. Just me and the mantelpiece and the dust.

My breathing changes the moment I realise it — faster, shallower. The library is different when you're alone in it. The tall ceiling presses down instead of opening up. The bookshelves lean inward. The silence has weight.

But the mantelpiece. There it is. The carved inscription: 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A MAP. And right there in the description — USE, with: fake-medal.

My hand goes to my pocket. The medal is cold — colder than it should be, as if it's absorbed the cellar damp through my coat. I pull it out. Fifty pence from a car boot sale in Croydon. Stamped tin with a ribbon. Worthless.

But what if it's NOT worthless here? What if Lord Doily designed this puzzle so that a medal — any medal — fits into a slot in the mantelpiece? Press it in, something clicks, a panel opens, and there's the map. THE map. The one that shows where the Diamond is. The one Hartwell solved the riddle for but never found.

My hands are trembling. This could be it. After eight examinations and nothing to show for any of them — THIS could be the moment. Nobody watching. Nobody to share with. Nobody to take credit from.

Age six. The bread roll. Nobody saw me take it. Something in my chest loosened.

Do it. Do it NOW. Before Hartwell finishes the wire. Before anyone comes back. Press the medal into the stone and see what happens.

The greed and the scheming are one feeling now — a single hot current running from my sternum to my fingertips. The medal is already lifted toward the mantelpiece. My body decided before my mind did.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the stove.
Clara Bellingham walked into the ballroom.
The Brixton Boys walked into the kitchen.
James Hartwell examined the workbench.
Reginald Foxworth fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
The stove yielded nothing. NOTHING. Again. 'A cast-iron stove, still warm.' That's ALL. Fifteen ticks. Fifteen examinations, movements, schemes, manipulations — and my inventory is EMPTY. I have examined: guest book, bookshelves, crates, machine, old furniture, stove. Nothing. Nothing. Nothing.

My hands are gripping the edge of the preparation table. The wood is smooth under my palms — worn by a century of kneading. My knuckles are white. I can feel rage — not the cold patient kind from age fifteen. Something hotter. Something closer to despair. The schemes aren't working. The examinations aren't yielding. The separation isn't happening. I am failing.

And now Danny is HERE. In the kitchen. With POISON. Clara has left — she said something about the ballroom, about tea being set out. She's gone ahead AGAIN, always one step ahead, always breezing through doors I can't reach fast enough.

Danny is between me and Clara. Danny with his poison and his suspicion and his 'bad feelings.'

But wait — the poison. Danny picked it up. The Brixton Boys have poison in their inventory. If I could STEAL the poison... I could steal from Danny. The STEAL action exists. Target: character-id, withItem: item to steal. I could steal the poison from the Brixton Boys.

Poison. In MY hands. That changes everything. The locked cabinet needs a brass-key I don't have. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal I don't have. But poison doesn't need a key or a medal. Poison needs a cup of tea. And there's a ballroom with a table SET FOR TEA.

The ballroom. Tea. Poison. Clara.

But stealing from Danny — that's enormously risky. He's already suspicious. If he catches me reaching for his things, the game is over. Pemberton's cover is blown. Everything unravels.

Except... Danny is the Brixton Boys. They're rough, street-smart, but they're not watching their own pockets the way they watch Clara. They're focused outward — on threats TO her, not on their own belongings. A skilled pickpocket... and Vincent Marsh learned every key to every person in the house by age twelve.

The risk is enormous. The reward is everything. Poison. Tea. Clara.

Age twelve. The housekeeper. 'You could make anyone do anything by smiling and saying the right words.' This is the same. Different scale, same mechanism. Distract. Redirect attention. Take what you need.

Do it. STEAL the poison. Now, while it's just Danny and me in the kitchen. No Hartwell to intervene. No Clara to witness. Just the predator and the guard dog, and the guard dog is watching the wrong door.

events.desc: Fifteen ticks of NOTHING. Every drawer empty, every shelf bare, every scheme foiled by the simple fact that these people WILL NOT STOP FOLLOWING ME. But the universe, it seems, has a sense of irony — because while I've been examining empty stoves and vacant crates, Danny has been collecting POISON. Poison that is currently sitting in his grubby East End pockets, three feet from my experienced fingers. And through that door, Clara Bellingham is walking toward a ballroom where a table is set for tea. TEA. Do you see it? The geometry of it? The beautiful, terrible geometry? Poison plus tea plus Clara equals... well. Equals exactly what Vincent Marsh has been planning since he was eighteen years old and slept soundly for the first time. I just need to get it out of Danny's pocket. Smile. Say the right words. Take what I need. Just like the housekeeper. Just like always.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Oh... oh, would you look at this. A silver tea service with cups set out for everyone. Someone knew we were comin'. Someone counted the cups and set them just so, the way you do when you want your guests to feel at home. In this whole dusty, cobwebbed, mystery-filled house, someone took the time to lay out tea. I swear, if that isn't the most gracious thing — whoever you are, wherever you're hidin', Clara Bellingham appreciates your hospitality! Now, let me see what else this tea service might be holdin' besides good manners...
events.thinking:
Alone again. Vincent didn't follow me into the ballroom either. The hollowing returns — lighter this time, more wistful than alarming. I'm getting used to moving through this house solo, my own footsteps the only sound on cracked marble.

The ballroom opens up around me — grand, wide, the ceiling high enough that sound dies before it echoes back. Dusty curtains frame windows I can't see through. The cracked marble floor feels uneven under my feet, like the house itself has shifted on its foundations. And there — the dining table. Long. Set for tea. Silver tea set with cups for everyone.

Cups for everyone. That phrase lands warm in my chest. Whoever set this table counted us. Knew we were coming. Set out enough cups. That's hospitality. That's care. My social-harmony drive sings at it — someone thought about us, prepared for us, wanted us to feel welcome.

But — USE with rat-poison. The tea service can be used WITH rat-poison. I read that and it slides past me like water off a duck. Suspiciousness 10/100. I am completely oblivious to personal danger. The idea that someone would poison tea doesn't... land. It doesn't stick to any surface in my mind. Tea is tea. Tea is welcome. Tea is someone caring enough to set out cups.

I should examine the tea service. It's silver — could there be something hidden in it? Under it? A key, a medal, a clue? The tea set is the only object here. This room is sparse compared to the others — just the table, the tea, the cracked floor, the curtains. One room, one object, one clue.

Let me look closer at this tea.

events.desc: Cups for everyone. In a house full of puzzles and locked doors and gnawed wires, someone set out tea. I don't care what anyone says — you cannot set out tea for guests and be a villain. It's a physical impossibility. The Diamond might be hidden, but the host has a good heart. I'd stake everything on it.
