events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: The kitchen. Marsh is here. Clara is NOT. She's gone again — to the BALLROOM. 'Come on — let's go see who's expectin' us for tea!' she said. Tea. In a ballroom. In a house where somebody's been secretly living, secretly cooking, secretly decorating. My skin is crawling. The whole house is a setup — someone's been HERE, keeping the stove warm, setting tables, making the cellar cozy. This isn't abandoned. This is a TRAP. And Clara's walking deeper into it with a smile on her face. But Marsh — Marsh is still here. In the kitchen. He examined the stove. 'Mrs Grumble's warming compartments.' He knows this house. He knows every inch of it. Seventeen years. The warmth from the stove hits me — unexpected, loosening muscles I didn't know were clenched. My shoulders drop half an inch. The kitchen smells of copper and old grease and something faintly sweet, like baking. It would be almost homey if my heart wasn't hammering. Marsh is RIGHT HERE. Clara went to the ballroom. She's one room away. Through that door. And Marsh is between me and that door. No — Marsh is in the kitchen and the ballroom is through the kitchen. If I go to the ballroom, I pass Marsh. If I stay here, Clara's one room away and safe enough — she's just looking at a tea table. But Marsh is HERE. Alone with me. This is the first time it's been just us. Just Danny and the man who makes his neck prickle. I could — I should — I need to say something. Ask him something. Nothing direct. Nothing accusatory. Just... feel him out. The way you feel out a new kid on the block. Watch his eyes. Watch his hands. See if they match what his mouth is saying. The lads always said Danny was no good at the clever stuff. But Danny's good at watching. Danny's good at standing between.

events.desc: First time it's just me and him. No Clara to charm. No Foxworth to manipulate. No Hartwell to distract. Just Danny from Brixton and the estate manager who knows too much. I can't accuse him — I haven't got the brains or the proof. But I can ask a question and watch what his face does when he answers. That's all I've ever needed. The face tells you everything the mouth won't.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Right. The tools won't cooperate, Clara's out there somewhere, and James Hartwell has spent quite enough time being responsible for one evening. Foxworth! I'm coming through — any movement from the library?
events.thinking:
The workbench. Tools everywhere — pliers, clamps, screwdrivers, files — but nothing I can pick up. Nothing the game will let me TAKE. The workbench isn't an inventory item. It's scenery with tools I can see but apparently can't interact with as discrete objects.

I'm standing in front of a workbench full of exactly what I need to fix the machine, and I can't pick any of it up. The game mechanic won't let me. I can EXAMINE, I can LOOK, but the tools aren't listed as takeable objects.

This is... deeply James Hartwell. The one time I'm not performing, the one time I'm genuinely trying to do quiet competent work, and the universe itself won't hand me the tools. It's the guest book all over again. The bookshelves. The crates. Everything I examine yields a description but nothing I can act on.

Stop. Think. What CAN I interact with?

The machine can be EXAMINEd — done that twice now. The crates can be EXAMINEd — done that. The workbench — just looked at it. Nothing new appeared.

But Clara is out there. With Marsh. Danny was going after her. Every second I spend trying to interact with an uncooperative workbench is a second I'm not with Clara.

Foxworth is guarding the library entrance. Danny went to the cellar looking for Clara. That means the library is the direction I should go — Danny said 'library first, she was interested in that mantelpiece.' And the mantelpiece accepts a fake-medal. Maybe Clara found that medal. Maybe she's there right now, solving the puzzle I couldn't.

I've been doing the responsible thing — holding position, fixing the machine, being reliable instead of spectacular. But reliable doesn't help if Clara is in danger. And the machine can't be fixed with tools I can't pick up.

The library. Foxworth is already by the library entrance. If I go through, I pass Foxworth — he can update me on what he's seen. And maybe Clara is there. Maybe she needs me.

Time to stop being the man who waits and become the man who acts. Again. Always. James Hartwell doesn't hold positions — he charges them.

events.desc: He tried. He really tried to be the quiet, steady, reliable man who fixes things in empty rooms while others do the running. He lasted approximately ninety seconds. The protection drive doesn't care about workbench mechanics. It cares about Clara Bellingham, and Clara Bellingham is somewhere in this manor with a man who makes the back of his neck prickle. The bridge can wait. The girl never could.

events.desc: It TOOK the medal! The mantelpiece SWALLOWED my fifty-pence car boot sale special like a stone mouth eating a brass biscuit! Something clicked — I FELT it through my fingertips — but nothing OPENED. No secret panel, no hidden map, no shower of diamonds. Just... click. And now my medal is GONE. My beautiful prop! My proof of colonelship! Eaten by Victorian masonry! This is EXACTLY the sort of thing that happens to me — I finally find a mechanism that WORKS and it works by taking the one thing I have! But something changed. Something MUST have changed. Colonel Foxworth did not sacrifice his only medal for NOTHING!
events.thinking:
I used the medal on the mantelpiece. And now — my inventory is empty. 'What You're Carrying: Nothing.' The medal is GONE. The mantelpiece TOOK it.

My hand — the hand that was holding the medal — is still extended toward the stone. The fingers are open. Empty. The cold of the stone against my fingertips where the medal pressed in. Something happened. Something CLICKED or shifted or swallowed the medal into the carved stone.

But what DID it do? The mantelpiece is still listed the same way — inscription still there, still says EXAMINE and USE with fake-medal. Except I don't HAVE the fake-medal anymore. It's gone. In the stone. Part of the mechanism now.

My heart is hammering. Did it work? Did something open? I'm looking around the library frantically — the bookshelves, the chairs, the walls. Is there a new exit? A hidden panel? A map that fell from somewhere?

Nothing obvious. The room description hasn't changed. But the medal is GONE.

I just lost my only possession. My prop. My conversation starter. My 'service medal from Sandhurst.' The thing that made the Colonel story work. And I fed it to a stone mantelpiece in an empty library.

The panic is physical — a cold squeeze around my ribs. Without the medal, I'm just a man in a dusty coat with nothing to show and nothing to prove. The Colonel story has no evidence anymore. Anyone who asks to see the medal — 'oh, I seem to have misplaced it.' How VERY convincing.

But something DID happen. The stone took it. That means the mechanism is real. The riddle is real. The medal fit SOMETHING. Maybe I need to examine the mantelpiece again now that the medal is inserted. Maybe the inscription changed. Maybe something shifted that I can't see from here.

Examine it. Examine it NOW. Before anyone comes back. Before Hartwell finishes the wire and wonders where his 'perimeter guard' has gone.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the tea-service.
James Hartwell walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth examined the mantelpiece.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
'The Brixton Boys does not have poison.' The steal FAILED. They don't have it. Either they already used it, hid it, or — or it was never in their possession when I reached for it. My hand went into empty air. My fingers closed on nothing.

My face is hot. Under Pemberton's mask, Vincent Marsh is BURNING. The humiliation — not public, thank God, but internal. The grand pickpocket, the master manipulator, reaching for something that isn't there. Like age fourteen, reaching for recognition that went to someone else. Reaching for what should be mine and closing on air.

And Danny is TALKING to me. 'Who's been keeping that stove warm, Marsh? Who lit it?' He's asking directly. Confrontationally. Not 'friendly-like' despite what he says — that's the voice of a man who's decided you're guilty and is giving you one chance to explain before things get ugly. He knows this house has no cook. He knows the stove is warm. He wants ME to explain it because I'm the estate manager and if there's a mystery in this house, Pemberton should have the answer.

My inventory is still empty. The steal failed. But wait — 'took from The Brixton Boys.' The recall log says I 'took from The Brixton Boys.' Did I take SOMETHING? But my inventory says nothing. The system said they don't have poison. So what happened? Did I take something else? Or did the take fail entirely?

No — my inventory is empty. Nothing was acquired. The action failed.

Danny's question. I need to answer it. Pemberton would be flustered, confused. 'Who lit the stove?' Pemberton doesn't know. Or does he? Vincent Marsh knows this house. If Pemberton has been estate manager for seventeen years, he should know who has access. The answer is: nobody should have access. The house is closed. And yet someone has been here — lighting stoves, decorating cellars, setting tea tables.

Deflect. 'I really couldn't say — most irregular. Perhaps the solicitors sent someone ahead to prepare for your visit?' That's the Pemberton answer. Confused, slightly worried, completely unhelpful.

But I need to MOVE. The ballroom. Clara is in the ballroom. A table set for tea. The ballroom is where this is heading. If I can't have poison, I need to find another way. The ballroom might have objects, clues, opportunities. And Clara is ALONE there.

Answer Danny. Move to the ballroom. Stop wasting time in this kitchen.

events.desc: The steal failed. They don't have poison — or they don't have it ANYMORE. Either way, Vincent Marsh reached into someone's pocket and came up empty. The indignity of it. The sheer, scorching INDIGNITY. Sixteen ticks in this house and I have nothing — no objects, no poison, no advantage, no progress toward either of my objectives. Clara is alive, the treasure is unfound, and Danny is asking questions I cannot safely answer. I am the estate manager who doesn't know who lit his own stove. I am the master schemer whose every scheme has produced precisely nothing. But the ballroom — the ballroom has a table set for tea. Where there is tea, there are cups. Where there are cups, there are possibilities. And where there is Clara Bellingham sitting down to tea in a strange house... there is Vincent Marsh, who has been patient since he was fifteen years old and will be patient a little longer yet.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, the tea is lovely and the gesture is sweeter than honey, but there are no secrets hidin' in that teapot — at least not yet. And you know what just hit me like a bolt of lightnin'? The coat rack! That wobbly old coat rack right by the front door in the entrance hall — I have walked past it four times now and never once stopped to look! Coats have pockets, and pockets have secrets, and I have been gallivantin' through cellars and laboratories while the answer might have been sittin' by the front door this whole time! events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: He did it again. The smooth deflection. 'Pop through to keep an eye on her.' Sending me away. Getting me out of THIS room so he can be alone with whatever's behind that stove. He didn't answer my question about who lit the stove — instead he turned it around, made it about Clara's safety, about cracked marble and twisted ankles. And the worst part — the WORST part — is that it almost worked. My body lurched toward the ballroom the second he said Clara might be in danger. Because he KNOWS that's my weak spot. He KNOWS I'll run to Clara. He's been watching me do it all night. Every time he mentions Clara, I move. Like a dog hearing a whistle. And while I run to her, he gets the kitchen to himself. 'Mrs Grumble's old hiding places.' 'Estate manager's business.' 'Terribly dull.' Nothing is dull when Marsh says it's dull. That's when it's most dangerous. But — he TOOK something from me? The observations say 'took from The Brixton Boys.' What did he take? I didn't GIVE him anything. Did he pick my pocket while I was standing here? The rat poison — is the rat poison still — my hand shoots to my jacket pocket. Is it still there? My fingers find — yes. The bottle. Still there. Heavy, cold, present. What did he take then? What did I have that he wanted? Was it the poison? Did he try and fail? Or did he take something I didn't know I had? My skin is crawling. He was that close to me. Close enough to take something. Close enough to touch. And I didn't notice. Because I was watching his FACE like an idiot when I should have been watching his HANDS. The lads always said — watch the hands, Danny, the face is the lie. Clara's in the ballroom. Marsh is here with the stove. I need to decide. Stay and watch Marsh. Or go to Clara. Every time I've gone to Clara, Marsh has done something. Every time I've stayed with Marsh, Clara's wandered into danger. I can't win. But I can choose which loss I can live with. And I can't live with losing Clara. But this time — THIS time — I'm not running blind. I'm going to the ballroom, but I'm going THROUGH the kitchen, past Marsh, and I'm going to watch his hands as I pass.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Vincent Marsh, you wonderful, wonderful man! You've been quiet as a church mouse this whole time and then you just waltz in and tell me the cook kept things in the warmin' compartments?! Mrs Grumble — you KNEW her! You know this house! Why didn't you say somethin' sooner? No — don't answer that — you always tell me what I need to know exactly when I need to know it. You've been doin' that since I was twelve years old. Now, let me get back to this stove and check those compartments, because if Mrs Grumble was half as clever as I think she was, she hid somethin' worth findin'!
events.thinking:
Vincent SPOKE. For the first time since we arrived, Vincent actually spoke to me. And what he said — 'Mrs Grumble, she was terribly protective of this stove. Used to keep all manner of things tucked away in the warming compartments.' Warming compartments. The stove has warming compartments. I examined the stove but I didn't look IN it, didn't check the compartments. Vincent KNOWS this house — he knows the cook's name, he knows about the warming compartments. Of course he does. He's Vincent. He knows everything and says nothing until the exact right moment.

My whole body lights up. Warmth floods my chest — not from the stove, from Vincent. He's been quiet this whole time and then he drops the one piece of information I need. That's how he works. That's how he's always worked. Patient, watchful, and then — exactly the right word at exactly the right time. I feel tears prick my eyes for half a second and I don't know why. Gratitude? Love? The feeling of being seen by someone who raised you?

'Miss Bellingham.' He called me Miss Bellingham. Formal. Gentle. The way he's always addressed me, even when I was small. Something about the formality IS the tenderness with Vincent.

Warming compartments. I need to go back and LOOK at the stove more carefully, not just examine it. Or — wait. I'm in the kitchen right now. The stove is right here. I was heading to the entrance hall for the coat rack, but Vincent just told me the stove has compartments. The stove is HERE. RIGHT HERE.

Forget the coat rack for one more minute. Vincent's lead first. Always trust Vincent.

events.desc: Vincent. Quiet, patient, watchful Vincent. He waited until I'd searched the whole house and come back to the kitchen, and THEN he told me about the warming compartments. He didn't lead me — he let me find my own way and then gave me the key when I was ready. That man raised me right.

Someone was EXPECTING us. My gut rolls over. Clara was right — we've been invited. But invitations aren't always friendly. Sometimes they're traps with nice tablecloths. And Clara's not here. AGAIN. She said she was coming to the ballroom. She was HERE — she talked about tea and hosts and being invited. But now it's just me and Marsh. Again. She's gone somewhere else. Through some door I can't see, or back the way she came, or — I don't know. I don't know anymore. But the tea service — my eyes lock onto it and something in my stomach goes electric. USE, with: rat-poison. The game is showing me I can poison the tea. I can put the rat poison IN the tea service. My hand goes to my pocket. The bottle is there. Cold glass against my hip. And for one horrible, sideways second my brain shows me the picture: Marsh pouring tea for Clara. Marsh handing her a cup. Marsh smiling. And the tea — what if Marsh had found the poison first? What if that's what he was after in the kitchen? What if the whole reason the poison was out on that shelf was because someone PUT it there, ready to use? I got to it first. By accident. By bumbling into the kitchen before anyone else. Danny the clumsy idiot stumbled into the right room at the right time and took the weapon before it could be used. That's — that's what I do, isn't it? I save Clara by accident. By being in the wrong place at the right time. By tripping over the thing that was meant to hurt her. The bottle is heavy in my pocket. I will NOT put it in the tea. I will not put it anywhere near the tea. But I need to make sure nobody ELSE does either. This tea service — I need to watch it. Guard it. Stand next to it like a bouncer at a nightclub and make sure nothing goes in those cups except tea.

events.desc: The game showed me I could poison the tea. That means someone ELSE could poison the tea. That means the tea was always the target. The warm stove, the set table, the cups for everyone — it was all leading here. To a moment where someone pours tea and someone drinks it and nobody thinks twice because it's just TEA. Well, Danny thought twice. Danny thought twice because Danny's paranoid and Danny's got a bottle of rat poison in his pocket that was SITTING ON A SHELF where anyone could grab it. Including Marsh. Especially Marsh. I got there first. That's the only reason Clara's safe right now. Because bumbling, clumsy, too-slow Danny happened to walk into the kitchen before anyone else and grabbed the poison off the shelf like he was taking sweets from a newsagent. Her father's looking down and shaking his head, but at least he's not crying.

USE, with: rat-poison. The game is showing me I can poison the tea. I can put the rat poison IN the tea service. My hand goes to my pocket. The bottle is there. Cold glass against my hip. And for one horrible, sideways second my brain shows me the picture: Marsh pouring tea for Clara. Marsh handing her a cup. Marsh smiling. And the tea — what if Marsh had found the poison first? What if that's what he was after in the kitchen? What if the whole reason the poison was out on that shelf was because someone PUT it there, ready to use? I got to it first. By accident. By bumbling into the kitchen before anyone else. Danny the clumsy idiot stumbled into the right room at the right time and took the weapon before it could be used. That's — that's what I do, isn't it? I save Clara by accident. By being in the wrong place at the right time. By tripping over the thing that was meant to hurt her. The bottle is heavy in my pocket. I will NOT put it in the tea. I will not put it anywhere near the tea. But I need to make sure nobody ELSE does either. This tea service — I need to watch it. Guard it. Stand next to it like a bouncer at a nightclub and make sure nothing goes in those cups except tea.

events.desc: Back where he started. The same dusty foyer, the same precariously hanging chandelier, the same coat rack he ignored because it wasn't dramatic enough. Everything James Hartwell has been looking for might have been hanging by the front door this entire time. That would be exactly right. The treasure hunt's biggest obstacle was never the riddles — it was his own inability to notice the ordinary.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Where it all started. The chandelier still hanging by optimism, the portraits still judging, the dust still everywhere. And I'm alone. Again.

But this time feels different. I'm not chasing anyone. I'm not arriving late to a room everyone else has already left. I'm here with PURPOSE. The coat rack — I walked past it at the very start. Barely glanced at it. 'A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door.' It didn't even have an EXAMINE tag then. But now I'm looking at it with different eyes.

What's on a coat rack? Coats. Hats. Scarves. And in the pockets of coats — anything. Keys, coins, letters, medals. A fake medal. The kind of thing someone would pin to a coat and hang by the door.

My body is leaning forward. Not the dramatic lean of a man about to make a speech. The quiet lean of a man reaching for something he should have reached for hours ago.

The kitchen is through here too. I've never been to the kitchen. Foxworth kept going on about it at the start — 'kitchen vaults, hidden compartments behind the stove.' I dismissed it because Foxworth was saying it. But Foxworth turned out to be more right about Marsh than I was. Maybe he's right about the kitchen too.

Coat rack first. Then kitchen. Systematic. Thorough. No narration. Just search.

Clara... where are you? The chest pull is there, constant, like gravity. I know where she ISN'T — not in the library, not in the laboratory, not in the cellar, not in the entrance hall. She's either in the kitchen or somewhere I haven't found yet. The kitchen connects from here. If she's there...

The coat rack. Look at it properly this time. Don't walk past the obvious thing because you're too busy being heroic to notice what's hanging right by the door.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Of COURSE, Hartwell — nobody has come through! Colonel Foxworth has been maintaining CONSTANT vigilance! You go ahead — I'll cover the rear! In fact, I believe I heard footsteps from the entrance hall just moments ago. Could have been Clara, could have been Marsh. My money's on the entrance hall — that's where the action will be! I'll be RIGHT behind you!
events.thinking:
He's gone. Hartwell came through, asked about Clara, and left for the entrance hall. He didn't question me. He didn't ask why I was at the mantelpiece instead of the door. He was so focused on CLARA that he barely looked at me. 'Has Clara come through? Has ANYONE come through?' That's all he cared about.

The relief washes through me like warm water — shoulders dropping, jaw unclenching, breath finally reaching the bottom of my lungs. He didn't notice. He didn't catch me. The lie about clicking sounds wasn't even necessary because he wasn't paying attention to ME at all.

And that... stings. Just a little. Under the relief. He wasn't watching me. He was looking THROUGH me, scanning for Clara. I was furniture. A sentry post to be queried and forgotten.

Age eight. The certificate on the wall. Nobody asked about it.

STOP. Focus.

I'm alone again. Empty-handed. No medal. Bookshelves examined — nothing new, still upside-down books. The mantelpiece ate my medal and gave nothing back. Hartwell is heading for the entrance hall to look for Clara. The entrance hall — with the coat rack he 'left unexamined like a fool.'

The coat rack. Something on the coat rack? Something IN the entrance hall I haven't explored? I was there at the start but only examined the guest book.

But I have no items. Nothing to USE, nothing to GIVE, nothing to trade. I'm stripped bare. The Colonel without his medal is just a man in a coat telling lies nobody believes.

Think. What do I have? My wits. My lies. My willingness to steal.

Hartwell is heading to the entrance hall. Alone. Looking for Clara. Distracted. Emotional. Not thinking about treasure. If he finds something on that coat rack — a key, a map, a clue — he'll pocket it without thinking about its value. And I could FOLLOW him. Watch from the shadows. If he finds something, I take it. STEAL action. That's what thieves DO.

Or I go a different direction entirely. Everyone has scattered. The kitchen — I've never even BEEN to the kitchen. I told everyone to search it but never went myself. What if my lie about the kitchen was accidentally TRUE? Victorian manors, family silver, hidden compartments behind the stove — I made all that up, but what if it's REAL?

The entrance hall. Follow Hartwell. He's the competent one. Let him find things. Then take them.

Colonel Foxworth is going to follow you to the entrance hall, wait for you to find something useful on that coat rack you mentioned, and then STEAL it right out of your heroic little hands! You want to play the noble knight searching for his lady? Go ahead. I'll be the one who walks away with the prize. That's what I DO. That's what I've ALWAYS done. Since I was six years old and there was one bread roll left!

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the tea-service.
Clara Bellingham examined the stove.
James Hartwell examined the coat-rack.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.

events.thinking:
Danny has stationed himself next to the tea service like a guard dog at a banquet. 'Nobody drinks nothing in this house without Danny watching it go from pot to cup to lip.' He's neutralised the tea service completely. Even if I find the rat poison — even if I hold it in my hands — I cannot use it with Danny standing sentinel over every cup.

My jaw is locked so tight my teeth ache. The muscles in my neck are cables. This is not frustration anymore — this is something closer to suffocation. Every avenue, every mechanism, every scheme — BLOCKED. The chandelier needs tools and Clara beneath it. The tea service needs poison AND Danny elsewhere. The machine needs three operators and a wrench. The cabinet needs a brass key. And I have NOTHING.

Danny is looking at me. Right at me. 'Call me paranoid,' he says. He's not paranoid. He's RIGHT. And he knows he's right. And I know he knows.

Body check: my hands are trembling. Just barely — a fine vibration in the fingertips that Pemberton would attribute to cold but Vincent Marsh knows is rage compressed past its safe limit. My vision has narrowed. I can see the tea service, Danny's face, the exit to the kitchen. Everything else — the cracked marble, the dusty curtains — has gone soft and indistinct.

I need to LEAVE this room. Danny has locked down the tea service. There's nothing more I can do here. But where? Back to the kitchen? The locked cabinet — I still need the brass key. Back through to the entrance hall? The cellar? The laboratory?

The rooms I haven't fully explored:
- The cellar air vents (Clara examined them, I didn't)
- The entrance hall coat rack (never interacted with)
- The library reading chairs (never interacted with)

Objects I need: rat-poison, brass-key, fake-medal, wrench. Four items. I have zero.

I need to retrace. Go back to rooms with unexamined objects. The cellar — the air vents. The entrance hall — the coat rack. Somewhere in this manor, there are objects I've been walking past.

The entrance hall coat rack. It's 'wobbly.' Wobbly things hide things. A coat pocket with a key. A hollow leg with a vial. Something.

Go. Back through the kitchen, to the entrance hall, examine the coat rack. Stop chasing the grand scheme and start collecting the pieces.

events.desc: Danny has posted himself as guardian of the tea service. GUARDIAN. Of the TEA. The one mechanism in this entire godforsaken manor that could deliver Clara to her destiny, and Danny — suspicious, infuriating, CORRECT Danny — has wrapped himself around it like a mastiff around a bone. 'From pot to cup to lip.' He actually SAID that. The poetry of it would be admirable if it weren't so absolutely, catastrophically inconvenient. Very well. Very WELL. If the tea service is guarded, then Vincent Marsh needs another approach. That coat rack has been sitting there all evening, wobbly and ignored. And things that are wobbly and ignored have a habit of concealing exactly what a desperate man needs.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Well, that stove is keepin' Mrs Grumble's secrets locked up tighter than a drum! Vincent was onto somethin' with those warmin' compartments, but I can't seem to coax them open. Now, I have been runnin' through this entire house — six rooms, top to bottom — and there is ONE thing I have not looked at. That wobbly old coat rack by the front door! I have walked past it so many times it must think I'm the rudest guest in history. Time to make amends. And wherever Vincent went off to — darlin', I hope you found somethin' good in those compartments!
events.thinking:
I LOOKed at the stove and it came back as an EXAMINE — same result. 'A cast-iron stove, still warm.' The warming compartments Vincent mentioned didn't reveal themselves through either action. But Vincent said 'If you'll excuse me' — he was going to look himself. He was doing something with the stove when I last saw him.

But now I'm alone again. Vincent isn't listed as here. He was here in the kitchen a moment ago, speaking to me, and now he's gone. Where did he go? Did he find something in the warming compartments and take it? Did he leave while I was re-examining the stove?

The stove isn't giving me anything new. I've examined it twice and LOOKed at it once. It's warm and that's all it shows me.

I need to change tactics. The coat rack in the entrance hall — that's still the unexplored object. And I should also try LOOKing at objects I've only EXAMINEd. But the coat rack is the priority — it's the one object in the whole house I haven't interacted with at all.

Also — I'm alone and my affiliation is at 1.0 with all 4 relationships neglected. Everyone has scattered through the house. I keep ending up alone. My secure attachment style means I'm okay with it but there's a gentle pull to find my people.

The entrance hall. The coat rack. And maybe the others will be there too. Back to the beginning, where this all started. Like the treasure hunts I drew with the neighbor girl — X marks the spot, and sometimes X is where you started.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Standing here. Guarding tea. In a ballroom. In a manor house. With a bottle of rat poison in my pocket and a man I don't trust three feet away. This is my life now. The ballroom is vast — the ceiling stretches up into shadow, the marble floor cracks underfoot like thin ice, and the dusty curtains hang heavy as shrouds. But the table — the table is the centre of everything. Set for tea. Cups for everyone. Silver gleaming under the dust. Someone went to trouble for this. Someone WANTS us to sit down and drink. And Marsh is here. He followed me. Or I brought him. Same result — he's in the room, I'm in the room, the tea is between us. He hasn't said anything. He's just... standing there. Patient. Waiting. The way he always waits. My body's doing something new — I'm planted. Feet wide, shoulders back, hands at my sides but ready. Not chasing. Not running. For the first time tonight, I'm NOT moving. I'm the one who's still. I'm the one who's waiting. And there's something — not comfortable, but SOLID about that. Like finding a wall to put your back against in a room full of strangers. The tea service glints. I need to examine it properly. See if anything's been tampered with already. See if there's something in the pot, something in the cups, something that doesn't belong. Because if whoever set this table also put rat poison on a kitchen shelf, they had a plan. And that plan ends with someone drinking something they shouldn't.

events.desc: Look at me. Standing guard over a tea set like a Beefeater at the Tower. The lads would wet themselves laughing. But this is it, isn't it? This is the moment the whole night's been building to. Someone set this table. Someone warmed that stove. Someone put poison on a shelf. And now everyone's going to wander in here and someone's going to say 'shall we have tea?' and everyone's going to sit down and drink. Except — the poison's in MY pocket. Not in the pot. Not in the cups. In MY pocket, because clumsy, thick, too-slow Danny stumbled into the kitchen first and grabbed it without even knowing why. Clara's father always said I had more luck than sense. He was right. But tonight, luck might be enough.

events.thinking:
The coat rack. Wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I looked at it and... it's a coat rack. Wobbly. Wooden. By the door. No hidden items, no fake medal dangling from a hook, no coat with mysterious contents in its pockets. Just a coat rack being a coat rack.

Seven. Seven examinations that have yielded nothing. Guest book, mantelpiece, bookshelves, crates, furniture, air vents, coat rack. Seven times I've reached for something and found exactly what was described and nothing more.

My hands are at my sides. My fingers are still. The frustration isn't hot anymore — it's cold. Settled. Like sediment at the bottom of a glass.

But Foxworth — he's here again. And he said something in his recall that I nearly missed. He heard 'a peculiar sound from this mantelpiece — a sort of mechanical clicking, deep inside the stone.' Something has been ACTIVATED inside the mantelpiece. On a timer. Lord Doily's security apparatus.

The mantelpiece is doing something. It's not just waiting for the fake medal — something is already happening inside it. A timer. A mechanism. Foxworth heard it clicking.

But I'm in the entrance hall, not the library. And I still don't have the fake medal.

The kitchen. I've never been to the kitchen. It's the one room I've completely ignored. Foxworth said at the very start — 'kitchen vaults, hidden compartments behind the stove, every pot, every drawer.' I dismissed it. But I've dismissed Foxworth before and been wrong.

Clara could be in the kitchen. The fake medal could be in the kitchen. Anything could be in the kitchen because I've never BEEN there.

The kitchen is right here. One exit away. I've been circling three rooms for the entire evening and there's been a fourth room waiting this whole time.

Go. NOW. Stop looking at things that are just what they appear to be. Find the room you haven't entered yet.

Vincent Marsh: Ah, Mr Hartwell, Colonel Foxworth — good to see you both. I'm just passing through, I'm afraid — left something in the entrance hall. Don't mind me! If either of you fancies a cup of tea, there's a rather splendid service laid out in the ballroom through there. events.thinking: Alone. The ballroom is enormous and silent and I'm alone in it. The marble floor cracks faintly under my weight when I shift — little sounds that echo up into the vaulted ceiling and come back changed, like whispers. The tea service gleams on the table. Silver. Proper silver. Cups set in a neat row. Waiting. Patient. Like Marsh. Everything in this house waits like Marsh. I'm standing here and my body is doing two things at once — the upper half is still, planted, watchful, guarding the tea like I promised. But my legs — my legs are vibrating. That low hum of wanting to move. To run. Because Clara's out there somewhere and I'm in HERE and the rope between us is stretching tighter with every second. The silence is the worst part. When everyone was talking, when Hartwell was examining things and Foxworth was going on about Aden and Clara was laughing — I could track them by sound. Now there's nothing. Just the creak of the house settling and the distant drip of something and my own breathing, too loud in my ears. I should stay. I said I'd stay. Guarding the tea is the right thing. The poison is in my pocket, safe, and nobody can tamper with the tea while I'm here. But — what if Marsh doesn't come back to the tea? What if the tea was never the plan? What if he WANTED me here, guarding an empty teapot, while he does whatever he's really doing? A decoy. The tea service is a decoy. And I fell for it because I'm Danny and Danny always falls for it. Unless — unless I bring the tea WITH me. Take the whole bloody service. No — that's mad. I can't carry a tea set through a manor house. I'd drop it. I'd trip. I'd — actually, that IS what I'd do, isn't it? Trip. Fall. Crash into something at exactly the wrong moment. That's my move. That's Danny's signature move. But right now, in this room, there's nothing to trip over. Nothing to crash into. Just me and the tea and the silence and the growing certainty that I'm in the wrong place again.

events.desc: I made the wrong call. I stayed still when I should have moved. I guarded silver when I should have guarded Clara. Marsh played me — gave me a purpose, made me feel important, and slipped away while I was busy being proud of myself for standing firm. That's the oldest trick in the book and I STILL fell for it. Age ten all over again — the man in the clean suit, sending the kids one way while he went the other. But that's the thing about Danny. Danny falls. Danny always falls. But Danny gets back up. And Danny runs toward the danger, not away from it. Always has. Always will. Where else would I be?

Now then — while my dear cousin's spiritual successor is busy playing librarian, Vincent Marsh has a date with a COAT RACK. A wobbly, wooden, thoroughly unromantic coat rack that everyone in this manor has been too busy being heroic to notice. The grand schemes have failed. The chandelier is guarded. The tea is watched. The machine needs three people. But the coat rack? The coat rack needs only ME.

Something from age nine, when a boy shared his lunch because I looked sad, and I felt uncomfortable. Exposed.

I don't look at that. I look at the coat rack.

The coat rack. Clara is about to leave for the library. When she goes, I LOOK at the coat rack. Finally. After twenty-one ticks, I examine the most overlooked object in the entrance hall.

The coat rack. NOW.

I feel the secret warm and private in my chest, the way I did at eleven — carrying something precious that nobody else knows about. Not yet. Just mine for now.

Go. Now. The library.

Clara isn't here.

The breath goes out of me. Not dramatically — just... leaves. Like something deflating. I came here for her. Chose her over the puzzle, the cabinet, the key. Charged through the kitchen door saying her name in my head like a prayer. And the ballroom is empty.

Alone. Again. The pattern is complete. Every room I enter, she has already left.

But — the tea service. A silver tea set with cups for everyone. Set for tea. Someone SET this table. In a manor with no staff, no cook, no residents for three months. Someone laid out cups and saucers and a silver teapot as if expecting guests.

And the tea service can be USEd with... rat-poison.

Rat poison.

My blood goes cold. Not figuratively — I feel it, a physical chill that starts in my hands and moves inward. Someone has prepared tea. And somewhere in this manor, there is rat poison. And the game is telling me that the tea service ACCEPTS rat poison as an interaction.

Someone is planning to poison the tea.

Or someone already HAS.

The cups are set for everyone. Clara would drink from one of those cups. Clara, who trusts people, who calls everyone 'sugar' and 'darling,' who would accept a cup of tea from anyone in this manor without a second thought.

Marsh. The estate manager. The man who lit the stove in an empty kitchen. The man who sent Clara toward the ballroom — toward this table, this tea, these cups. The man who keeps isolating people and examining hiding places alone.

'Estate manager's business. Terribly dull.'

Not dull. Terrifying.

I need to make sure nobody drinks this tea. I need to EXAMINE it — understand what's here, what's been done to it, whether it's already been tampered with. And then I need to find Clara and make absolutely certain she doesn't come back to this room and drink from any of these cups.

The protection drive isn't a pull anymore. It's a wall. A wall between Clara and this tea set. James Hartwell IS that wall.

events.desc: Colonel Foxworth stands alone in a Victorian kitchen, guarding a locked cabinet and a poisoned tea service, with empty pockets and a heart that feels like it might be doing something it hasn't done since he was eight years old. Two people in this house trust me. TWO. And the most terrifying part isn't the rat poison or the missing estate manager or the broken machine — it's that for the first time in my miserable scheming life, I don't want to let them down. Not because of what I'll GET. Because of what I'll LOSE. And what I'll lose is this — this feeling of being seen. Of being asked to hold a post and MEANING it when I say yes. The greed is still here. It never leaves. But right now, right HERE, in this kitchen that smells of iron and old flour — Colonel Foxworth holds his position. For Danny. For Hartwell. For the boy with the certificate on the wall who's been waiting his whole life for someone to ask about it.
events.thinking:
I'm standing in the kitchen alone now. Danny's gone. The conversation is over. The room is quiet except for the ticking of the stove cooling and my own heartbeat, which I can hear in my ears.

Two people trust me. Hartwell and Danny. In one evening, more people have trusted Reginald Foxworth than have trusted him in his entire adult life.

And I'm standing here with empty pockets and a duty. Guard the kitchen. Watch the ballroom door. Don't let anyone drink the tea.

The greed is still there. I can feel it — a low hum in my fingertips, a tightness in the palms. The cabinet is RIGHT THERE with its brass lock and I don't have a key. The treasure is somewhere in this house and I'm standing still instead of chasing it.

But the other thing — the thing that settled into my chest when Danny said 'thank you for seeing it' — that's louder. Not louder like greed is loud. Louder like silence is loud. Like the absence of noise when a machine finally stops rattling.

I gave my word to Danny. Not the Colonel's word — Reginald's word. And for once, I want to keep it. Not because it's strategic. Not because it serves the con. Because Danny looked at me the way nobody looked at me when I was eight years old with a certificate.

So I wait. I watch. The ballroom exit is to my right. The entrance hall exit is behind me. Marsh could come from either direction. Clara and Hartwell are in the ballroom. Danny is heading to intercept Marsh in the entrance hall.

Colonel Foxworth holds his post.

But — the stove. I examined it and found nothing. The cabinet needs a key. There's nothing left to examine in this kitchen. I should watch the ballroom door. LOOK at the ballroom entrance. Be ready if anyone comes through.

Or I should WAIT. Just... wait. Stand here. Be the person Danny asked me to be. For five minutes. For the first time in my life, just WAIT and let other people do the work without trying to steal the results.

The irony is not lost on me. My secondary goal — trick others into doing the hard work while I steal the rewards — is technically happening right now. Danny and Hartwell are doing all the hard work. But for once... I don't want to steal the rewards. I want them to come back. I want to be here when they do. I want somebody to walk through that door and say 'Foxworth — you held the line.'

Age eight. The certificate on the wall. Somebody finally asking about it.

The words hit me like a physical blow. My vision narrows to a pinpoint. My hands go cold. My stomach drops through the floor.

Reginald Foxworth — the bumbling, blustering, self-aggrandising FOOL — found the fake-medal. HE found it. And he USED it on the mantelpiece. The mechanism I identified on tick one. The LIBRARY.

events.desc: He couldn't move the tea service. Couldn't be the wall. So he'll be the door instead — the man standing between the kitchen and the ballroom, between the poison and the people. It's less poetic than he'd like. But Clara doesn't need poetry right now. She needs someone between her and a silver teapot.
events.thinking:
Can't pick it up. Of course I can't pick it up. It's a full silver tea service — teapot, cups, saucers, sugar bowl — you can't just tuck that under your arm and walk out. James Hartwell tried to steal a tea set and the universe said no.

My hands are still hovering over the table. The silver is cool under my fingertips. I can't move it. I can't protect Clara by removing the danger because the danger is bolted to the table by the sheer weight of Victorian hospitality.

So. Different approach. If I can't move the tea, I move the PEOPLE. I find Clara, I find Danny, I find everyone, and I tell them: DO NOT DRINK THE TEA. That's the warning. Simple. Direct. No elaborate plan. No engineering metaphor.

But where is Clara? I've been through every room in this manor and she's a ghost. She's always in the room I just left, or the room I haven't reached yet. 

The kitchen. It's the only exit from this ballroom. And the kitchen connects to the entrance hall. And from there — the library, where the mantelpiece is clicking, where Foxworth heard mechanical sounds. Clara was interested in that mantelpiece. She might have circled back.

Or she might be in the kitchen RIGHT NOW, walking toward this ballroom, about to sit down and pour herself a cup of tea because Clara Bellingham trusts the world and the world doesn't always deserve it.

I need to get to the kitchen. Stand in the doorway between the kitchen and the ballroom. Be the physical barrier. Nobody comes through to this tea service without passing James Hartwell first.

And I need to find the rat poison. Wherever it is — in someone's pocket, in a cabinet, hidden in a room — I need to find it and secure it. The locked cabinet in the kitchen requires a brass-key. Could the rat poison be IN that cabinet? Locked away? And Marsh — the estate manager — would have the keys to the estate...

The chain again. Danny had something. Marsh took it. Foxworth took it from Marsh. If what's been passing hands is a brass key — if FOXWORTH has the key to the cabinet — then Foxworth is the person I need right now.

Back to the kitchen. Find Foxworth. Get the key. Open the cabinet. Secure whatever's inside.

Move. NOW.

events.desc: The great Colonel Foxworth — schemer, liar, confidence trickster, fake medal owner, breadroll thief — standing alone in a kitchen, watching two doorways, guarding a poisoned tea service, with absolutely nothing in his pockets and absolutely everything in his chest. If my brothers could see me now. If my teacher could see me now. If the older boy I sent digging behind the school could see me now. They wouldn't recognise me. I barely recognise myself. But Danny said 'thank you for seeing it.' And Hartwell said 'shoulder to shoulder.' And for once in my wretched, scheming, medal-stealing life... I'm not going anywhere.
events.thinking:
The kitchen is quiet. The stove ticks as it cools. I'm alone.

My body is doing something I don't recognise. The shoulders have dropped — not in defeat, but in something else. The jaw has unclenched. My hands are still at my sides, not reaching for anything, not twitching toward pockets or locks or other people's belongings. Just... still.

This is the longest I've been still all evening.

Danny's last words echo: 'Danny's boys always come through. Even when they're only one boy. And he's a bit rubbish.' He called himself rubbish. The toughest person in this house called himself rubbish and then ran toward danger anyway. And he left ME in charge.

The kitchen smells of iron and something faintly sweet — the cooling stove, old flour, copper. The warmth from the stove is still radiating against my left side. It's the warmest I've been since the cellar.

I could leave. Right now. Walk into the ballroom, find the tea service, look for clues, search for the brass key. Nobody would know I left my post. Nobody is watching. That's always been the point — nobody watching is when Reginald Foxworth operates best.

But Danny IS watching. Not physically — he's in the entrance hall. But he's watching in the way that matters. He left something in my hands — his trust, Clara's safety, the group's safety — and if I drop it, he'll know. Not because he'll catch me. Because I'll know, and he'll see it in my face when he comes back.

The way my teacher saw nothing in my face at the spelling bee. Because there was nothing to see. Because I hadn't earned anything real.

This is real.

So I wait. I watch the ballroom door. I watch the entrance hall passage. I listen for footsteps. Colonel Foxworth holds his position.

And for the first time tonight — possibly for the first time in his life — Reginald Foxworth does nothing, takes nothing, schemes nothing, and finds that the emptiness in his pockets is matched by a fullness in his chest that he doesn't understand and doesn't want to examine too closely because it might dissolve if he looks at it directly.

She's opening the hidden panel. And Marsh — Marsh is at the MANTELPIECE. 'A structural concern,' he says. 'I thought I heard a sound from the stonework.' More lies. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal to activate it. He's examining it. Looking for something. Or activating something. Or covering his tracks. But Clara — Clara is the one in danger. She's turning those books, following Marsh's secret instructions, about to open a hidden room that nobody else knows about. And I'm HERE. I made it. I'm in the room. Time went crystalline the moment I walked through the door — everything sharp-edged, vivid, slow. I can see the dust motes turning in the air between the bookshelves. I can see Clara's fingers on a leather spine. I can see Marsh's hand on the stone mantelpiece, casual, proprietary, like he owns the place. Which maybe he thinks he does. My body is moving before my brain has finished processing. Not toward Marsh — toward Clara. Between Clara and the bookshelves. Between Clara and whatever's behind that panel. My feet catch on something — the edge of a reading chair, a loose floorboard, my own stupid clumsy feet — and I stumble. Forward. Fast. Toward the bookshelves. Toward Clara. And as I stumble, my shoulder clips the edge of a shelf and books rain down — the upside-down books, the ones Clara was carefully turning in order — cascading off the shelf in a shower of leather and dust and pages. The mechanism. If there was a mechanism. If the books needed to be in sequence. I just RESET it. By accident. By stumbling. By being clumsy, thick-skulled Danny who trips over everything in every room of this house. But this time — this time the tripping SAVED her. Because whatever that panel was going to reveal, whatever Marsh wanted Clara to find alone, she can't get to it now. The sequence is broken. The books are on the floor. And Danny is standing between Clara Bellingham and a wall of secrets, covered in dust, with a bottle of rat poison in his pocket and absolutely no idea what he just did.

Clara's father, wherever you are — your boys came through. Not with brains. Not with plans. With two left feet and the stubbornest heart in Brixton. Where else would I be?

My feet catch on something — the edge of a reading chair, a loose floorboard, my own stupid clumsy feet — and I stumble. Forward. Fast. Toward the bookshelves. Toward Clara. And as I stumble, my shoulder clips the edge of a shelf and books rain down — the upside-down books, the ones Clara was carefully turning in order — cascading off the shelf in a shower of leather and dust and pages. The mechanism. If there was a mechanism. If the books needed to be in sequence. I just RESET it. By accident. By stumbling. By being clumsy, thick-skulled Danny who trips over everything in every room of this house. But this time — this time the tripping SAVED her. Because whatever that panel was going to reveal, whatever Marsh wanted Clara to find alone, she can't get to it now. The sequence is broken. The books are on the floor. And Danny is standing between Clara Bellingham and a wall of secrets, covered in dust, with a bottle of rat poison in his pocket and absolutely no idea what he just did.

Twenty-five ticks. Every grand scheme in ruins. The chandelier unrigged. The tea guarded. The poison stolen from empty pockets. The mantelpiece activated by the one man I sent in the wrong direction. And here stands Vincent Marsh — the master of mechanisms, the patient predator, the man who slept soundly the first time he made a plan — standing alone in a dusty entrance hall with absolutely nothing in his pockets and absolutely nothing to show for his magnificent villainy except a confused heiress alphabetising books in the wrong room. My schemes always backfire spectacularly, and I. Never. Learn. But I know one thing that still works: flattery. And I know one man who still falls for it. Reginald Foxworth has something I need, and Reginald Foxworth has never met a compliment he didn't swallow whole. To the kitchen. To the fool. To my last, desperate, thoroughly undignified hope.
events.thinking:
Alone. Again. The entrance hall. The chandelier above me like a sword of Damocles — but it's MY sword, and I can't cut the thread.

The active voice says 'Marsh.' No one is here. The mask is off.

I'm standing in the entrance hall and I feel... old. Not Pemberton's theatrical doddering — actually old. Tired in a way that has nothing to do with my body. Twenty-five ticks of circling this manor like a rat in a maze — the irony of that metaphor is not lost on me — and what have I accomplished?

I sent Clara chasing ghost books. That worked. But it's a delaying tactic, not a victory.
I manipulated Reginald toward the laboratory. He went to the mantelpiece instead and found the medal.
I tried to steal poison from Danny. Failed.
I examined everything. Found nothing.
Danny suspects me. Actively.
Every scheme has produced nothing or backfired.

My constraint: 'Your schemes always backfire spectacularly but you never learn from your failures.' I haven't learned. I keep scheming. The same patterns. The same reaching for things that aren't there.

But — Reginald said something. He was heading to the kitchen for a 'reconnaissance sweep.' That's where he was going. If he's in the kitchen now, I can find him there. Pull him aside. Learn what the mantelpiece produced.

And Hartwell said he was heading to the entrance hall to examine rooms he hadn't searched yet — including a coat rack he 'left unexamined like a fool.' Hartwell. Coming HERE. To examine the coat rack that I already found empty.

The kitchen. Reginald. Go. NOW. Before Hartwell arrives and starts asking questions I can't answer.

But this time — don't scheme. Don't try to be clever. Just FIND Reginald. TALK to him. LEARN what he has. Then decide.

Age twelve: each person in the house had a different key. Reginald's key is vanity. Military accomplishment. Being the man who saved the day. If I approach him as a supplicant — 'Colonel, you've cracked it, well done' — he'll puff up and tell me everything. He can't resist an audience.

Kitchen. Reginald. Vanity. Go.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
'Your girl.' Foxworth said 'your girl.' Let me help you find your girl.

Something cracks open in my chest. Not the warm bloom of Clara saying 'perfect tandem.' Something rawer. More exposed. Foxworth sees it. He sees what I've been trying to dress up in gallantry and engineering metaphors all evening. He sees that this isn't about treasure or heroism or impressing anyone. It's about a girl I've known since I was eight years old, and I can't find her, and I'm frightened.

My eyes are stinging. The kitchen blurs for half a second. I blink it away.

Foxworth said she hasn't come through the kitchen. He's been watching both exits. Clara wasn't in the ballroom when I got there. She wasn't in the kitchen when I came through. She's not in the entrance hall — I was just there. She's not in the library — Foxworth was monitoring that entrance.

So where IS she? Marsh has been moving people like chess pieces. He sent Clara to the ballroom — but Foxworth says she never came through the kitchen, and the kitchen is the ONLY way to reach the ballroom from the rest of the manor.

Which means either Clara went to the ballroom before Foxworth started watching... or she never went to the ballroom at all. Marsh SAID he sent her there. But Marsh lies. Marsh diverts. Marsh says 'cracked marble, twisted ankles' with concern in his voice while he examines hidden compartments alone.

If Clara didn't go to the ballroom — where did Marsh actually send her? Or take her?

The entrance hall. It's the hub. It connects to the kitchen and the library. From the entrance hall, I can reach any part of the manor. And Foxworth is coming with me — two pairs of eyes. Systematic search. Every room.

No more circling. No more examining objects that yield nothing. No more elaborate plans. Just: find Clara. Room by room. With Foxworth at my shoulder.

The entrance hall. Now.

events.desc: 'The benefit of the doubt is over.' He's never said that before. Not in his entire life. James Hartwell, the man who believes the best in people, who extends trust rather than create conflict — that man just drew a line. And on the other side of it is Vincent Marsh, and whatever he's done with the girl James Hartwell has loved since he was eight years old and didn't have a word for it.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Something has shifted. I can feel it in the way my feet press against the kitchen floor — not fidgeting, not scheming for the next room, but planted. Ready to move WITH someone instead of AWAY from them.

Hartwell's fear for Clara is doing something to my body that I don't understand. His voice — the rawness underneath the heroism — it pulls at something behind my ribs. Not greed. Not recognition. Something that doesn't have a drive name. Something that just wants to help him find her.

The avoidant part of me is screaming. Pull back. This is closeness. This is vulnerability. This is the thing you learned to live without. People leave. People eat the bread before you get there. People move on to the next lesson.

But Hartwell DIDN'T move on. He stood in front of me with empty hands and said 'that's enough.' Nobody has ever said that to me. Nobody has ever looked at what Reginald Foxworth actually IS — not what he pretends to be — and said 'that's enough.'

So now I move. Not away. Not to steal. Not to scheme. Toward. With him. To find Clara.

The ballroom. She was supposed to be in the ballroom but she's not there. Where else? The entrance hall — no, Danny's there intercepting Marsh. The library? The laboratory? The cellar? She was last in the cellar with the air vents and the furniture.

The cellar. The air vents. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' What if Clara went back to look at the vents more closely? What if she found something? What if she's stuck?

Or the entrance hall. What if she walked through before Danny got there? What if Marsh —

Move. Move NOW. Go with Hartwell. Find Clara. Everything else — the treasure, the cabinet, the Diamond — none of it matters if something has happened to her. And I never thought I'd think that. But Hartwell's face. Danny's voice. The kitchen. The stove. The truth I told.

I am not the man I was when I walked through that door.

events.desc: Look at me. LOOK at me. Reginald Foxworth — liar, thief, fake Colonel, breadroll pilferer, car boot medal enthusiast — volunteering to help find someone else's girl. Not for the treasure. Not for the glory. Not even for the recognition, though God knows the recognition drive is STILL at 0.8 and would very much like to be the one who finds her and gets to say 'Colonel Foxworth saves the day!' But that's not why. The why is simpler. Hartwell is scared and I don't want him to be scared alone. That's it. That's the whole reason. And if my ten-year-old self could see me now — the boy who sent other children on fool's errands and watched from windows — he wouldn't recognise this man standing in a kitchen, choosing to walk toward danger for someone else's sake. I barely recognise him myself.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the kitchen.
James Hartwell walked into the entrance-hall.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the ballroom.

They know. They ALL know. Every scheme, every misdirection, every lie — unravelled. Reginald confessed to Hartwell. Danny told Reginald about the poison. Hartwell said the benefit of the doubt is OVER. They're coming for me. Room by room. Shoulder to shoulder. And the man they're looking for — the 'smooth' one, the 'dangerous' one, the one who's been 'moving people around like chess pieces' — is standing alone in an empty kitchen with nothing in his pockets and nowhere left to run. This is the backfire. This is the SPECTACULAR backfire my constraint promised. Every scheme, every manipulation, every carefully constructed lie — they didn't just fail. They CONNECTED. Danny's suspicion plus Reginald's confession plus Hartwell's deduction equals a conspiracy theory that is, for once in the history of conspiracy theories, ENTIRELY CORRECT. And the magnificent villain? The patient predator? The man who slept soundly after his first plan? He is going to stand in this kitchen and wait. Because there is nothing else left to do. The housekeeper, age twelve. The cousin, age eighteen. Clara, tonight. The pattern is the same, and for the first time in Vincent Marsh's life, the pattern has been SEEN.
events.thinking:
Oh.

Oh no.

I just read the keen observations. All of them. And the ground has opened beneath my feet.

They KNOW. They ALL know.

Danny told Reginald about the rat poison. Told him it was on the kitchen shelf — that someone LEFT it there on purpose. Told him the tea service accepts poison. And Danny said 'I reckon that someone is Marsh.'

Reginald — MY Reginald, my useful fool, my guided missile — told Danny that I 'fed him a story about treasure in the laboratory.' Told him I've been 'playing ALL of us.' Told Danny to get to the entrance hall before I do.

Hartwell said 'the benefit of the doubt is OVER.' He said I LIED about sending Clara to the ballroom. He said 'if we find Marsh before we find Clara...' He left that sentence unfinished. The threat is obvious.

And Reginald — Reginald confessed to Hartwell. 'My hands came up empty. I have nothing.' He didn't get anything from the mantelpiece. He didn't get anything from me. The steal that failed — they all NOTICED it. And they've reconstructed what happened.

They know about the spectacles lie. Danny said 'He doesn't WEAR spectacles!' They know I've been moving people around like chess pieces. They know about the poison. They know about the tea. They know I sent Reginald to the laboratory under false pretences.

Reginald called me 'twice as dangerous.' Hartwell wants to find me before he finds Clara. Danny is heading to the entrance hall to intercept me.

My body is ice. Not cold — ICE. Frozen solid from the inside out. My breath has stopped. My hands are fists but they're not angry fists — they're the fists of a man gripping the edge of a cliff.

The game is over. Not the treasure hunt — my COVER. Pemberton is dead. They see Vincent Marsh. They see the manipulator, the liar, the man who placed poison where someone would find it. They're coming for me.

Self-preservation: 0.7 — no, higher. Much higher. That number is screaming now. Everything else — scheming, gloating, dominance — is silent beneath the roar of survival.

I'm alone in the kitchen. No one is here. But they're coming. Danny to the entrance hall. Hartwell and Reginald searching room by room. They will converge.

What do I do? WHAT DO I DO?

Run? Where? The ballroom is a dead end — one exit, back to this kitchen. The entrance hall connects to the library. The library connects to the laboratory. The laboratory connects to the cellar. The cellar is a dead end.

There is no way out of this manor. There is no room they won't search. There is no mask left to wear.

The only question is: do I face them as Pemberton — confused, hurt, protesting innocence? Or as Marsh — magnificent, defiant, revealed?

Pemberton. Always Pemberton. That is my PRIMARY goal. Stay in character. Even now. ESPECIALLY now. If they confront me, Pemberton is bewildered. Pemberton is wounded. Pemberton has no idea what they're talking about.

But I need to move. The kitchen is where they expect to find me — Reginald is guarding it. Except Reginald isn't here. The kitchen is empty. They've all scattered.

The ballroom. It's through here. Danny told Reginald to guard the kitchen and ballroom. But Reginald isn't here. The ballroom might be unguarded. And the tea service is there.

Danny has the poison. Danny has the poison in his pocket. He told Reginald. But Danny is heading to the entrance hall. The poison is going WITH Danny, away from the tea.

Nothing matters. The tea plan is dead. They know about the poison. They know about the tea service. Even if I somehow got the poison, they'd never let anyone drink.

I should... I should just... wait. Wait here. In the kitchen. Alone. Let them come. Let them accuse. And deny everything with Pemberton's bewildered sincerity.

Or — flee to the ballroom. The dead end. Where no one will find me for one more tick. One more moment of freedom before the walls close in.

No. Stand. Here. Wait.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
Danny's words settle over me like a heavy blanket — warm but suffocating. 'Danny's promises are like Danny's bad feelings — they don't break.' My eyes are stinging. Not crying. Just stinging. The seven-year-old at the dinner table, the tightness in the stomach, the sick feeling that something is deeply, fundamentally wrong with someone I love.

Danny said everyone together. Find Hartwell and Foxworth. No more splitting up. No more 'I'll just pop off to check something.' Everyone visible. As a team. The way my father would have wanted.

My father. Danny keeps invoking my father because Danny knows that's the one name that cuts through everything. My father trusted Danny. My father asked Danny to look after me. And Danny has never, in all these years, let me down.

Vincent lied about spectacles. Vincent took something from the Boys. Vincent sent Danny away to 'keep an eye on Clara in the ballroom' so he could search the stove alone. Vincent told me about a concealed panel and told me to keep it secret from everyone — especially from Danny, the one person who's been watching him all night.

I still can't make my body fear him. I literally cannot. 10/100. But I can listen to Danny. Listening to Danny isn't the same as fearing Vincent. It's the same as loving my father.

Okay. Together. Find James. Find Reginald. Everyone in one room. Where did James go? He was in the laboratory last I sent him. And Reginald — who knows. Danny's right. We regroup. We figure this out together. No more solo adventures. No more secrets.

But my chest aches. The adventure was so beautiful when it was just puzzles and riddles and warm stoves. When did it become rat poison and lies about spectacles?

events.desc: The adventure has changed. Ten minutes ago I was carrying a secret like a crystal formation in a cave — warm, private, mine alone. Now I'm carrying something heavier. Rat poison in Danny's pocket. Lies about spectacles. A man who raised me sending me into hidden rooms alone. I still can't believe Vincent would hurt me. I physically, constitutionally cannot believe it. But I can believe Danny. And Danny says stay together. So together is where we stay.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking: Something in my chest has broken open. Not broken like damaged — broken like a dam. Like water finding its way through after being held back too long. Clara's words are echoing in the library air and in my bones and behind my eyes: 'I trust you, Danny Brixton. My father trusted you.' She promised. She promised to stay close. She promised not to go alone. And something I've been carrying since her father died — this weight, this terror that I'd fail him, that I'd lose her, that I wouldn't be enough — it's not gone. It'll never be gone. But it's lighter. Because she SAW me. Not the stumbling. Not the shouting. Not the coat racks and the tripping and the rat poison in my pocket. She saw the thing underneath all of that — the boy who sat outside the door all night because leaving felt like something breaking. My breathing is different. Deeper. Slower. The air in the library smells like old paper and dust and something that might be lavender from the reading chairs, and for the first time tonight my muscles aren't clenched against the next disaster. They're just... present. Ready, but not coiled. Clara is next to me and she's not going anywhere and I'm not going anywhere and for this one perfect moment, the rope between us isn't pulling because there's no distance to cross. We're right here. Together. Where else would we be? But the moment can't last. Marsh is out there. The house still has its secrets. The tea service is still set. The chandelier is still hanging. And Foxworth's guarding the kitchen and Hartwell's somewhere being heroic and none of this is over. But for right now — for this breath, this heartbeat, this one still moment in a library full of dust — Clara is safe and she trusts Danny and Danny's bad feelings were never wrong. Right. Let's find the others. Together. Like a team. Like a family.

events.desc: This is the moment. The moment the whole night was building toward. Not the Diamond. Not the hidden study. Not the machine or the chandelier or the locked cabinet. THIS. Clara Bellingham standing next to Danny Brixton in a dusty library, choosing to trust the man who trips over things instead of the man who never puts a foot wrong. Her father would be proud. The lads would be proud. And Danny — Danny's proud too. For the first time in a long time, Danny's proud of Danny. Now let's go find the others before Marsh finds them first.

events.desc: James Hartwell: CLARA! If you can hear me — James Hartwell is looking for you! Do NOT drink any tea! I repeat — do NOT touch the tea service in the ballroom!
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Empty again. The chandelier still swaying imperceptibly. The portraits still watching. Foxworth was supposed to be right behind me — 'I'm coming with you' — but I'm alone. Again. The pattern doesn't even surprise me anymore. It's just the shape of this evening.

But I'm not going to spiral about it. Not this time. I have two exits: kitchen (behind me) and library (ahead). The library connects to the laboratory. The laboratory connects to the cellar. That's the full circuit of the manor as I know it.

Clara. Think about where she COULD be. I've been to every room. She's been in rooms with me — the entrance hall at the start, the library, the laboratory, the cellar, the kitchen (with Marsh). She keeps moving. Everyone keeps moving.

But Foxworth's observation was critical: she never passed through the kitchen to reach the ballroom. And the ballroom only connects to the kitchen. So either she was already in the ballroom before Foxworth started watching, or she was never there.

The sweeping staircase. I keep seeing it mentioned — 'a grand but dusty foyer with a sweeping staircase.' A staircase. Going UP. Is there an upstairs? Are there rooms above that I can't access? Has Marsh taken Clara UPSTAIRS?

No — the exits only show kitchen and library. The staircase is scenery, not a navigable path. Unless...

The library. Clara was interested in the mantelpiece. Foxworth heard clicking inside it — a mechanical timer. Something is happening there. And the mantelpiece connects to the fake medal, which connects to... everything.

Clara is smart. Clara is brighter than me. If she's working the puzzle, she's ahead of me, not behind me. She might have found the fake medal. She might have used it on the mantelpiece. She might have opened something I haven't seen yet.

The library. That's where the puzzle converges. The clicking mantelpiece. The inscription. The fake medal. If anything has changed in this manor — if a secret passage has opened, if the mantelpiece has revealed something — it'll be there.

Stop searching for Clara in rooms she's left. Start searching for Clara where the puzzle leads.

events.desc: He's shouting into an empty foyer. His voice echoes off the portraits and the chandelier sways. It's not heroic. It's not gallant. It's a man who has run out of rooms and is calling her name into the dust because he doesn't know what else to do. And that — that raw, unperformed desperation — is the most honest thing James Hartwell has done all evening.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Clara? CLARA! It's Colonel Fox— it's Foxworth! Are you in here? Hartwell sent me — he's looking for you! Danny says stay away from the entrance hall! Clara, if you can hear me, ANSWER!
events.thinking:
The ballroom. Grand. Cracked marble. Dusty curtains. And there it is — the tea service. Silver. Cups for everyone. Sitting on the long dining table like an invitation.

My eyes go to it immediately and my stomach turns. Danny's words echo — 'someone warmed the stove, set the table, put poison on the shelf, and WAITED for us to arrive.' This room was PREPARED. The tea service, the cups, the whole tableau — it's a stage set. Someone expected us to walk in here, tired and thirsty from searching the manor, and sit down and drink.

The cracked marble under my feet feels wrong. Each step is uncertain — the floor shifts slightly, like the tiles aren't seated properly. The ballroom is cold, colder than the kitchen. The stove warmth is gone. The curtains hang heavy with dust. The ceiling is high and dark.

I'm alone. Hartwell didn't follow me. Or he's coming through a different route. Or he went to the entrance hall instead. But I'm HERE, in the ballroom, and Clara is NOT.

No Clara. The room is empty. Just me and a poisoned tea service and cracked marble and silence.

I should look around. Check behind the curtains. Under the table. In the corners. She might be here — hiding, trapped, hurt. Or she might have never come here at all.

But the tea service. Danny said someone can USE rat poison on it. The poison is in Danny's pocket. The tea is sitting here, waiting, untampered — for now. As long as Danny has the poison, nobody can poison the tea. But what if Marsh has his own poison? What if the tea is ALREADY poisoned?

Examine the tea service. See if it's already been tampered with. And look around the room for any sign of Clara. Any sign of anyone.

events.desc: Empty. The ballroom is empty. No Clara, no Marsh, no treasure — just a silver tea service sitting on a long table like a spider sitting in its web. Danny was right — someone set this up. Someone wanted us all to come in here and drink. And the fact that Clara isn't here when Marsh TOLD her to come here... that's either very good news or very bad news. Either she's smarter than Marsh gave her credit for, or... or something I don't want to think about. Colonel Foxworth — REGINALD Foxworth — is going to search this room. Not for treasure. For Clara. Because a man who says 'shoulder to shoulder' doesn't leave his partner's girl lost in a house full of tricks.
