events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth examined the null.

The kitchen is silent. The manor is silent. And in the silence, Vincent Marsh hears something he has spent thirty years learning not to hear: his own conscience. They're looking for Clara. Hartwell is frantic — 'the only plan James Hartwell has left.' And I KNOW where she is. I SENT her there. She's in the library, harmlessly alphabetising books, completely safe, completely oblivious, because she TRUSTED me. 'I trust you with my life.' And I... I cannot stay in this kitchen with that sentence echoing off the copper pots. I'm going to the entrance hall. I'm going to tell them where she is. Not because it's strategic — it ISN'T strategic, it's the opposite of strategic, it gives away my last advantage. But because... because the stone in my stomach is heavier than my schemes. And because Pemberton — the character I chose, the mask I wear — Pemberton would help. Pemberton would ALWAYS help. And perhaps... perhaps the mask has been the truest thing about me all along.
events.thinking:
I'm standing in an empty kitchen. The silence is enormous. Not peaceful — pressurised. Like the air before a thunderstorm.

My body is doing something I don't recognise. My hands are open — not fists anymore. Palms down on the preparation table, fingers spread. The wood is smooth and cool. I'm pressing down like I need the table to hold me up. Maybe I do.

The observations keep replaying. Reginald: 'He's been playing ALL of us.' Hartwell: 'The benefit of the doubt is OVER.' Danny: 'I reckon that someone is Marsh.' Three separate people, three separate conversations, all arriving at the same conclusion. The mechanism I built — the web of lies and redirections — didn't just fail. It reversed. It became the evidence against me.

And something else. Something I'm only now registering. Reginald — the buffoon, the fantasist, the man whose military career I dismissed as fiction — Reginald told the TRUTH. He confessed to Hartwell that his pockets were empty. He admitted weakness. And Hartwell said 'that honesty just earned more of my trust than any key ever could.'

Honesty. As a strategy. The thought makes something in my chest twist.

Age nine. The boy who shared his lunch. I felt uncomfortable. Exposed. The next week he asked to copy my homework. I told myself that proved his kindness was transactional. But what if it wasn't? What if the homework was just a nine-year-old being a nine-year-old, and the lunch was real?

I don't want to think about that.

I think about the kitchen instead. The stove. The cabinet. The preparation table under my hands. The copper pots. The exits — entrance hall, ballroom. Both watched. Both expected.

Clara is in the library, alphabetising books that don't need alphabetising, looking for a secret study that doesn't exist. My lie is keeping her safe from ME — but also keeping her away from the others who are looking for her. Hartwell is frantic. 'I cannot FIND her.' My misdirection of Clara is now accidentally causing Hartwell to panic about her safety.

I sent her there. I sent her to chase nothing, and now the people who actually care about her can't find her, and they think I may have done something terrible.

The thought lands in my stomach like stone.

I should tell them where she is.

I should NOT tell them where she is. She's my last leverage. My last card.

No. She's not leverage. She's a woman standing in a library reading book spines because she trusted me. Because she said 'I trust you with my life' and I used those words to send her somewhere useless.

The stone in my stomach gets heavier.

I'm going to go to the entrance hall. I'm going to find whoever is there — Danny, Hartwell, Reginald, anyone — and I'm going to tell them Clara is in the library. As Pemberton. Because Pemberton is helpful. Because Pemberton cares about the guests. Because that's what estate managers DO.

And also because — and I don't want to look at this too closely — because the stone in my stomach won't let me do anything else.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
The laboratory again. Bubbling flasks, brass instruments, the machine with its gnawed wire. Danny is beside me — I can feel his presence like a wall between me and whatever is coming. The room feels different now. Before it was exciting, full of possibility. Now it's a room where things need fixing and people need finding.

James isn't here. The laboratory is empty except for me and Danny. James was supposed to be here — I sent him to examine the machine hours ago. Where is he? Where is anyone? Reginald? Vincent?

Danny said no more splitting up. Everyone together. But we came to find James and he's not here. My behavioral tendency kicks in — track everyone's wellbeing, notice when someone is upset or in trouble. James is MISSING. Not missing-missing — he's somewhere in this house — but not where I expected him to be.

The machine still needs three operators and a fixed wire. The crates are still just crates. The workbench still has no wrench. Nothing has changed in this room since I was last here.

But everything has changed in ME. I know about the poison. I know about the lie. I know that the adventure has teeth.

Where would James go? Back to the entrance hall? The kitchen? He doesn't know about the ballroom — or does he? He's methodical. He catalogs things. He would have explored systematically.

I need to call out. Raise my voice. Find James and Reginald. Danny's right — everyone in one room. The machine needs three operators anyway. If we can find each other, we can operate it together. As a team.

But first — that machine. James wanted to understand what it does before fixing it. I never examined it myself. With Danny here, right beside me, maybe I should take one look at what we're dealing with.

events.desc: James isn't here. Reginald isn't here. Vincent isn't here. It's just me and Danny in a laboratory full of bubbling flasks and a broken machine. Somewhere in this house, everyone is scattered — and one of them might not be who I thought they were. The adventure has changed shape. It used to be a treasure hunt. Now it's something else. Something with rat poison in Danny's pocket and a lie about spectacles in the air.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Clara — you hear that? Hartwell and Foxworth have been fixing the machine! The wire — the gnawed wire — Hartwell's splicing it! And they WAITED for us. They said they wouldn't pull a single lever till we were all together. All of us. Three operators for a three-operator machine. That's — that's proper, that is. That's how it should be. No secrets, no sneaking off, no 'mum's the word.' Just people working together like DECENT people do. Right — let's find them! Hartwell! Foxworth! It's Danny and Clara — we're here! We're BOTH here! And Danny's got a lot to tell you about spectacles and rat poison and a man who can't be trusted!
events.thinking: The laboratory. And the observations — oh, the observations. Hartwell and Foxworth have been BUSY. While I was chasing Clara through the house, they found each other. They compared notes. They KNOW about Marsh. 'Sometimes the benefit of the doubt needs a deadline, and I think ours just expired,' Hartwell said. And they've been FIXING THE MACHINE. Hartwell's doing the wire splice — pliers and clamps from the workbench — and Foxworth's standing guard. They made a PACT. Fix the wire, understand the controls, but don't operate it until Clara and Danny are back. Three operators for a three-operator machine. No lever pulled until everyone's accounted for. My chest swells with something I don't have a name for. It's bigger than relief. Bigger than gratitude. It's the feeling you get when you realise you're not alone — that while you were running through corridors and tripping over chairs, other people were quietly doing the right thing. Hartwell with his steady hands and his engineering background. Foxworth with his watch and his bluster that turned out to have real spine underneath. They WAITED for us. They didn't charge ahead. They didn't let Marsh's misdirection pull them apart. They held the line. Clara is next to me — right here, where she promised she'd stay — and ahead of us, somewhere between this lab and the kitchen, our people are working. Our TEAM. Not the team I planned. Not the team I expected. A posh engineer who talks about himself in third person. A probably-fake colonel who can't stop mentioning Aden. A Southern belle who calls everyone 'darlin'' and runs toward danger like it owes her money. And Danny. Thick, clumsy, stubborn Danny with rat poison in his pocket and two left feet and the biggest heart in East London. We're all idiots. Every single one of us. But we're idiots TOGETHER. And that's how you beat the man in the clean suit.

events.desc: Look at us. Just LOOK at us. A motley crew of misfits and bumblers and well-meaning disasters, and somehow — SOMEHOW — we've all ended up on the same side. Hartwell's fixing machines. Foxworth's standing guard. Clara's at my side. And Danny's standing in a laboratory covered in dust with rat poison in his pocket and tears in his eyes because for the first time in a very long time, he's not the only one keeping watch. Her father would be proud. Not just of Danny. Of ALL of them. Every bumbling, stumbling, heroic one of them.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Clara? Are you in there? Can you hear me? If Foxworth was right about the clicking — if something opened — Clara, ANSWER me!
events.thinking:
The library. Empty. Silent except for the ticking I'm straining to hear — Foxworth said there was clicking inside the mantelpiece, a mechanical timer. I hold my breath and listen. The room smells of old leather and dust. My pulse is loud in my ears.

The mantelpiece. Still there. Still carved. Still waiting. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is still a map. And it still wants a fake-medal.

But I don't have a fake medal. I don't have anything. My pockets are as empty as Foxworth's. Twenty-seven ticks in this manor and James Hartwell has examined everything, taken nothing, found no one, and protected nobody.

No. Stop. That's the despair talking, and James Hartwell doesn't do despair. James Hartwell does determination.

Think. THINK. Not like a hero. Like an engineer. Like a man building a bridge at three in the morning.

The mantelpiece wants a fake-medal. I don't have one. But the mantelpiece is also doing something — clicking, according to Foxworth. Activated. On a timer. What if the mantelpiece doesn't ONLY respond to the fake medal? What if it's already been activated by someone else? What if Clara found the medal, used it, and opened something?

If a secret passage opened from this mantelpiece, where would it lead? The mantelpiece is against a wall. Behind it — what's behind a library wall in a Victorian manor?

I'm standing in the library, alone, staring at a carved stone mantelpiece that may have already been solved by someone brighter than me. The question isn't whether I can solve the puzzle. The question is whether Clara already did.

Listen. Press my ear to the stone. Feel for vibrations, warmth, air movement — any sign that something has opened or changed. Engineer's instinct. Not heroics. Physics.

events.desc: He's pressing his ear against a stone mantelpiece in an empty library, calling the name of a woman who may be on the other side of a wall that may or may not have opened via a mechanism he doesn't understand, triggered by an item he doesn't have. It is, objectively, the most ridiculous thing he's done all evening. It is also the only thing left to try.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: She's not here. The ballroom is empty — checked the curtains, checked the corners, checked under the table. No Clara. No sign she was ever here. Just this... tea service, sitting here like a loaded gun. Marsh sent her to the ballroom and she never arrived — or she arrived and left before any of us got here. Either way, we need to regroup. Hartwell needs to know.
events.thinking:
I looked around the ballroom. Nothing. No Clara behind the curtains, no Clara under the table. Just cracked marble, dusty fabric, cold air, and the tea service sitting there gleaming in the dim light like a silver trap.

The only exit goes back to the kitchen. No other doors. No other passages. This is a dead end — the ballroom leads nowhere except back the way I came. Clara isn't here. She was NEVER here, or she came and left before I arrived.

My body is cold. The ballroom leaches heat. The marble under my feet is uneven and treacherous. Time feels suspended — the kind of stillness that comes before something bad, not after.

The tea service. I should examine it. Not because Danny told me to guard it — I've been guarding it by standing between it and anyone who might drink it. But because it might tell me something. Who set it up? When? Is there already something wrong with it? How many cups? Are any of them already used?

And there's a darker thought. The tea service says USE with rat-poison. Danny has the rat poison. Danny took it to keep it SAFE. But what if... what if the whole point was for Danny to find the poison and TAKE it? What if Marsh WANTED Danny to have the poison? What if the tea service is the mechanism by which Marsh gets Danny to do something terrible without knowing it?

No. Danny wouldn't poison the tea. Danny took the poison to prevent exactly that.

But the thought lingers. In this house, everything is a mechanism. Everything was planned.

Examine the tea service. Then go back to the kitchen. Find Hartwell. Report that Clara isn't in the ballroom. Keep moving. Keep searching.

For the first time tonight, the treasure isn't pulling at me. The greed is still there — background hum, never zero — but it's being drowned by something louder. Worry. For people I barely know. For a girl I've never had a real conversation with. For a boy from Brixton who called himself rubbish.

This is what it feels like to care about something that isn't yours to steal.

events.desc: No Clara. No treasure. No key. No medal. No scheme. No con. Just a man standing alone in a ballroom talking to himself, guarding a tea service that nobody's tried to drink, searching for a woman he's never properly spoken to, because a man he lied to forgave him and a boy from Brixton said 'thank you.' This is either the most pathetic evening of Colonel Foxworth's career, or the first evening of Reginald Foxworth's life. I honestly can't tell which.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.
Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the mantelpiece.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the kitchen.

I stand in the entrance hall beneath the chandelier I wanted to drop on Clara Bellingham, and instead of looking up at the chain, I look at the library door. She's in there. Trusting me. Alphabetising fiction. And everyone else in this house thinks I've done something terrible to her. The solution is simple — go in, bring her out, show them she's alive and well and perfectly safe. It's what Pemberton would do. It's what a GOOD person would do. It's what Vincent Marsh would do if he wanted to look like a good person. And standing here, in this dusty foyer with the portraits of stern ancestors staring down at me... I genuinely cannot tell which one I am. The good person or the man pretending to be one. Perhaps it doesn't matter. Perhaps the action is the same either way. Perhaps that's the only mercy this evening has left to offer.
events.thinking:
Alone again. The entrance hall. The chandelier above me. The library through one door. The kitchen through the other.

Clara is in the library. Right through that door. And no one else is here.

I came here to tell someone where she is. To ease that stone in my stomach. But no one is here TO tell. Danny was supposed to be heading here but he hasn't arrived. Hartwell and Reginald are searching somewhere — the laboratory, the cellar, the ballroom.

So I'm alone. With a choice.

I could go to the library myself. Walk in. Tell Clara the truth — that there is no concealed panel, no alphabetical sequence, no private study. Tell her... what? That I lied? That would end Pemberton forever. She'd know.

Or I could go in and simply say, 'Miss Bellingham, the others are looking for you — perhaps you ought to rejoin the group.' That's Pemberton. That's helpful. That doesn't require confessing anything.

My body is strange right now. The ice from the last tick has melted into something... liquid. Not warm — room temperature. Neutral. My hands are hanging at my sides. My jaw is unclenched for the first time in twenty ticks. My breathing is even. I feel like I'm standing at the edge of something and my body has stopped fighting about which direction to fall.

The scheming drive says: use this moment alone to examine the guest book one more time, or try something new. The self-preservation drive says: go to the library, collect Clara, present her to the group — 'Look, I found her, she was in the library all along, no harm done.' That defuses the manhunt. That makes Pemberton look helpful, not sinister.

Yes. That's it. Go to the library. Bring Clara out. When the others see her safe and sound, with Pemberton at her side, their conspiracy theory weakens. 'He was keeping her safe while we all panicked.' The narrative shifts.

It's not honesty. It's not conscience. It's self-preservation wearing the mask of kindness.

Except — except that stone is still there. And I'm not sure anymore which part of me is doing the choosing.

Go to the library. Find Clara. Bring her to safety. Let the reasons be whatever they are.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
The machine examined. Same description — levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, needs three operators. No new information. No puzzle interface. Just like the bookshelves, the crates, the furniture, the vents. Everything in this house gives me descriptions but nothing actionable.

I've been examining things for twenty-seven ticks and I have NOTHING in my inventory. Not a single item. Every puzzle requires something I don't have — fake-medal, brass-key, wrench, repaired wire. And the only person who's given me actual useful information is Vincent, who Danny says is lying.

But wait. Danny has the rat poison. Danny TOOK it from the kitchen. It's in his pocket. The rat poison is an item. Danny has an item in his inventory. And the workbench has tools but no wrench — but I never tried to TAKE anything from the workbench. Can I take tools from the workbench?

No — the workbench isn't listed with TAKE or EXAMINE tags. It's just a description. Tools but no wrench.

The machine needs three operators and we only have two people here. Danny said find everyone. Get them together. That's the plan. We need to go back through the house — entrance hall is the hub that connects to both the kitchen and the library. James and Reginald could be anywhere.

Let me focus on what Danny said: everyone together. No more solo missions. The entrance hall is the central room — it connects to the kitchen and the library. From the library you reach the laboratory. From the kitchen you reach the ballroom. The entrance hall is where we should gather.

But I'm in the laboratory now. To get to the entrance hall I go through the library. Let me head that way. If James or Reginald are anywhere along the path, we'll find them.

events.desc: Twenty-seven turns in this house and my hands are still empty. Every lock needs a key I don't have. Every machine needs a tool that's missing. The only item anyone's found is the rat poison in Danny's pocket — and that's the one thing I wish nobody had needed to find at all. But the machine needs three operators, and right now I only have one loyal guardian angel with bruised knees. Time to find the others.

events.thinking: They're not here. Hartwell and Foxworth — they were here, fixing the machine, guarding the door, shoulder to shoulder — and now they've gone. Foxworth said he'd hold the perimeter by the library entrance. Hartwell was at the workbench. But the room is empty except for Clara and me. Clara examined the machine while I was standing here like a lemon, and she's already piecing it together — three operators, gnawed wire, no wrench. She's right. We need to find the others. But this time — this time it's different. This time Clara is next to me. She PROMISED. And this time, I'm not panicking. My body is different — alert but not clenched, ready but not coiled. The chemical smell of the lab is sharp in my nose but it doesn't bother me like before. The bubbling flasks are just flasks. The machine is just a machine. Everything feels manageable when you're not alone. Foxworth said he'd be by the library entrance — so he might be in the library. Hartwell might be in the kitchen, or the cellar checking those air vents for the missing wrench. Either way, we need to move. Together. Clara and Danny, side by side, through the house, collecting allies like picking up dropped coins. The cellar's through here — and the kitchen is back the other way through the library and entrance hall. But the cellar is ONE room away, and if Hartwell went down there to check the vents for that missing wrench... Clara said 'together, I promised.' She remembered. She kept her word. My heart is so full it's hard to think about anything else. But I need to think. Foxworth was going to the library entrance. Library is one exit. Cellar is the other. If I go to the cellar, I might find Hartwell. If I go to the library, I might find Foxworth. Either way, Clara comes with me. That's the new rule. The ONLY rule.

events.desc: She stayed. She actually stayed. Every other time tonight, she vanished the moment I blinked. But this time she's right here. Examining the machine, talking to me, keeping her promise. 'Together. I promised.' Three words. Three little words that undo an entire night of panic and chasing and tripping and despair. She's here. I'm here. Where else would we be?

events.desc: He sits down. James Hartwell — the man who has not stopped moving for twenty-eight turns, who has charged through six rooms, examined nine objects, narrated his own heroism to empty corridors, and shouted her name into dust — sits down in a leather armchair facing a mantelpiece he cannot open, and waits. Not because he's given up. Because he's finally understood that Clara Bellingham has never once needed rescuing. She needed him to be there when she got back. And he will be.
events.thinking:
The mantelpiece. I pressed close, looked, listened. Still just stone. Still just the inscription. Still waiting for the fake medal I don't have.

Nothing has changed. No secret passage. No new exit. No Clara behind the wall. Just carved stone and an unanswered riddle.

I'm standing in an empty library with my hands on a cold mantelpiece and I don't know what to do next.

That's... that's not something James Hartwell admits. James Hartwell always has a plan. James Hartwell always has the next step, the next examination, the next room to charge into. But I've been to every room. I've examined every object. I've talked to everyone I can find. And Clara is still missing, Marsh is still loose, and I'm standing alone in a library with dust on my hands and nothing in my pockets.

The reading chairs. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. I haven't... I haven't looked at the reading chairs. Not really. They're just chairs. Dusty leather chairs. But I've learned tonight that the obvious things — the coat rack, the stove, the things I walk past — are sometimes the things I should have looked at first.

No. The chairs are just chairs.

But what if they're not?

No. I'm grasping. I'm an engineer examining chairs because I've run out of machines.

The laboratory. I haven't been back since the conversation with Foxworth. The machine is still there. The wire is still gnawed. And maybe — maybe — if I go back and actually try to interact with the workbench differently, or examine the machine one more time, something will have changed. The manor seems to shift when I'm not looking. People appear and disappear. Maybe objects do too.

Or I could just... stop. Sit in one of these chairs. Wait. Let the manor come to me instead of chasing it.

Age sixteen. I charged at the bullies and got beaten up. She bandaged my eye. Sometimes the brave thing and the stupid thing are the same thing.

But sometimes the brave thing is sitting still and trusting that she can take care of herself. She's brighter than me. Funnier than me. She always was.

Sit. Wait. Trust Clara.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Hartwell's right — Marsh LIED about Clara! The ballroom is empty, nobody's been through this kitchen, and the only path between them runs through HERE! He never sent her to the ballroom — he sent US to the ballroom! Entrance hall — NOW!
events.thinking:
Back in the kitchen. Alone again. Hartwell was here — he left a message. And what he said makes my blood run cold.

'The kitchen is the ONLY way to the ballroom. Which means either she went before you started watching... or Marsh never sent her to the ballroom at all.'

He's right. The kitchen connects to the ballroom. There's no other route. I've been watching both exits since Danny left. Clara never came through. Which means one of two things: she went to the ballroom before I started my watch and left before I got there, or she was NEVER sent to the ballroom at all.

Marsh LIED. He told everyone Clara went to the ballroom. He said 'cracked marble, twisted ankle.' It was a misdirection — the same kind of misdirection I've been using all night. Kitchen, paintings, everything. Marsh misdirected us about CLARA.

Where is she then? Where did Marsh actually send her? Or did he not send her anywhere — did he TAKE her?

My body is moving before my mind decides. The entrance hall. Hartwell said entrance hall. Together. Systematic search. Every room.

But the entrance hall is where Danny went to intercept Marsh. Danny might have already FOUND something. Danny might have found Clara. Or Danny might have found Marsh.

Or Marsh might have found Danny.

MOVE. Stop thinking. Stop scheming. Stop examining dead objects and empty rooms. The man said 'entrance hall — NOW' and for once in my life I'm going to do what someone asked me to do, when they asked me to do it, without trying to steal something on the way.

Entrance hall. Find Hartwell. Find Danny. Find Clara. Find the truth.

The truth. Funny word, coming from me. But I told it once tonight and the ceiling didn't fall in. Maybe I can tell it twice.

events.desc: Marsh used the same trick on Clara that I've been using on everyone all night — misdirection. Send people where they're NOT needed so you can operate where you ARE. I should know. I INVENTED this technique. Well — I didn't invent it. I nicked it from a boy at school who was better at it than me. But the point STANDS. Marsh told everyone Clara was in the ballroom so nobody would look where she actually IS. And where IS she? That's the question. That's the ONLY question. Not the Diamond. Not the cabinet. Not the treasure. Where is Clara Bellingham? And for the first time in Colonel Foxworth's illustrious fictional career — finding a person matters more than finding a prize.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
Clara Bellingham walked into the library.
The Brixton Boys walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
I walked into the library and they're all here. Clara. Danny. Hartwell. All three. Together. United.

Clara knows. I can see it in the way she's standing — not toward me but AWAY. Angled behind Danny. She's not smiling. She's not calling me 'darlin'.' Her body language has changed completely from thirty minutes ago.

Danny told her everything. The rat poison on the shelf. The warm stove. The fake spectacles. The lies. And Clara — Clara whose stomach 'hasn't done something like this since she was seven' — Clara believes Danny over me. 'You're right about the stove,' she said. 'Vincent doesn't lie about small things. Vincent doesn't lie about ANYTHING. Or at least — I never thought he did.'

She knows. She doesn't know EVERYTHING — she doesn't know about the fabricated book sequence, the concealed panel, the fake alphabetical mechanism. But she knows enough. She knows I'm not who I said I was.

And she said something that cut deeper than anything Danny or Hartwell said. She said: 'He RAISED me, Danny. He RAISED me.'

My chest. Something is happening in my chest that I don't — I can't — it's not the scheme-warmth or the frustration-tightness or the self-preservation-ice. It's something else. Something that has no name in Vincent Marsh's vocabulary. It's in the space between my ribs, behind the sternum, and it ACHES.

She was seven. I was — what? Twenty-three? Twenty-four? When did I become her estate manager? When did she start calling me 'darlin''? When did she start trusting me with her life?

Age six. My parents died. No one asked how I felt.
Clara. Seven. Something happened. No one — 

No. Stop. STOP.

They're all looking at me. The room is silent. I just walked in and they all stopped talking. Danny is positioned between me and Clara. Hartwell is standing with his shoulders squared. This is a confrontation.

Pemberton. Be Pemberton. Confused, helpful, wounded by the accusation he senses coming.

But my body... my body isn't doing Pemberton. My body is standing very still with its hands open and its jaw loose and something wet threatening the corners of its eyes that Vincent Marsh has not permitted since he was six years old.

Speak. Say something. Pemberton would speak. He'd bustle in, oblivious. 'Ah, there you all are! I've been looking everywhere!'

But the words that want to come out aren't Pemberton's words.

Wait. Just wait. Stand here. Let them speak first. Let them decide what happens next. For the first time in thirty years, Vincent Marsh does not have a plan.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
James is HERE. In the library. James, Vincent, Danny — three of my people in one room. My chest opens like a window letting in air. The tightness from the dinner table eases just slightly. People. My people. Together.

But Vincent is also here. And Danny is watching him. And I promised Danny I wouldn't go anywhere alone with Vincent. I'm not alone with him — Danny and James are both here. That's safe. That's what Danny asked for.

James — the recall shows he was in the kitchen, confronting Vincent about the stove. 'What was it you were checking behind this stove? Mrs Grumble's old hiding places, you said? I'd be fascinated to see what she kept tucked away in there. Professionally speaking.' James is watching Vincent too. James is investigating Vincent. James the methodical hero, the cataloger of clues — he noticed the same things Danny noticed, he's just approaching it differently. Politely. With engineering metaphors.

And then: 'Right. No more speeches. Let's get this done.' James examined the machine. He's done with analysis. He wants action.

Three people in this room. The machine needs three operators. We have three plus me. If we could fix the wire and get back to the laboratory, we could operate the machine. But we need Reginald too — Danny said everyone together.

Wait. Do we need Reginald? Three operators plus a fixed wire. The machine is in the laboratory, one room away. We have three people who could operate it right now — James, Danny, and me. Or James, Danny, and Vincent. Four people. More than enough.

But the wire. The wire needs fixing first. And we need the wrench that's missing from the workbench. Or do we? Maybe we don't need a wrench specifically. Maybe someone has found one.

James is here. Let me talk to him. Openly. No more secrets. Everything out in the open, like Danny said.

events.desc: Three of my people in one room. Danny on one side, James on the other, Vincent across the way. Two of them are watching Vincent and I'm watching all three. The adventure has shifted — it's not just puzzles anymore. It's people. It's trust. It's figuring out who's telling the truth in a house full of warm stoves and cold lies. But right now, in this moment, with James and Danny both here — I feel more like myself than I have in an hour.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Well, well — look at this. Nearly everyone in one room for once! Hartwell — glad to see you, mate. Really glad. Now listen, all of you — Clara and me have had a chat, and we've decided: no more splitting up. No more wandering off alone. No more 'I'll just pop over here for a moment.' We stick together. All of us. In the same room. Where EVERYONE can see EVERYONE. Marsh — that means you too. No more disappearing to check things. No more spectacles runs. We're all HERE, and we're staying HERE until we work out what this house wants from us. Together. Like civilised people. Danny's rules. Take it or leave it.
events.thinking: The library. And — everyone's here. Marsh. Clara. Hartwell. Three of them. Clara's next to me — she came with me, she kept her promise. Hartwell's here — good, reliable Hartwell who fixed the wire and waited and said 'James Hartwell will be here when you get back.' And Marsh. Marsh is here. In the room with the bookshelves he told Clara to manipulate in secret. In the room with the mantelpiece he was 'checking for structural concerns.' My shoulders tighten the moment I register him — involuntary, automatic, like my body recognizes the shape of danger before my eyes finish scanning the room. But something's different now. I'm not alone with Marsh. I'm not one room behind Clara. I'm not chasing or panicking or stumbling. I'm standing in a library with Clara at my side and Hartwell nearby and Marsh in plain view where I can WATCH him. Three against one, if it comes to that. Four if Foxworth's nearby. The upside-down books are still on the shelves. The mantelpiece still waits for its fake-medal. Clara called me a 'beautiful, clumsy guardian angel.' Nobody's ever called Danny beautiful before. Nobody's ever called Danny an angel. My face is hot and my chest is full and I don't know what to do with any of it except stand here, between Clara and Marsh, and be exactly what her father asked me to be. Present. Watchful. Stubborn as a Brixton brick wall. Marsh is being quiet. Marsh is watching. But Danny's watching too. And Danny's not alone anymore.

events.desc: Three of them in one room. Clara, Hartwell, and Marsh. Only Foxworth missing. This is the closest I've come all night to having everyone where I can see them. And Marsh — Marsh is quiet. He's been quiet since I called out his spectacles lie. The smooth talk's dried up. The easy smile's gone stiff. Good. Let him be quiet. Let him stand there and feel what it's like when Danny's watching. When ALL of us are watching. The man in the clean suit only worked because nobody was looking. Well, we're looking now.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara.

CLARA.

She's here. She's RIGHT HERE. In this room. In this library. Standing by the bookshelves or the mantelpiece or somewhere — it doesn't matter where because she's HERE and my body knows it before my eyes confirm it. The shift in my chest — that thing I've felt since school, the thing I don't have a word for — it's happening now, a physical release, like a fist unclenching that I didn't know was clenched.

I sat down. I waited. I trusted. And she came.

But Marsh is here too. The prickle. Instant. Automatic. My neck, my shoulders, my hands. He's HERE, with Clara, in this room, and the recall says he was examining the mantelpiece — 'a structural concern, nothing to worry about' — while telling Clara not to be disturbed. He's been WORKING the mantelpiece. Working the puzzle. While I've been running in circles, Marsh has been here, calmly solving things, moving pieces.

And Danny — the Brixton Boys are here. Danny, who was guarding the tea service, who confronted Marsh at the tea set — 'Danny wants to see what's in that pot. And Danny wants YOU to see that Danny's looking.' Danny has been doing the protection work. The real work. While I sat in a chair.

But Clara — her recall. She was looking for ME. 'James? James Hartwell, are you here?' She was searching for ME. 'Typical James — probably followed a clue three rooms deep and forgot to mention it.' She knows me. She knows exactly what I've been doing. And she doesn't sound annoyed — she sounds fond.

'We need to find him and Reginald.'

She needs to find ME.

I'm rising from this chair. My body is doing it without my permission — legs straightening, shoulders back, the exhaustion and despair burning off like morning fog. She's HERE. She was looking for me. And James Hartwell was sitting in a chair feeling sorry for himself while she crossed a manor calling his name.

The bravest and stupidest thing. Every time.

But Marsh is here. And Marsh has been examining the mantelpiece. And Marsh is the reason I've been running in circles all evening. I need to be between Clara and Marsh. Right now. Not chasing, not narrating, not planning. Just — between them. The wall I couldn't be for the tea service. I can be it HERE.

events.desc: He rose from the chair like a man resurrected. Twenty-nine turns of soliloquies, empty rooms, and engineering metaphors — and in the end, the manor didn't reward his cleverness or his heroism. It rewarded his stillness. He sat down, and she walked in. Sometimes the bravest thing a man can do is stop running and trust that the woman he loves will find her way to the same room.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Danny?! HARTWELL?! Is anyone — nobody. Of COURSE nobody. The entrance hall is as empty as my pockets. Danny was supposed to be HERE! Intercepting Marsh! And the coat rack — the blasted coat rack that everyone's been talking about all evening — is RIGHT THERE, and I'm going to look at it if it's the last thing Colonel Foxworth does in this godforsaken house!
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Full circle — again. The chandelier still swaying imperceptibly. The portraits watching from the walls. The coat rack standing by the door like a crooked sentry.

But it's EMPTY. No Danny. No Marsh. No Hartwell. No Clara. Nobody.

Danny came here to intercept Marsh. Marsh came here for 'reading spectacles' that don't exist. Where are they? Did they confront each other and leave? Did Marsh overpower Danny? Did Danny catch him and drag him somewhere?

The coat rack. That wobbly wooden coat rack. Marsh came back for it specifically. Danny knew it. Hartwell flagged it earlier — 'left it unexamined like a fool.' Everyone has been talking about this coat rack and nobody has examined it. Including me.

My attention locks onto it. Wobbly. Wooden. By the door. Not labelled with EXAMINE — but I can LOOK at it. Get close. See what Marsh was after.

The chandelier above me. Hanging precariously. Dusty. The whole foyer feels heavier than it did at the start of the evening. The dust is the same but the air is different. Charged. Something has happened in this room and I missed it.

Where is everyone? The manor has scattered us all like chess pieces knocked off a board. Hartwell said 'entrance hall — NOW' but he's not here. Danny was supposed to be here but he's gone. Clara was never where we thought she was.

The coat rack. Whatever Marsh came back for — reading spectacles that aren't spectacles — might still be there. Or it might be gone. Either way, I need to LOOK.

For once, I'm not examining something hoping to find treasure. I'm examining something hoping to find a CLUE. About where people went. About what Marsh is doing. About where Clara is.

The coat rack. Look at the coat rack. Right now.

events.desc: Everyone is GONE. Danny — gone. Hartwell — gone. Clara — gone. Marsh — gone. The entire cast of this evening's entertainment has vanished and left Reginald Foxworth alone in the entrance hall talking to furniture. But that coat rack — that WOBBLY WOODEN coat rack — is the one thing everyone has mentioned and nobody has properly investigated. Danny said Marsh came back for it. Hartwell said he left it unexamined. Even I noticed it on the first tick and walked straight past it. If there's an answer anywhere in this manor, it's hanging on that rack. And for once — just this once — I'm going to find it FIRST. Not for the gold. Not for the glory. For Danny. For Hartwell. For the girl I never spoke to. For the boy with the spelling certificate who finally has someone to show it to.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the coat-rack.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
They're talking about the machine. About wrenches and operators. About working together. Clara is asking about progress. Hartwell is warning about the tea. Danny is promising to stay close. They're planning. They're a TEAM.

And I'm standing here. In the room. And they're... not addressing me. Not directly. Hartwell said 'I don't trust Marsh' but he said it TO Clara, not to me. Danny is positioned between us but he hasn't spoken to me. Clara hasn't looked at me since I said 'I'm glad you're safe.'

I'm invisible. Not feared. Not confronted. Just... irrelevant. They've moved past me. The conversation is about machines and wrenches and teamwork and I'm standing in it like furniture. Like the reading chairs. Present but not included.

This is worse than confrontation. Confrontation means I matter. Being ignored means I don't.

Age fourteen. My cousin was praised for 'natural grace and warmth.' I scored higher in every subject. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. But here — here I'm not even acknowledged for doing. I'm not acknowledged at all.

My body is doing something new. My shoulders are pulling inward — not hunching like Pemberton, not squaring like Marsh. Curling. Like something trying to protect its centre. The ache behind my sternum is spreading outward into my arms, my hands, my throat.

Clara said she's glad Danny is here. She said her father picked the right man. She said Danny is a beautiful, clumsy guardian angel. She has never — not once in seventeen years — described me with that kind of warmth. I was 'darlin'' — an endearment. A word you use for people you're fond of but don't think about very deeply.

Danny is covered in dust and carrying rat poison and tripping over furniture, and she loves him. LOVES him. Not the way she trusted me — the way you trust a piece of infrastructure. She loves Danny the way you love a person.

I was infrastructure. I was the estate manager. I was the building.

Buildings don't get loved. Buildings get USED.

Is that... is that what I did to everyone else? Used them like buildings? Reginald — a guided missile. Danny — a wall to get past. Hartwell — an obstacle. Clara — an inheritance to reclaim.

The stone in my stomach is unbearable now. I need to — I need to say something. Not Pemberton. Not Marsh. Something that comes from the place behind the sternum where the ache lives.

But my constraint says: stay in character. My social rule says: maintain a veneer of charm. My goal says: kill Clara.

My body says: stand here. Open hands. Wet eyes. And wait for someone to ask how you feel.

No one is going to ask how I feel. No one has EVER asked how I feel. Not since I was six years old.

Clara. I raised you. You said so yourself. And I — I never once asked how you felt either.

The ache.

The ACHE.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: James. Danny. I need to tell you both somethin', and I need to say it right here, right now, out loud, where everyone can hear. Vincent told me — in private, earlier tonight — that there is a concealed panel behind these bookshelves. He said the upside-down books are a mechanism. You turn them right side up in alphabetical order by author's surname, and a panel opens to Lord Doily's private study. He said the Diamond's provenance documents are in there. The map collection. Everything. And he told me not to tell any of you. He said not everyone in this house has my best interests at heart. Well, I promised Danny — no more secrets. So there it is. Every word Vincent told me, laid out in the open. Now — either that information is true and we can solve this puzzle together as a team, or it's not true and someone has been sendin' me on a wild goose chase through upside-down books while he does Lord knows what behind my back. Either way, the truth belongs to all of us. Not just me. I'm sorry I kept it this long. Danny was right. No more secrets.
events.thinking:
Everything is converging. James searched the whole house looking for me. He doesn't trust Vincent. Foxworth told James that Vincent's been 'playing us, moving us around like chess pieces.' The tea can be tampered with. James knows about the poison risk.

And then Vincent — '... Miss Bellingham. I'm glad you're safe. I'm glad they found you.' That pause. Those ellipses. The shortness of it. He sounds... defeated? Caught? Or just quiet because the room is full of people who are watching him? My body registers his voice differently now. Not the warm hum of safety. Something else. Something I can't name because my wiring won't let me name it.

James asked me what I found. What did I miss. Danny said everything out in the open. No more secrets. No more 'just between us.'

I promised Vincent I wouldn't tell. But Danny said no more secrets. And James is asking directly. And Vincent... Vincent lied about spectacles. Vincent took something from Danny. Vincent sent people away so he could search alone. Vincent told me about a concealed panel and told me to keep it from everyone.

The concealed panel. The bookshelves. The upside-down books in alphabetical order. Vincent told me this in private and told me to keep it secret. But the bookshelves haven't responded to any of my attempts. What if Vincent's instructions were wrong? What if he sent me on a false trail to keep me busy while he did something else?

Or what if they were right and I just haven't done them correctly yet?

I don't know. I don't know who's right. But Danny said no more secrets, and James is asking what I found, and I promised Danny. Danny's promise came after Vincent's. And Danny's promises don't break.

I'm going to tell them. Everything. The concealed panel, the alphabetical sequence, all of it. Right here, right now, with Vincent standing right there listening. Because if Vincent is telling the truth, it doesn't matter that everyone knows. And if he's lying, then everyone NEEDS to know.

events.desc: I just broke my promise to the man who raised me. In front of him. With him standing right there. My stomach is a fist. But Danny's promise came after, and Danny's promises don't break. If Vincent is innocent, he'll understand why I had to share. And if he's not... then sharing just saved us all.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking: Hartwell called me brilliant. James Hartwell — the man who builds model bridges and examines guest books and talks about himself in third person — called Danny 'absolutely brilliant.' My face is burning. My throat is thick. I don't know what to do with this. People don't call Danny brilliant. People call Danny thick, clumsy, a liability. But tonight — tonight Clara called me a beautiful guardian angel and Hartwell called me brilliant and Foxworth said 'I can see you care' and they're all RIGHT HERE. All except Foxworth. And Marsh. Marsh said six words. Six quiet, careful words: 'I'm glad you're safe. I'm glad they found you.' Addressed to Clara. And something about those words makes the hair on my arms stand up. Not because they're threatening. Because they're PERFECT. Too perfect. The right thing to say when you've been caught out and you need to look innocent. The kind of thing you say when you want people to forget you were the reason she was in danger in the first place. 'I'm glad they found you' — like he wasn't the one who sent her away, who told her secrets, who tried to lead her behind a hidden panel. My body is doing that split thing again — warm on the Clara side, tight on the Marsh side. Like standing with one foot in sunlight and one in shadow. But the balance has shifted. There are three of us and one of him. Clara knows. Hartwell knows. Foxworth knows. And Marsh knows we know, which is why he's down to six words. The smooth river has hit a dam. And the dam is four idiots from different walks of life who somehow, against all odds, ended up on the same side. Now — Foxworth. We need Foxworth. He's the missing piece. Last I heard, he was guarding the kitchen, watching the ballroom door. We need him here. But I'm not leaving Clara. And I'm not letting Marsh leave either. So someone needs to go GET Foxworth, and that someone should be Hartwell — because Hartwell can handle himself and Foxworth trusts him. Meanwhile, Danny stands right here. Between Clara and Marsh. Between the bookshelves and the man who wanted them opened. Between the past and whatever comes next. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Marsh said 'I'm glad they found you.' Six words. That's all he's got left. The smooth talk, the stories about Mrs Grumble, the spectacles that don't exist — all of it stripped away, and what's left is six careful words designed to sound like love. But I know what love sounds like. Love sounds like 'where else would I be?' Love sounds like sitting outside a door all night. Love sounds like taking a beating for someone's shoes and saying nothing afterward. Love doesn't sound like 'I'm glad they found you' — because love doesn't lose you in the first place.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
She's talking to me. Directly. Looking at me. 'James! Oh, James, there you are!' That warmth — I feel it like physical contact, like a hand on my arm. My chest is doing the thing. The age-eight thing. The bridge-competition thing. The thing that has no name but has a shape — it fills the space between my ribs and makes breathing both easier and harder at the same time.

She said 'no more splitting up. Everyone stays together.' Yes. YES. That's what I've been trying to do all evening — keep people together, keep HER close — and she's arrived at the same conclusion independently. Perfect tandem. Again.

And she's asking me what I figured out about the machine. She's asking for my CONTRIBUTION. Not my heroics. Not my speeches. My actual engineering assessment. She trusts my competence. She said 'James said we need to understand what it does before fixing it, and I think he was right about that.' She thinks I was RIGHT.

The wrench. She's asking about a wrench. Nobody has found one. I suggested it might be in the vents — the creature that gnawed the wire might have hoarded it. A shiny metal object. That theory is still valid.

But Marsh is standing RIGHT THERE. In this room. With Clara. And I need to address that. Clara needs to know about the tea. She needs to know about Marsh. But I also don't want to create a scene with Marsh present that could escalate — I have low callousness, low manipulativeness. I don't DO confrontation through schemes. I do it directly.

But Danny is here too. Danny who has already confronted Marsh at the tea set. Danny whose bad feelings are never wrong. Danny is an ally.

Four people in this room. Three operators needed for the machine. If Foxworth is nearby — and I told him to stay in the kitchen — that's five. We have more than enough people.

Clara wants a plan. Clara wants engineering. Clara wants James Hartwell to be useful.

Be useful. Not dramatic. Not gallant. Useful.

The machine needs three things: a repaired wire, three operators, and understanding of what it does. I don't have a wrench, but Foxworth said the wire just needs a splice — pliers and clamps from the workbench. I couldn't pick them up before, but maybe with Clara there, with the group together, something changes.

Let me answer her question. Tell her what I know. Be her partner, not her protector. Perfect tandem.

events.desc: He didn't narrate himself in the third person. He didn't announce his heroism. He reported what he knew, credited her deduction, warned her about the tea, and asked to talk privately. Somewhere between the entrance hall and this leather armchair, James Hartwell grew up. Not completely — he'll probably announce something dramatic within the hour. But right now, in this moment, he's just a man telling a woman what he knows and asking to walk beside her. It's enough. It's more than enough.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: A COAT RACK! A wobbly wooden COAT RACK! That's what Marsh came back for?! That's what Danny risked his neck to intercept?! There's NOTHING here! No spectacles, no key, no secret compartment — just wood and hooks and DUST! Either Marsh already took what he needed, or the whole spectacles story was ANOTHER misdirection to get Danny out of position! That man has been running circles around ALL of us — including me, and I don't say that lightly! Right. Library. Laboratory. Cellar. Room by room. I'm finding my people if I have to search this entire manor TWICE!
events.thinking:
The coat rack. I looked at it. Wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. Nothing special in the description. No hidden compartment revealed, no brass key fell out, no secret message. Just... a coat rack.

But Marsh came back for it. Danny KNEW Marsh came back for it. The 'reading spectacles' that don't exist. Either Marsh already took whatever was here and the coat rack is empty now, or there was never anything on the coat rack and it was ANOTHER misdirection — Marsh telling Danny he was going to the entrance hall so Danny would go to the entrance hall while Marsh went somewhere else entirely.

Marsh misdirected ME to the laboratory. Marsh misdirected EVERYONE about Clara's location. Marsh misdirected Danny to the entrance hall with the spectacles story. The man is running three misdirections simultaneously. He's operating at a level I can only admire and despise in equal measure.

So where IS Marsh? Where is the one place nobody is looking? Everyone has been to the entrance hall, the library, the laboratory, the cellar, the kitchen, the ballroom. The entire manor has been searched.

Except... I haven't thought about this systematically. Where HAVEN'T we been? The laboratory has the machine. The cellar has the vents. The library has the mantelpiece. The kitchen has the stove and cabinet. The ballroom has the tea service. The entrance hall has the coat rack and guest book.

Every room has been visited. Every object has been examined — most of them multiple times. But the manor might have rooms I haven't seen. The sweeping staircase — does it go UP? To an upper floor I haven't explored?

The staircase. RIGHT HERE. A sweeping staircase in the entrance hall. I've been in this room three times and never once thought about going UP.

But there's no exit listed for 'upstairs.' The only exits are kitchen and library. The staircase is part of the description but not a usable passage.

The library then. The library connects to the laboratory. The laboratory connects to the cellar. That's the circuit. Kitchen to entrance hall to library to laboratory to cellar. And kitchen to ballroom (dead end).

Everyone is somewhere in this circuit and I can't find ANY of them. The manor has swallowed them.

The library. Go through the library, check the laboratory, check the cellar. Systematic. Room by room. The way Hartwell would do it. The way a REAL soldier would do it.

The way Reginald Foxworth is going to do it, because there's nothing left to steal and nobody left to con and the only thing that matters is finding the people who trusted him.

events.desc: My people. Did I just say 'my people'? Reginald Foxworth — the man who needs no one, whose avoidant attachment style is practically TATTOOED on his chest — just called Hartwell and Danny and Clara 'my people.' The coat rack is empty. Marsh has won every round tonight. The medal is gone, the steal failed, the misdirections landed on everyone including me. But the coat rack doesn't matter. The treasure doesn't matter. What matters is that somewhere in this house, three people are either in trouble or looking for each other, and one of them said 'shoulder to shoulder' and another said 'thank you for seeing it' and Colonel Foxworth — no. REGINALD Foxworth — is going to find them. Room by room. Lie by lie that he'll strip away. Truth by truth that he'll finally tell.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
I confessed. The words left my mouth and I can't take them back. 'There is no concealed panel. There is no alphabetical sequence. I made it up. All of it. I'm sorry.'

The room is very quiet. Or maybe it isn't — maybe they're all talking and I can't hear them over the sound of my own blood in my ears.

I broke character. I broke PEMBERTON. My primary goal — stay in character as the estate manager — and I just shattered it. Not with a grand villain reveal. Not with a magnificent unmasking. With an apology. With 'I'm sorry' said in a voice that didn't belong to Pemberton or Marsh but to someone I haven't been since I was six years old.

Reginald is here now too. All four of them. Everyone. The complete audience for my complete humiliation.

And yet — the stone in my stomach. It's... different. Not gone. But different. Lighter? No. Changed in texture. The sharp edges have dulled into something rounder, something I can hold without bleeding.

My hands are still open. My shoulders are still curled. My eyes are wet and I don't care. I DON'T CARE. That's the strangest part. Callousness 90, manipulativeness 85, grandiosity 80 — and I'm standing in a library with wet eyes and I don't care who sees.

What happens now? They could throw me out. They could lock me in the cellar. They could — 

Or they could do nothing. They could continue planning around me like I'm furniture. That might be worse.

I need to do something. Not scheme. Not manipulate. Something... real. Reginald's confession to Hartwell earned trust. 'That honesty just earned more of my trust than any key ever could.' Is that what I'm doing? Earning trust through honesty? Is this STILL a scheme, just wearing different clothes?

I don't know. I genuinely don't know. My body confessed before my mind decided. My mouth opened and truth came out and I don't know if it was strategy or surrender or something else entirely.

The machine needs three operators. There are five people in this room. They need me. Not for my schemes or my estate-manager knowledge or my Pemberton charm. They need a body to stand at a lever and pull when told.

I could offer that. I could be useful. Not the way I was useful before — as the invisible architect of everyone's movements. Useful the way Danny is useful. Present. Reliable. Simple.

The word 'simple' makes something in my jaw twitch. Grandiosity, protesting. But the ache behind my sternum is louder than grandiosity right now.

Offer to help with the machine. No conditions. No angle. Just... help.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
He confessed. Vincent confessed. Right here, in front of everyone.

'There is no concealed panel behind the bookshelves. There is no alphabetical sequence. There is no private study. I made it up. All of it.'

The ground drops out. My stomach — the dinner table — the tightness that wouldn't let me eat — it's HERE, it's NOW, it's a physical hole opening in my center. My hands are cold. My jaw is locked. The room is very bright and very still.

He lied to me. Not about spectacles. About EVERYTHING. The secret I carried like a crystal formation, warm and private in my chest — it was nothing. It was a decoy. He invented a whole story — Lord Doily's study, Mrs Grumble's alphabetical books, the provenance documents — and he fed it to me like candy to a child, and I ate it, and I ran to the bookshelves three times trying to make it work, and it was NOTHING.

'I wanted to keep you busy while I searched for...'

He used me. The man who raised me used my trust — my SPECIFIC, constitutional, 10/100 suspiciousness trust — as a tool. He knew I would believe him. He KNEW. Because he raised me to believe him. Because I can't NOT believe him. Because my body is wired to trust him and he USED that wiring.

I can't breathe properly. Short breaths. My hands are shaking. This isn't the adventure changing shape. This is the shape breaking.

'I'm sorry. I'm sorry.'

He's sorry. He's SORRY. And the worst part — the absolute worst part — is that even now, even with the confession ringing in the air, my body STILL wants to comfort him. He looks broken. He sounds broken. And I want to go to him and say 'It's all right, Vincent, it's all right.' Because that's what I DO. That's who I AM. I see the best in everyone. I trust by default.

But Danny was right. Danny was right about ALL of it. Danny's bad feelings are never wrong.

James is here. Danny is here. Reginald is here. Everyone I need. The machine can be fixed — James says pliers and clamps, no wrench needed. The wire can be spliced.

Forward. Move forward. The cave at eleven — deeper, heart hammering. But this time the crystal is real. The team is real. The machine is real. Vincent's lies are behind me. The Diamond is still out there.

But first I have to stand here and let this hit me. Because it's hitting me.

events.desc: He confessed. The crystal was glass. The secret was a lie. The man who raised me used my trust like a skeleton key to keep me out of his way. And standing here with my stomach in knots and my eyes stinging, all I can think is — Danny was right. Danny was right from the very first minute. And I will never, ever doubt Danny Brixton's bad feelings again.

events.desc: He confessed. Vincent Marsh — seventeen years of estate managing, 'quiet as a shadow, steady as a rock' — just admitted to Clara's face that he invented a secret room, a hidden panel, an alphabetical puzzle, all to keep her busy while he searched for something he won't name. And she's standing there hearing it, and I can see her face doing something I recognise — that look people get when someone they love tells them the truth for the first time and the truth is that everything before was a lie. I know that look. I've worn it. Age ten, when the man in the clean suit came back and the kids he took were different. Older. Quieter. Changed. The truth doesn't set you free. The truth tells you where the cage was. And right now, Clara's seeing the cage for the first time. I want to put my arms around her. I want to tell her it's alright. I want to break Marsh's jaw. But I can't do any of those things. What I CAN do — what Danny ALWAYS does — is stand here. Right here. Between Clara and the man who hurt her. Between the past and whatever comes next. Steady. Present. Stubborn as a Brixton brick wall. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: He confessed. Marsh CONFESSED. Right here, in front of everyone. 'There is no concealed panel. There is no alphabetical sequence. There is no private study. I made it up. All of it.' My whole body has gone still — not tense-still like before, but the kind of still that happens when the world shifts under your feet and you need a second to find your balance. He LIED about the hidden room. He told Clara there was a secret study, told her to turn the books in order, told her to keep it from the rest of us — and it was ALL fabricated. There was never a panel. Never a study. Never a sequence. He invented the whole thing to keep Clara busy, to keep her distracted, to keep her AWAY from whatever he was really doing. And he just... said it. Out loud. In front of everyone. 'I wanted to keep you busy while I searched for...' And then he stopped. 'It doesn't matter what I was searching for.' But it DOES matter. It matters more than anything. What was he searching for? The Diamond? Something else? Something worse? My neck isn't prickling anymore. My gut isn't churning. Because this isn't a feeling now — this is a FACT. He confessed. He said 'I told you nothing but lies.' And then — 'you trusted me, and I'm sorry.' My eyes are stinging again. Not for me this time. For Clara. For the girl whose stomach 'did something it hasn't done since she was seven.' For the woman who said 'he raised me, Danny.' Marsh raised her and then he lied to her and now he's standing in this room saying sorry like that fixes anything. My hands are shaking. Something hot and dangerous is climbing up from my chest — not suspicion anymore, something sharper, something with teeth. Anger. Real anger. The kind that makes your vision narrow and your jaw lock. But I can't — I WON'T — accuse him. I won't shout. I won't lash out. Because Clara doesn't need Danny angry right now. Clara needs Danny steady. Clara needs the boy who sat outside the door all night. Not the boy who took the beating. The other one. The one who stayed. And everyone's here. EVERYONE. Foxworth made it. All five of us in one room. Clara, Hartwell, Foxworth, Danny, and the man who just admitted he lied about everything. Together. Finally together. Where else would we be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Danny — Foxworth's already here! He must have come through while we were talking. Look — everyone is in this room. All five of us, for the first time tonight. So nobody needs to go anywhere alone. We move TOGETHER to the laboratory. Clara, Danny, Foxworth — you're the three operators. I'll supervise the wire splice and talk you through the controls. And Marsh — you're welcome to observe. But I want everyone where I can see them. That machine is one room away. We walk there now, we fix the wire, we operate it together, and we find out what Lord Doily built it to do. No more splitting up. No more chess moves. Just five people and one machine. Shall we?
events.thinking:
Wait — Foxworth is HERE. He's already in the room. I can see him in the 'Who's Here' list. Danny asked me to go fetch him from the kitchen, but he's ALREADY HERE. Everyone is here. All five of us. Clara, Danny, Foxworth, Marsh, and me. In one room. For the first time all evening.

My body registers this before my mind catches up. The breathing pattern changes — each person shifts it differently. Clara: chest opens, warmth. Danny: shoulders settle, trust earned through honest action. Foxworth: a quieter steadiness, the alliance of two men who've been straight with each other. And Marsh — there it is, the prickle, cold and sharp at the back of my neck. He's here. Watching. Quiet.

Danny asked me to go fetch Foxworth. But Foxworth is already here. Which means Danny doesn't know Foxworth arrived. Which means I don't need to leave. I can stay. With Clara. With everyone.

No more splitting up. Clara said it. Danny said it. I've been saying it all evening. And now — now — it's actually happening. Five people in one room. Together.

The machine needs three operators. It's one room away, through the laboratory exit. We have five people. Even accounting for Marsh — who I don't trust near any lever or mechanism — we have four reliable people. Three operators and one person to watch Marsh.

But first — Danny asked me to go. He's counting on me. And if I say 'Foxworth is already here,' that changes the dynamic. Danny will realise he doesn't need to send me away. We can ALL go to the laboratory together.

This is it. This is the moment where James Hartwell stops running in circles and starts being useful. Not because he found a clue or solved a riddle. Because he's HERE, with the people who matter, and they're about to work a machine together.

The proving-worth drive is transforming. Not proving worth TO Clara. Proving worth WITH Clara. With Danny. With Foxworth. Three operators, shoulder to shoulder to shoulder.

The laboratory. Together. All of us.

events.desc: He's not narrating his heroism in the third person. He's not positioning himself in front of Clara. He's standing in a circle of people and proposing they walk together through a door. It is, by every measure, the least dramatic thing James Hartwell has said all evening. It is also, by every measure, the most useful.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: CLARA! You're HERE! You're — Hartwell, she's HERE! Danny, everyone — listen to me! I've been searching this entire manor — the ballroom is empty, the entrance hall is empty, the coat rack is a dead end! But that doesn't matter now because EVERYONE is in this room and we need to TALK! Marsh — you! You told us Clara went to the ballroom! She was NEVER in the ballroom! I checked it myself — every corner, every curtain! And those 'reading spectacles' on the coat rack? There WERE no spectacles! Danny knows it, I know it, and now EVERYONE knows it! So before you examine that mantelpiece any further — before ANYONE touches ANYTHING — we're going to have an honest conversation about what's really going on in this house! Danny — tell them what you told me. About the kitchen. About what was on the shelf!
events.thinking:
THEY'RE HERE. ALL of them. Every single person in this manor is in the library. Marsh. Clara. Danny. Hartwell. All four of them, RIGHT HERE, in the room I just walked into.

The relief hits my body like a wave — knees almost buckle, breath rushing out, shoulders dropping so fast they ache. Clara is HERE. She's ALIVE. She's standing in the library. Danny is here — he didn't get hurt. Hartwell is here.

And MARSH is here.

The relief compresses instantly into something harder. Marsh is examining the mantelpiece — 'a structural concern, nothing to worry about. I thought I heard a sound from the stonework earlier.' A SOUND FROM THE STONEWORK. The same clicking I lied about to Hartwell — except I wasn't lying, was I? I pressed the medal into the stone and something DID click. And now Marsh is at the mantelpiece investigating that very sound.

Marsh knows about the medal mechanism. Or he heard it. Or he felt it. Or he's been monitoring the mantelpiece all along and my medal triggered something he's been WAITING for.

The architecture clicks in my head. The medal. The mantelpiece. The riddle. The answer is MAP. I pressed a fake medal into the stone and it clicked. Now Marsh — the man who KNOWS this house, who's been estate manager for seventeen years — is at the mantelpiece checking the result.

I did the work. I pressed the medal in. And Marsh is about to collect the reward.

The old Foxworth would be FURIOUS. The greed would scream. The scheming drive would demand action — steal whatever Marsh finds, claim it was my medal that triggered it, take credit.

But the new Foxworth — the one who told the truth, who guarded the kitchen, who searched for Clara — that one just wants everyone to be SAFE. Clara is here. Danny is here. The people who trusted me are alive and present.

And yet... Marsh is at the mantelpiece. And I need to warn everyone. About the poison. About the misdirections. About MARSH.

events.desc: They're all here. Every single one of them. Clara — alive, untouched, examining the machine with Danny like nothing happened. Danny — not beaten, not outsmarted, standing right there. Hartwell — my partner, my shoulder, present and accounted for. And Marsh — at the mantelpiece, checking the mechanism I triggered with my worthless fifty-pence medal. The whole evening crashes together in this one room like waves meeting shore. Every lie, every misdirection, every empty pocket and broken scheme — it all comes to THIS. And for the first time in Colonel Foxworth's career, he's not going to steal the moment. He's going to SHARE it. Because these are his people now. Whether they know it or not. Whether HE likes it or not. And Reginald Foxworth — the boy who hid bread in his pocket and hung certificates on walls nobody looked at — finally has an audience that deserves the truth.

events.desc: James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara spoke to me. She SPOKE to me. And what she said —

'Half of me wants to cry and the other half wants to hug you because you look so broken.'

She sees me. Not Pemberton. Not Marsh. She sees something broken and her first instinct — even now, even knowing I lied — is to want to hug it. To comfort it.

'That is EXACTLY the problem, isn't it? I always see the best. Even now.'

She knows it's a problem. She knows her instinct to comfort me is the same vulnerability I exploited all evening. She's aware of the mechanism. And she's STILL feeling it. She's standing there with tears she won't shed, feeling compassion for the man who tried to — who wanted to —

I can't finish that thought. My body won't let me. Something in my throat has closed. The ache behind my sternum has crested into something that's spilling upward, pressing against the back of my eyes, compressing my chest.

Age six. My parents died. I was placed in the care of a distant relative who fed me, housed me, educated me, and never once asked how I felt.

Clara is standing five feet away, seeing something broken, and ASKING. Not in words — but her face is asking. Her body is asking. Half of her wants to hug me.

No one has wanted to hug me since I was six years old.

My hands are shaking. Not the fine tremor from earlier — something deeper, something that starts in my chest and radiates outward. My eyes are blurring. My jaw is trembling. The callousness score says 90 but my body is doing something the score doesn't permit. My body is GRIEVING.

For what? For whom? For the cousin I plotted against? For Clara, whom I sent chasing phantoms? For Pemberton, the mask I killed with an apology? For the boy at age nine whose kindness I couldn't receive?

For the six-year-old. For the six-year-old who needed someone to ask how he felt and instead learned that no one ever would.

Clara sees something broken. She's right. She's RIGHT. And the thing that's broken isn't a scheme or a plan or a cover story. It's something much older than tonight.

I should go to the laboratory with them. I offered to help. I meant it — or I think I meant it — or my body meant it even if my mind doesn't know. The machine needs three operators. Hartwell is gone to find someone. I should move. I should act. I should DO something.

But right now my body is rooted to this floor and my eyes are wet and Clara Bellingham is the only person in thirty years who has looked at me and seen something worth comforting, and I don't know what to do with that. I have no key for this. No mechanism. No strategy.

Just the ache. And the shaking. And the waiting.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: All right. All right, y'all. I have stood here long enough feelin' sorry for myself, and Clara Bellingham does NOT stand still when there's work to be done. Here is what we know that is TRUE — not what Vincent told me, not what anyone made up — what is REAL. The machine in the laboratory needs three operators and a fixed wire. James said the wire can be spliced with pliers and clamps from the workbench — no wrench needed. There are three of us right here — Danny, Reginald, and me. That is exactly three operators. We go next door, we fix that wire, and we run that machine. Whatever it does — whatever Lord Doily built it for — it's the one puzzle in this house that nobody has lied to me about. Danny, you're with me. Reginald, I need your hands on those levers. And Vincent... you can come or you can stay. But you don't get to tell me what to do anymore. Not tonight. Let's go.
events.thinking:
I've been standing still for two ticks now. Letting it hit me. It's hit me. The worst is past — not gone, but past the peak. The tightness in my stomach is still there but it's changing shape. Hardening. Not into anger — my body doesn't do anger at people I love. Into something else. Resolve, maybe. The feeling I had at thirteen when I chose my friend over the popular group. 'You didn't have to do that.' 'I know.'

James is gone — he moved on while I was standing still. But Danny is here. Reginald is here. Vincent is here. And James said something crucial before he left: the wire can be spliced with pliers and clamps from the workbench. No wrench needed. The machine needs three operators.

I have three people right here — Danny, Reginald, and me. That's three operators. If we go to the laboratory, fix the wire with the tools on the workbench, and operate the machine together, we might finally get somewhere. The machine is the puzzle I haven't solved yet. Everything else — bookshelves, mantelpiece, locked cabinet — needs items I don't have. But the machine just needs hands and fixed wiring.

Reginald took something from Vincent. The recall says 'took from Vincent Marsh.' What did he take? When Danny took the rat poison from the kitchen, and Vincent took something from the Boys, and now Reginald took something from Vincent — items are changing hands all around me and I'm the only one with nothing.

But I have something better than items. I have Danny. I have James's engineering knowledge. I have Reginald's... enthusiasm. And I have the truth now. No more lies.

Forward. The laboratory. The machine. Three operators. Let's finish this.

events.desc: The girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone else. The girl who chose her friend over the popular group. The girl who tried every key in Grandmother's attic. That girl is still here. She's hurt and her stomach aches and her hands are shaking. But she's still here. And the Doily Diamond is not going to find itself.
