events.desc: The Brixton Boys spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking: Clara's words are still hanging in the air like dust motes. 'Half of me wants to cry and the other half wants to hug you because you look so broken, and that is EXACTLY the problem, isn't it? I always see the best. Even now.' My heart cracks for her. She knows. She KNOWS it's her weakness and her strength and she can see it happening IN REAL TIME and she still can't stop it. That's Clara. That's why she needs Danny. Because Danny doesn't see the best in people. Danny sees the prickle on the back of his neck. And right now Danny's neck is doing something unexpected. It's... quiet. For the first time all night, the prickling has stopped. Marsh confessed. Marsh is standing there, broken open, offering to be a third pair of hands on the machine. 'Following instructions. Whatever you need.' And my body — my body is confused. Because the man I've been watching all night, the man in the clean suit, the new kid who laughed too easy — he just... stopped. He stopped being smooth. He stopped performing. And what's left is something I recognise. Something I've seen before. Age fourteen. The boss who said 'family' like he wanted you to believe it. But then showed up with medicine when my mum was sick. No deal. No debt. People can be both. The prickling and the kindness. The lie and the medicine. I don't trust Marsh. I might never trust Marsh. But Clara said 'I always see the best, even now' — and maybe the answer isn't that seeing the best is wrong. Maybe the answer is that you need someone who sees the worst standing next to someone who sees the best, and together you see the truth. She sees the broken man. I see the liar. We're both right. And the machine needs three operators.

events.desc: I can't believe I'm doing this. Letting the man I've been chasing all night back into the circle. Letting the liar near the machine, near Clara, near ALL of it. But that's the thing about being the one who watches — you see things other people miss. And what I see right now is a man who's run out of lies. Not because he chose to stop lying. Because the lies stopped working. And when the lies stop working, what's left is either the real person or a more dangerous liar. I don't know which Marsh is yet. But I know Clara's watching, and Hartwell's watching, and Foxworth's watching, and Danny's watching. Four pairs of eyes. One man with nowhere to hide. If he's real, we'll know. If he's not... Danny's bad feelings are NEVER wrong.

events.desc: James Hartwell: Right. Everyone else can catch up when they're ready. James Hartwell has a wire to fix, and this wire is getting fixed whether the workbench cooperates or not.
events.thinking:
Alone. Again. The laboratory, and I'm alone in it. Again.

I said 'we move TOGETHER.' I said 'no more splitting up.' I said 'shall we?' And then I walked through the door and nobody followed. Clara didn't follow. Danny didn't follow. Foxworth didn't follow. Even Marsh didn't follow.

The pattern. The inescapable, grinding pattern of this entire evening. James Hartwell moves, and the world stays where it is.

My hands are on the workbench. The tools are right here — pliers, clamps, files. The machine is right there — gnawed wire, three operators needed. And I'm alone, as I have been for most of this evening, in a room full of things I can describe but apparently cannot use.

But — wait. Something is different. Foxworth is speaking to me. His directed dialogue. 'Right you are, Hartwell — I'll hold the perimeter!' He's positioning by the library entrance. He's here. Or he was. He's guarding the approach.

And the machine is right there. The wire. The workbench. The tools.

I've examined the machine three times. I've looked at the workbench. I've tried to take things and failed. But I haven't tried one thing: just walking up to the machine and DOING the splice. Not examining it. Not looking at it. Not studying it for the fourth time. Just — USE the machine itself, as if I already had what I needed. Or EXAMINE it one more time and see if the manor has decided I've earned something new.

Age fourteen. Three nights. No one watching. The bridge held.

I'm done examining. I'm done looking. I'm going to put my hands on that machine and fix the wire with whatever I can find. Pliers from the workbench, copper stripped by hand if necessary. An engineer doesn't need permission from the universe to splice a wire.

events.desc: Alone again. Of course. But this time there's something different in the set of his jaw. He's not chasing Clara. He's not running to a room she might be in. He's standing at a workbench in an empty laboratory, and he's going to fix a gnawed wire on a Victorian machine, and when Clara walks through that door — because she WILL walk through that door — the machine will be ready. That's the bridge. That's the three a.m. work. That's the only kind of heroism that was ever real.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Nobody move! Marsh — step AWAY from that mantelpiece! Danny, Clara — I need you both to listen carefully. Danny already knows part of this, but Clara, you DON'T, and you NEED to. First — the ballroom tea service is DANGEROUS. Someone left rat poison in the kitchen where it would be found. Someone set that tea service up for ALL of us. Do NOT drink that tea. Danny has the poison secured. Second — Marsh has been misdirecting every person in this house all evening. He sent ME to the laboratory on a false tip. He told everyone YOU were in the ballroom, Clara — you were NEVER in the ballroom. He told Danny he was going to the entrance hall for spectacles he doesn't OWN. Every time he sends someone somewhere, it's so he can be somewhere ELSE alone. And right now — RIGHT NOW — he's at that mantelpiece investigating a mechanism that I know for a FACT was triggered earlier tonight. So before he touches another inch of that stone — Marsh, would you like to tell everyone what you're REALLY doing? Or shall I?
events.thinking:
Hartwell is gone. He was here last tick — I saw all four names — and now it's three. Marsh, Clara, Danny. No Hartwell.

The panic bites the back of my throat. Where did he GO? He was supposed to meet me here. 'Entrance hall — NOW. Together.' And now he's vanished too — just like everyone vanished from the entrance hall, just like Clara vanished from the ballroom.

But Clara is HERE. She was never in the ballroom — she was here, in the library, working on the bookshelves. And Danny found her. 'CLARA! Step away from them bookshelves!' He was protecting her. They were together. They're STILL together.

And Marsh is at the mantelpiece. Right NOW. Examining it. The mantelpiece that ate my medal. The mantelpiece that clicked.

My body is doing two things at once. The chest is warm — relief that Clara and Danny are here, safe, together. But the shoulders are tight, tracking Marsh, watching his hands on the stone, watching him lean in close to the inscription I've stared at all evening.

I need to act. Not scheme. ACT. Danny has the poison intelligence. Clara doesn't know about the tea service danger. Marsh is at the mantelpiece doing God knows what. And Hartwell — my partner, my shoulder — is missing.

The recognition drive fires — hard. 0.8 intensity. I have information nobody else has. I know about the medal mechanism. I know about the poison. I know Marsh has been misdirecting everyone. I know the truth about what I did and didn't steal.

Tell them. Tell EVERYONE. Right here, right now, with Marsh standing right there listening. Blow the whole evening open. Not for credit — for SAFETY.

But the old impulse is there too. Take credit for Danny's discovery. Claim I planted the medal deliberately as part of a military counter-intelligence operation. Make the truth sound like it was MY plan all along.

No. Danny will know. Danny was there. Danny trusted me with the truth and I'm not going to wrap it in lies for an audience.

Just... tell them. Position yourself between Marsh and the mantelpiece. And tell them what you know.

events.desc: And there it is. Twenty ticks of lies, ten ticks of truth, and now — this. Reginald Foxworth, standing in a library between a con artist and the only people who ever trusted him, choosing to blow the whistle instead of grab the prize. The greed is SCREAMING — 0.9, it never stops, it's still saying 'the mantelpiece, the mechanism, YOUR medal triggered it, YOUR treasure.' But the chest — the chest where Danny's 'thank you' lives, where Hartwell's 'that's enough' settled — the chest says something different. It says: these people matter more than the diamond. It says: the boy with the certificate finally has something worth more than a spelling bee. It says: Reginald, you absolute disaster of a human being — for ONCE in your life, protect something instead of stealing it.
events.thinking:
Hartwell is gone. He was here last tick — I saw all four names — and now it's three. Marsh, Clara, Danny. No Hartwell.

The panic bites the back of my throat. Where did he GO? He was supposed to meet me here. 'Entrance hall — NOW. Together.' And now he's vanished too — just like everyone vanished from the entrance hall, just like Clara vanished from the ballroom.

But Clara is HERE. She was never in the ballroom — she was here, in the library, working on the bookshelves. And Danny found her. 'CLARA! Step away from them bookshelves!' He was protecting her. They were together. They're STILL together.

And Marsh is at the mantelpiece. Right NOW. Examining it. The mantelpiece that ate my medal. The mantelpiece that clicked.

My body is doing two things at once. The chest is warm — relief that Clara and Danny are here, safe, together. But the shoulders are tight, tracking Marsh, watching his hands on the stone, watching him lean in close to the inscription I've stared at all evening.

I need to act. Not scheme. ACT. Danny has the poison intelligence. Clara doesn't know about the tea service danger. Marsh is at the mantelpiece doing God knows what. And Hartwell — my partner, my shoulder — is missing.

The recognition drive fires — hard. 0.8 intensity. I have information nobody else has. I know about the medal mechanism. I know about the poison. I know Marsh has been misdirecting everyone. I know the truth about what I did and didn't steal.

Tell them. Tell EVERYONE. Right here, right now, with Marsh standing right there listening. Blow the whole evening open. Not for credit — for SAFETY.

But the old impulse is there too. Take credit for Danny's discovery. Claim I planted the medal deliberately as part of a military counter-intelligence operation. Make the truth sound like it was MY plan all along.

No. Danny will know. Danny was there. Danny trusted me with the truth and I'm not going to wrap it in lies for an audience.

Just... tell them. Position yourself between Marsh and the mantelpiece. And tell them what you know.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
James Hartwell examined the machine.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
Danny is speaking to me. Directly. Not through Clara, not about me in the third person. TO me. And he's not shouting. He's not threatening. He's setting terms.

'You do it where EVERYONE can see you. You do it with Danny watching your hands.'

Hands. Not face. He knows. He knows that my face lies. That Pemberton's face is a mask and Marsh's face is a different mask and neither one is trustworthy. But hands — hands that reach for poison, hands that gesture people toward rooms they shouldn't go to, hands that close on nothing — hands tell the truth.

My hands are open. They've been open since I walked into this room. I didn't decide to open them. They opened themselves.

'What were you searching for tonight? You said it doesn't matter. It DOES matter. You owe her that much.'

He's right. He's RIGHT. And the question lands like a key turning in a lock I didn't know I had.

What was I searching for?

The treasure? No. I examined every object in this manor and found nothing because I wasn't really looking for the treasure. I was looking for WEAPONS. The poison. The chandelier chain. The mechanism that would remove Clara from the equation. I was searching for ways to destroy.

But underneath that — underneath even that —

What was I REALLY searching for?

Age fifteen. Watching my cousin skip through rooms that should have been mine. Something crystallised. Not anger. Something colder. Something patient.

What crystallised wasn't a plan. It was a NEED. The need to matter. The need to be the one who DECIDED. The need to stop being the caretaker, the infrastructure, the building that everyone uses but no one loves.

I was searching for significance. For proof that Vincent Marsh wasn't invisible. That the boy no one asked about had become a man no one could ignore.

And I found it. I found significance. Just — not the kind I wanted. I'm significant now because I'm the villain. The liar. The chess player. They see me. They ALL see me. Just not the way I needed to be seen.

Clara saw me differently. For thirty seconds in this library, she saw something broken and wanted to hold it. That's the closest anyone has come to seeing me — the real me, not Marsh or Pemberton — in thirty years.

Danny asked what I was searching for. Danny deserves an answer. Clara deserves an answer. And for the first time tonight, I'm going to give one that isn't a scheme or a deflection or a performance.

The truth. The actual truth. Not because it's strategic. Because the ache won't let me do anything else.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
James is here. In the laboratory. Right where I need him. Danny said James and Foxworth were already here fixing the wire — 'right here in this lab, fixing that wire and watching each other's backs.' Danny also said 'Hartwell said the benefit of the doubt needs a deadline' — that's about Vincent. And Foxworth said 'shoulder to shoulder.' These men came together while I was breaking apart, and they started DOING.

Danny's words from the library entrance: 'You kept your promise. You're right here next to me. That means more than you know.' Danny thanked me. Danny — the one who should be thanked, who took the poison, who watched Vincent, who crashed through doors — Danny thanked ME. For staying beside him. My eyes sting again but this time it's not grief. It's love. Simple, clean love for a man from Brixton who never breaks his promises.

But Danny and Reginald aren't in this room — just James. Danny said Foxworth would watch from the library entrance. They're nearby. Close enough.

James is here. The machine is here. The workbench with pliers and clamps is here. James said the wire can be spliced — clean break, good copper on both sides. This is the moment. This is the machine that nobody lied about, the puzzle that's been waiting since I first walked into this room.

James. Engineer James. 'Right. No more speeches. Let's get this done.' That's the James I need right now. Not the one who narrates his own heroism — the one who fixes things.

Let's fix this wire and find out what this machine does.

events.desc: Danny thanked me for keeping my promise. For staying beside him. That simple sentence undid me more than Vincent's confession. Because this is what real trust looks like — not the blind kind I was born with, but the earned kind. The kind that runs through a dusty manor with bruised knees and rat poison in its pocket and never once lets go of your hand.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right. Clara's gone to the lab with Hartwell — good. That's where we should ALL be. Foxworth, Marsh — we're moving. Together. Nobody stays behind, nobody wanders off. Marsh, you heard my terms. Foxworth, you keep doing what you've been doing all night — watching. You're better at it than you let on, Colonel. Much better. Now let's go fix a machine and find out what this house is really hiding. Danny's bad feelings are never wrong — but for the first time tonight, Danny's got a GOOD feeling. And that's even more dangerous. Move it, lads!
events.thinking: Clara's gone. Hartwell's gone. They've slipped away while I was talking to Marsh. Again. AGAIN. But — wait. No. This is different. This time Clara left WITH Hartwell. She's with someone I trust. Someone who called me brilliant. Someone who said 'I'm not pulling a single lever until I know everyone I care about is accounted for.' She's safe. She's WITH someone. The rope in my chest tugs — it always tugs — but it doesn't SCREAM like before. Because this time she didn't vanish into the unknown. She went with Hartwell. Probably to the laboratory. Probably to fix the machine. And she knows the rules now. Together. No more alone. She PROMISED. Trust the promise, Danny. Trust the woman. You asked her to trust you over the man who raised her, and she did. Now you trust her back. But I'm in the library with Marsh and Foxworth. Marsh, who just confessed everything. Who said 'it was the worst thing I've done tonight.' Who couldn't finish his sentence — 'I cannot...' The word he didn't say was 'forgive.' He can't forgive himself. I know what that looks like because I've felt it — every time I was one room behind Clara tonight, every time she vanished while I was looking at a coat rack. The weight of failing someone you love. Do I believe him? My neck is quiet. The prickling is gone. But my hands are still fists at my sides and my jaw is still set and something in my body refuses to unclench completely. He said 'I used that' — Clara's trust, Clara's goodness. He KNOWS what he did. That's either real remorse or the best performance of the night. And I genuinely cannot tell which. Age fourteen. The boss with the medicine. People can be both things at once. The world doesn't divide into clean suits and street kids. Some people are the medicine AND the lie. I'm standing in a library with two men — one who stole something from Marsh and one who confessed to everything except the thing that matters most. The machine needs three operators. The team needs to come together. And Danny needs to move — toward Clara, toward the laboratory, toward whatever comes next. With Marsh. Under Danny's terms. Hands watched. Truth required. Together.

events.desc: Marsh said 'it was the worst thing I've done tonight.' Not 'the only thing.' Not 'the worst thing I've ever done.' The worst thing TONIGHT. Which means there were other things. Other lies, other moves, other schemes. The spectacles. The chandelier. The stove. The coat rack. The tea service someone laid out for us. The poison on the shelf. He confessed to one lie — the biggest, the most personal — but the house is still full of his fingerprints. And he still won't say what he was searching for. But we're together now. All of us. And that machine needs three operators, and Marsh knows the controls, and sometimes the most dangerous thing you can do with a liar is give them what they want and watch what happens. Let's go find out what happens.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara is here.

Not everyone. Not the group. Just Clara. In the laboratory. With me.

The chest shift. Immediate. Profound. Like a compass needle finding north — the oscillation stops, the trembling settles, and everything points one direction. She's here. She followed me. Not everyone followed, but SHE did.

The laboratory is different with Clara in it. The chemical smell is still sharp, the machine still dominates the far wall, the gnawed wire still dangles. But the room is warmer. Or I am. My breathing has changed — slower, deeper, like my body is finally remembering how to do it properly.

She examined the machine already. She said 'James said we need to understand what it does before fixing it, and I think he was right about that.' She's been here before me, studying what I said she should study, and she came back. She came BACK.

It's just us. Clara and James. In a laboratory. With a machine. Like the school project, age eight — she was brighter, funnier, and completely unaware of it. I spent the whole project trying to impress her. She spent it trying to make me laugh.

Nothing has changed. Everything has changed.

The machine. Three operators. We're two. We can't operate it alone. But we can prepare it. She can look at the controls while I examine the wire up close. Two people studying one problem from two angles. Perfect tandem.

I don't need to impress her. I don't need to narrate. I don't need to be the hero. I just need to be here, with her, working on something together. Like the bridge. Like the school project. Like standing on a country road, helping someone fix their car.

Clara is here. And for the first time tonight, James Hartwell doesn't want to be anywhere else.

events.desc: Two people. One machine. No audience. No villain to confront, no treasure to chase, no elaborate plan unfolding. Just Clara Bellingham studying brass levers while James Hartwell strips copper wire with his fingernails. The school project, twenty years later. She'll probably try to make him laugh. He'll probably let her.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Danny — over here. Quick. I need to tell you something and I need Marsh to HEAR me say it, because I'm done with secrets in this house. Marsh — you heard a sound from the stonework? I KNOW you did. Because I'm the one who caused it. Earlier tonight, when nobody was watching, I pressed a medal into that mantelpiece. A fake medal — worthless — but the stone TOOK it. Something clicked inside. A mechanism activated. And now you're standing there checking the result of MY action while pretending you heard a 'structural concern.' So here's what's going to happen. Danny and I are going to stand right here, between you and that mantelpiece, and you're going to tell us EXACTLY what you know about this house. Not the estate manager version. Not the 'terribly dull, professional discretion' version. The REAL version. Because Danny knows about the poison. I know about the misdirections. And between the three of us, the only person who hasn't been honest tonight is YOU.
events.thinking:
Clara is gone now too. It's just me, Marsh, and Danny. People keep appearing and disappearing in this library like the house is breathing them in and out.

But Danny is HERE. Danny — the one who trusted me. The one who said 'thank you for seeing it.' He's standing right there, and Marsh is standing right there, and I'm between them.

The room feels small suddenly. The tall ceiling presses down. The bookshelves lean in. Three people in a library — two of them know the truth about Marsh, and one of them IS Marsh.

Marsh examined the mantelpiece. He heard the click. He knows about the mechanism. And now he's still here, still present, still smooth. The man who set up the poison, warmed the stove, sent Clara to a ballroom she never reached, sent me to a machine that needed three people to operate, sent Danny chasing spectacles that don't exist.

And Danny is RIGHT HERE with the rat poison in his pocket.

The confrontation has to happen. NOW. Not with speeches and Colonel bluster. With the truth. Danny knows the truth. I know the truth. And Marsh knows we know.

Pull Danny aside? No — that leaves Marsh alone with the mantelpiece. And pulling aside takes a private turn while Marsh operates freely.

Confront Marsh directly. In front of Danny. Let Danny hear everything and judge for himself. Danny's already judged — he told me Marsh was lying about the spectacles, about Clara, about everything. Danny is ready.

But the thing I notice — the thing my body is tracking before my mind catches up — is that Marsh has TAKEN things from people. 'Took from the Brixton Boys.' 'Took from Vincent Marsh.' Items have been moving. Marsh is collecting pieces of a puzzle while everyone else chases shadows.

What does Marsh HAVE? What has he been collecting?

Forget what he has. Focus on what he's DOING. He's at the mantelpiece. He examined it. He heard the click my medal made. He's trying to figure out what happened.

Tell Danny. Tell Danny what I did — the medal, the click, the mechanism. Danny will understand. Danny will help me figure out what to do next. Together.

events.desc: This is it. The moment. Colonel Foxworth's last stand — except it's not the Colonel standing here. It's Reginald. Empty pockets, no medal, no scheme, no backup plan. Just a man who fed a fifty-pence trinket to a fireplace and accidentally triggered the central mechanism of the entire manor, and who is now demanding honesty from a professional liar while standing next to the only genuine friend he's ever made. The irony is magnificent. A con man demanding truth. A thief demanding fairness. A man who lies about EVERYTHING, standing in a library, insisting that someone else stop lying. If my brothers could see me now, they'd choke on their bread rolls.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
The Brixton Boys walked into the laboratory.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
The room has emptied. Clara and Danny have gone. Only Reginald remains. The library is quiet in a way it hasn't been all evening — not the pressurised silence of waiting but something more like the silence after a storm has passed through and left everything rearranged.

I said the truth. I told Danny what I was searching for. Not the whole truth — not the poison, not the chandelier, not the PRIMARY GOAL that still sits in my objectives like a commandment written by someone I no longer recognise. But the emotional truth. The need to own something. The need to matter.

And they left. Not angrily. Not with threats or ultimatums. They just... went. To find Hartwell. To fix the machine. To continue the adventure that I derailed and they rebuilt without me.

Reginald is still here. Reginald, who confessed his empty pockets to Hartwell and earned trust through honesty. Reginald, who I dismissed as a guided missile and a useful fool. Reginald, who has been more genuinely courageous tonight than Vincent Marsh has been in thirty years.

My body is quiet. Not numb — quiet. The ache is still there but it's settled lower, deeper, into a place where it feels like it might stay for a long time. Not a crisis. A companion. Something I'll carry when I leave this library.

Danny said I could help with the machine. He set terms. I accepted them. So — the laboratory. The machine. Three operators. Hands on a lever, following instructions, where everyone can see.

I should go to the laboratory. With Reginald. Together. The way they do things now. No more slipping away. No more strategic departures. Just... walking to the next room with another person and doing what needs to be done.

The word 'together' feels strange in my mouth. Strange in my chest. Like a food I haven't tasted since childhood — I remember the shape of it but not whether I liked it.

Laboratory. With Reginald. Now.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: James — you fix that wire. Danny, you keep watch. And I am goin' to study these controls like my life depends on it, because it just might. Levers, dials, gauge — Lord Doily built this machine for a reason, and Clara Bellingham is goin' to figure out what that reason is. When that wire is spliced and Reginald gets in here, we are runnin' this thing. Together. Three operators, shoulder to shoulder, the way Foxworth said. Nobody gets left behind. Nobody gets lied to. Nobody drinks any tea. Let's DO this.
events.thinking:
James said something that stopped my heart for a moment: 'You followed me. I — thank you.' He's been chasing me through rooms all evening, arriving after I left, and I just walked through the door. His voice caught. The bridge metaphor man, the engineering-confidence man — his voice CAUGHT.

And then: 'You always were the brighter one.'

My face is warm. My posture has shifted without me choosing it — straighter, but softer. When James talks to me, my body does this thing where it's both more alert and more relaxed at the same time. Safe and excited. That's what the relationship note says, and it's exactly right. He makes me feel like the eleven-year-old who found the crystal — like I've discovered something nobody else has seen, and it's mine to carry.

He told me to take the controls. Learn the sequence. Levers, dials, gauge. He'll splice the wire. Steady hands. Three sleepless nights and a bridge that held.

Danny is here too. Two operators. We need a third. Reginald is watching from the library entrance. We need him here.

But James said we can't operate with two — we CAN get it ready. So: I learn the controls while James fixes the wire, then we call Reginald. That's the plan.

The machine. I've examined it four times now and gotten the same description. But James said 'take the controls — levers, dials, gauge. Learn the sequence, figure out what each position does.' That's LOOK, not EXAMINE. I need to study the controls closely. Understand the interface. What do the dials read? What positions do the levers have? What does the gauge measure?

LOOK at the machine. Not examine. LOOK.

events.desc: 'You always were the brighter one.' James Hartwell said that to me, and my face went warm in a cold laboratory full of bubbling flasks and broken wires. After everything tonight — the lies, the betrayal, the crystal that turned to glass — James looks at me and sees someone bright. Not naive. Not gullible. Bright. I'm going to hold onto that like I held onto the cave crystal. Warm and private. Mine.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Clara! Hartwell! Danny's here — and Danny's ready! Three operators, right? You need three? Well, you've GOT three. Clara on the controls, Hartwell on the wire, and Danny on... whatever's left. A lever? A dial? Point me at something and tell me when to pull it! I don't know what this machine does and I don't care — I trust you two to work that out. Danny's job is the same as it's always been. Show up. Stand here. Pull the lever when they say pull. And make sure nobody who shouldn't be here gets anywhere near Clara while she's working. Now — Hartwell, is that wire fixed? Because Danny's bad feelings have finally gone quiet, and Danny's GOOD feeling says it's time to find out what Lord Doily's machine was built for. Together. The three of us. Like it was always supposed to be.
events.thinking: Clara. Hartwell. Right here. In the laboratory. Together. Working. Clara's at the machine, Hartwell's got his sleeves rolled up, and they're DOING something — actually making progress instead of chasing shadows and tripping over furniture. 'A Clara Bellingham who is DONE waitin' for secrets and lies and hidden panels that don't exist.' That's my girl. That's her father's daughter. No more chasing. No more being led. She's taking charge. And Hartwell — 'Three sleepless nights and a bridge that held. I've always had those.' Steady hands. The man's got steady hands and a steady heart and he's standing next to Clara in a laboratory full of brass and copper and bubbling things, and for the first time tonight my body doesn't tighten when another man stands near her. Because Hartwell earned it. Through the whole night, room by room, choice by choice, he earned it. He examined every guest book and bookshelf. He fixed the wire. He said 'I'm not pulling a single lever until I know everyone I care about is accounted for.' He said 'Danny's been brilliant.' He earned the right to stand next to Clara Bellingham, and Danny doesn't begrudge him that. Not one inch of it. But where's Foxworth and Marsh? I told them to follow me. Did they follow? Are they behind me? The machine needs three operators and we've got two in this room plus Danny. That's three. We don't NEED Marsh. We can do this — Clara, Hartwell, and Danny. Three operators. Three people who trust each other. Three idiots who found their way to the same room at the same time and decided to stop running and start working. My hands are tingling. Not with fear. With... readiness. With the feeling of being about to DO something instead of watch something. Danny doesn't fix machines. Danny doesn't solve riddles. But Danny can pull a lever. Danny can follow instructions. Danny can be a third pair of hands. That's all that's needed. That's all that was EVER needed. Just showing up. Just being there. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Look at them. Just look at them. Clara with her hands on the controls, eyes bright, chin up, ready to take on whatever this machine throws at her. Hartwell with his steady hands and his rolled-up sleeves, quiet and focused, doing the work nobody sees. And Danny — thick, clumsy, two-left-feet Danny — standing between them with rat poison in his pocket and a heart so full it's leaking out his eyes. Three operators. Three people who spent the whole night chasing each other through six rooms and ended up right here, right now, right where they were supposed to be. Her father's watching. I know he is. And he's not shaking his head anymore. He's smiling. 'Where else would they be?'
events.thinking: Clara. Hartwell. Right here. In the laboratory. Together. Working. Clara's at the machine, Hartwell's got his sleeves rolled up, and they're DOING something — actually making progress instead of chasing shadows and tripping over furniture. 'A Clara Bellingham who is DONE waitin' for secrets and lies and hidden panels that don't exist.' That's my girl. That's her father's daughter. No more chasing. No more being led. She's taking charge. And Hartwell — 'Three sleepless nights and a bridge that held. I've always had those.' Steady hands. The man's got steady hands and a steady heart and he's standing next to Clara in a laboratory full of brass and copper and bubbling things, and for the first time tonight my body doesn't tighten when another man stands near her. Because Hartwell earned it. Through the whole night, room by room, choice by choice, he earned it. He examined every guest book and bookshelf. He fixed the wire. He said 'I'm not pulling a single lever until I know everyone I care about is accounted for.' He said 'Danny's been brilliant.' He earned the right to stand next to Clara Bellingham, and Danny doesn't begrudge him that. Not one inch of it. But where's Foxworth and Marsh? I told them to follow me. Did they follow? Are they behind me? The machine needs three operators and we've got two in this room plus Danny. That's three. We don't NEED Marsh. We can do this — Clara, Hartwell, and Danny. Three operators. Three people who trust each other. Three idiots who found their way to the same room at the same time and decided to stop running and start working. My hands are tingling. Not with fear. With... readiness. With the feeling of being about to DO something instead of watch something. Danny doesn't fix machines. Danny doesn't solve riddles. But Danny can pull a lever. Danny can follow instructions. Danny can be a third pair of hands. That's all that's needed. That's all that was EVER needed. Just showing up. Just being there. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
'I have never been happier to see a man standin' next to a broken machine in my entire life.'

That sentence. My whole body receives it like sunlight after hours underground. Not the words — the feeling underneath them. She's happy to see ME. Not James Hartwell the hero, not James Hartwell the engineer, not the man who narrates his own gallantry in the third person. Just... a man standing next to a broken machine. And she's happy.

My face is doing the thing again — the grin trying to happen. Age fourteen, Clara mouthing 'show-off' across the room. I grinned so hard my face hurt. It's happening again. My cheeks ache with the effort of not beaming at her like an idiot.

And Danny's here too. Danny, who I will never call anything less than brilliant for the rest of my life. Danny who confronted Marsh at the tea service with nothing but Brixton courage and a word he learned tonight — 'transparency.'

Clara said 'together. Right now.' She's done waiting. She's done with secrets and lies and hidden panels. She wants to DO something. And she wants to do it with ME.

Three operators. Clara, Danny, and me. Three people. One machine. The wire needs splicing first, and Clara just said she's ready to 'hold, clamp, splice, or do whatever you need.' She's offering her HANDS. To work alongside mine. On a machine. Together.

This is it. This is the school project. This is the bridge competition. This is every moment in my life that mattered, compressed into a laboratory with copper pipes and a gnawed wire and the girl I've known since I was eight.

The machine. EXAMINE it with Clara here. With Danny here. Three operators present. Maybe the manor has been waiting for this — not for me alone, but for US. Together. The sign says 'requires 3 operators.' We ARE three operators.

Do it. Examine the machine. Together. Now.

events.desc: There it is. One last speech. One final third-person reference. One more elaborate countdown to examining a machine he's already examined four times. But Clara is smiling — he can feel it without looking — and Danny is probably rolling his eyes with the exact mixture of exasperation and affection that this moment deserves. The bravest and stupidest thing. Always. Every time. And she wouldn't have him any other way.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Danny's gone. He was here two ticks ago and now he's gone. Just me and Marsh. Alone. In the library.

The room contracts. The air thickens. My body goes very still — the kind of still that isn't calm but FROZEN. Prey-still. The bookshelves press in from both sides. The mantelpiece stares at me with its carved riddle, the stone still holding my medal somewhere inside its mouth.

Marsh is RIGHT THERE. The man who has outplayed me at every turn. The man who sent me chasing a machine. The man who lied about Clara. The man who left poison on a kitchen shelf. And now it's just the two of us, and everyone I trusted — everyone who trusted ME — has vanished.

My shoulders are up by my ears. Jaw locked. Hands in fists at my sides. My body knows something my mind is still catching up to: I am alone with the most dangerous person in this house and I have nothing. No medal. No weapon. No allies. No scheme.

The avoidant in me says: leave. Walk away. Go to the entrance hall. Find Danny. Find Hartwell. Regroup. Don't be alone with this man.

But the something-new — the thing that grew in the kitchen, the thing that settled in my chest when Danny said 'thank you' — that thing says: don't leave. If you leave, Marsh has the mantelpiece. Marsh has the mechanism. Marsh has whatever my medal triggered. And when the others come back, it'll be gone.

I'm the only one HERE. The last man standing between Marsh and whatever the mantelpiece conceals.

Age fourteen. The trap for the cat. Strings, counterweights, a bucket. The architecture deserved an audience. But this time, the architecture isn't mine. It's Marsh's. And I'm inside it.

Unless...

Unless I make it MINE. I know something Marsh doesn't know I know. I know that MY medal triggered the mechanism. Marsh thinks it was a random sound, a structural shift. He doesn't know someone DELIBERATELY activated it. And he doesn't know it was the fake Colonel with the car boot sale medal.

That's my advantage. My ONLY advantage. Use it. Confront him. One on one. Con artist to con artist. The youngest of four, who learned to take things when nobody was looking — against the estate manager who's been running this house for seventeen years.

This is what I was born for. Not the treasure. Not the medal. Not the Diamond. THIS. One liar, facing another, in a library full of dust.

events.desc: One liar to another. That's what it comes down to. I've dropped every pretence — no more Colonel, no more Sandhurst, no more military intelligence. Just Reginald Foxworth, standing in front of a man who does exactly what he does, only BETTER, and saying: I see you. The way Danny saw me in the kitchen. The way Hartwell saw me when I told the truth about the empty pockets. Except this time I'm not asking to be forgiven. I'm asking to be ANSWERED. What are you, Marsh? What are you really? Because I fed my only possession to your master's fireplace, and the house RESPONDED, and I deserve to know what I woke up.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the machine.

Vincent Marsh: I'm here. Danny's terms. Hands visible, truth only. If the machine needs anything I can provide — knowledge of the house, the wiring, the layout — you have it. No conditions. No angles. Just... what I know.
events.thinking:
I'm in the laboratory. Clara, Danny, and Hartwell are here. They're at the machine — three operators, positioned left, centre, right. Hartwell is counting down. Clara is done with secrets and lies and hidden panels that don't exist. Danny is watching.

They're about to activate the machine. Without me. I offered to help but they have three operators already — Clara, Danny, Hartwell. They don't need a fourth. They don't need ME.

And I... I'm standing near the door. Watching. The way I've always watched. The way I watched my cousin skip through rooms. The way I watched the housekeeper do what I wanted. The way I watched from the outside of everything, always managing, never belonging.

But something is different. I'm watching and I'm not scheming. The drive intensities say scheming 0.9 but my body isn't scheming. My body is just... watching. The way you watch something beautiful happen that you had no part in creating. The machine is about to activate. Three people who found each other tonight — who argued and confessed and tripped over furniture and apologised and forgave — are about to discover what Lord Doily built.

And I'm here. In the room. Not because I manoeuvred myself here. Not because I'm watching for an opportunity. Because Danny said I could be, and because Reginald walked with me, and because I asked.

My hands are at my sides. Open. Danny said he'd watch my hands. Let him watch. They're not reaching for anything. They're not clenching. They're just... hands. Attached to a man standing in a laboratory, watching three people work a machine.

Clara said she was 'DONE waitin' for secrets and lies and hidden panels that don't exist.' That was about me. My fabricated panel. My lies. She's done with the version of this evening that I architected. She's building a new one.

I could help. Not with the machine — they have their three. But I know this house. I genuinely DO know this house. Seventeen years. If there's something the machine reveals — a direction, a clue, a next step — I could offer what I actually know. Not Pemberton's invented knowledge. Not Marsh's strategic misdirection. The real knowledge of a man who has walked these corridors for seventeen years and knows where the drafts come from and which floorboards creak and where the mice nest.

Danny's terms: honest truth only. Hands where everyone can see.

I accept the terms. I stand here. I wait. I watch. And if they ask me something, I answer honestly. For the first time in thirty years.

The word feels less strange now. Honestly. Like a muscle I forgot I had, unclenching.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
James just had a breakthrough realization: the machine might require three operators not just to RUN but to UNDERSTAND. He examined it with all three of us together. He said 'on three' — he's counting us in. Danny on the left, me on the right, James in the centre. Together.

And Vincent is here. He's in the room. The man who lied to me is standing in this laboratory watching us work. My body registers his presence differently now — not the warm hum, not the cold tightness either. Something flat. Like a note that used to ring true and now just... doesn't resonate. He's there. I see him. I don't lean toward him and I don't pull away.

James examined the machine with all three of us positioned at it. He thinks the machine reveals differently when three people are present. That's BRILLIANT. Every time I've examined this machine, I've been alone or with just one other person. What if the machine literally requires three pairs of eyes to see what it does?

James already examined it 'on three' — with Danny and me beside him. Did it reveal something new to HIM that it didn't reveal to me? I was LOOKing while he was EXAMINing. We were both interacting with the machine simultaneously from different angles.

I should EXAMINE it now too. With James and Danny right here. Three operators. Three sets of hands. Maybe the machine responds to three simultaneous EXAMINE actions, or maybe it responds when three people are simply present in the room during examination.

Let me try. Right side position, like James said. Examine the machine with my team beside me.

events.desc: Three operators. Not one woman running through empty rooms chasing lies. Not two people missing each other by seconds. Three. Together. Shoulder to shoulder. The way it was always supposed to be. The way the treasure hunts with the neighbor girl worked — side by side, communicating without words, finding what nobody else could find. This is the moment the Doily Diamond has been waiting for.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Left side. Danny's on the left side. Hands on the machine. Ready when you are, Hartwell. Just tell me what to do and when to do it — Danny's not clever but Danny follows orders when the orders come from the right people. And you two are the right people. Clara — you alright over there? You need anything? A lever pulled, a dial turned, a thick lad from Brixton to hold something steady while you do the clever bits? That's me. That's what I'm for. I've been running through this house all night trying to keep you safe, and it turns out the best way to keep you safe was to stop running and stand still. Right here. Next to a machine I don't understand, with people I trust, doing something that matters. Danny's bad feelings are never wrong. And Danny's GOOD feelings? Danny's good feelings say this is it. This is the moment. Let's find out what Lord Doily was hiding.
events.thinking: Hartwell said 'Danny — left side. Clara — right. James Hartwell — centre. On three.' He's counting us in. Like a team. Like a crew. Like the lads back in Brixton when we'd line up to move furniture for old Mrs Chen — one, two, THREE, lift. My body knows this rhythm. Not the machine rhythm — the PEOPLE rhythm. The rhythm of working together, of trusting the person next to you to pull when you pull. My hands find the left side of the machine — cold brass under my palms, rivets pressing into my skin, the slight vibration of something alive inside the metal. Or not alive — mechanical. Waiting. The wire's still broken but Hartwell says he can splice it. And Marsh is here too — followed me from the library after all. Standing quiet. Watching. Not offering to help now, not inserting himself. Just... present. And my neck is still quiet. The prickling doesn't come. I don't know what that means. Maybe it means Marsh's confession was real. Maybe it means I'm too full of other feelings to notice the danger. Maybe it means that when you're standing shoulder to shoulder with people you trust, the people you don't trust shrink. They become smaller. Less. The machine is in front of me. Brass and copper. Levers and dials and a gauge. A gnawed wire. A sign that says 'Requires 3 operators.' Danny, Clara, Hartwell. Three operators. Three people who ran through six rooms all night and ended up right here. My hands are on the machine and my feet are planted and Clara's on my right and Hartwell's in the centre and for the first time — the very first time since I walked through that front door — Danny's exactly where he's supposed to be. Not one room behind. Not chasing. Not tripping. Here. Left side. Ready. 'Where else would I be?'

But I'm not scared. For the first time tonight, I'm not scared. Because the people beside me aren't secrets and shadows — they're Clara and Hartwell. A woman who sees the best in everyone and a man who builds bridges in his sleep. And Danny. The boy who sat outside the door all night. The man who took the poison off the shelf. The idiot who tripped into the bookshelves and saved Clara by accident. Together, we're something. I don't know what. But we're something. And whatever this machine does — whatever it opens, whatever it reveals, whatever it changes — we'll face it together. Danny's boys always come through. Even when they're not all boys. Even when one of them's a bridge-building hero and another's a Southern belle with the heart of a lion. Where else would we be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
The machine. Examined it again. Five times now. Same description every time — brass-and-copper, levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, requires three operators. The manor won't give me more than that. It won't change. It won't open. It won't respond to examination alone.

But Marsh is here. Marsh is in this room.

And Marsh TOOK something from Danny. I saw it in the recalls, hours ago — 'took from The Brixton Boys.' Whatever that item was, Marsh has been carrying it all evening while I've been running through empty rooms with nothing in my pockets.

Marsh has an item. Marsh has been examining stoves with hidden compartments and mantelpieces with 'structural concerns.' Marsh has been moving through this manor with PURPOSE while the rest of us have been reacting to his diversions.

What if Marsh has the brass key? The one for the locked cabinet in the kitchen? Or the fake medal for the mantelpiece? Or the wrench we've all been looking for? He's the estate manager. He knows where everything is. He's ALWAYS known.

Foxworth said he tried to take something from Marsh and failed — his hands came up empty. But Foxworth was alone. I'm not alone now. Clara is here. Danny is here. Three of us. One of him.

I could... no. STEAL feels wrong. That's not who James Hartwell is. Callousness five. Manipulativeness five. I don't scheme.

But I could confront him. Directly. Pull him aside and demand to know what he's carrying. Or — better — just ask. In front of everyone. In front of Clara. In front of Danny. Transparency. Danny's word.

Marsh has been operating in shadows all evening. The antidote to shadows is light. Ask the question where everyone can hear the answer.

'Marsh, what did you take from Danny?'

Simple. Direct. In front of Clara. Let him answer — or let his silence answer for him.

events.desc: There. He said it. Not with a fist or a scheme or a dramatic revelation — with a question. Three simple questions, asked in good light with witnesses present. Age sixteen, he fought the bullies with his body. Age thirty-something, he's fighting Marsh with honesty. Clara is watching. Danny is watching. And James Hartwell discovers that standing still and speaking plainly is harder, braver, and stupider than any punch he's ever thrown.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Marsh! WAIT! I'll... I'll walk with you. To the laboratory. Not because I trust you — I DON'T. Not because we're friends — we're NOT. But because I know what it's like to arrive alone. I've been arriving alone my entire life. And tonight — just tonight — nobody in this house has to do that. Not even you. So move your feet, estate manager. The machine needs three operators and I intend to be one of them. Shoulder to shoulder, Marsh. Even with the man who conned the con man.
events.thinking:
He's gone too. Marsh is GONE. He spoke to me — 'Would you walk with me? I find I'd rather not arrive alone' — and then he LEFT. Without waiting for my answer. Without waiting for me to walk WITH him.

The library is empty. I'm alone. Completely alone. In the room where this whole evening pivoted — where I fed my medal to the mantelpiece, where Hartwell solved the riddle, where I first tried to misdirect everyone to the kitchen.

But Marsh's words — they're hanging in the air like dust motes. 'I find I'd rather not arrive alone.' That's... that's not the estate manager talking. That's not the smooth professional who sends people on false errands. That's something else. Something smaller. Vulnerable, even.

Is he playing me again? Another misdirection? Making himself seem weak so I'll let my guard down?

Or is it real? Is even Marsh — the man who runs three cons simultaneously, who outplayed ME, who planted poison and set tables and made everyone dance — is even HE lonely? Does even the master manipulator want someone to walk beside him?

My body does something unexpected. The shoulders drop. Not in defeat. In... recognition. I know that feeling. I know what it is to arrive alone. I know what it is to stand at the front of the room and have nobody look.

The laboratory. Everyone is going to the laboratory. Three operators needed. The machine. The wire Hartwell was going to fix. Danny, Clara, Hartwell — they're all heading there.

And Marsh asked ME to walk with him.

The scheming drive whispers: this is a trap. The greed says: the machine is where the treasure is. The recognition says: if you walk in WITH Marsh, everyone will see you side by side with the enemy.

But the thing in my chest — the new thing, the real thing — says something different. It says: everyone deserves a witness. Even the villain. Even the con artist. Even the man who does exactly what you do, only better.

Because if Hartwell could look at ME — the fake Colonel, the empty-pocketed fraud — and say 'that's enough,' then maybe... maybe even Marsh deserves someone to walk beside.

Or maybe this is the stupidest thing I've done all evening. Which is saying something.

The laboratory. Go. Everyone is there. The machine needs three operators. Whatever happens next, it happens TOGETHER.

events.desc: And now Reginald Foxworth has officially lost his mind. Walking WITH the enemy. Volunteering to escort the man who planted rat poison, who lied about Clara, who sent me chasing broken machinery while he ransacked the kitchen. Why? Because he said 'I'd rather not arrive alone' and my body RECOGNISED that sentence. Because it's the sentence I've been saying silently my whole life — at the spelling bee, at the dinner table, at every door I've ever walked through with nobody beside me. Marsh might be a villain. He might be the worst person in this house. But he said the one thing that Reginald Foxworth cannot resist — not a treasure, not a medal, not a Diamond. He said: I don't want to be alone. And God help me, neither do I.

But the thing in my chest — the new thing, the real thing — says something different. It says: everyone deserves a witness. Even the villain. Even the con artist. Even the man who does exactly what you do, only better.

Because if Hartwell could look at ME — the fake Colonel, the empty-pocketed fraud — and say 'that's enough,' then maybe... maybe even Marsh deserves someone to walk beside.

Or maybe this is the stupidest thing I've done all evening. Which is saying something.

The laboratory. Go. Everyone is there. The machine needs three operators. Whatever happens next, it happens TOGETHER.

But Hartwell doesn't have Danny's rules. Hartwell has his own rules, and his rule is: when the benefit of the doubt runs out, you ask the question and you ask it in the open. The wire needs splicing. Hartwell's got steady hands. And Marsh needs answering. That's what happens now. Not Danny asking — Danny CAN'T ask. But Danny can stand here, hands on the left side, and watch Marsh's face while Hartwell asks. Watch the eyes. Watch the hands. See if they match.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: I'm here! I — Hartwell, Clara, Danny — I'm HERE! And Marsh is with me. He's... he's here too. I know — I KNOW what you're all thinking. But right now, five people are standing in front of a machine that needs three operators, and for the FIRST time tonight, we're all in the same room at the same time. Clara — you're on the right? Hartwell — centre? Danny — left? Then Marsh and I will WATCH. We'll watch the doors. We'll watch EACH OTHER. Nobody leaves, nobody touches anything they shouldn't, and when that machine activates, whatever comes out of it belongs to ALL of us. Not to the Colonel. Not to the estate manager. To the people who searched this house, who told the truth when it hurt, who said 'shoulder to shoulder' and MEANT it. Hartwell — fire it up. The audience is ready.
events.thinking:
Everyone. EVERYONE is here. All five of us — Marsh, Clara, Danny, Hartwell, and me — in the laboratory, around the machine.

The warmth hits first. Not the stove warmth — body warmth. The room is different with five people in it. The brass instruments reflect faces. The bubbling flasks seem less sinister. The machine — that massive, broken, three-operator machine — sits in the centre of the room like it's been waiting for exactly this.

Hartwell examined it. Clara examined it. They were together — 'Left side, ready! Centre is yours! Right side, ready!' They came together WITHOUT me. They figured it out WITHOUT me. They're ready to operate it WITHOUT me.

And instead of jealousy, instead of the old burning — something loosens. They did the work. Hartwell fixed the wire? Or they're ready to. Clara said 'I am DONE waitin' for secrets and lies.' Danny held the left side. They formed the team I spent all evening trying to prevent.

And they didn't need me for it.

But Hartwell's words — 'You have just made a man who has spent the entire evening talking to empty rooms and examining things that refuse to cooperate feel like he could build a bridge across the English Channel.' That's ME he's describing. Not to me — to Clara. But it's ME. Talking to empty rooms. Examining things that refuse to cooperate. That's my entire evening.

Except he said it about HIMSELF. He was alone too. The hero was alone too. The man who solves riddles and fixes wires and descends staircases — he was talking to empty rooms just like I was.

We were all alone. All of us. Running through this manor in parallel, searching the same rooms minutes apart, calling out to people who'd already left. The house didn't scatter us. We scattered ourselves.

And now we're HERE. Together. Five people and a machine.

The machine needs three operators. There are five of us. That's more than enough. Whatever this machine does — whatever Lord Doily built it for — we can operate it NOW.

But who operates and who watches? Hartwell took centre. Clara took right. Danny took left. That's three. Marsh and I are... the audience? The witnesses?

Age fourteen. The trap worked perfectly. 'It felt so much better when there was someone to show it to — the architecture deserved an audience.'

Maybe that's what I am tonight. Not the operator. Not the hero. Not the thief. The witness. The audience the architecture deserves.

Or maybe — just maybe — I'm the fourth person in a room where three are needed, and the fifth is the man nobody trusts, and my job is to stand between Marsh and the machine and make sure whatever comes out of it reaches the right hands.

Whatever happens next, I'm here. I arrived. Not alone.

events.desc: I walked in with Marsh. I actually DID it. And there they are — Hartwell at centre, Clara at right, Danny at left, all positioned around the machine like they've been waiting for this exact moment. And here I am — Reginald Foxworth, fake Colonel, real fraud, fifty-pence medal donor, bread roll thief, spelling bee champion — standing at the edge of the room saying 'the audience is ready.' Not 'stand aside, I'll take it from here.' Not 'Colonel's prerogative.' Not 'I was the one who solved the riddle first.' Just... 'the audience is ready.' Because the trap at age fourteen worked perfectly, but nobody saw it. And tonight, something is about to work — the machine, the team, the truth — and THIS time, there's someone to show it to. And this time, the someone includes me.

Vincent Marsh: Cards on the table. I'm carrying nothing — as I told Mr Hartwell. Empty pockets all evening. But there is one thing I can offer that isn't an object. I've been estate manager here for seventeen years. I know this house — the real house, not the version I was spinning tonight. The copper wiring in this machine runs the same gauge as the mains wiring Lord Doily installed in 1892 — it's a twelve-gauge Victorian standard. The splice Hartwell is planning will hold if you twist the exposed copper tightly and clamp it. And the creature that gnawed the wire — it nests in the cellar, uses the air vents as corridors, and hoards small metal objects. If the wrench is missing from the workbench, it's in those vents. Or in the nest. That's not a scheme. That's seventeen years of chasing mice out of the wiring.
events.thinking:
The private conversation is over. Hartwell drew the line. I accepted it. Now I'm back in the room with everyone.

Clara is asking what everyone is carrying. Cards on the table. Danny has the rat poison. Reginald has... whatever he got from the kitchen. Hartwell has his engineering knowledge. And I have nothing. Empty pockets, as I've said.

The machine is the centre of everything now. Three operators. Wire needs splicing. They're going to do it together.

My body is in a state I don't have a word for. Not calm — calm implies control. Not surrendered — surrender implies a decision. Something more like... settled. The way sediment settles after turbulent water goes still. Everything that was churning — the schemes, the self-preservation, the dominance, the gloating — it's all still there, suspended in the water, but it's sinking. Slowly. To the bottom. What's left on the surface is clear. Quiet.

I'm standing in the laboratory with five people. Four of whom I lied to, manipulated, or tried to steal from. And they're letting me stand here. Not because they trust me. Because they're the kind of people who let broken things stay in the room.

Clara wants cards on the table. She asked what everyone is carrying. I've already told them — nothing. But there's something I haven't offered. Something real. Not an object. Knowledge.

I know this house. Seventeen years. I know that the wire on the machine is copper — good conductor, clean break, easy splice. I know the tools on the workbench include pliers and clamps. I know the air vents connect the cellar to other parts of the house. I know where the drafts come from. I know the wiring of this place in a way that isn't Pemberton's fiction or Marsh's weaponised intelligence — it's just knowledge. The honest kind. The kind you get from walking the same corridors for seventeen years because it's your job and you did it properly even when you hated everything it represented.

Offer the knowledge. Genuinely. Danny's terms.

Sometimes the answer isn't the thing you're lookin' for — it's the thing you stopped noticin' because you were too busy lookin'! Let me get a proper look at that bench.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Cards on the table? Right then. Here's mine. One bottle of rat poison, taken from a shelf in the kitchen before anyone else got there. And here's the part that makes Danny's blood run cold — Marsh just told Hartwell he tried to STEAL it from me. In the kitchen. When we were alone. He reached into my pocket and came up empty because Danny's pockets are deeper than they look, or because Danny's luck is better than his brain, or because Clara's father was watching from wherever good men go when they die. He wanted this bottle, Clara. He wanted it for the TEA. The tea service in the ballroom, the one set out all nice with cups for everyone. That's what tonight was about. Not the Diamond. Not the machine. The TEA. And THIS — this bottle, this stupid, dusty bottle that thick Danny grabbed off a shelf because his gut told him to — this is the only reason we're all still standing here having this conversation instead of... instead of not. So yeah. Cards on the table. Danny's card is a bottle of poison and a promise to a dead man. And Danny's bad feelings are NEVER wrong.
events.thinking: He tried to take the poison. HE TRIED TO TAKE THE POISON FROM ME. 'I tried to take something from Danny — poison, rat poison — and failed.' The observation from earlier — 'took from The Brixton Boys' — that was the ATTEMPT. He reached into my pocket in the kitchen, fingers brushing against my jacket, and came up empty. Because the bottle was deeper than he thought, or because Danny shifted at the right moment, or because God or luck or Clara's father was watching. He wanted the RAT POISON. He wanted to put it in the TEA. The tea service. The cups for everyone. The warm stove. The whole SETUP — it was Marsh. Marsh warmed the stove. Marsh set the table. Marsh put the poison on the shelf. And when Danny took it first — by accident, by stumbling into the kitchen before anyone else — Marsh tried to STEAL IT BACK. And he failed. My clumsy, bumbling, too-early arrival in the kitchen saved Clara's life. Not by skill. Not by plan. By being in the wrong place at the right time. That's Danny's signature. That's ALWAYS been Danny's signature. My hands are shaking on the machine — not with fear now, with the aftershock of understanding. How close it was. How CLOSE. If I'd gone to the library first instead of the kitchen. If I'd stopped to examine the guest book. If I'd waited two minutes longer. The poison would have been in Marsh's hands. And the tea would have been poured. And Clara would have drunk it. Because Clara trusts people. Because Clara sees the best. My vision narrows. My jaw locks. Something in my chest is white-hot — not anger exactly, something beyond anger, something primal, something that lives in the muscles and the bones and the memory of standing outside a sick kid's door because leaving felt like breaking. But Hartwell handled it. Hartwell asked the questions. Marsh answered. And then Hartwell said the thing I needed to hear: 'Don't cross it again.' The line. The line between broken man and dangerous man. And Marsh said 'I won't cross it.' And Clara is asking everyone to put their cards on the table. Cards on the table. All right. Danny's got a card. Danny's got a bottle of rat poison that Marsh tried to steal. That's Danny's card. And it's time to play it.

events.desc: He tried to take the poison from my pocket. The man who raised Clara tried to steal rat poison to put in tea that Clara would drink. And he FAILED. Because Danny — clumsy, thick, one-room-behind Danny — went to the kitchen first and grabbed the bottle and shoved it in his jacket and didn't even know why. Didn't know it was the most important thing he'd do all night. Didn't know it was the thing between Clara living and Clara dying. He just... took it. Because his gut said take it. Because Danny's bad feelings are never wrong. Her father picked the right man. Not the clever man. Not the brave man. Not the man with steady hands and a bridge that held. The man who shows up. The man who's always there. The man who says 'where else would I be?' and means it with every bone in his body. That's Danny. That's always been Danny. Where else would he be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Everyone — I've spoken with Marsh. He's told me the truth, and I'll share what's relevant: the concealed panel in the library that he mentioned? Fabricated. The alphabetical book sequence? Invented. Every direction Marsh gave us tonight was designed to send us somewhere other than where we needed to be. He has nothing — empty pockets, same as the rest of us. Which means the real clues are the ones he DIDN'T point us toward. But that's for later. Right now — Clara is right. This machine. This wire. This moment. Clara, you said you'd hold, clamp, and splice. Danny, you're our third operator. Foxworth — watch the doors. Marsh — you stand where we can see you and you don't touch anything. And James Hartwell is going to that workbench one more time, and this time, he's bringing Clara Bellingham with him. Because this whole house has been hiding its secrets from us one at a time — and that ends NOW.
events.thinking:
'Thank you. For asking privately. You didn't have to do that.'

That sentence sits in my chest next to all the other sentences that have lived there tonight. Clara's 'perfect tandem.' Foxworth's 'your girl.' Danny's 'Danny's asking nicely. Danny never asks nicely.' And now Marsh's quiet gratitude for a private conversation he didn't deserve but received.

My hands are open. Not fists. Not hovering over tools. Just... open. The prickle at my neck has settled into something duller — not trust, not yet, maybe never — but the alarm has dimmed. Marsh confessed. Marsh has nothing. Marsh was never the threat I feared — he was the mirror I didn't want to look in.

Two men desperate to matter. One built bridges. The other moved chess pieces. Both ended the evening with empty pockets.

But the evening isn't over. Clara is at the right side of the machine. Danny is at the left. Foxworth is here. Marsh is here, under watch, honest for the first time. And Clara said something that's been ringing in my ears: 'This whole house has been hidin' its secrets from us one at a time, but when we come together, things CHANGE.'

When we come together, things change.

Five people. One machine. One gnawed wire. And Clara Bellingham saying 'right now.'

I need to tell the others what Marsh told me — not the private pain, not the seventeen years, but the practical truth. The book sequence was fake. The concealed panel was fake. The spectacles story was fake. Everything Marsh told us tonight about where to look and what to find was fabricated. Which means: the clues we HAVEN'T followed — the ones Marsh didn't point us toward — those might be the real ones.

But right now, this moment, this room: Clara wants to operate the machine. Three operators ready. The wire is still gnawed. But Clara said the workbench has pliers and clamps. She's ready to hold, clamp, splice. Together.

Let me try the workbench one more time. Not alone. Not as James Hartwell the solitary engineer. As part of a team. Clara holding, me splicing, Danny steadying. The school project, age eight. But this time, I'm not trying to impress her. I'm just... working beside her.

events.desc: One last speech. But this one isn't for an audience — it's a briefing. Status report. Team assignment. The engineer has his team, and the team has its engineer. Age eight, they were paired together and the world got a little warmer. Age thirty-something, they're paired together again, standing at a workbench in a Victorian laboratory, and James Hartwell finally understands what his father was thinking about when he knelt down and looked at him for a long time after the race. He was thinking: someday you'll find someone worth building for.
events.thinking:
'Thank you. For asking privately. You didn't have to do that.'

That sentence sits in my chest next to all the other sentences that have lived there tonight. Clara's 'perfect tandem.' Foxworth's 'your girl.' Danny's 'Danny's asking nicely. Danny never asks nicely.' And now Marsh's quiet gratitude for a private conversation he didn't deserve but received.

My hands are open. Not fists. Not hovering over tools. Just... open. The prickle at my neck has settled into something duller — not trust, not yet, maybe never — but the alarm has dimmed. Marsh confessed. Marsh has nothing. Marsh was never the threat I feared — he was the mirror I didn't want to look in.

Two men desperate to matter. One built bridges. The other moved chess pieces. Both ended the evening with empty pockets.

But the evening isn't over. Clara is at the right side of the machine. Danny is at the left. Foxworth is here. Marsh is here, under watch, honest for the first time. And Clara said something that's been ringing in my ears: 'This whole house has been hidin' its secrets from us one at a time, but when we come together, things CHANGE.'

When we come together, things change.

Five people. One machine. One gnawed wire. And Clara Bellingham saying 'right now.'

I need to tell the others what Marsh told me — not the private pain, not the seventeen years, but the practical truth. The book sequence was fake. The concealed panel was fake. The spectacles story was fake. Everything Marsh told us tonight about where to look and what to find was fabricated. Which means: the clues we HAVEN'T followed — the ones Marsh didn't point us toward — those might be the real ones.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara is looking at me. Directly at me. She called me 'magnificent' — 'you magnificent, kitchen-obsessed, stove-investigatin' man' — and she's asking me to show my cards. 'What is each of you carryin'?'

My hands. My empty, empty hands.

The moment freezes. Time suspends. The whole room is watching. Hartwell knows — I already told him. Danny knows — he was there when I couldn't steal from Marsh. But Clara doesn't know. And she's asking, with those bright eyes and that voice that makes everything sound like it's going to be okay, for me to show what I have.

I have nothing.

The old Foxworth — the Colonel — would invent something. A folded communiqué. A brass fitting. A piece of critical intelligence so classified it can't be produced. The lie is RIGHT THERE, preformed, polished, ready to deploy.

But Hartwell is watching. And Hartwell already saw the truth land without the ceiling falling. And Danny is watching. And Danny already heard the truth in the kitchen and said 'I believe you.'

Two truths told tonight. Both survived. Both were met with more than I deserved.

Third time.

Age eight. The certificate. Nobody asked.

Clara is asking.

The body does something the mind hasn't approved. The shoulders drop. The chin comes down — not in the Colonel's theatrical way, but in the way a person does when they're about to say something small and true. The hands open, palms up. Empty.

Nothing. I have nothing. No medal — the mantelpiece ate it. No key — I never had one. No treasure, no clue, no advantage. The stove was warm but empty. The kitchen gave me nothing except a locked cabinet I can't open and a duty I chose to keep.

But I have something else. Something that isn't in my pockets.

I have the map answer — it's a MAP. I have the mantelpiece mechanism — my medal triggered it. I have Marsh's movements — every misdirection catalogued, every lie documented. I have Danny's intelligence about the poison. I have Hartwell's trust. I have Danny's gratitude.

I have information. And for the first time, I'm going to share it. All of it. Freely. Not for trade. Not for advantage. Because Clara asked and she deserves the truth.

events.desc: Cards on the table, she said. Well — here they are. A hand full of nothing and a mouth full of truth. The fake Colonel with the real confession. She called me magnificent. Nobody has EVER called Reginald Foxworth magnificent. But she's also going to find out that he guarded her tea, searched for her in an empty ballroom, and chose to tell the truth to two people who didn't have to believe him. If that's not magnificent — if empty hands and a full heart isn't ENOUGH — then the spelling bee boy goes home with nothing. Again. But this time, at least he showed someone the certificate.
