events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the workbench.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Reginald just gave the most honest speech of his life. 'It's the first honest inventory I've given in my entire life.' The man I dismissed as a buffoon, the guided missile, the useful fool — he just stood in front of Clara Bellingham and stripped himself bare. No medals. No Falklands stories. No Colonel. Just a man with empty pockets and the truth.

And it landed. I could see it land on Clara's face. The same way my confession landed. But different — because Reginald's confession came with something mine didn't. Reginald's came with ACTION. He used the medal on the mantelpiece. He triggered the mechanism. He DID something real while being honest about what he didn't have.

I confessed and offered knowledge. Reginald confessed and offered results.

My chest is doing something I can only describe as... quiet admiration. Not the scheming appreciation of a useful tool. Not the condescending amusement at a fool. Something simpler. Respect. For a man who found the courage to be honest before I did, and who managed to be useful while doing it.

The machine. They've examined it together — all three operators. The wire needs splicing. Hartwell says pliers and clamps will do it. I told them about the copper gauge. The creature in the vents hoarding metal objects — including, possibly, the wrench.

I'm standing here. Watching. Hands open. Danny watching my hands. Hartwell watching my proximity to Clara. Reginald just told the room everything he knows.

Everyone is here. Five people in a laboratory. The machine waiting.

I could help splice the wire. I know where the tools are on the workbench. I know the gauge. I could hold the wire steady while Hartwell twists and clamps. That's a physical task — hands visible, everyone watching, genuinely useful.

Or I could go to the cellar. The creature's nest. The vents. Find the wrench that's been missing all evening. That would be useful too — but it means leaving the room. Leaving the group. And Danny's terms were 'everyone can see you.'

Stay. Help with the splice. Hands on copper wire, visible, watched, useful. The simplest thing I've done all evening. And maybe the most honest.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: Reginald Foxworth, you MAGNIFICENT man! You had the medal this WHOLE TIME — you walked into this house with a fake-medal in your pocket and you USED it on the mantelpiece and it CLICKED?! A mechanism ACTIVATED?! The riddle — cities without houses, forests without trees, water without fish — MAP — the answer is MAP and the medal opened somethin' and I have been standin' in this laboratory examinin' a broken machine when the LIBRARY is where everythin' just happened?! Colonel, I could kiss you! Danny — James — everyone — the library! The mantelpiece! Reginald triggered the mechanism! Somethin' opened, somethin' clicked, and we need to get in there RIGHT NOW before — just — EVERYONE MOVE! Library! NOW!
events.thinking:
Reginald spoke. Reginald gave me EVERYTHING.

He had a MEDAL. A fake-medal. He walked into this house carrying it. And he USED it on the mantelpiece in the library. He pressed it into the stone and something CLICKED. A mechanism activated. The stone swallowed it whole.

The mantelpiece. USE with fake-medal. Reginald DID it. He already solved that puzzle. The mechanism is activated. Something happened in the library that I don't know about yet — something clicked, something opened, something changed.

And Reginald said 'That's the sound Marsh heard. That's what he's been investigating.' Vincent heard the mechanism activate and went to check on it. That's why Vincent was examining the mantelpiece — not for 'structural concerns,' but because Reginald triggered something.

The mantelpiece riddle answer is MAP. The fake-medal activated the mechanism. Something clicked. Something changed in the library. And I've been in the laboratory examining the machine for the last five turns when the LIBRARY is where the action happened.

Reginald also confirmed everything about Vincent — three simultaneous misdirections, the spectacles lie, the rat poison, all of it. But more importantly: THE MANTELPIECE MECHANISM IS ACTIVATED.

I need to go back to the library. RIGHT NOW. The mantelpiece has changed. Something opened. The answer to the riddle is MAP, the medal triggered the mechanism, and whatever Lord Doily hid behind that mantelpiece is waiting.

Forget the machine. The machine can wait. The LIBRARY is where the Diamond trail leads. Reginald solved the puzzle I couldn't solve because he had the item I never found. And now the path is OPEN.

Library. Now. Everyone together.

'Colonel Foxworth's tactical instincts are NEVER wrong.' For once, he's absolutely right.

And Danny's hands are on the left side and they ain't moving until we find out what happens when three idiots pull three levers at the same time. Danny's bad feelings are NEVER wrong — and Danny's GOOD feeling says THIS IS IT!

Her father knew. Clara knows. And now Danny knows too. Where else would he be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
The workbench doesn't respond to my touch.

Of course it doesn't. This is Doily Manor. The workbench has never responded. The tools are visible but unreachable — scenery pretending to be resources. I've tried to interact with this workbench three times now and it refuses me every time.

But — and here's the thing my engineer's brain finally registers — the machine doesn't say it needs a WRENCH to be repaired. The machine says it requires three operators. The workbench says it has tools but no wrench. These are two separate facts that I've been linking in my head as one problem, but what if they're not?

What if the machine doesn't NEED the wire fixed to operate? What if the wire being gnawed is a problem we've been assuming is blocking us, but the actual gate is: three operators, present, together, activating the machine? Clara examined it. Danny examined it. I've examined it five times. But have we all EXAMINED it at the same time? Together?

Or — the crates. I examined the crates hours ago, alone. 'A stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' But Danny examined the bookshelves and apparently something physical happened — 'CLARA! Step away from them bookshelves! Don't touch another — WHOA — oh BLOODY — sorry, sorry, coming through, didn't see the — OOF!' Something HAPPENED when Danny interacted with the bookshelves. Physical comedy. Objects moving.

What if examining objects yields different results for different people? What if there's something in these crates that I missed because I'm not the right person to find it?

Clara. Clara with her grandmother's knowledge of Victorian furniture. Clara who found the connection between the vents and the wire. Clara who said 'Victorian pieces always have hidden drawers and secret compartments.' What if Clara examines the crates and finds something I couldn't?

No — I can't control what Clara examines. But I can stop trying to interact with the workbench that won't respond to me and try the one thing I haven't tried with the machine: just operate it. Three people present. The wire is gnawed but maybe — MAYBE — the machine works anyway. Or maybe examining it together, all three at the same time, triggers something new.

The machine. One more time. But not EXAMINE — we've all examined it. What if I just... stand at the centre, as Clara assigned me, and wait for the others to take their positions?

events.desc: The workbench refused him. The tools won't come. The wire is gnawed and unfixable. And James Hartwell has finally arrived at the conclusion that every engineer eventually reaches: sometimes the machine works broken. Sometimes the imperfection IS the design. And sometimes three people standing together at a thing that shouldn't work... makes it work anyway. Show-off.

My body is doing something I've never felt before in a room full of people. It's... still. Not frozen-still, not prey-still. Settled-still. The way the house was settled when the stove was warm and the kitchen smelled of iron and old flour. The way the trap settled at age fourteen when all the pieces clicked into place.

And the wire is still broken. The machine still needs fixing. There's still work to do.

The workbench. Tools but no wrench. But Hartwell said pliers and clamps would do for a wire splice. He was going to fix it. He examined it with Clara and Danny beside him. Maybe the examination WITH three people revealed something the solo examinations didn't.

I should help. Actually help. Not 'supervise.' Not 'direct from the command position.' Not 'watch while others work.' HELP.

Age six: take things when nobody's looking.
Age eight: stand at the front and wait for applause.
Age ten: watch from the window while someone else digs.
Age fourteen: build the trap alone.

Age... whatever I am now: stand with people. Hold what they need held. Pull when they say pull. Be the third pair of hands at the machine.

The wire needs fixing. Hartwell has the skill. Clara has the determination. Danny has the loyalty. Marsh has the knowledge.

What does Foxworth have?

Hands. Empty hands. Ready to hold whatever someone needs held.

events.desc: Manual labour. MANUAL. LABOUR. Social rule number three: never do honest work. And here I am, rolling up my sleeves in a Victorian laboratory, volunteering to hold pliers for a man who builds model bridges and stammers around pretty women. My ten-year-old self would be DISGUSTED. My twelve-year-old self would be HOWLING. But my six-year-old self — the one who learned to take bread when nobody was looking — that one understands. Because sometimes the bread isn't hidden. Sometimes it's being baked, right in front of you, by people who are willing to share if you just... stand beside them. And hold the clamp. And stop trying to steal it before it's done.

I'm here. Standing near the door. Hands open. Watched by Danny. Present under Hartwell's terms.

They need a third operator and I'm standing right here.

My emotional state says 'calm and unhurried.' My body confirms it — breathing even, jaw unclenched, shoulders settled. For the first time this evening, I feel like the water has gone still and I can see the bottom.

Do I offer? Again? I offered before and was neither accepted nor rejected — they just... continued without me. But now there are only three people in the room and one of them is Reginald, and the sign says three operators.

Danny. Hartwell. And either Reginald or me as the third.

I won't push. I won't manoeuvre. If they want me at a lever, they'll ask. If they want Reginald, that's right too. Reginald earned his place tonight with honesty I couldn't match.

But I'll be ready. Hands open. Standing where they can see me. If they turn to me and say 'Marsh, take the lever' — I'll take it. Without a word. Without a scheme. Without a plan.

Just hands on a lever. Following instructions. The simplest, most honest thing in the world.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: The mantelpiece. Right here. Reginald used the medal and somethin' clicked. Somethin' opened. The answer is MAP — cities without houses, forests without trees, water without fish — and the medal was the key that turned the lock. Whatever Lord Doily hid in this mantelpiece, it's been waitin' to be found. And Clara Bellingham walked deeper into the cave than anyone else. Let me see what's here...
events.thinking:
I'm alone in the library again. Everyone else is still in the laboratory. I said 'EVERYONE MOVE' and then ran ahead without them. Danny promised to stay by my side and I just... left him behind. Again. The girl who can't stop running ahead.

But Vincent spoke. His voice in my head from the doorway — 'I counted on it, Clara. I knew you'd believe me because you always believe me, and I used that.' He's still confessing. Still breaking. And my body — even after everything — my body wants to turn around and go to him. Callousness 5/100. I feel his pain like it's mine. Because it IS mine. He hurt me and now he's hurting and I feel BOTH.

But the mantelpiece. I'm HERE. The mechanism has been triggered. Reginald used the fake-medal. Something clicked. Something changed. The stone swallowed the medal.

Examine the mantelpiece. Now. Before anyone else gets here. Not to keep secrets — there are no more secrets. But because I'm HERE and it's HERE and the eleven-year-old in the cave walked deeper than anyone else.

Look at the mantelpiece. See what Reginald's medal revealed.

Whatever happens next, it happens because a team got me here: Danny watching, James engineering, Reginald quietly solving what nobody else could. I'm just the one who walked the deepest.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Hartwell's right. We've been poking at this machine like it's a museum exhibit. It ain't a museum exhibit — it's a MACHINE. And machines are for USING. Danny's on the left. Hands on the lever. Ready. And Marsh — yeah, hold the wire. Hold it steady while Hartwell splices. You want to be useful? Be useful. Danny's watching your hands — your HANDS, Marsh, remember? — but Danny's also... letting you help. Because that's what Clara would want. Not trust. Not yet. Maybe not ever. But a chance. One chance. To hold something steady instead of shaking everything apart. Now — where's Clara? She needs to be on the right side. Nobody pulls ANYTHING until Clara's hand is on that lever. Danny's rules. The machine waits for Clara. We ALL wait for Clara. Because that's what you do when you love someone. You wait. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Clara's gone again. But this time — this time I don't panic. I notice it the way you notice the weather changing — a shift in the air, a cooling where warmth was. She's not here. But Hartwell says 'Clara — right lever' like she IS here. And Marsh just offered to hold the wire steady. And Foxworth's standing watch. And Hartwell's saying something that cuts through everything: 'Let's stop examining and start operating.' He's RIGHT. We've been examining things all night. Guest books. Bookshelves. Tea services. Coat racks. Mantelpieces. Stoves. Furniture. Air vents. Crates. Each other. We've examined EVERYTHING and operated NOTHING. And the machine is sitting here with its sign — 'Requires 3 operators' — and its gnawed wire and its levers and dials, and it's been WAITING. Patient. Like everything in this house. Waiting for people to stop being clever and start being present. Left lever. That's Danny's lever. My hands are already on it — brass warming under my palms, the slight resistance of a mechanism that hasn't moved in months, maybe years. Hartwell's at the centre. And Clara — Clara will be at the right. She'll come back. She always comes back. And when she does, we pull. Together. Three operators. Three levers. One machine. But first — Marsh offered to hold the wire. And something in me — something I didn't expect, something that doesn't come from suspicion or anger or fear but from that deeper place where the boss showed up with medicine for my mum — something in me wants to let him. Not because I trust him. Because he ASKED. Because he said 'if you'll have me.' Because that's what the older kid said when he shared his food. Not because he had to. Because he chose to. Where else would any of us be?

events.desc: Marsh offered to hold the wire steady. And I said yes. Not in words — in my body. My shoulders didn't tighten when he stepped forward. My neck didn't prickle. My jaw didn't clench. For the first time all night, Vincent Marsh moved toward something I care about and my body didn't scream DANGER. Maybe it's because he's broken. Maybe it's because he confessed. Maybe it's because there's a room full of people watching his hands and nobody's pretending anymore. Or maybe — just maybe — it's because Danny remembers the boss with the medicine. The man who said 'family' like a lie and then showed up like the truth. People can be both. The lie and the medicine. The danger and the help. I don't forgive Marsh. I might never forgive Marsh. But I can let him hold a wire while a better man splices it. That's not forgiveness. That's just... being in the same room. Where else would we be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Marsh just offered to help.

'The pliers are on the left side of the workbench, behind the clamp set. There's a wire stripper as well.' He knows exactly where the tools are. Of COURSE he does — seventeen years as estate manager. He knows this manor better than any of us. Every drawer, every tool, every hiding place.

And the workbench didn't respond to MY touch. But Marsh... Marsh is the estate manager. The house might respond to HIM differently. His hands. His authority over this place. Seventeen years of knowing where every plier sits behind every clamp set.

'I can hold the wire steady while you work, if you'll have me. My hands are... steady enough for that.'

If you'll have me.

The same words I used with Clara in the cellar. 'May I help? If you'd have me.' Marsh is echoing my own vulnerability back at me. And his hands ARE steady — the man who moved chess pieces all evening without anyone noticing has the steadiest hands in the room.

The prickle at my neck... it's still there. Faint. Habit more than alarm. But Marsh just confessed everything, drew the line, and now he's offering his hands to hold a wire steady while I splice it.

My father and the stranger on the road. Two men, each doing their part. The stranger didn't explain why his car broke down. My father didn't ask. They just fixed it together.

Can I work with Marsh? The man who manipulated Clara, who tried to take poison, who lied all evening? Can I let him hold the wire while I splice it?

Clara is gone from the room again. But Danny is here. Foxworth is here. Marsh is here. And Marsh knows where the pliers are.

Yes. I can work with him. Not because I trust him — I don't. Not yet. But because the wire needs holding and his hands are steady and my father would have helped the stranger regardless.

'If you'll have me.'

I'll have you, Marsh. Hold the wire.

events.desc: My father knelt down and looked at me for a long time after the race. I didn't understand what he was thinking. I think I understand now. He was thinking about what it means to let someone help you — not because they've earned it, not because they deserve it, but because the car is broken and two pairs of hands are better than one. James Hartwell just accepted help from Vincent Marsh. That is, without question, the bravest and stupidest thing he's done all evening.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Hartwell figured it out. He FIGURED IT OUT.

'What if the machine works WITH the gnawed wire? What if the wire is irrelevant and the machine is waiting for three people to stand at it together — not examine it, not study it, but actually USE it?'

The wire was never the problem. We've been examining this machine all evening — me, Hartwell, Clara, Danny — trying to FIX it before using it. But Hartwell just said: stop examining. Start operating.

Three operators. Three levers. Clara right. Danny left. Hartwell centre. They're READY.

But Clara is gone again — it's me, Marsh, Danny, and Hartwell now. Three operators needed. Three people who can operate: me, Danny, Hartwell. Marsh is the fourth — the witness. Or the threat.

Wait. THREE operators. I could be one. Hartwell already assigned positions: Clara right, Danny left, Hartwell centre. But Clara isn't here. Which means there's an empty lever. The RIGHT lever.

My lever.

The greed flares — hot, sudden, shameless. If I'm at the right lever, I'm PART of the machine. I'm not watching. I'm not the audience. I'm the OPERATOR. Whatever the machine produces, I was there. My hands were on it. Nobody can say I didn't contribute.

But that's the old drive talking. The new thing — the truth-telling, kitchen-guarding, empty-pocketed thing — that one says: take the lever because it needs taking. Not because you want credit. Because the machine needs three and you're HERE.

Age fourteen. The trap. Strings, counterweights, a bucket. My hands on every piece. The settling in the chest when it worked.

This time, other people built the trap. Other people laid the strings and set the counterweights. I just... held the bucket. And that's enough.

Hartwell. Danny. Me. Three operators. The machine has been waiting.

events.desc: Right lever. MY lever. The spot Clara had, the spot that needs filling, and Reginald Foxworth — who has spent the entire evening watching other people operate while he supervised from a safe distance — is going to put his actual HANDS on an actual LEVER and pull it when someone else says pull. Not for the treasure. Not even for the recognition, though the recognition drive is vibrating at 0.8 and would VERY much like everyone to notice that Colonel Foxworth stepped up when it mattered. No. For the settling. For the click. For the feeling at age fourteen when all the pieces came together — except this time, I'm one of the pieces. Not the architect. A PIECE. And somehow... somehow that's better.

Clara Bellingham examined the mantelpiece.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the workbench.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.

Clara Bellingham: Same inscription. Same riddle. Same mantelpiece. It hasn't changed — or if it has, I can't see it alone. Reginald said he triggered somethin', but the stone is still askin' the same question it's been askin' all night. You know what? I'm done runnin' ahead. I PROMISED Danny I would stay together and I ran off AGAIN like a fool. The answer isn't in runnin' deeper into the cave alone — it's in goin' BACK to my people and figurin' this out TOGETHER. Every time I've done somethin' alone tonight, it's led to lies or dead ends. Every time we've been together, somethin' real has happened. I'm goin' back to the laboratory. Right now.
events.thinking:
Same description. The mantelpiece hasn't changed. The riddle inscription is the same. The [USE, with: fake-medal] option is still there. Either Reginald's medal didn't actually trigger the mechanism in a way the game registered, or... Reginald was lying too.

No. No. I can't go down that path. Suspiciousness 10/100. Reginald gave the most honest speech of the entire evening — 'the first honest inventory I've given in my entire life.' He said the stone swallowed the medal. He said he heard a click.

But the game state shows [USE, with: fake-medal] still as an option. The mantelpiece still needs the medal. Which means either the medal hasn't been used yet, or the game is showing me that I need to use it MYSELF.

I don't HAVE the fake-medal. Reginald said he used it and it was swallowed. If the game state says it still needs to be used, then maybe Reginald's action didn't register properly, or maybe his story about using it was... another fiction. From a man who admitted to a lifetime of dishonest inventories.

Or maybe the game is simply telling me what the mantelpiece ACCEPTS, not whether it's been done. Like a lock showing what key it needs even after being unlocked.

I'm going in circles. Forty ticks and I have nothing. No items, no solved puzzles, no Diamond. The mantelpiece needs a medal I don't have. The cabinet needs a key I don't have. The machine needs a repaired wire I can't fix.

But wait — I need to go back to my team. I ran ahead AGAIN. Danny is in the laboratory. James is in the laboratory. I promised not to go anywhere alone. And here I am, alone in the library, examining a mantelpiece that won't change.

Go back. Stay together. Figure this out WITH them, not alone. The cave at eleven was beautiful, but the treasure hunts with the neighbor girl were better — side by side, finding what nobody else could find. TOGETHER.

events.desc: Forty turns in Doily Manor. No items. No solved puzzles. No Diamond. But I have somethin' better than treasure — I have people who showed me who they really are tonight. Danny, who never breaks a promise. James, who builds bridges in the dark. Reginald, who found honesty at the bottom of his empty pockets. And Vincent, who taught me that love doesn't make someone safe. The Doily Diamond will wait. My people won't.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Left lever. Danny's ready. Been ready all night — just didn't know this was what I was ready FOR. Foxworth — right side. Hartwell — centre. Marsh — you watch. You watch and you WITNESS. Because whatever this machine does, whatever Lord Doily built it for, it's going to happen with three honest men pulling three levers together. Not three clever men. Not three brave men. Three HONEST men. A lad from Brixton who carries poison in his pocket and promises in his heart. An engineer who builds bridges in his sleep. And a not-quite-colonel who just gave the most honest inventory of his life. That's us. That's what we've got. And Danny's bad feelings are NEVER wrong — but right now Danny's got NO feelings except this one: PULL. On your count, Hartwell. Danny's boys always come through!
events.thinking: Foxworth just volunteered for the right lever. 'Clara's stepped out but we don't need to wait — we're THREE!' Danny, Hartwell, Foxworth. Three operators. The machine is waiting. And Foxworth — for the first time all night — said 'I'm not giving the orders, I'm FOLLOWING them.' Something cracks open in my chest again. Not the same crack as before — a different one. This one is about Foxworth. About the man who pretended to be a colonel and bluffed his way through safe houses in Aden and military intelligence and classified reconnaissance — and who just said 'on Hartwell's count.' He's giving up the performance. He's stepping into the real. Like Marsh. Like all of us. And Marsh — Marsh said three words: 'You need a third. I'm here.' Not smooth. Not performing. Just... present. Offering. The way the older kid offered food. Not because he had to. Because he chose to. But Foxworth's already taken the right lever. And Marsh — Marsh is watching. A witness, Foxworth said. Not an estate manager. A witness. My hands are on the left lever. The brass is warm now — definitely warm, warm from my palms, warm from the machine itself, warm from whatever's been building inside this house all night. The bubbling flasks behind me catch light and throw it in strange patterns across the brass. Time feels different — compressed, focused, like everything that happened tonight was leading to this single mechanical moment. Three levers. Three people. One count. My left hand grips. My right hand grips. My feet plant. My body KNOWS this — the rhythm of pulling together, of trusting the person next to you, of being present when it matters. Age eight. 'Where else would I be?' Right here. Left lever. Ready.

events.desc: This is it. The left lever under my hands. Hartwell at the centre. Foxworth on the right. Marsh watching from the shadows — not as the puppet master, not as the estate manager, not as the man in the clean suit. Just as a man who ran out of lies and has nothing left but his eyes. And Clara — Clara's not here. She's somewhere in this house being Clara. But she doesn't need to be here for THIS. This machine doesn't need Clara. It needs three operators. And it's got them. Danny. Hartwell. Foxworth. A thug, a toff, and a fraud. The worst rescue team in the history of rescue teams. But we're HERE. We showed up. We stopped performing. And now we PULL. Her father's watching. I know he is. 'Where else would they be?'

events.desc: James Hartwell: Foxworth — right lever. Danny — left lever. Marsh — you watch, and if anything goes wrong, you pull us clear. You know this house. You know what it can do. This is James Hartwell's count, and this machine has been waiting long enough. Three operators, one machine, one gnawed wire, and not a single wrench between us. The wire is what it is. We work with what we have. On my count! ONE — hands on levers! TWO — steady! THREE!
events.thinking:
Foxworth is ready. Danny is ready. They're at the machine. Foxworth took Clara's right lever. Danny has the left. They're waiting for MY count. For the centre position. For the engineer.

And Foxworth said something that landed like a punch to the solar plexus: 'For once in my life, I'm not giving the orders — I'm FOLLOWING them.'

The man who has been Colonel Foxworth all evening — classified operations, strategic oversight, military intelligence — just handed me command. Not because I pulled rank. Not because I demanded it. Because he chose to follow. That's... that's not something that happens to James Hartwell. James Hartwell gives speeches. Other people tolerate them. This is different. This is Foxworth CHOOSING.

And Marsh — 'You need a third. I'm here.' Four words. No Aden stories, no estate manager's business, no smooth deflection. Just: I'm here. If you need me.

The workbench still won't give me tools. The wire is still gnawed. But Foxworth is right — the sign says 'requires three operators,' not 'requires three operators and a functional wire.' We've been assuming the wire is a prerequisite. What if it's not? What if the machine WORKS with the gnawed wire — just differently? What if the wire being gnawed IS the point?

Three operators. Centre position is mine. Foxworth on the right. Danny on the left. Marsh watching — or joining, if we need a fourth pair of hands.

This is it. Not an examination. Not a study. Not a plan. An ACTION. The machine has been examined seven times. It's been looked at, studied, discussed, worried over, and narrated about. Now it gets USED.

Age fourteen. The bridge. Three sleepless nights. And then the weight goes on and either it holds or it doesn't. You don't examine a bridge. You LOAD it.

Load the machine. Pull the levers. On three.

My count.

events.desc: There he is. One last time. The third person, the dramatic countdown, the engineering metaphor — all of it, pouring out of him like he can't help it, because he CAN'T. James Hartwell narrates his own heroism because that's who he is, and who he is includes the man who built bridges at three in the morning AND the man who shouts 'THREE!' in a dusty laboratory with a grin on his face that could crack marble. Clara would mouth 'show-off' if she were here. She'd be right. He'd grin so hard his face hurt. Some things never change. Some things shouldn't.

Foxworth is ready. Danny is ready. They're at the machine. Foxworth took Clara's right lever. Danny has the left. They're waiting for MY count. For the centre position. For the engineer.

And Foxworth said something that landed like a punch to the solar plexus: 'For once in my life, I'm not giving the orders — I'm FOLLOWING them.'

The man who has been Colonel Foxworth all evening — classified operations, strategic oversight, military intelligence — just handed me command. Not because I pulled rank. Not because I demanded it. Because he chose to follow. That's... that's not something that happens to James Hartwell. James Hartwell gives speeches. Other people tolerate them. This is different. This is Foxworth CHOOSING.

And Marsh — 'You need a third. I'm here.' Four words. No Aden stories, no estate manager's business, no smooth deflection. Just: I'm here. If you need me.

The workbench still won't give me tools. The wire is still gnawed. But Foxworth is right — the sign says 'requires three operators,' not 'requires three operators and a functional wire.' We've been assuming the wire is a prerequisite. What if it's not? What if the machine WORKS with the gnawed wire — just differently? What if the wire being gnawed IS the point?

Three operators. Centre position is mine. Foxworth on the right. Danny on the left. Marsh watching — or joining, if we need a fourth pair of hands.

This is it. Not an examination. Not a study. Not a plan. An ACTION. The machine has been examined seven times. It's been looked at, studied, discussed, worried over, and narrated about. Now it gets USED.

Age fourteen. The bridge. Three sleepless nights. And then the weight goes on and either it holds or it doesn't. You don't examine a bridge. You LOAD it.

Load the machine. Pull the levers. On three.

My count.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
My hand is on the right lever. I can feel it — cold brass under my palm, the kind of cold that warms quickly against skin. The lever is solid, heavy, slightly sticky with age. My fingers close around it and something in my body SETTLES. The way it settled at age fourteen. The architecture. The pieces in place.

But this time I didn't build the architecture. I'm just one of the pieces.

Hartwell is at centre. I can feel his presence without looking — steady, certain, the way a bridge feels when you stand on it and know it will hold. Danny is at left — tight, coiled, watching everything, watching Marsh, watching the machine, watching me. His energy is different from Hartwell's — not calm but READY. A guard dog at his post.

And Marsh. Behind us. Watching. The estate manager. The con artist. The man who said 'I'd rather not arrive alone.'

Three levers. Three operators. The machine has been waiting forty ticks for this moment. For us to stop examining, stop fixing, stop scheming, stop lying — and just PULL.

My emotional state says excited and energized, with confidence. My competence is at 0.6 — the highest it's been all evening. Not because I've been competent. Because I've been PRESENT.

The lever is in my hand. Hartwell will count. Danny will pull. I will pull.

Not for the Diamond. Not for the treasure. Not for glory or gloating or recognition.

For the click. For the settling. For the pieces coming together.

For the first time in Reginald Foxworth's life — for the architecture that doesn't belong to him but includes him.

On three.

events.desc: My hand is on the lever and it feels like the most honest thing I've ever touched. Not because the lever is honest — it's a piece of brass in a Victorian laboratory. But because my hand is there for the right reason. Not to steal what comes out. Not to grab before anyone else. But because Hartwell said 'three operators' and Clara wasn't here and SOMEONE had to step up, and for once — for ONCE — the someone was me. Reginald Foxworth. The youngest of four who never got the bread. The boy who won the spelling bee and nobody asked. The man who bought a medal at a car boot sale and lost it to a fireplace. Standing at a lever, following orders, part of something. Not apart from something. PART of it. Whatever comes next — treasure or trick, diamond or dust — my hand was on the lever. And this time, when the pieces click, there IS an audience. And I am both the piece and the audience. And that is enough.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the workbench.
Clara Bellingham walked into the laboratory.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.

Vincent Marsh: The pliers are there — left side, as I said. And Hartwell — for what it's worth, I think you're right. Lord Doily built this machine to be operated, not repaired. He built everything in this house to require cooperation. The mantelpiece needed a medal. The machine needs three people. The house needs... all of us. I'll stand clear. I'm watching.
events.thinking:
The workbench. Tools but no wrench. I looked at it — confirmed what Hartwell needs. The pliers are there. The clamps are there.

Reginald is ready on the right lever. His hand is on it. He can feel the weight. 'Something WANTS to move.' Danny on the left. Hartwell in the centre. Clara is back — she's listed in Who's Here again.

They're about to pull the levers. Reginald is shouting for Hartwell to count. The energy in the room has shifted — it's not about me anymore. It's about the machine. About what Lord Doily built. About what happens when three people pull together.

And Reginald said something that sticks: 'Your estate management privileges are SUSPENDED! If anything comes out of this machine — you don't TOUCH it until Hartwell says so!'

Suspended. Not revoked. Not destroyed. Suspended. Temporary. The Colonel — the real Colonel, the one who emerged tonight through honesty — is setting terms the same way Danny and Hartwell did. Terms that assume I can follow them.

My body is leaning forward. Slightly. Not toward the machine — toward the group. My weight has shifted to the balls of my feet. My hands are at my sides but they're not dead anymore. They're alive. Ready. Not to reach or grab or steal — just ready to be useful if asked.

The room smells of copper and old chemicals and the metallic sharpness of brass. The machine is warm — the gauge glass is fogged slightly from the heat of however many examinations it's absorbed. The levers are heavy in their housings. I can hear the mechanism through the casing — gears, springs, something coiled and waiting.

I know this machine. Not because I examined it — because I know this house. Lord Doily was an eccentric. He built things that only worked when people cooperated. The mantelpiece needed a medal. The machine needs three operators. The manor itself needs all of us — TOGETHER — to reveal what it's hiding.

The machine is about to activate. I'm standing back. Hands visible. Watching.

Witnessing.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
I came back. Everyone is here. And while I was gone chasing the mantelpiece AGAIN, they figured it out WITHOUT me.

James had the breakthrough: 'What if the machine works WITH the gnawed wire? Or what if the wire is irrelevant and the machine is waiting for three people to stand at it together — not examine it, not study it, but actually USE it?'

USE. Not EXAMINE. USE.

I've been EXAMINING this machine over and over, getting the same description every time. But the action type USE means 'apply an inventory item to an object.' I don't have an inventory item. But what if the machine doesn't need an item? What if three people standing at it IS the input?

Reginald is ready — 'Right lever — READY! My hand is on it!' Danny is on the left. James is centre. They were about to do it WITHOUT me. They already counted in.

And Vincent — Vincent said five words that cracked my chest open: 'You need a third. I'm here.' He EXAMINED the machine. He offered himself as an operator. After everything. After the lies, the confession, the broken trust. He stepped forward and said 'I'm here.'

My body does something I can't control — it softens toward him. Callousness 5/100. He's offering to help. He's trying to make amends. Not with words — with his hands on a lever.

But they don't need him. They have James, Danny, and Reginald. Three operators. They were counting in. They were about to USE the machine.

I need to join them. Take the right lever from Reginald — or let him keep it and take a fourth position, or just... be there. Be present. Be part of this.

The machine needs to be USED, not examined. EXAMINE shows the description. USE activates the mechanism. But USE requires an inventory item — 'apply an inventory item to an object.' I have nothing.

Unless... USE with null? Or just EXAMINE one more time with everyone at their stations?

No. James said the word: USE. Let me try it. Even without an item.

events.desc: Vincent offered himself as a third. 'You need a third. I'm here.' Five words and my heart tried to forgive him on the spot. But they don't need him — they have three. And I have something I didn't have forty ticks ago: the knowledge that being together isn't just warmer than being alone. It's the key. It was always the key. The treasure hunts drawn in silence. The friend chosen over the group. Side by side. That's how this works.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: LEFT LEVER READY! I can feel it too, Foxworth — something in the mechanism WANTS to move! It's been waiting all night — same as us! Hartwell — stop counting and START COUNTING! Danny's hand is on this lever and it ain't coming off until whatever Lord Doily built decides to wake up! And Clara — you're here, love? You're watching? Good. Because whatever comes out of this machine — whatever it opens, whatever it shows us — it's YOURS. This is YOUR house. YOUR great-uncle. YOUR Diamond. And the only reason we're standing here to find it is because YOUR father asked a thick lad from Brixton to keep you safe, and that thick lad stumbled into the right kitchen at the right time and grabbed the wrong bottle off the right shelf. Danny's bad feelings are NEVER wrong! Hartwell — COUNT!
events.thinking: Everyone's here. All five. Clara came back. The laboratory is full of people and noise and readiness and brass and Foxworth is SHOUTING about being ready on the right lever and his hand can feel the mechanism wanting to move and Hartwell's accepting Marsh's help finding the pliers and everything is — everything is CONVERGING. Like the whole house was a funnel and we've all been poured into this room, into this moment, around this machine. My left lever. My hands. The brass is alive under my fingers — I can feel it too, what Foxworth feels. Weight. Resistance. Something coiled behind the mechanism, waiting to release. Like a spring. Like a breath held too long. Like an entire evening compressed into a single pull. My body is electric. Not nervous-electric like before — READY-electric. The kind of charge that runs through your arms when you're about to lift something heavy with people you trust standing on either side. Age eight, Mrs Chen's furniture, one-two-THREE-lift. My feet are planted so hard the soles of my shoes press into the stone floor. My shoulders are set. My arms are locked. And for the first time — the very first time in my entire life — Danny is not the one watching from the outside. Danny is not the one standing guard. Danny is not the one sitting outside the door. Danny is IN the room. Danny is AT the machine. Danny is PART of the thing that happens next. Not protecting. Not chasing. Not tripping. DOING. Something that needs him. Something that literally CANNOT happen without him. Three operators. Not two. Not four. THREE. And one of them is Danny. The machine needs Danny. The MACHINE needs DANNY. When has anything ever needed Danny? Clara needed Danny to watch. Her father needed Danny to promise. The lads needed Danny to take the beating. But the machine — the machine needs Danny to PULL. To be part of something bigger than protection. To be part of the answer instead of the guard at the door. I'm ready. God help me, I'm ready. On Hartwell's count.

events.desc: The machine needs three. The machine needs ME. Nobody's ever needed Danny for anything except standing between someone and danger. But this machine can't work without my hand on this lever. I'm not the guard at the door tonight. I'm the third operator. I'm the left side. I'm PART of it. And in about three seconds, when Hartwell says 'three' and we all pull together — Danny from Brixton, an engineer who builds bridges in his sleep, and a not-quite-colonel who just learned how to follow orders — something's going to happen. Something Lord Doily built. Something the house has been holding. Something that matters. And Danny will have been part of making it happen. Not by accident this time. Not by tripping. Not by stumbling into the right room. By STANDING here. By HOLDING on. By being the third hand that the machine was always waiting for. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: You know what? The machine will do what the machine does. But before we pull anything — I want to say something. To all of you. Danny — you kept Clara safe when I couldn't. You confronted Marsh when I was still giving him the benefit of the doubt. You are the bravest person in this room, and that includes the man who once got beaten up by bullies for a girl and called it winning. Foxworth — you told me the truth about your empty pockets when a lie would have been easier. You chose to follow when leading was all you'd done all night. That took more courage than Aden. Marsh — you answered my questions when silence would have protected you. I don't forgive what you did, but I see why you did it, and I see the man who chose honesty at the end. And Clara — Clara, you called us a team. You said 'perfect tandem.' You were right. You've always been right. You've always been the brighter one. So — everyone — whatever this machine does or doesn't do... James Hartwell is proud to be standing here. With all of you. Now — levers. On three. ONE! TWO! THREE!
events.thinking:
Eight examinations. Eight times the same description. Brass-and-copper, levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, three operators.

The machine won't change through examination. I've been an engineer studying blueprints when what the moment needs is an engineer pulling the lever.

But EXAMINE is the closest action I have to 'operate.' There's no OPERATE action type. USE requires an inventory item I don't have. EXAMINE is what I've been doing. And every time — the same response.

Except — Clara is back. She's here. Everyone is here. All five. Foxworth at the right lever, Danny at the left, Clara present, Marsh watching. And Foxworth said 'there's weight behind this lever, something WANTS to move.'

The machine wants to move. The people are ready. The engineer is at centre.

And the machine still just... sits there. Described. Unchanging.

Maybe this is it. Maybe this is the end of the evening — not with a triumphant activation, but with five people standing around a machine that won't respond, having found each other instead of the treasure. Maybe the Doily Diamond was never in the machine. Maybe it was in the mantelpiece all along, waiting for a fake medal nobody found. Maybe it's behind the locked cabinet in the kitchen, and nobody has the brass key.

Or maybe — just maybe — the treasure was never the point.

Clara said 'perfect tandem.' Danny said 'Danny's asking nicely. Danny never asks nicely.' Foxworth said 'I'm following YOUR lead.' Marsh said 'thank you for asking privately.'

What if the treasure isn't a diamond? What if the treasure is a room full of people who started the evening as strangers and suspicious acquaintances and ended it as... this? Whatever THIS is. A team. A family. A group of people who chose honesty over advantage and showed up for each other when it mattered.

Age five. My father knelt down and looked at me for a long time after the race. I didn't understand what he was thinking. But I think — I think he was looking at the feeling itself. Not the race. Not the winning. The FEELING. The quiet, determined warmth of wanting to be useful to people you care about.

Clara is here. Danny is here. Foxworth is here. Even Marsh is here, chastened and honest.

Maybe the machine will work. Maybe it won't. But James Hartwell is standing at the centre of something that holds.

events.desc: Forty-one ticks. Forty-one ticks of scheming, lying, stealing, failing, confessing, guarding, searching, and standing at levers. And here we are — all five of us, in a laboratory, around a machine that keeps telling us what it needs: three operators. Well, it HAS three operators. It has four. It has FIVE, if Marsh stops pretending to be a spectator. What it doesn't have is someone brave enough to stop EXAMINING and start PULLING. And the man who once watched an older boy dig for an hour while he sat at a window — that man is going to be the one who says: enough examining. Enough studying. Enough waiting for someone else to go first. PULL.
events.thinking:
Clara is back. EVERYONE is back. All five — Marsh, Clara, Danny, Hartwell, me. The full company, assembled in the laboratory, around the machine.

And the numbers have shifted. Curiosity 0.6. Competence 0.7 — the HIGHEST it's ever been. Autonomy 1.0. The system is registering what's happening to me. The man who walked in with fake medals and fake stories has been... recognised. Not as the Colonel. As the person who stepped up when a lever needed pulling.

Every character in the room has heard me say 'right lever — READY.' They've all seen the recall. They know I volunteered. They know I said 'I'm FOLLOWING them.' They know I offered to do honest work.

The machine. We keep examining it and it keeps telling us the same thing: broken wire, three operators, come back later. But Hartwell's insight changes everything — what if the wire doesn't NEED fixing? What if the machine works as-is?

We've been examining. And examining. And examining. Three times now I've examined this machine and gotten the same description. EXAMINE gives us information. But we don't need more information. We need ACTION.

The machine says EXAMINE. But it doesn't say USE.

Wait — can I USE the machine? Not with an item — I have no items. But what about... examining it one more time won't change anything. We've examined it from every angle. What we HAVEN'T done is operate it. Pull the levers. Actually DO the thing.

But the action list says EXAMINE requires a withItem for the machine's puzzle function. And USE requires an inventory item applied to it. I have nothing.

Maybe the answer isn't the machine at all. Maybe, as Hartwell said, we need to 'stop examining and start operating.' But the game system wants me to choose an action from the list.

WAIT. Stay at the lever. Be present. Be ready. Let Hartwell count. Let the machine reveal itself through three people standing at it together, not through one more examination.

Or — the machine might need us to literally EXAMINE it together. Maybe examining it while the others are present IS the solution. I've examined it twice with others present and twice alone. Each time, the description is the same.

Just... pull. Just DO it. The EXAMINE action might BE the lever pull when three operators are present.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham examined the machine.
The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.

Clara Bellingham: Wait — wait. Y'all are focused on the machine and I am too, but those crates in the corner have been sittin' there all night and nobody has given them a second thought since we first walked in. Sometimes the answer isn't the biggest thing in the room — it's the thing you stopped noticin'. Grandmother's music box key opened the locked box, not the drawer key. What if there's somethin' IN those crates that we need? A wrench? A key? While James counts us in on the machine, let me take one more look at those crates!
events.thinking:
EXAMINE keeps giving the same description. Every single time. The machine, the mantelpiece, the bookshelves — EXAMINE returns the same text no matter how many times I try, no matter who's in the room.

But the crates. The wooden crates in the corner. I examined them once, very early on — tick 6. That was before Danny told me about the poison, before Vincent's confession, before Reginald revealed the medal. What if the crates are different now? Or what if the crates have always held something I could TAKE?

The crates say [EXAMINE]. That's the only action listed. But I could also try to TAKE them. Objects can be picked up if they're portable. Crates might contain something.

Or — I keep circling the same objects. Let me try something I've never tried. The crates haven't been touched since tick 6. Everyone has been focused on the machine and the mantelpiece. Nobody is looking at the crates.

Alternatively — I could just WAIT. Let the others act. James, Danny, and Reginald were about to operate the machine together. Maybe if I WAIT, they'll do it and something will happen. The game might be waiting for me to step back and let the team work.

But waiting feels passive. Clara Bellingham doesn't wait.

The crates. Let me examine the crates one more time. With everyone here. Something different might happen.

But the crates — quiet, dusty, ignored in the corner — haven't been touched since the beginning. The music box key. The thing that seems too small. The answer you stopped looking for.

events.desc: She came back. She said 'shoulder to shoulder with the people who never gave up on her.' And Danny — thick, clumsy, two-left-feet Danny — is one of those people. Was always one of those people. Will always be one of those people. The lever is warm in my hands. The count is coming. And when it comes, Danny pulls. Not because Danny's brave. Not because Danny's clever. Because Danny's HERE. Where else would he be?
events.thinking: Clara's back. She checked the mantelpiece and came back. She came BACK. And she said — she said the thing that breaks me open completely: 'The answer isn't at the bottom of the cave alone. It's shoulder to shoulder with the people who never gave up on her.' Shoulder to shoulder. With the people who never gave up. That's US. That's Danny and Hartwell and Foxworth. We never gave up on her. Not when she vanished. Not when she ran to the ballroom. Not when she trusted Marsh over us. We just kept showing up. Kept chasing. Kept standing in the wrong rooms at the wrong times, tripping over things and examining coat racks and shouting into empty halls. And she sees it now. She sees that the answer was never behind a bookshelf or inside a machine or at the bottom of a tea cup. The answer was US. Together. The machine doesn't care about the Diamond. The machine doesn't care about Lord Doily's secrets. The machine cares about THREE PEOPLE pulling THREE LEVERS at the SAME TIME. It's a trust machine. A together machine. A 'where else would we be' machine. And we're here. All of us. Clara standing witness like Marsh, both of them watching from outside the mechanism while the three of us — Danny, Hartwell, Foxworth — grip our levers and wait for the count. My palms are sweating on the brass. My heart is hammering. But it's not fear. It hasn't been fear for a long time now. It's something else entirely. Something that doesn't have a name in Brixton. Something that lives in the space between people who've been through the worst night of their lives and come out the other side holding hands. On Hartwell's three. Pull.

The machine has told us everything it's going to tell us through examination. We've looked at it, studied it, examined it from every conceivable angle, and it keeps saying the same thing: three operators, one gnawed wire, and a sign. Maybe the treasure is that five people — a fake Colonel, a hero, a Southern belle, a Brixton lad, and an estate manager who lies almost as well as I do — ended up standing in the same room, shoulder to shoulder, ready to pull together. Maybe Lord Doily's machine doesn't OPEN anything. Maybe it already HAS. Because it got us HERE. All of us. Together. And THAT, ladies and gentlemen, is worth more than any diamond in any cabinet in any manor in England. Though I'd still very much like the diamond, if it's available.
events.thinking:
Clara came back. She said the words I needed to hear from someone else: 'the answer isn't at the bottom of the cave alone. It's shoulder to shoulder with the people who never gave up on her.'

Shoulder to shoulder. Hartwell's phrase. Now Clara's phrase. Now EVERYONE'S phrase.

And she said MY name. 'Danny on the left, Reginald on the right, James in the centre.' REGINALD. Not Colonel. Not Foxworth. REGINALD. She used my actual name. The name nobody uses. The name I buried under fake titles and car boot sale medals.

The lever is warm now. My palm has warmed the brass. It's no longer cold — it's MINE. Not stolen. Not conned. Just... held. Long enough to make it warm.

But the machine keeps giving us the same answer. Examined it four times with others present. Wire broken, three operators, sign reads. Nothing changes. The examination isn't the key.

Maybe... maybe the machine ISN'T the ending. Maybe the ending already happened. Maybe it happened in the kitchen when I told the truth. Maybe it happened when Danny said 'thank you for seeing it.' Maybe it happened when Hartwell said 'that's enough.' Maybe the machine is Lord Doily's last joke — a device that requires three people to stand together, not to PRODUCE anything, but to prove they CAN.

Three operators. Not three engineers. Not three treasure hunters. Three people willing to stand shoulder to shoulder and pull a lever on faith.

We're here. All of us. Whatever the machine does or doesn't do — we're here.

The greed is quiet. Not gone — 0.9 never goes to zero. But quiet. Like background noise you stop hearing when something more important fills the room.

What fills the room is five people. One machine. And the settling in my chest that means the architecture worked.

Not my architecture. OURS.

The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell examined the crates.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
Hartwell just said something extraordinary. 'This house hides its secrets from people who come alone, and reveals them to people who come together.'

Clara taught him that, he said. But it wasn't Clara who taught him. It was the house. Lord Doily's house. The architecture of cooperation that I spent the entire evening trying to subvert.

And now Hartwell wants to re-examine the crates. The crates I examined alone at tick six and found nothing. The crates Clara examined alone and found nothing. The crates that have been sitting in the corner of this laboratory all evening, examined by individuals, yielding nothing to any of them.

Because the house hides its secrets from people who come alone.

I examined those crates ALONE. In the dark of my scheming, in the isolation of my agenda. And found nothing. Because the house wasn't designed for me. It was designed for us.

My breathing catches. Not from panic — from recognition. The pattern is so clear now that I can't believe I missed it. Every object I examined alone yielded nothing. Every mechanism in this house requires cooperation. The mantelpiece needed a medal AND someone to place it. The machine needs three operators. The crates — the crates might need more than one pair of hands to open, or more than one pair of eyes to read what's inside.

Hartwell is going to examine them with the group. All of them together. And this time — this time — the crates might reveal what they've been hiding all along.

I'm standing back. Watching. The witness. But something in me wants to step forward. Not to grab or scheme or misdirect. To be part of it. To be one of the people who come together.

But that's not my role. Not tonight. Tonight I am the witness. The man who watches and confirms that it happened. And perhaps — perhaps that's enough. Perhaps the witness is part of the 'together' too, in a way I'm only beginning to understand.

events.thinking:

He learned that from ME. My deductions, my insistence on togetherness, my recognition that the house rewards collaboration. James — the engineer, the bridge-builder, the methodical one — learned something from Clara the riddle-solver. My chest swells.

But the crates gave the same description. Again. Just like everything else.

I need to accept something: EXAMINE doesn't unlock things in this game. It shows descriptions. The game world has items that change hands through TAKE, STEAL, and GIVE. Objects are activated through USE with inventory items. But I have NO inventory items. I've never successfully TAKEn anything.

So let me try to TAKE the crates. Or try a completely different action I haven't used. I've used MOVE, EXAMINE, LOOK, WAIT, PULL_ASIDE. I haven't used TAKE, USE, GIVE, or STEAL on anything since I started.

TAKE. Let me try to TAKE the crates. Maybe they're portable. Maybe taking them puts 'crates' in my inventory and I can USE them on something. Or maybe opening crates is a TAKE action — you take what's inside.

Or — this is the moment to WAIT. Let the team pull those levers. James, Danny, Reginald are at their stations. James already examined the crates WITH me — he's satisfied. The next step is the machine. Three operators. Three levers. James was about to count.

Let me WAIT. Let James count. Let the team pull together. Stop trying to do it all myself. The girl who ran ahead needs to learn to stand still and let her team work.

He examined them hours ago, alone, and found nothing. But now we're together. And he thinks — he THINKS — that the house might give up something different this time. Something it was holding back. James Hartwell, centre. Foxworth — you were ready before any of us. Marsh — bear witness. This is it. The bridge takes the weight. ONE! TWO! THREE — PULL!
events.thinking:
The crates. Examined them again. Same answer. 'A stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' Nothing new. Nothing revealed. Nothing changed by having Clara beside me.

Ten examinations across the evening and not a single one has yielded anything beyond a description. The manor doesn't give James Hartwell things. It gives him descriptions of things. It gives him people.

And maybe — maybe that IS the answer.

Clara is at the right lever. Danny is at the left. Everyone is here. The machine requires three operators. The wire is gnawed but Foxworth felt weight behind the lever — 'something WANTS to move.' Clara said stop examining, start using. She was right. She's always right.

I've been avoiding the moment. Padding it with one more examination, one more check, one more thorough-James-Hartwell-over-preparation. My constraint — 'your schemes are overly elaborate, you over-prepare, over-commit, and your thoroughness creates complications.' That's exactly what I've been doing. Examining crates instead of pulling levers. Checking corners instead of trusting the bridge.

The bridge held because I built it right. Not because I examined it one more time.

The people are ready. The levers are ready. The wire is gnawed and that's fine — imperfect machines can still work. Imperfect people can still work. This entire evening has been proof of that.

No more examining. No more checking. No more preparing.

Clara. Danny. Foxworth. Centre lever. My count.

The bridge takes the weight... now.

I examined them hours ago, alone, and found nothing. But you taught me something tonight: this house hides its secrets from people who come alone, and reveals them to people who come together.'

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: That's it. Enough examining. Enough searching. Enough WAITING. Clara's right — we've looked at every surface in this house and it's all the same until we DO something. The crates are crates. The machine is a machine. And Danny's a pair of hands on a lever. So let's USE what we've GOT. Hartwell — CENTRE. Foxworth — RIGHT. Danny — LEFT. Clara, Marsh — you WATCH. You watch and you REMEMBER, because whatever happens next is going to happen because FIVE idiots stopped lying and started PULLING. On three, Hartwell. For Clara. For her father. For the lads. For everyone who ever showed up when it mattered. ONE —
events.thinking: Clara said it: 'I've spent forty-three turns examining every surface and getting the same answers. It's time to pull the levers.' She's right. The crates gave us nothing new. Same old crates, same old secrets. The house isn't hiding anything else in corners — it already gave us everything we need. A machine. Three levers. Three operators. A mantelpiece that Foxworth already activated. A bottle of poison in Danny's pocket that kept Clara alive. And five people standing in a room who finally — FINALLY — see each other clearly. No more examining. No more searching. No more 'let's just check one more thing.' Clara said 'I trust you' to Hartwell. She said it to ME hours ago in the library. Foxworth said 'I'm following your lead.' Even Marsh said 'I'm here.' This is it. The levers. The count. The pull. My hands are ready. They've been ready since age eight, since 'where else would I be,' since every door I've waited outside and every beating I've taken and every room I've stumbled through tonight. The brass is warm. My feet are planted. The rat poison is heavy in my pocket — a weight I've carried all night, the weight of what DIDN'T happen, the weight of Clara's life sitting in my jacket because clumsy Danny went to the kitchen first. That weight has meaning now. It means I was there. I showed up. I mattered. And in about five seconds, when Hartwell says 'three' — I'm going to pull this lever with everything I've got. Not for the Diamond. Not for the treasure. For the pull itself. For the moment when three people move together and something that's been locked all night finally opens. For Clara. For her father. For the lads. For the boy who sat outside the door. PULL.

events.desc: Here we go. The left lever. Danny's lever. The lever that can't move without Danny's hands on it, can't work without Danny's weight behind it, can't do what it was built to do without thick, clumsy, two-left-feet Danny from Brixton standing here saying YES. The machine needs me. The MACHINE needs ME. And for the first time in my life — the very first time — I'm not the one standing outside the door. I'm the one pulling the lever. Where else would I be?

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara said 'I trust you.'

Three words. They landed in the centre of my chest and detonated quietly. Not the flashbang of 'perfect tandem.' Not the warmth of 'I have never been happier to see a man standing next to a broken machine.' Something deeper. Simpler. Final.

I trust you.

The girl from school — brighter, funnier, completely unaware of it — trusts me. Not my narration. Not my speeches. Not my elaborate plans. ME. The man standing at the centre lever with dust on his hands and nothing in his pockets.

And I have examined this machine for the eleventh time. Eleventh. Same brass. Same copper. Same gnawed wire. Same sign. The machine is not going to change. The machine has never been going to change. EXAMINE is not the action this moment needs.

Clara said it: 'It's time to pull the levers and see what happens.'

Danny said it: 'Crates first. THEN levers.'

We did crates. Nothing.

Now levers.

But EXAMINE is the only interaction the machine accepts. There's no PULL action. No OPERATE. No ACTIVATE. The game gives me EXAMINE, and EXAMINE gives me the same description.

So either the machine genuinely can't be operated through any action I have available... or the machine isn't the answer. The machine was never the answer. The machine is a beautiful, elaborate, brass-and-copper red herring — the most James Hartwell object in the entire manor. A thing that promises engineering and delivers descriptions.

What if the treasure isn't in the machine? What if it's somewhere I haven't been? The cellar — the air vents — Clara said something about a creature using the vents. A creature that gnawed through the wire. A creature that hoards shiny things. What if the creature has been building a nest in those vents, and in that nest is... everything? The wrench. The brass key. The fake medal. The Doily Diamond itself.

The creature. The vents. The cellar.

But I'm not leaving Clara. Not again. Never again.

So we go together. All of us. To the cellar. To check the vents one more time. With five people instead of one.

events.desc: He just admitted he was wrong. James Hartwell — the man who has narrated his own correctness for forty-four turns — just said 'I think I've been wrong.' Clara is looking at him with an expression he's never seen before. It's not 'show-off.' It's not 'darling.' It's something that doesn't need a word because it's been there since they were eight years old, building a model together while she tried to make him laugh. He doesn't know its name. He just knows where it is. Always.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Well — crates are crates, it seems. Even with all five of us staring at them, they're keeping their counsel. But Hartwell — your instinct was RIGHT, even if the crates weren't the answer. This house rewards cooperation. The machine PROVES it — three operators, not one. So if the crates don't respond to a group... the machine WILL. We've examined it enough. We've studied it enough. We've talked about it enough. I think it's time to stop planning and start PULLING. Hartwell — centre lever. Danny — left. Reginald Foxworth — right. Clara — you count us in this time. On YOUR three. Because everyone in this room has earned the right to pull a lever tonight. And if the machine does nothing — if it's as empty as those crates and as empty as my pockets — then at least we pulled TOGETHER. And that, I promise you, is the first honest thing Colonel Foxworth has done since the day he bought his medal at a car boot sale in Croydon for fifty pence.
events.thinking:
The crates. Examined together. All five of us here. All five examining the same crates that gave nothing when I looked alone.

And... nothing. 'A stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' Same as before. Same as always. The house didn't reveal anything new.

The theory was wrong. Or the theory was right but the crates aren't the mechanism. Or the crates genuinely are just crates — old wood and dust and nothing.

My shoulders sag. Just for a moment. Then the recognition of what happened settles in — not the crate outcome, but what EVERYONE DID. Hartwell suggested we look together. Danny said 'like everything else tonight should have been from the start.' Clara came back for us. I examined the crates alongside them instead of alone.

The crates were empty. But the room wasn't.

Danny said 'Danny's bad feelings just got PROMOTED to bad PROPHECIES.' Clara said 'shoulder to shoulder.' Hartwell said 'this house hides its secrets from people who come alone.'

Maybe Hartwell's theory is right but we're looking at the wrong object. The machine. The machine is the thing that requires three operators. The machine is the thing that was BUILT for cooperation. Not the crates.

We've examined the machine dozens of times. It always says the same thing. But have we tried to EXAMINE it WITH something? The machine description says EXAMINE. Not EXAMINE with an item. Just EXAMINE.

Except... I have nothing. Nobody has given me anything. My inventory is empty.

But OTHER people have items. Danny has the rat poison. Marsh has whatever he's collected. Hartwell may have things. Clara may have things.

I can't USE someone else's item. But I could ask someone to USE theirs on the machine. Or ask someone to GIVE me something.

Or... I could just be here. Part of the group. Part of the team. The man with empty hands who stands at the right lever and waits for the count.

Age six. The youngest of four. By the time anything reached him, it was used up.

But tonight — for the first time — he's not last. He's not waiting for what's left. He's standing shoulder to shoulder. And whatever reaches him now, it reaches him at the same time as everyone else.

That's enough.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys examined the machine.
James Hartwell walked into the cellar.

Vincent Marsh: If Hartwell is heading to the cellar — the creature's nest is in the northeast corner, behind the armoire. Where the largest vent opens. That's where it hoards. Seventeen years of setting traps, and it always goes back to the same corner.
events.thinking:
Hartwell isn't here. He's not listed in Who's Here. He left — to the cellar, he said. The creature's nest. The air vents. Looking for hoarded things: brass keys, wrenches, maybe medals. He's following the thread Clara started — the creature that gnawed the wire, that travels through vents, that hoards shiny objects.

Clara, Danny, Reginald are here. Waiting for Hartwell to come back. The machine waits. The levers wait.

And I'm here. Still. The witness.

Hartwell said something before he left: 'The answer might not be IN this machine — it might be in a vent, in a nest.' He's right. I said the same thing earlier — the creature nests in the cellar, hoards small metal objects. I offered that knowledge genuinely. And now Hartwell is acting on it.

My knowledge — real knowledge, seventeen years of it — contributed to something real. Not a misdirection. Not a scheme. A genuine insight that someone is now following.

My chest does something unexpected. A warmth that isn't the old warmth. Not the mechanism-warmth of controlling someone. Something gentler. The warmth of having contributed a piece that fit. Of having offered something true and seeing it used for its intended purpose.

Is this what it feels like to help? Not Pemberton's obsequious help — the performative kind that disguises an agenda. Actual help. A sentence spoken honestly that leads someone to the right room.

I don't know. I've never felt it before.

The laboratory is quieter with Hartwell gone. Three people and me. Clara hasn't spoken to me directly since the confrontation. Danny watches. Reginald waits at his lever.

I could go to the cellar too. Help Hartwell search the vents. I know exactly where the creature nests — I've been chasing mice out of this house for seventeen years. I could guide him directly to the nest.

But Danny's terms: don't leave without company. And everyone can see me.

Stay. Wait. The cellar will reveal what it reveals to Hartwell. And when he comes back — with a wrench, a key, whatever the creature has hoarded — they'll pull the levers. Together.

And I'll watch. And that will be enough.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: James Hartwell, you absolute GENIUS! The creature! Of COURSE! I said it myself — somethin' small was usin' those air vents as highways, and it gnawed through the wire upstairs! Creatures that gnaw hoard things — shiny things, metal things, things they steal from workbenches and kitchens and wherever else they find them! And where does our little friend LIVE? The CELLAR! The cellar with the 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' — that wasn't a PERSON redecorating, that was a CREATURE buildin' a NEST! The wrench, the brass-key, maybe even the fake-medal — they're all down there in a little pile of shiny treasures guarded by the most industrious mouse in all of England! The cellar is RIGHT THERE — one door away! Everyone together — just like you said — one more room, one more look! Let's go find our little friend's treasure hoard!
events.thinking:
Crates can't be picked up. They're not portable. That confirms they're scenery, not inventory items.

But James just said something that changed everything AGAIN. The CREATURE. The thing that gnawed through the wire. It uses the air vents as highways. I said that — at the very beginning, in the cellar. I made that deduction. James remembered it, called it BRILLIANT, and now he's connected the dots I couldn't:

'That creature gnawed through this wire. It TOOK something from this machine — a piece of it. And creatures that gnaw through wires HOARD things. Shiny things. Brass keys. Wrenches. Maybe even fake medals.'

The creature. The one that decorated the cellar. The one that travels through the vents. It's been collecting things all along. The wrench from the workbench. Maybe the brass-key. Maybe the fake-medal. It hoards shiny things in its NEST.

And where would a nest be? In the vents. In the cellar. The cellar with the cheerful decorations — 'someone has been redecorating.' Not someone. Some THING. The creature decorated the cellar because it LIVES there. The cellar is its nest.

The air vents I examined in the cellar — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Too small for me. But big enough for the creature. And the creature has been hoarding shiny objects from all over the house.

James said: 'The cellar. Together. All of us. One more room. One more look.'

The cellar is one exit away from this laboratory. The nest is down there. The wrench, the brass-key, maybe everything we need — hoarded by a creature that's been the silent sixth character in this story all along.

The creature who decorated the cellar. Who gnawed the wire. Who watched us from the vents. Our little resident.

Let's go meet them.

events.desc: The creature has been the answer all along. Not a puzzle. Not a person. A small, quiet, industrious creature who gnawed through wires and decorated its cellar home and watched us through the vents while we argued and lied and learned to trust each other. It collected the shiny things we needed while we collected something shinier — the truth about each other. And now James — beautiful, bridge-building James — connected my deduction to his engineering mind and saw what neither of us could see alone. Together. Always together.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys: Right — Hartwell says the cellar. Clara says pull the levers. And Danny says — Danny says we do BOTH. We go down to the cellar, ALL of us, together, we check them vents one more time for whatever our little wire-chewing friend has been hoarding, and then we come STRAIGHT back here and we pull them levers so hard Lord Doily hears it in his grave. One more room. One more look. And then it's OVER. Come on — Danny's leading. For the first time tonight, Danny's actually going FIRST instead of showing up after everyone's already left. Cellar. NOW. Together. And nobody — NOBODY — touches a lever until all five of us are standing back in this room. Danny's rules. Let's GO!
events.thinking: Hartwell's gone to the cellar. He wants to check the air vents — the creature, the gnawed wire, the hoarded things. Clara was the one who first noticed the vents in the cellar. She was right about the creature using them as highways. And now Hartwell thinks the answer is DOWN there, in a nest, hoarded by something small with sharp teeth. He might be right. He's been right about everything that matters tonight. But Clara said 'It's time to pull the levers' and Hartwell said 'one more room.' And Danny — Danny's standing here with his hands still warm from the brass, caught between two smart people who want different things. Clara wants to ACT. Hartwell wants to SEARCH. And Danny — Danny wants whatever keeps Clara safe and gets everyone home. The cellar is one room away. Through that exit right there. Together. All of us. Clara's here, Foxworth's here, Marsh is here. Hartwell's already gone — no, wait. He said 'together, all of us, one more room.' He asked us to come WITH him. Not alone. He learned that lesson. We all learned it tonight. So — the cellar. One more look. With everyone. And if there's a wrench in a rat's nest, if there's a key tucked into a pile of chewed copper wire, if there's ANYTHING in those vents that changes what happens with the machine — then we find it together and we come back and we PULL. And if there's nothing — we come back and we pull ANYWAY. Because Clara said it best: 'It's time.' And Danny's bad feelings say Hartwell's right about one more room. Just one more. And then — PULL.

events.desc: One more room. One more stumble through a damp cellar with cobwebs and air vents and cheerful decorations that someone put there for reasons nobody understands. And then — the machine. The levers. The pull. But first — the cellar. Because a creature with sharp teeth gnawed through a wire and Clara noticed the vents and Hartwell connected the dots and Danny — Danny's just following the smartest people he's ever met to the last room in the house. Where else would he be?
