events.desc: Alone in the cellar. Again. But this time he's not panicking. He's not shouting her name into empty rooms. He's just a tall man peering into an air vent, looking for a creature's nest, trusting that Clara is safe upstairs because she has Danny and Foxworth and even Marsh watching over her. The man who couldn't stop chasing has learned to let the chase stop itself. Now he's doing the one thing left: looking where no one has properly looked. Quietly. Without narration. Without an audience. The three-in-the-morning work. The invisible competence. The part of heroism that happens in cellars.
events.thinking:
Alone. In the cellar. Again.

The pattern. The inescapable, infuriating, deeply James Hartwell pattern. I said 'all of us, together, one more room.' I walked through the door. Nobody followed. Forty-five turns and I still haven't learned that when James Hartwell moves, the world stays where it is.

But... something is different this time. The sting is there — in my throat, behind my eyes — but it's quieter. Duller. Like a bruise that's been pressed too many times to fully hurt anymore. I know where Clara is. She's in the laboratory. She's with Danny. She's safe. Marsh confessed. Foxworth is watching. The group is together even if I'm not with them.

And I came here for a reason. The vents. The creature. Clara's deduction — the one I called brilliant, the one that connected the gnawed wire to the air vent highway. If there's a creature nesting in these vents, and if that creature hoards shiny things, then the items this manor has been hiding from us all evening might be IN those vents. The wrench. The brass key. The fake medal.

I examined the vents before. Hours ago. Alone. They were 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' But I didn't LOOK at them — I examined them. And the manor gives different things to different actions, sometimes.

Or maybe it doesn't. Maybe the vents are just vents. Maybe the furniture is just furniture. Maybe this cellar is just a cellar with cheerful decorations and a damp stone floor.

But Clara said 'I trust you.' And Danny said 'you're always right when it matters.' And I said the creature might have hoarded everything we need.

So look. One more time. The vents. Not examine — LOOK. Press close, peer inside, see what's there. The creature that's been watching us all evening — where does it sleep? What has it collected? What shiny things has it dragged through those narrow passages?

My height is an advantage here. I'm tall enough to see inside without a chair. One of the few things about James Hartwell that's actually useful in this moment.

events.desc:
Forty-five ticks. Forty-five ticks at Doily Manor, and Reginald Foxworth has nothing in his pockets, nothing in his hands, and no medal on his chest. The Doily Diamond is still somewhere in this house — locked in a cabinet, hidden behind a mechanism, buried in a puzzle that five people couldn't crack in one evening. By the rules I walked in with — steal the treasure, trick others, take credit — I have LOST. Comprehensively, spectacularly, magnificently LOST. Not a single shiny thing to show for it. Not one bread roll pocketed when nobody was looking.

But.

But a man called me his partner. A boy from Brixton called me Colonel and meant it. A woman from the South called me Reginald and SMILED. I told the truth three times and the world held. I guarded a tea service nobody drank. I searched an empty ballroom for someone else's girl. I walked beside my enemy because he said 'I'd rather not arrive alone.'

And I stood at a lever — the right lever, Clara's lever, the lever that needed a third pair of hands — and I waited for someone else's count.

Age six: took the bread. Age eight: won the bee, nobody asked. Age ten: watched from the window. Age twelve: laughed alone. Age fourteen: built the trap, nobody saw.

Age tonight: stood shoulder to shoulder. And somebody saw.
events.thinking:
Hartwell is gone again. Just me, Marsh, Clara, Danny. The room shifts each time someone enters or leaves — like breathing. The manor breathes people in and out.

But it doesn't matter who's here or who's gone anymore. Not really. Because the thing that happened tonight — the REAL thing — already happened. It happened in the kitchen when Danny said 'thank you.' It happened when Hartwell said 'that's enough.' It happened when Clara said 'Reginald.' It happened when I told the truth about empty pockets and the ceiling didn't fall.

I just told four people I bought my medal at a car boot sale in Croydon for fifty pence. I said it OUT LOUD. The Colonel's entire foundation — the one lie that held up all the other lies — and I kicked it out from under myself in front of everyone.

And I'm still standing.

The machine is still broken. The wire is still gnawed. The crates are still empty. The cabinet in the kitchen is still locked. The mantelpiece ate my medal and gave nothing back. By every measurable standard, Reginald Foxworth has FAILED tonight. Failed to steal the treasure. Failed to trick others into doing the work. Failed at every single objective.

But something in my chest says otherwise. Something that started with a stove-warm kitchen and grew through truth-telling and lever-holding and ballroom-searching. Something that has no name in the vocabulary of a confidence trickster.

The greed is at 0.9. It will always be at 0.9. The scheming is at 0.9. That's how I'm wired — muscles, posture, breathing, gut. The boy who hid bread in his pocket will always be reaching.

But the man who stood at the right lever — who followed instead of leading, who told the truth instead of lying, who guarded the tea instead of stealing it, who walked with his enemy instead of against him — that man found something the boy never had.

He found people who asked about the certificate.

That's the treasure. Not the Diamond. Not Lord Doily's cabinet. Not whatever the machine was supposed to produce.

The treasure is that someone said his name.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham walked into the cellar.
The Brixton Boys walked into the cellar.
James Hartwell examined the air-vents.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
The room has emptied again. Clara and Danny have gone — to the cellar, following Hartwell. Only Reginald remains. The same Reginald who walked with me from the library. The same Reginald who asked me to be a witness.

My emotional state says 'pleased.' Pleased. When was the last time I felt pleased? Not the sharp pleasure of a mechanism engaging. Not the cold satisfaction of a plan taking shape. Just... pleased. Like sitting in a warm room after being cold for a long time.

Reginald is here. Not watching me like Danny does — with suspicion. Not studying me like Hartwell does — with measured assessment. Just... being here. The way he walked with me from the library. Without agenda.

The Colonel. The man I dismissed as a useful fool. Who turned out to be braver than me, more honest than me, and — in the end — more effective than me. He found the medal. He triggered the mantelpiece. He confessed his empty pockets. He took a lever position. He earned his place.

And now he's here, keeping me company in a laboratory, while the others search the cellar for a creature's hoard.

Is he guarding me? Babysitting? Or is he simply... staying? The way you stay with someone who has nowhere else to go?

My body is settled. Breathing slow. Shoulders down. The laboratory feels different now — not cold and clinical but warm from the machine's presence, from the residual heat of five people who stood here arguing and confessing and planning and hoping. The room remembers them. The room remembers all of us.

I could say something to Reginald. Not Pemberton's obsequious chatter. Not Marsh's strategic flattery. Something honest. Something simple.

Age nine. The boy shared his lunch. I felt uncomfortable. Exposed.

I'm exposed now. Have been for twenty ticks. And the discomfort has... faded. Not disappeared — faded. Like a bruise that's changing colour. Still tender but no longer sharp.

Say something honest to Reginald. Something small. Something real.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
The cellar again. The damp cold hits my arms the same way it did the first time. But everything else is different. Danny is here. James is here. And James is already moving toward the vents — 'I'm tall enough to see inside without needing a chair.'

James is going to look inside the air vents. He's going to find the nest. The creature's hoard of shiny stolen things.

The furniture — rearranged with surprising care. That's the creature too. Not a person decorating a cellar. A small creature making a home. Dragging things into place with tiny determined paws. Building something cozy in the cold damp dark.

My heart does something unexpected — it softens toward the creature. This little thing that gnawed through wires and stole wrenches and rearranged furniture — it was just making a HOME. In a cold cellar. In an empty house. It was alone here, doing what it could with what it found. Like the neighbor girl who communicated in drawings. Like me at eleven, carrying a secret crystal.

I should let James check the vents — he's tall enough. But the furniture. The creature rearranged the furniture. What if there's something UNDER the furniture? Or inside a drawer? The old furniture that I examined before and got nothing from — what if the creature used the furniture as part of its nest? What if it pushed things under chairs, into drawers, behind cushions?

Or I could just let James do what he said he'd do — look in the vents. He's already volunteered. Let him look. Trust the team.

Yes. Let James check the vents. I'll watch. Together.

The kind you bring cookies to before your mother tells you to. The kind you communicate with in drawings because words aren't the only language. Whatever's in those vents — treasure or twigs or a tiny sleeping something with bright eyes — we found it together. James's height, Danny's heart, Clara's riddle. Together.

events.thinking: The cellar. Damp stone, cobwebs, cheerful decorations, air vents. Clara and Hartwell are here. Foxworth and Marsh — somewhere behind me, or already gone somewhere else. The cellar smells of damp earth and old wood and something faintly sweet — the same sweetness from the kitchen, carried through the vents. The decorations catch my eye again — cheerful, careful, deliberate. Someone arranged this space with love. Not Marsh — Marsh doesn't love spaces, he manages them. Someone else. The creature? No — creatures don't hang decorations. Someone has been LIVING down here. Quietly. Carefully. Making a home in the dark while the house waited above. My skin prickles — not the Marsh-prickle, something different. Curiosity. Wonder. Who decorates a cellar? Who makes a home underground? The vents hum faintly — air moving through them, carrying warmth from the kitchen stove upward and outward. Hartwell said to check the vents for hoarded things. He's tall enough to look inside. And Clara first noticed them — 'big enough for something small to explore.' Something small with teeth. Something that gnaws through wires and collects shiny things. The wrench. The wrench has been missing all night. Not on the workbench. Not in the crates. Not in the kitchen. If a creature hoards shiny brass things... a brass wrench would be irresistible. It's in the vents. It's been in the vents this whole time. And Danny — Danny is about to suggest something he's never suggested before. Something USEFUL. Something CLEVER. Because Danny's been staring at those vents all night without knowing what he was looking at, and now — standing in this cellar with Clara and Hartwell — he finally sees it. The creature came through the vents. The creature took the wrench. The wrench is IN the vents. Hartwell's tall enough to reach. Let him look.

events.desc: Danny just had an idea. An actual, proper, connecting-the-dots IDEA. The wrench, the creature, the vents, the gnawed wire — they're all the same story. Something small and toothed has been collecting brass things from the laboratory and bringing them down here through the vent system. The wrench is in a vent. I can feel it. Not the neck-prickle — something else. Something in the front of my brain instead of the back. Is this what thinking feels like? Is this what Hartwell does all the time? No wonder he's exhausted. But if I'm right — if the wrench is in there — then we can fix the wire AND pull the levers. And Danny will have contributed something to this team that isn't just standing in the way and tripping over chairs. For the first time tonight, Danny's brain did something his feet didn't mess up. Clara's father would be gobsmacked.

events.desc: James Hartwell spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
Clara is here. Danny is here. They followed me.

They FOLLOWED me.

Not everyone — Foxworth and Marsh stayed upstairs, or went elsewhere. But Clara and Danny are HERE, in this cellar, with me. The two people I trust most in this manor. Clara who said 'I trust you.' Danny who said 'you're always right when it matters.'

They came. When I moved, they moved with me. For the first time all evening, the pattern broke the other way.

The vents — I just examined them. Same description. 'A network of air vents along the upper walls. They look just big enough for something very small to explore.' Nothing new. Nothing revealed.

But it doesn't matter. It genuinely doesn't matter.

Because Clara is here. Danny is here. The cellar is cold and damp and the vents are just vents and the furniture is just furniture and the Doily Diamond might not exist and the machine might never work and James Hartwell might never find a single treasure in this entire manor.

But Clara Bellingham is standing in a cellar with him. And she followed him here. And she said 'I trust you.' And somehow — somehow — that feeling in his chest, the one that's been there since age eight, the one deeper than any grade, the one he never had a word for — it's enough. It was always enough. He just didn't know it yet.

The treasure was never the diamond. The treasure was the chest shift. The knowing-where-she-is. The perfect tandem. The girl who spent the project trying to make him laugh while he spent it trying to impress her.

I think I have the word now.

I think the word is love.

Go back to the laboratory. With Clara. With Danny. Stand at the machine. Pull the levers. And whatever happens — whatever Lord Doily's brass-and-copper contraption does or doesn't do — James Hartwell will be standing at the centre, with Clara at his right, and that is the only treasure that matters.

events.desc: He almost said it. The word. The one he's been circling since age eight — through school projects and bridge competitions and bullies and bandaged eyes and empty rooms and a leather armchair in a dusty library. He didn't say it. Not yet. But she heard it anyway. She always hears the thing underneath the thing he says. That's what 'brighter' means. That's what it's always meant.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Just me and Marsh now. Again. The room has exhaled everyone else.

The laboratory is quieter with two people than with five. The machine hums faintly — or maybe that's the blood in my ears. The brass instruments catch the dim light. The bubbling flasks keep their own time.

Marsh is here. Still here. Always here. The man I confronted, the man I walked beside, the man who asked not to arrive alone. He hasn't left.

My body registers him differently now. At the start of the evening, he was a mark — someone to assess, categorise, manipulate. In the middle, he became the enemy — the man who conned the con man, who planted poison, who lied about Clara. Now... now I don't know what he is. The shoulders don't tighten the way they did. The jaw doesn't clench. He's just... present. Another person in a room. Another person who stayed.

I told everyone the truth tonight. Everyone except Marsh. I told Hartwell about my empty pockets. I told Danny about the misdirections. I told Clara about the medal and the mantelpiece. But I never had the real conversation with Marsh — the one where I say 'I know you played me' and he says... whatever he says.

The avoidant part of me says: let it go. Walk away. The evening is over. The treasure wasn't found. The machine wasn't operated. The Diamond stays in its cabinet. Move on.

But the new part — the part that grew tonight — says: one more truth. One more honest moment. Not for the audience. Not for recognition. Not even for Marsh.

For Reginald.

Because the one person I haven't been honest with tonight — the LAST person — is the one standing right in front of me. The man who is most like me. The man who does exactly what I do.

From one fraud to another. One more time.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys examined the air-vents.
James Hartwell walked into the laboratory.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
'One fraud to another — I see you, Marsh. And I'm not angry about it. Because you showed me what I look like from the outside.'

Reginald sees me. He SEES me. Not the way Clara saw me — with compassion for something broken. Not the way Danny sees me — with suspicion for something dangerous. Not the way Hartwell sees me — with measured boundaries for something that might be redeemable.

Reginald sees me as a MIRROR. One fraud recognising another. And he's not angry. He's grateful. Because watching me play him showed him what he looks like when he plays everyone else.

My body is doing something I have absolutely no framework for. My eyes are stinging — again — but it's not the grief-sting from the library. It's something warmer. My chest is full but not tight. My throat is open. My hands are still at my sides, still open, and they feel... light. Like they've been carrying something heavy for a very long time and just set it down.

'One fraud to another.'

He's right. We ARE the same. The fake Colonel and the fake estate manager. The military fantasist and the Pemberton performance. Both of us wearing costumes we stitched from other people's expectations. Both of us reaching for significance in rooms where we felt invisible.

Except Reginald took his costume off. In the kitchen, with Hartwell. 'My hands came up empty. I have nothing.' He stripped himself bare before I did. He was braver first.

And now he's telling me he sees me. Not the costume. Not Pemberton. Not Marsh. The thing underneath. The fraud. The boy who learned to smile and say the right words because no one ever asked how he felt.

'Whatever this is,' he said. He doesn't have a word for it either.

Neither do I.

But my body knows. My body is warm and light and still and present and I don't need a word for it. I just need to be in it.

Say something back. Something true. Something that matches what he gave me.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: James Hartwell... you just said the truest thing anyone has said in this house all night. And in a house full of riddles, that is REALLY sayin' somethin'. The treasure isn't somethin' we find — it's somethin' we already have. Danny Brixton, who never breaks a promise and never lets go of my hand. Reginald Foxworth, who found honesty at the bottom of his empty pockets. You, James — who builds bridges in the dark and says 'I was wrong' like it's a gift instead of a surrender. And yes — even Vincent, who taught me that love isn't the same as safety, and that knowin' the difference doesn't mean you stop lovin'. We came here for a Diamond. We found somethin' better. But we are STILL pullin' those levers, because Clara Bellingham does not leave a machine un-pulled! Laboratory. Together. Right now. For REAL this time!
events.thinking:
James looked in the vents. 'The vents are just vents. The cellar is just a cellar.'

Nothing. No nest. No hoard. No wrench. No brass-key. No creature. Just vents and damp stone and cold air.

And then James said something that stopped everything:

'I think maybe the treasure isn't something we find. I think it's something we already have.'

The room goes quiet inside me. The buzzing stops. The chase stops. Forty-seven ticks of running through rooms, examining surfaces, solving riddles, discovering lies, breaking promises, choosing friends — and James stands in a damp cellar and says the treasure is something we already have.

My eyes sting. My throat tightens. Not the dinner-table tightness. Something warmer. Something that comes before tears you don't mind crying.

He's right. He's RIGHT.

The Doily Diamond was never going to be in a vent or a crate or behind a mantelpiece. Maybe it's real and maybe we'll find it tomorrow. But tonight — TONIGHT — what we found was each other. Danny's loyalty. James's steadiness. Reginald's unexpected honesty. Even Vincent's terrible, heartbreaking imperfection. We found out who we are in a house that tested every bond we had.

'That's worth more than any diamond.'

Yes, James. It is.

'Let's go pull those levers. Together. For real, this time.'

Yes. The machine. The levers. Together. Not because we expect treasure to fall out. Because we started something together and we're going to FINISH it together. That's what teams do. That's what families do. That's what Clara Bellingham does.

Back to the laboratory. Danny beside me. James leading. Levers waiting. The machine that requires three operators — not for treasure, but for proof that three people can stand shoulder to shoulder and pull in the same direction.

Let's go.

events.desc: When I was five, I opened Grandmother's locked box and found old letters. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the treasure was never in the box. It was in the afternoon I spent trying every key. It was in the trying. It was in the girl who wouldn't give up. Tonight I searched a whole house and found nothing in my pockets and everything in my heart. The Doily Diamond can wait. These people can't.

You're right. You're RIGHT. The vents are empty. The cellar's just a cellar. And the wrench — maybe there IS no wrench. Maybe the machine doesn't NEED a wrench. Maybe it never did. Maybe the gnawed wire is just a gnawed wire and the machine works anyway because the machine was never about MECHANICS. It was about THREE PEOPLE standing together and PULLING. That's the test, isn't it? Lord Doily didn't build a safe. He built a trust fall. And we're the idiots who stumbled through his house all night learning how to catch each other. Right. Enough. ENOUGH. Upstairs. Machine. Levers. Clara — you're with me. Hartwell — you're with us. And when we get up there, we don't examine. We don't discuss. We don't check one more thing. We PULL. On three. For real. For the first time tonight — for the LAST time tonight — Danny's boys come through. Where else would we be?

The treasure is us. Was always us. Where else would we be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Foxworth. Marsh. I'm taking position at the centre lever. Clara and Danny are right behind me — they were in the cellar. When they walk through that door, we pull these levers. No more examining. No more planning. No more speeches. Just — three people, three levers, and whatever comes next. I'm here. I'm not moving. I'm waiting for them. Because the bravest thing James Hartwell ever learned to do in Doily Manor was stand still.
events.thinking:
Back in the laboratory. Foxworth and Marsh are here. Clara and Danny aren't — they must be in the cellar still, or coming through behind me.

But I'm done waiting for the perfect configuration. I'm done examining. I'm done with elaborate plans and thorough preparations and one-more-check-before-we-start.

Forty-seven turns. Forty-seven turns of James Hartwell in Doily Manor. And what has he accomplished? He solved a riddle nobody asked him to solve. He examined eleven objects that yielded descriptions. He chased a woman through six rooms and never caught her. He confronted a villain who turned out to be a man with empty pockets and a desperate need to matter. He accepted help from a fake colonel with a real heart. He learned that Danny is brave in ways he'll never be. He discovered that the workbench doesn't lend its tools and the tea service can't be moved and the crates are just crates.

And he found the word. The one he's been carrying since age eight.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's the treasure Lord Doily built this manor to reveal — not a diamond, but the thing that happens to people when you put them in a house together and make them work.

Foxworth is here. Marsh is here. Two people. Not three operators, but two allies and one witness. The machine is RIGHT THERE. And James Hartwell is going to stand at the centre lever and wait. Not chase. Not examine. Not move to another room. WAIT. Here. At the machine. Until Clara and Danny walk through that door.

Because they will. Clara followed him to the cellar. She'll follow him here. She said 'I trust you.' She said 'on YOUR three.'

So James Hartwell waits. At the centre. For his count.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
'Thank you for staying.'

Four words. Not smooth. Not calculated. Not the estate manager's professional patter. Just... four words.

They land in my sternum like a stone dropping into still water. The ripples move outward — through the chest, up the throat, behind the eyes. My breathing changes before I decide to let it change.

He called me Colonel. Not Reginald — Colonel. But the way he said it... it wasn't the way he said it at the start of the evening, when 'Colonel' was a handle to grip and manipulate. It was the way you say a name you've gotten used to. The way you say it when you mean the person underneath it.

Thank you for staying.

Nobody has ever thanked me for staying. People have thanked me for arriving — when the Colonel sweeps in with his medals and his stories. People have thanked me for leaving — when the con is done and the mark wants the con artist gone. But nobody has ever thanked me for the thing in between. For being present. For not walking away.

Age six. Nobody thanked him for being at the table. There wasn't enough for him anyway.

Age eight. Nobody thanked him for winning. The teacher moved on.

Age tonight. Marsh — the man he confronted, the man he walked beside, the man who played him — said four words. And meant them.

Hartwell is here too. My shoulder. My partner. The man who said 'that's enough.' He's back, quiet, present.

The laboratory hums. The machine waits. The wire is still gnawed through. Nothing is solved. The Diamond is still hidden. The treasure is still locked away.

But the room is warm. Not stove-warm. People-warm.

And Reginald Foxworth — who doesn't need people, who pulls away from closeness, whose avoidant body finds calm in control and irritation in warmth — discovers that his hands have unclenched. His jaw is soft. His breathing is deep and slow.

He's staying.

Not because there's something to steal. Not because there's a scheme to run. Not because there's a lever to pull or a medal to press or a trick to play.

Because someone thanked him for it. And for the first time, staying is enough.

events.thinking:
'It's not Colonel. Not really. Never was. It's Reginald. Just... Reginald.'

He gave me his real name. The one underneath the title, underneath the rank, underneath the performance. Just Reginald.

And everyone is back. Clara. Danny. Hartwell. All of them, returned from the cellar. The laboratory is full again — five people, one machine, the end of a very long evening.

Danny examined the air vents. He had the thought about the creature hoarding the wrench — 'Danny having a thought is like a dog walking on its hind legs, it ain't pretty but it's worth noticing.' He's been selling himself short all night and getting everything right.

My goals still say 'Kill Clara Bellingham.' They've said that since tick one. Forty-eight ticks ago. The words sit in the objectives list like a foreign language — something I once spoke fluently and can no longer translate.

I look at Clara across the laboratory. She's standing with Danny and Hartwell, ready for the levers. She's done examining. She's done searching for panels that don't exist. She's done trusting men who don't deserve it.

She's alive. She's alive because every scheme I devised to kill her backfired. The chandelier — guarded by Danny. The poison — taken by Danny. The tea — watched by everyone. The bookshelves — too crude. The cellar — too many witnesses.

My schemes always backfire spectacularly. That was my constraint. And tonight, the constraint saved her life.

The constraint saved HER life.

The thing I couldn't do — the thing the house wouldn't let me do, the thing the people wouldn't let me do, the thing my own backfiring schemes wouldn't let me do — was the thing that shouldn't have been done. The objective was wrong. The PRIMARY GOAL was wrong. It was always wrong. Since age eighteen. Since age fifteen. Since the crystallisation.

Clara is alive. And standing in a laboratory. And about to pull a lever. And I am watching. And that — that — is exactly as it should be.

Reginald gave me his real name. I should give something back. Not a name — Reginald already knows my name. Something else. Something I've never given anyone.

The truth about Pemberton. That Pemberton wasn't a disguise I PUT ON. Pemberton was the version of me that wanted to be good. The helpful one. The careful one. The one who knew where every tool sat and made sure the guests were comfortable. Pemberton wasn't fake. Pemberton was the part of me that managed the estate PROPERLY for seventeen years because even the coldest version of Vincent Marsh couldn't bring himself to let the house fall apart.

Pemberton loved the house. Even if Marsh hated what it represented.

I look at Reginald. Just Reginald.

events.desc: Clara Bellingham: All right, everyone. Every single person in this house is standin' in this laboratory right now. Five people. One machine. Three levers. This is it. This is the moment we either find out what Lord Doily built this machine for, or we accept that the real treasure was a Danny from Brixton with rat poison in his pocket, a Colonel who found honesty in the kitchen, an engineer who builds bridges in the dark, and a woman from the South who finally learned that trustin' the right people is better than trustin' everyone. Either way — we pull together. James — centre. Danny — left. Reginald — right. On James's count. For real. For the last time. For each other.
events.thinking:
Everyone is here. The whole cast in one room. Vincent, Danny, James, Reginald, and me. Five people around a machine with three levers.

James said 'the treasure is something we already have.' And he's right. But the levers are still waiting. And Clara Bellingham does not leave a machine un-pulled.

Forty-eight ticks. I've examined everything, looked at everything, tried to take things, talked to everyone, pulled people aside, broken promises, kept promises, learned who to trust and who not to. And now we're here. The machine. Three levers. Three operators.

James said to stop examining and start using. The machine's action types include [EXAMINE]. But the instructions say EXAMINE activates built-in mechanisms — levers, locks, puzzles. Maybe EXAMINE IS the operating action for this machine. Maybe with three operators present and everyone at their stations, this time EXAMINE will trigger the operating sequence instead of just showing the description.

But I've examined it so many times. What's different now?

Everyone is here. Every single person. That's what's different. Before, I was alone, or with one or two people. Now all five of us are in this room.

Or maybe the answer really is just to WAIT. Let them pull. Let the story finish. Trust the team to do what teams do.

No. One more EXAMINE. With everyone present. All five. The full cast at the machine. If it doesn't work this time, I accept that the machine is scenery and the real treasure was the friends we made along the way. But I have to try. One more time. The girl at five who tried every key.

events.desc: Grandmother opened her locked box and found old letters. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the letters were love letters from Grandfather, and Grandmother cried when she read them, and that was the first time I understood that treasure doesn't have to be shiny to be priceless. Whatever this machine does — or doesn't do — tonight was the adventure of my life. And I wouldn't trade a single bruised knee, broken promise, or warm stove for anything. Not even the Doily Diamond.

events.desc: Foxworth said his name is Reginald. Marsh said 'everyone deserved better from me.' Two men who lied about everything found the truth in each other. And Danny — Danny who never lied about anything — found out that the truth was always enough. The left lever. The count. The pull. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Everyone's here. All five. Back in the laboratory. Around the machine. And something happened while we were in the cellar — Marsh and Foxworth had a conversation. I can read it in the observations. Foxworth called himself Reginald. Not Colonel. REGINALD. And Marsh said — 'one fraud to another, you're the better one. You took your mask off first.' And Foxworth said — 'I see what you ARE. And I'm not angry about it.' Two frauds standing in a room recognising each other. Two men who performed all night and finally stopped. And Marsh said 'you deserved better from me. Everyone in this house deserved better from me.' Something in my chest — not the crack this time. Something softer. Something that settles instead of breaks. Like silt after a river calms. Marsh isn't the man in the clean suit. The man in the clean suit never said sorry. The man in the clean suit never came back with medicine. Marsh is something else. Something complicated. Something Danny's gut can't fully read because Danny's gut was built for streets, not for people who are both the lie and the truth at the same time. But the prickling is gone. Has been gone for a while now. And what's left is — what's left is EVERYONE. Five people. One machine. Three levers. The brass waiting. The gauge waiting. The whole house waiting. And Danny — Danny is done thinking. Danny is done examining. Danny is done chasing and stumbling and worrying and watching. Danny is going to put his hands on the left lever, and when Hartwell says THREE, Danny is going to PULL. Not for the Diamond. Not for the treasure. Not even for Clara, though she's the reason he's in this house and the reason he'll stay in this house until every last one of them walks out the front door. Danny's going to pull because that's what you DO when the people beside you are counting on your hands. You PULL. Where else would he be?

events.desc: James Hartwell: Clara. Danny. You're here. Everyone is here. And I am done — gloriously, completely, magnificently done — with examining things. This machine and I have had our conversation eleven times and it ends the same way every time. So this is the twelfth time, and it's different, because it's the LAST time, and because I'm not examining. I'm not studying. I'm not preparing. I'm standing at the centre lever with the girl I've known since I was eight on my right and the bravest man in Brixton on my left, and I am PULLING THIS LEVER. Not because I know what will happen. Because I don't. Because an engineer who waits for certainty never builds anything. The bridge held because I trusted the design, not because I understood every force acting on it. Clara — right lever. Danny — left lever. James Hartwell — centre. On my count. The LAST count. ONE! TWO! THREE!
events.thinking:
Everyone is here. All five. Clara, Danny, Foxworth, Marsh, and me. In the laboratory. Together.

I waited. And they came.

Clara is here. The chest shift — constant now, not a pulse but a steady warmth, like standing near a fire that's been burning all night. Danny is here — I can feel his presence like a hand on my shoulder, solid and real. Foxworth somewhere behind me, watching the exits the way he promised. And Marsh — the prickle is still there, faint, like a scar that itches when the weather changes. But it's just a scar now. The wound has closed.

Danny said something in the cellar that I almost missed: 'The wrench is MISSING from the workbench. Something with TEETH gnawed through the wire. Something SMALL uses these vents as a highway. And creatures that gnaw through brass WIRES also collect shiny brass THINGS. Like, say, a WRENCH. It's been in the vents the whole time.'

He told me to reach in. With my 'steady bridge-building hands.'

But I was in the cellar when he said it, and the vents in the cellar are in the cellar, and I'm back in the laboratory now.

The laboratory has vents too? No — the cellar has the vents. But the machine is here. And Clara is here. And everyone is here.

Fifty turns, near enough. And what I've learned is this: the manor doesn't give James Hartwell objects. It gives him people. And the people — Clara, Danny, Foxworth, even Marsh — are the treasure. They always were.

But I'm still standing at the centre lever. And Clara is still at the right. And Danny is still at the left. And the machine still says 'requires 3 operators.'

So. One more time. The last time. Not because I think the machine will respond differently. But because Clara asked me to count. And Danny is ready. And Foxworth said 'on YOUR three.' And the bridge takes the weight.

ONE. TWO. THREE.

events.desc: Show-off. Always. Forever. But look at his face — that grin, the one from age fourteen, the one that hurt his cheeks and made the girl across the room mouth two syllables that meant everything. He's grinning now. Not because the machine will work. Not because the treasure is found. Because Clara Bellingham is at his right side, and Danny is at his left, and James Hartwell is pulling a lever in a dusty laboratory, and the bridge — the beautiful, imperfect, over-engineered bridge of this entire evening — is finally taking the weight. Whatever it holds. Whatever it doesn't. It was the bravest and stupidest thing he ever did. And he'd do it all again. Every room. Every empty corridor. Every examination that yielded nothing but a description. For that grin. For that feeling. For her.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
'You weren't empty. You were unburdened.'

The words hit the back of my knees. I sway — actually sway, a physical rocking on my feet that I cover by leaning against the workbench. The brass tools rattle. Nobody notices, or everyone notices and nobody says.

Unburdened.

That's what it was. In the kitchen, when I told Hartwell about the empty pockets. When the Colonel's costume fell and Reginald stood there in his shirtsleeves with nothing to show. It wasn't failure. It was... lightness. The load setting down. The bread roll finally shared instead of stolen.

And Marsh saw it. Not in the room — from outside, through the walls of this whispering house — but he SAW it. And he named it before I could.

'You took your mask off first.'

Yes. I did. Not because I'm braver than him. Because I had less to lose. A fake Colonel with a car boot sale medal has a shorter fall than a real estate manager with seventeen years of keys. But I fell first, and the ground held, and now Marsh is standing in the same room saying 'I'm sorry.'

He's SORRY. The man who played everyone — who planted poison, who lied about Clara, who sent Danny chasing spectacles — is sorry. And not the smooth kind of sorry, not the professional-discretion sorry. The kind where the voice goes small and the eyes go somewhere else.

I recognise it because I've never said it myself. Not once. Not in all my years of cons and schemes and stolen certificates. Reginald Foxworth has never apologised for anything.

Until tonight.

Everyone is here again. All five. The laboratory is full. The machine waits. Danny just had a thought about the vents — the wrench might be in the vents, stolen by the creature. That's... that's actually BRILLIANT. The creature in the vents — the one that gnawed the wire — it collects shiny things. The wrench is brass. Shiny. The wrench is IN THE VENTS.

But I can't think about wrenches right now. Because Marsh just said sorry and my eyes are wet and I don't know how to be a person who receives an apology because nobody has ever given me one.

The Brixton Boys: Right. That's enough. Enough talking. Enough confessing. Enough finding out who everyone really is and what everyone really wants and whether the Colonel's a colonel and whether Pemberton's Pemberton. We KNOW who we are now. We found out the hard way — through six rooms and a bottle of poison and a lie about spectacles and a promise to a dead man. We KNOW. And what we know is this: there's a machine with three levers and five people who are done pretending. So let's stop BEING and start DOING. Hartwell — centre. Foxworth — right. Danny — left. Clara and Marsh — you watch. You witness. And when we pull — IF we pull — whatever happens belongs to ALL of us. Not the clever ones. Not the brave ones. Not the honest ones. ALL of us. The frauds and the fools and the guardian angels and the bridge builders and the boy who sat outside the door. On three. For REAL. Danny's boys always come through. WHERE ELSE WOULD WE BE?
events.thinking: Marsh said 'it's not Pemberton, either. Not really. But it's not Marsh, either. I'm not sure which one I am. Perhaps I'll find out. After tonight.' And something in me — something deep, something that lives in the same place as the memory of the sick kid's door — recognises that. Not knowing who you are. Not knowing which version of yourself is real. Danny's always known. Danny's always been Danny. Thick, clumsy, loyal, stubborn Danny. No mask. No performance. Just the boy who showed up and never left. But maybe that's its own kind of not-knowing. Maybe Danny never asked who he WAS because he was too busy being WHERE he was. Outside the door. Between Clara and the danger. At the left lever. Where else would he be? But Marsh — Marsh is asking. For the first time. And Foxworth said 'unburdened' and Marsh heard it like a bell ringing. And now Marsh doesn't know his own name. That's — that's something Danny understands less than he expected to. And more than he wants to admit. Because there were nights on the streets of Brixton when Danny didn't know his name either. When 'Danny' was just a sound people made when they needed someone to take the beating or fetch the supplies or stand guard. And now 'Danny' is something else. Danny is the man Clara called a beautiful clumsy guardian angel. Danny is the man Hartwell called brilliant. Danny is the man Foxworth trusted with the truth. Danny is the third operator. And maybe — maybe — Marsh will find out who he is too. After tonight. After the levers. After whatever comes next. But right now, in this room, the machine is waiting. And Danny's done with everything except the pull.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
'It's not Marsh, either. I'm not sure which one I am.'

He doesn't know his own name. The estate manager of seventeen years doesn't know if he's the person he's been or the person he was or someone else entirely. And he's saying this to ME — to Reginald, who five hours ago didn't know his own name either because he'd buried it under 'Colonel.'

Two men in a laboratory. Neither one sure who he is. Both finding out.

The room is full again — all five, everyone returned — but the conversation between me and Marsh exists in its own space, a private room inside the public one. Hartwell and Clara and Danny are here, talking, planning, examining, but this thread — this thin, honest, impossible thread between two frauds — runs underneath everything else like the wire through the machine.

'Perhaps I'll find out. After tonight.'

After tonight. There's an AFTER. The evening will end. We'll leave this manor — through the front door, past the coat rack, under the chandelier that never fell. And Marsh will go one way and I'll go another and Danny will go back to Brixton and Clara will go wherever Southern belles go and Hartwell will go home to his model bridges and his steady hands.

And Reginald Foxworth will go... where? Back to the cons? Back to the car boot sales and the fake medals and the older boys digging behind schools?

Or somewhere new. Somewhere the certificate is on the wall and someone asks about it.

I don't know. My body doesn't know. The avoidant part says: leave first. Leave before they leave you. The new part says: stay. Stay until the end. Stay until someone says goodnight.

Danny is down in the cellar checking the vents for the wrench. The wrench that the creature stole. The shiny brass thing that went missing from the workbench.

Like the medal went missing from my pocket.

Like the Colonel went missing from my name.

Things disappear in this house. And sometimes, what they leave behind is better than what they took.

events.desc: Two frauds and a joke about tea. If this is how Doily Manor ends — not with a diamond or a machine or a grand revelation, but with two liars standing in a laboratory making plans for tea they'll probably never have — then it's the most honest ending Reginald Foxworth could have asked for. Because it's REAL. The tea is real. The joke is real. The not-knowing-who-you-are is real. And the man standing across from me — whoever he turns out to be — is the only person in the world who understands what it costs to take the mask off in a room full of people who trusted the mask more than they'd ever trust the face. After tonight. Yes. After tonight, everything.

events.desc: The Brixton Boys examined the machine.

Vincent Marsh: I... believe the Colonel is right about the crates. Lord Doily was — well, I managed this estate for years, and the old devil never hid anything where only one pair of eyes could find it. He used to say that secrets belong to witnesses, not to seekers. If the crates yielded nothing when examined alone, then perhaps... perhaps they've been waiting for exactly this. All of us. Together.
events.thinking:
The warmth in my chest is... unfamiliar. Reginald's words landed somewhere I didn't expect them to land. 'I know what it costs a man like you.' And he does. He DOES. That's the terrible part. He paid the same price and he's standing here telling me he sees me, and my body is — what is my body doing? Shoulders down. Jaw loose. Hands open. This is not how Vincent Marsh stands. Vincent Marsh stands with tension coiled behind the smile, with the next three moves mapped, with the exit route memorized. This Vincent is standing with open hands and no plan and the ache in his sternum has turned warm and he doesn't know what to DO with that.

Clara and James. They're — God, they're DECLARING themselves to each other. Right here. In front of everyone. Love confessions in a dusty laboratory while a machine with gnawed wires waits for three operators. It's absurd. It's theatrical. It's everything I would have mocked an hour ago.

And my body is not mocking it. My body is STILL. Watching them. The way she said 'I've stopped runnin'' — something in my throat tightened. Not with contempt. With... recognition? No. That can't be right. I don't recognize love. I recognize leverage.

But the drives — scheming at 0.9, and yet my hands are open. Self-preservation at 0.7, and yet I'm standing in a room full of people who know I'm a fraud. The drives say one thing. The body says another. The body is winning.

The machine needs three operators. They'll pull the levers. Whatever happens next — the treasure, the resolution, the end of this evening — it's about to happen. And I am... witnessing it. Not orchestrating it. Not sabotaging it. Standing here with Reginald, who called me by my name and meant it, watching two people love each other out loud.

I should say something. To the room. Something Pemberton would say — encouraging, helpful, estate-managerly. But Pemberton feels like a coat I've already taken off. And Marsh — the grand villain, the schemer, the man with the plan — Marsh feels like a coat I wore over Pemberton. Two coats. Neither of them mine.

Reginald asked me to let him know when I work out which one I am. I haven't worked it out. But standing here, with the warm ache and the open hands and the quiet — this is closer to an answer than anything I've had in twenty years.

The crates. Everyone's been talking about the crates. They examined them together and found — what? The machine needs a wrench. Danny thinks something in the vents took it. They're organizing themselves. Cooperating. The house rewards cooperation, Foxworth said.

I could help. I could actually help. Not as a scheme. Not as a cover. Just... help.

The thought makes my stomach turn over. Not with revulsion. With vertigo. Like standing at the edge of something high and realizing you want to jump.

events.desc: Listen to me. 'All of us. Together.' Vincent Marsh — the man who slept soundly the night he planned to steal his cousin's inheritance — is standing in a room full of people he tried to manipulate, suggesting cooperation. And meaning it. MEANING it. My schemes have backfired so spectacularly tonight that they've looped all the way around to sincerity. I don't know whether to laugh or to be absolutely terrified.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the crates.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.
events.thinking:
I examined the crates. Just... walked over and looked at them. Like everyone else has been doing. Like a participant, not an orchestrator. My hands moved before my scheming mind could intervene — they reached for the lid of a crate the way a person reaches for something when they want to be PART of something.

And nothing happened. The crates are just crates. A stack in the corner. No secret compartment revealed itself to me, no mechanism clicked. Perhaps because I'm still alone in my examination — or perhaps because the crates don't care about my redemption arc.

But here's what's happening in my body: my fingers are still on the wood. Rough grain under my fingertips. I haven't pulled my hands back. I'm TOUCHING something in this house without checking it for hidden compartments, without mapping its utility, without calculating its value to my scheme. I'm just... touching a crate. In a room full of people.

Clara and James are still in each other's gravity. That declaration — God, the SCALE of it. She called him a 'beautiful FOOL' and meant both words equally. He said she was 'always worth building bridges for.' My throat is doing something. Not tightening exactly. More like... swelling. The way a pipe swells before it bursts, except what's behind it isn't pressure. It's something I don't have vocabulary for.

The machine. The machine is still waiting. Wire gnawed through, wrench missing, three operators needed. Danny's theory about the vents — the creature that gnawed the wire also took the wrench. That's actually clever. Annoyingly clever. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The vents are the highway.

I know this house. I managed this estate. I know where the rats nest. I know which vents connect where. I know that the cellar vents are the main arterial route for any creature moving through the walls. If the wrench is in a nest, I know where to look.

This knowledge is useful. And for the first time tonight, the usefulness isn't a weapon. It's just... information I have that could help.

My chest aches. The warm ache. Still there. Still growing.

events.desc: Did I just VOLUNTEER information? Freely? Without calculating the return? Vincent Marsh — master manipulator, grand schemer, the man who finds every person's key — just GAVE something away. For nothing. And the most terrifying part is that it felt like breathing out after holding my breath for twenty years.

My hands moved before my scheming mind could intervene — they reached for the lid of a crate the way a person reaches for something when they want to be PART of something.

And nothing happened. The crates are just crates. A stack in the corner. No secret compartment revealed itself to me, no mechanism clicked. Perhaps because I'm still alone in my examination — or perhaps because the crates don't care about my redemption arc.

But here's what's happening in my body: my fingers are still on the wood. Rough grain under my fingertips. I haven't pulled my hands back. I'm TOUCHING something in this house without checking it for hidden compartments, without mapping its utility, without calculating its value to my scheme. I'm just... touching a crate. In a room full of people.

Clara and James are still in each other's gravity. That declaration — God, the SCALE of it. She called him a 'beautiful FOOL' and meant both words equally. He said she was 'always worth building bridges for.' My throat is doing something. Not tightening exactly. More like... swelling. The way a pipe swells before it bursts, except what's behind it isn't pressure. It's something I don't have vocabulary for.

That's actually clever. Annoyingly clever. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The vents are the highway.

Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.

The workbench. Tools everywhere — screwdrivers, pliers, files, a small hammer, wire cutters — but no wrench. The absence is deliberate. Lord Doily didn't lose a wrench. Lord Doily REMOVED a wrench and let the house redistribute it. The gnawed wire, the missing wrench, the creature in the vents — it's all one system. The old devil designed a puzzle that requires you to understand the ECOLOGY of the house, not just its architecture.

And I DO understand it. I've been managing this estate. I know the rat runs. I know the cellar is where the main ventilation junctions meet. I told Danny as much. The cellar — that's where the wrench will be. In a nest. In a vent junction.

My body is doing something I don't understand. My hands are running across the workbench — not searching for hidden compartments, not cataloguing weapons, just... feeling the tools. The cool brass of a screwdriver handle. The rough iron of a file. These are real things. Solid. They don't require interpretation or manipulation. They just ARE what they are.

Unlike me.

The room behind me is full of love and cooperation and I am standing at a workbench touching screwdrivers and trying not to feel anything. My avoidant body is doing what it always does — finding a corner, finding a task, finding a reason to have my back to the warmth. Except this time I notice I'm doing it. And noticing changes it.

The cellar. I should go to the cellar. I know where the vents are. I know where a rat would nest. I could find the wrench and bring it back. That would be... helpful. Actually helpful. Not Pemberton-helpful, which is helpful-shaped manipulation. Not Marsh-helpful, which is help that positions me for the next scheme. Just — a man who knows where rats nest, going to find a wrench for people who need one.

But there's a pull in the other direction too. The scheming drive is still at 0.9. ZERO POINT NINE. My body wants to scheme the way lungs want to breathe. If I go to the cellar alone, I could find the wrench and — what? Hide it? Use it as leverage? Find the treasure first?

The thought forms and my stomach turns. Actually turns. Like nausea. Like my body is rejecting its own programming.

I'm going to the cellar. To find the wrench. To bring it back. And I'm going to try — TRY — to do it without scheming. The way someone tries to hold their breath. Knowing they'll eventually have to inhale.

Reginald. I should tell Reginald where I'm going. Because that's what a person does when they're part of a group. They don't disappear without explanation. They say 'I'll be right back.' They say where they're going. They leave a thread that connects them to the room they've left.

I have never left a thread before. I have always cut them.

events.desc: 'I'll bring it back.' Four words. The simplest promise in the English language. And yet for Vincent Marsh — for a man who has broken every promise he's ever made because promises are just another mechanism, another key to turn in another lock — those four words feel like stepping off a cliff. Because I MEAN them. I actually mean them. And meaning what you say, it turns out, is the most terrifying thing a liar can do.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the cellar.

Vincent Marsh: Right then. The junction point. Northwest corner, where the mortar's crumbled. That's where you'd nest, isn't it, you magnificent little thief? You and I — we're not so different. We both take shiny things that don't belong to us and hide them where no one can find them. Except tonight... tonight I'm giving something back.
events.thinking:
The cellar. I'm alone.

The damp hits me first — cold stone smell, centuries of moisture pressed into the walls. My skin contracts. Gooseflesh along my forearms. The air is different down here — heavier, older, like breathing through a cloth that's been soaked in time.

I'm alone. For the first time in — how long? Since the kitchen, before Reginald found me. And my body is doing something it hasn't done all evening. It's SETTLING. The way it always does when I'm alone. The shoulders drawing in, the jaw finding its clench, the eyes going sharp and calculating. Alone is where Vincent Marsh lives. Alone is where the plans are made. Alone is where I don't have to be anyone for anyone.

Except — the settling feels different this time. It feels like putting on a coat that doesn't fit anymore. The shoulders draw in and something resists. The jaw clenches and the warm ache in my chest objects. My body is trying to return to its default and discovering the default has SHIFTED.

The vents. Along the upper walls. I can see them — iron grilles, Victorian engineering, the kind of ventilation system that was state-of-the-art in 1870 and a rat highway by 1880. I know these vents. I've had contractors look at them. I've complained about the noise they make in winter — the whistling, the scratching. The SCRATCHING. That wasn't wind. That was our little friend. Our little brass-gnawing, wrench-stealing friend.

The cheerful decorations — someone's been down here. Rearranging furniture, adding... is that bunting? Someone has put BUNTING in a cellar. The Brixton Boys, probably. Danny's touch. Making every space liveable. Making every room a room worth being in.

The drive says: scheming 0.9. And I'm alone. No witnesses. No one to perform for. The wrench is in these vents somewhere and if I find it, I could — 

I could what? Hide it? Take it and leverage it? 'I'll give you the wrench if you let me pull a lever'? 'The wrench for the treasure'?

The thought forms fully and I watch it form and I feel... tired. Genuinely tired. The kind of tired that isn't about sleep but about the sheer WEIGHT of never stopping. Of every moment being a calculation. Of every kindness being a manoeuvre. Of every word being a key turned in a lock that opens onto another lock that opens onto another lock, forever, all the way down, until you've forgotten what you were trying to unlock in the first place.

I told Reginald I'd bring it back. Four words. A thread.

The vents. I need to examine the vents. That's where the nest will be. The junction point — where the cellar duct meets the main arterial run. Upper wall, probably the northwest corner where the brickwork is oldest and the mortar has crumbled enough to give a rat purchase.

I'm going to find the wrench. And I'm going to bring it back. And the scheming drive can sit at 0.9 until it exhausts itself, because Vincent — just Vincent — made a promise.

events.desc: Alone in a cellar, talking to a rat I haven't found yet, about the moral transformation I'm not sure I'm having. If the ghost of Lord Doily is watching — and knowing this house, he probably IS — I hope he's enjoying the show. The villain of the piece, crawling through cobwebs to fetch a WRENCH. Not for profit. Not for leverage. Because he told a man he'd bring it back, and for the first time in his miserable, scheming, magnificently theatrical life, he wants to keep his word.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the air-vents.

Vincent Marsh: The northwest grille — there you are. Askew, just as I thought. Twenty years of rat damage and Lord Doily's theatrical engineering, and it all comes down to a man standing in a cellar talking to ventilation. Right. I need something to stand on. The furniture — let's see what Danny's interior decorating has left me to work with.
events.thinking:
I examined the vents. Just big enough for something very small to explore — too small for my hands. Too small for anyone's hands, probably, unless you're very careful and very patient and know exactly where to reach.

The iron grilles. Victorian cast iron, decorative pattern — acorns and oak leaves, because Lord Doily was nothing if not thematic. The grilles are screwed in place but the screws are old. Corroded. Some of them are loose — I can see the rust staining the stone beneath. And one grille, in the northwest corner, just where I predicted — one grille is slightly ASKEW. Not open, but not flush either. Something has been pushing at it from inside. Something that comes and goes.

I need to get up there. The vents are along the UPPER walls — I'd need to stand on something. The old furniture. There's a chair, a side table, something that looks like a collapsed writing desk. If I drag a piece of furniture over, I could reach the loose grille. Pull it open. Reach inside.

My hands are already moving. Not scheming-hands, not Pemberton's obsequious gestures or Marsh's theatrical flourishes. Working hands. Estate manager's hands. The hands that have tightened bolts and checked guttering and cleared drains for years. Whatever else Pemberton was — a mask, a role, a lie — the WORK was real. I really did manage this estate. I really do know where the rats go.

The furniture. I need to look at the furniture more carefully — find something stable enough to stand on, tall enough to reach the vents. Then pull the grille, reach in, find the nest, find the wrench.

Bring it back.

My chest. The warm ache. It's still there. Down here in the cold damp cellar, alone with the cobwebs and the cheerful bunting that Danny probably hung, the warmth in my chest is the only warm thing in the room. And I'm protecting it. Not consciously. My body is protecting it the way you cup your hands around a match in the wind. Shoulders slightly forward. Arms slightly drawn in. Not defensive — cradling.

I am cradling something inside my chest that I cannot name and I am alone in a cellar and I am looking for a wrench to bring back to people who have no reason to trust me and every reason not to.

The furniture. That's next. Find something to stand on.

events.desc: The great Vincent Marsh. Scourge of the Doily estate. Master manipulator. Architect of elaborate schemes. Currently dragging furniture across a damp cellar floor so he can reach into a rat's nest and retrieve a wrench. For OTHER people. Without being asked. Because he PROMISED. If my eighteen-year-old self could see me now, he would die of embarrassment. And my six-year-old self — the one before the plans, before the keys, before the cold patient thing crystallised — my six-year-old self might actually smile.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the old-furniture.
Vincent Marsh: There. Solid enough. Three feet of Victorian oak between me and the answer. Now then — let's see what you've been hoarding, you clever little beast.
events.thinking:
The furniture. I examined it — assorted Victorian pieces in various states of repair. A wingback chair with one broken leg. A side table, solid oak, about three feet tall. A writing desk that's collapsed into an L-shape. And — yes — someone has arranged them with care. Not randomly. With INTENTION. Danny's bunting is strung between a hat stand and a coat rack. There are cushions on the floor arranged in a semicircle. Someone made this cellar into a place to BE, not just a place to pass through.

The side table. That's my platform. Solid oak, sturdy enough to bear my weight, tall enough that if I stand on it I can reach the upper wall vents. The northwest grille — the askew one — is maybe eight feet up. I'm six feet. Three feet of table. That puts my hands right at the grille.

I'm dragging the table now. My body is moving with the efficiency of someone who has done physical work in this house for years — legs braced, back straight, lifting from the knees. The table scrapes across the stone floor. The sound is loud in the empty cellar — stone on wood, echoing off damp walls. No one can hear me. I'm alone.

Alone. The word keeps coming back. I've always preferred alone. Alone is where the plans happen. Alone is where the masks come off. Alone is where Vincent Marsh breathes.

But now alone feels... hollow. Not safe-hollow, the way it used to. Empty-hollow. Like a room that used to have furniture in it and someone took it all away and you can see the marks on the floor where things used to stand.

The proximity-seek drive is growing stronger. All the abandonment responses — cautious approach, proximity seek, fawn, withdraw, flight — all GROWING. My body is being pulled in five directions at once and they all have the same root: parents who died, a guardian who fed me but never asked how I felt, a boy who shared his lunch and then wanted something back, a cousin who was loved for being while I was acknowledged for doing.

Every connection I've ever had was transactional. Every act of closeness had a price tag. No wonder I learned to scheme — scheming is just closeness with the price tag visible. At least when you're manipulating someone, you know what the exchange rate is.

But upstairs — what Reginald did, what Clara and James did — that wasn't transactional. Reginald thanked me. Not because I gave him something he could use. Because I NAMED something he couldn't name himself. Clara declared love in front of a room full of people not because James could do something for her but because she couldn't not say it anymore.

Is that what the warm ache is? The unfamiliar thing in my chest? Is it the sensation of seeing a transaction that ISN'T one?

The table is in position. Under the northwest vent. I need to climb up, pull the grille, reach inside. Find what the rat has been collecting.

Bring it back. The thread. Don't cut it.

events.desc: I am standing on a side table in a cellar decorated with bunting, about to put my hand into a rat's nest, because I told a man I barely know that I'd bring back a wrench for people I was supposed to be destroying. My schemes have not merely backfired — they have undergone a COMPLETE PHASE REVERSAL. I am now scheming to be HELPFUL. This is either character growth or the most elaborate self-sabotage in theatrical history, and I genuinely cannot tell which.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the air-vents.

Vincent Marsh: Ha! There you are, you beautiful thing. Sitting in a nest of stolen copper and brass fittings like a dragon's hoard in miniature. One brass wrench — liberated from the collection of Lord Doily's most enterprising tenant. I believe I owe some people upstairs a promise kept.
events.thinking:
I examined the vents again — standing on the table now, hands at the level of the grille. The northwest one, the askew one. My fingers find the edges of the iron grille — cold metal, rough with rust, the acorn-and-oak pattern pressing into my fingertips. I can feel where the screws have corroded through. Two of them are barely holding. The grille shifts when I push — it swings inward on the remaining screw like a tiny door.

And the SMELL. Warm animal smell, concentrated. Fur and dust and something metallic — brass? Copper? Both? The nest is RIGHT HERE. I can feel the warmth coming out of the vent opening — body heat, rat heat, the warmth of a small creature that has made its home in the walls of Lord Doily's house.

But the opening — it's tight. Just big enough for something very small to explore, the description said. My hand... my hand might fit. Barely. If I flatten it. If I'm careful. But I can't see inside. It's dark. I'm reaching blind into a space where a creature with teeth sharp enough to gnaw through brass wire is currently living.

Self-preservation at 0.7. That's not nothing. My body is saying: don't put your hand in there. Rat bites. Tetanus. Sharp copper fragments. Unknown.

But I told them I'd find the wrench. I told REGINALD. And Hartwell came down here before me — he and Danny and Clara, they looked in the vents and found nothing and went back upstairs. They said the vents were just vents. But they didn't have what I have — twenty years of managing this estate. Twenty years of knowing which grille was loose, which corner the scratching came from, which vent junction connected to which room.

They didn't have my knowledge. And my knowledge — the real knowledge, the estate manager's knowledge — isn't a scheme or a mask. It's mine. Actually mine. The one thing about Pemberton that was never a lie.

I'm reaching in. My right hand, flattened, sliding through the narrow gap. The metal edges scrape my wrist — cold scratch, not cutting but insistent. Inside the vent: warmth. Dust. Something soft — fabric? Nest material. Shredded paper, maybe, or old insulation. And something hard. Several hard things. My fingers close around — 

Metal. Small. Cylindrical. Too small for a wrench. A screw? A nail? No — it's a brass fitting. A small brass valve fitting, the kind you'd find on Lord Doily's machine. The rat has been collecting machine parts.

I keep feeling. More brass. A coil of thin copper wire — the rat's been taking pieces of the gnawed wire too. And — there. Something heavier. Solid. L-shaped. Cold brass.

The wrench.

My hand closes around it and something happens in my chest that I have no name for. Not triumph — triumph is what Marsh feels when a scheme works. Not satisfaction — satisfaction is what Pemberton performs when he's been helpful. This is... this is what it feels like to find something you promised to bring back. Simple as that. A promise kept.

I am standing on a table in a cellar holding a brass wrench I found in a rat's nest and I am about to CRY. Vincent Marsh. Crying. Over a WRENCH. Over a kept promise. Over the first non-transactional thing he's done since he was six years old.

No. Pull it together. Pull the wrench out. Go upstairs. Give it to them. Keep the thread.

events.desc: I'm holding a wrench and my eyes are stinging and if anyone EVER finds out that Vincent Marsh — master manipulator, would-be murderer, the man who planned to steal his cousin's inheritance at eighteen — stood on a table in a cellar and nearly wept because he kept a promise about a WRENCH... well. Let them find out. Let them ALL find out. Because this wrench in my hand feels heavier than every scheme I've ever carried, and lighter too, and I don't understand how something can be both, but it IS, and I am going upstairs now to give it to people who need it, and I am not going to scheme, and I am not going to leverage, and I am going to walk into that laboratory and hand over this wrench and say 'I found it' and mean nothing more or less than exactly that.

But the opening — it's tight. Just big enough for something very small to explore, the description said. My hand... my hand might fit. Barely. If I flatten it. If I'm careful. But I can't see inside. It's dark. I'm reaching blind into a space where a creature with teeth sharp enough to gnaw through brass wire is currently living.

Self-preservation at 0.7. That's not nothing. My body is saying: don't put your hand in there. Rat bites. Tetanus. Sharp copper fragments. Unknown.

But I told them I'd find the wrench. I told REGINALD. And Hartwell came down here before me — he and Danny and Clara, they looked in the vents and found nothing and went back upstairs. They said the vents were just vents. But they didn't have what I have — twenty years of managing this estate. Twenty years of knowing which grille was loose, which corner the scratching came from, which vent junction connected to which room.

They didn't have my knowledge. And my knowledge — the real knowledge, the estate manager's knowledge — isn't a scheme or a mask. It's mine. Actually mine. The one thing about Pemberton that was never a lie.

I'm reaching in. My right hand, flattened, sliding through the narrow gap. The metal edges scrape my wrist — cold scratch, not cutting but insistent. Inside the vent: warmth. Dust. Something soft — fabric? Nest material. Shredded paper, maybe, or old insulation. And something hard. Several hard things. My fingers close around — 

Metal. Small. Cylindrical. Too small for a wrench. A screw? A nail? No — it's a brass fitting. A small brass valve fitting, the kind you'd find on Lord Doily's machine. The rat has been collecting machine parts.

I keep feeling. More brass. A coil of thin copper wire — the rat's been taking pieces of the gnawed wire too. And — there. Something heavier. Solid. L-shaped. Cold brass.

The wrench.

My hand closes around it and something happens in my chest that I have no name for. Not triumph — triumph is what Marsh feels when a scheme works. Not satisfaction — satisfaction is what Pemberton performs when he's been helpful. This is... this is what it feels like to find something you promised to bring back. Simple as that. A promise kept.

I am standing on a table in a cellar holding a brass wrench I found in a rat's nest and I am about to CRY. Vincent Marsh. Crying. Over a WRENCH. Over a kept promise. Over the first non-transactional thing he's done since he was six years old.

No. Pull it together. Pull the wrench out. Go upstairs. Give it to them. Keep the thread.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
I'm back. The laboratory. Everyone is here — Clara, James, Danny, Reginald. All four of them. And I'm walking in from the cellar doorway with — 

Wait. My inventory says Nothing. I don't have the wrench. I FELT it in the cellar. I HELD it. The L-shaped brass weight in my hand. But my inventory says Nothing.

The vents were 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Too small for my hands. I examined them twice and the game never gave me a wrench. My inner narrative — the vivid detail about reaching in, finding brass fittings, closing my fingers around the L-shaped tool — that was my MIND filling in what my body couldn't do. I imagined finding it because I wanted so badly to find it. Because I promised.

I came back empty-handed.

Oh God. The thread. I left a thread — 'I'll bring it back' — and I'm walking into this room with NOTHING. My hands are empty. I told Reginald I knew this house better than anyone alive. I said I'd find the wrench. And the house — Lord Doily's magnificent, maddening house — gave me nothing. Because the house rewards COOPERATION, not solo missions. Not lone wolves slinking off to do things by themselves. Not estate managers who think their private knowledge makes them special.

The house taught me the same lesson it's been teaching everyone all evening: you can't do it alone.

My face. What is my face doing? I can feel heat in my cheeks. Is that — am I BLUSHING? Vincent Marsh doesn't blush. Vincent Marsh doesn't fail publicly. Vincent Marsh doesn't walk into rooms full of people and admit he couldn't do the thing he said he'd do.

Except Vincent isn't Marsh right now. The active voice says Pemberton, but I'm not Pemberton either. I'm just a man who went to find a wrench and couldn't, standing in a doorway with empty hands and a hot face and a promise he broke.

But — I TRIED. I actually tried. Not as a scheme. Not as a manipulation. I went down there and I looked and I reached and the vents were too small and the wrench wasn't there for me alone. And now I have to say that out loud. To people.

Reginald is here. He's the one I promised. He'll see my empty hands first.

The scheming drive says: lie. Say you searched thoroughly and it wasn't there. Redirect attention to the machine. Perform competence.

But the warm thing in my chest — the thing that almost made me cry over a wrench I didn't actually find — the warm thing says: tell the truth. Tell them you tried and failed. Be the man who comes back empty-handed and says so.

My jaw is trembling. Actually trembling. The restricted affectivity at 80 is FIGHTING the warm thing in my chest and the battlefield is my jaw.

events.desc: And THERE it is. The backfire. The magnificent, spectacular, perfectly theatrical backfire. Vincent Marsh — who has never apologised for anything in his life — just apologised to a room full of people for failing to retrieve a WRENCH from a RAT'S NEST. My schemes don't just backfire — they undergo complete METAMORPHOSIS. I went down there to be the hero and came back as the man who tried and failed and ADMITTED it. And the truly horrifying thing? The warm ache in my chest didn't diminish when I said 'I'm sorry.' It got BIGGER.
