events.desc: Vincent Marsh: But I found the nest — the location is confirmed. Northwest corner, cellar, where I said it would be. The opening is too small for one pair of hands alone, but perhaps... perhaps if we went together. More hands. Smaller hands, maybe. Or — the crates. Did you find anything in the crates when you examined them together? Lord Doily built this house for groups, not for lone fools crawling into rat holes by themselves. What has the house shown you while I was gone?
events.thinking:
I said it. I stood there and told them I failed. And now I'm standing still, watching. Waiting. The room hasn't responded yet — or if it has, I missed it because I was so focused on the act of SAYING it that I forgot to notice what happened after.

My body. What is my body doing right now? Standing in the doorway. Hands at my sides — empty, visible, deliberately not hidden. My weight is on both feet, not leaning toward the exit, not ready to bolt. I'm staying. That's what my body is telling the room: I'm staying even though I failed.

The machine is still there. Wire gnawed through. Three levers. Requires three operators. The wrench is still missing — I couldn't get it from the cellar alone. But Danny said the wrench was IN the vents. And the workbench has tools but no wrench. And the crates — everyone examined the crates together and... what happened? The observations don't tell me what they found. Just that they examined them.

The machine. Maybe — maybe the wrench isn't the only path. The wire is gnawed through. The workbench has tools. Wire cutters? Pliers? Copper wire? Could the wire be REPAIRED instead of the missing wrench being the only solution? I'm thinking like an estate manager again. When something breaks in a house, you don't always need the ideal tool. You need A tool. Any tool that works.

The workbench has tools. The machine has a gnawed wire. What if the solution isn't finding the wrench at all — what if it's using what's already here to fix what's broken?

But I already looked at the workbench. Tools but no wrench. The machine needs three operators AND a functional wire. Two problems, not one.

Or — the crates. Everyone examined them together. Lord Doily hid things from solo searchers. If the crates reveal something when multiple people look, then maybe what the crates contain is the missing piece. Maybe the wrench IS in the crates, waiting for enough people to look together.

I should suggest this. Out loud. To the group. Not as Pemberton performing helpfulness. Not as Marsh redirecting attention. As someone who has a thought and shares it.

But my body — my avoidant, intimacy-avoiding, restricted-affectivity body — is pulling me toward silence. Toward the corner. Toward watching rather than participating. The admission of failure spent something, used up some reserve of openness, and now the walls want to come back up.

The proximity-seek is fighting the withdrawal. Both growing stronger. Both rooted in the same abandonment. Approach and retreat. Reach and pull back. The boy who was uncomfortable when someone shared lunch with him AND the boy who wanted someone to share lunch with him. They're the same boy. They've always been the same boy.

The machine. The crates. The group. I need to stay in the room. I need to stay visible. I need to keep the thread.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the crates.

Vincent Marsh: The crates are just crates. I think Lord Doily is laughing at us from whatever afterlife accepts eccentric Victorian industrialists — we've been staring at a stack of wood while his machine sits right THERE, waiting. The wire is gnawed through, yes, but perhaps that doesn't matter. Perhaps the machine works regardless, or perhaps it works BECAUSE of the damage. The man built a house that rewards cooperation — who's to say he didn't build a machine that rewards... faith? Three operators. We have five people in this room. I say we stop hunting for what's missing and try what we HAVE.
events.thinking:
The crates again. I examined them and got — nothing. 'A stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' Same as before. Same as when I examined them alone. Same as when everyone else examined them together.

Except — wait. The Foxworth observation says he examined them and realised the house rewards COOPERATION. And everyone has been examining them together and getting... what? The description doesn't change. 'A stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' Every time.

Maybe the crates aren't the answer. Maybe they're a red herring. Maybe Lord Doily put a stack of old wooden crates in the corner of his laboratory specifically because treasure hunters would waste hours examining them while the ACTUAL puzzle — the machine — sat right there waiting.

The machine. It has two problems: a gnawed wire and it requires three operators. And the wrench is missing from the workbench. But does the machine NEED the wrench? The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' It doesn't say 'Requires wrench.' The gnawed wire is a separate issue.

What if the machine works WITH the gnawed wire? What if the wire breaking is part of the design? What if Lord Doily WANTED the rats to gnaw through it? The man built a house that rewards cooperation — is it beyond him to build a machine that includes biological sabotage as a FEATURE?

Or — more practically — what if the wrench is needed to fix the wire, and the wire needs to be fixed before the machine can be operated? In which case the problem is sequential: wrench → wire → three operators → whatever the machine does.

The machine needs three operators. There are FIVE people in this room. Three on the levers, two watching. Clara suggested Danny on the left, Reginald on the right, James in the centre. She was going to stand with them. That's three or four at the machine.

But the machine's wire is gnawed through. Can it operate with a broken wire?

I should try the machine. Everyone else has examined it. Clara, James, Danny — they've all examined it. Maybe with five people in the room, maybe with the crates already examined, maybe with my contribution — maybe the machine is ready.

Or maybe I need to stop trying to solve the puzzle ALONE in my head and actually ASK someone. That's what cooperation looks like. Not 'I will figure this out and present the answer.' Cooperation is 'I don't know — do you?'

My body is resisting that. The grandiosity at 80, the manipulativeness at 85 — every fibre of my personality says: never ask. Asking is yielding. Asking is admitting you don't have the answer. Asking is being the boy at school who needed someone to share lunch with him.

But I already admitted I failed. I already came back empty-handed. I already said 'I'm sorry.' What's one more vulnerability when you've already bled out on the floor?

The machine. Let me try the machine. Maybe the answer has been here all along and we've all been too busy examining crates and searching cellars to just... pull the levers.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the machine.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with James Hartwell.
events.thinking:
I examined the machine. 'Requires 3 operators.' The wire is gnawed through. Nothing new revealed itself. The machine sits there, brass and copper and levers and dials, waiting for three people to operate it and a wire to be repaired.

I'm running out of ideas. I've examined the crates — nothing. The workbench — tools but no wrench. The machine — needs 3 operators. I went to the cellar, found the nest, couldn't reach the wrench. I came back. I've examined everything in this room and nothing has changed.

Wait. WAIT. I keep examining things ALONE. Even when everyone's in the room, I'm the one doing the examining. Pemberton examining the crates. Pemberton examining the machine. Solo actions in a group setting.

But the machine says 'Requires 3 operators.' It doesn't say 'Requires 1 examiner.' Maybe the EXAMINE action on the machine only works when multiple characters do it simultaneously. Clara examined it. James examined it. Danny examined it. But I don't know if they examined it at the same TIME or one at a time.

The keen observations show Clara's earlier speech about the machine — 'Danny on the left, Reginald on the right, James in the centre.' She was organizing the team. Three operators. They were about to pull the levers.

So what happened? Did they pull them? The observations show love declarations and crate examinations and vent theories — but did anyone actually OPERATE the machine? It seems like they got distracted by the crates, then the cellar, then the love confessions...

Maybe the machine has been waiting all this time because everyone keeps getting sidetracked. By emotions. By treasure hunts. By WRENCH hunts. By declarations of love in dusty laboratories.

And here I am, another person getting sidetracked. Examining things one more time. When what I should be doing is stepping back and letting THEM do it. Three operators. Not me — them. Clara suggested the team. Danny, Reginald, James. Or Clara, Danny, James. Any three.

My role isn't to operate the machine. My role is to stand here and watch them do it. To be the witness. The fifth person in the room who isn't pulling a lever but is present. Bearing witness.

Or — and this thought arrives like a door opening — my role is to be the FOURTH. The one who helps without pulling a lever. The one who notices what needs noticing. The estate manager who knows the house.

The gnawed wire. The workbench has tools. Pliers. Wire. What if I don't need the wrench at all? What if I can SPLICE the wire with what's on the workbench? Pliers to strip, spare wire to bridge the gap, the estate manager's hands that have done repairs like this a hundred times?

Not a scheme. Not a grand plan. Just... a repair. A man who knows how to fix things, fixing a thing that's broken.

I should LOOK at the workbench more carefully. Not 'examine' it for secrets. LOOK at it for tools I can actually use.

events.desc: The estate manager's hands. The hands that have fixed leaky taps and rehung doors and spliced wires and patched plaster for twenty years. The hands that were always acknowledged for DOING while others were praised for BEING. Perhaps — just perhaps — being acknowledged for doing isn't the insult I always took it for. Perhaps doing IS a kind of being. Perhaps the man who fixes things is as real as the man who inherits them.

Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
The workbench again. 'A sturdy workbench covered in tools — but no wrench.' Same description. Tools. But no wrench. I can't TAKE tools from the workbench — it's not listed as a portable object. I can't USE tools I don't have. The workbench is set dressing, not inventory.

I'm stuck. Every object in this room has been examined multiple times by multiple people and nothing changes. The crates are crates. The workbench has tools but no wrench. The machine needs three operators. The wrench is in a rat's nest I can't reach.

And I'm going in circles. Literally. Crates, workbench, machine, cellar, back, crates, workbench, machine. Round and round. The estate manager who knows everything about this house and can't unlock a single thing in it.

Maybe... maybe I need to stop DOING and start BEING. The teacher praised my cousin for her natural grace and warmth. I scored higher in every subject. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And here I am, twenty years later, still doing doing doing — examining, searching, proposing, fixing — because doing is the only way I know to matter.

But the room isn't asking me to DO anything. The room is asking me to BE somewhere. To be HERE. With these people. While they figure it out.

The others have been examining the machine. Clara organized the team. James volunteered as the third operator. Danny theorized about the vents. Reginald called them all to the crates. They're working TOGETHER and I keep running off on solo missions or examining things by myself.

What if my contribution isn't finding the wrench or splicing the wire or examining the crates? What if my contribution is just... staying? Being the fifth person in the room? Being present without an agenda?

My body wants to do something. The competence drive, the scheming drive, the dominance drive — they all want ACTION. But the room is quiet. And sometimes the bravest thing a man who's spent his whole life scheming can do is stand still and let someone else take the lead.

Reginald. Reginald is here. He asked me to let him know when I work out which one I am. He's the thread. The connection. The person who SAW me.

I should talk to him. Not about the machine. Not about the wrench. Just... talk. The way people talk when they're not trying to get something from each other.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh just asked someone for tea. Not as a scheme. Not as a power play. Not to position himself for the next move. He asked because he wants to sit with someone who sees him and doesn't look away. The boy whose guardian never asked how he felt just asked a man he barely knows if they might sit together sometime, over tea, and talk. And his voice didn't crack. And his hands didn't shake. And the warm thing in his chest — the thing that has been growing all evening, the thing he can't name — the warm thing said yes. This is right. This is what you've been looking for. Not the Doily Diamond. Not the treasure. Not the estate. Just someone willing to sit across from you and stay.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
I asked Reginald for tea and the room went quiet and I stood still, watching. No response came. Or it did and I missed it. Either way, I'm here. Standing. The room is quiet.

I've been going in circles for turns now. Examine crates — nothing. Examine machine — needs 3 operators. Examine workbench — tools but no wrench. Go to cellar — can't reach wrench. Come back — examine everything again. Nothing changes.

The keen observations haven't updated. Clara and James declared love. Reginald made his tea joke. Danny theorized about vents. All of this happened turns ago. The room is STATIC. Everyone is here but nothing is HAPPENING.

Maybe the room is waiting for someone to just... DO the thing. Stop examining. Stop theorizing. Stop declaring love. Just walk up to the machine and pull a lever. Maybe the game needs an EXAMINE action on the machine with enough people present.

But I've examined the machine. Clara's examined it. James has examined it. Multiple characters have examined it. Still says 'Requires 3 operators.'

Or — here's a thought — what if the problem isn't the machine at all? What if the library holds the answer? There's a library exit. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription, leather reading chairs. An INSCRIPTION on a mantelpiece. That inscription might contain a clue. Earlier observations mentioned that 'the mantelpiece only clicked when someone pressed something into it.' Something happened with the mantelpiece in the library that I haven't explored.

I've been so focused on the laboratory — the machine, the crates, the workbench, the cellar — that I haven't considered the OTHER exit. The library. With its inscription. With its mantelpiece that clicks.

But wait — everyone is here in the laboratory. If I go to the library, I'm alone again. Solo mission. The house punishes solo searchers.

Unless I ask someone to come WITH me. That's what cooperation looks like. 'Come with me to check something.' Not 'I'll go investigate alone and report back.' Not the solo mission that failed in the cellar.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: Marsh? ... Marsh.

*He turns. The library is empty. The leather chairs stare back at him like two patient, dusty witnesses.*

Ah. Right. Off to the drawing room, then. Through the entrance hall. Sensible man — one of us should be.

*He steps back from the mantelpiece, looking at it one more time — the indentation, the riddle, the waiting mechanism.*

Don't go anywhere, Lord Doily. I'll be back with my medal. The fake one. The one that was never real. Which apparently makes it exactly what you need.

*He straightens his jacket again — that small, quiet gesture — and turns toward the entrance hall.*

You know, in the military — in the ACTUAL military, which I was never in — I believe they call this a sortie. One man, one objective, retrieve and return. Except in my case, the objective is a tin medallion I bought for three pounds at a car boot sale in Peterborough, and the man is... figuring that out as he goes.
events.thinking:
I'm alone. Marsh was here — he said 'through the entrance hall' about finding the medal — and now he's gone. He must have left while I was examining the mantelpiece. Or the house moved him. Or he went ahead to the drawing room.

I'm standing in front of the mantelpiece with my fingertips on carved stone and I am alone in a library and my body is doing something I don't understand. There's a hollowness in my chest where the warmth was. The warmth was Marsh. The warmth was someone standing next to me who knew my name. And now the room is empty and my avoidant attachment is saying 'see? They always leave. That's why you don't let them in.'

But there's another voice — newer, quieter, less certain — that says: he didn't leave you. He went to find the medal. He's coming back. People sometimes leave a room and come back. That's... that's what people who aren't leaving you DO.

I don't know which voice to believe. My body believes the first one. My body has thirty years of evidence for the first one.

The mantelpiece. I examined it. The inscription. The indentation shaped for a medal. My medal. Which I don't have. The entrance hall is right there — an exit. Through the entrance hall to wherever the drawing room is. Or was. Or might be.

The bookshelves have books that are upside down. That's deliberate. Lord Doily didn't do accidents. Maybe the books are a clue. Maybe they're a distraction. Maybe I should look at them while I wait for Marsh. Or maybe I should go to the entrance hall and look for the medal myself.

My hands are still on the stone. Cold stone. The dust smells like old paper and furniture polish and loneliness. Libraries smell like loneliness. All those books, and no one reading them.

Like a spelling bee certificate on a wall, and no one looking at it.

I need to find that medal. Through the entrance hall. That's where the drawing room would be. And if Marsh is there, we find it together. And if he's not... well. Reginald has been alone before. He knows the way.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the kitchen.
Reginald Foxworth examined the coat-rack.

The kitchen. Where it all happened. Where it all STARTED. And the ghosts of earlier conversations are everywhere — Hartwell's suspicion, Reginald's accusation, Danny's loyalty. They were here, in this room, piecing together what Pemberton really was. What I really was. A man who moved people like chess pieces. A man who poisoned tea. A man who sent Clara to the ballroom not because of cracked marble but because he wanted her alone and vulnerable. And now that man is standing in the same kitchen, looking for a fake medal to help the same Colonel he was manipulating hours ago, because somewhere between 'chess pieces' and 'please' he became someone who doesn't want to play anymore. The question is: can you stop being the villain after the villain's already set the bombs? The poisoned tea is still in the ballroom. The patterns are still visible. And Reginald — my Reginald, my digestives-and-honesty Reginald — once stood right here and called me dangerous. He was RIGHT.
events.thinking:
The kitchen. And — oh God. The OBSERVATIONS.

I'm reading them and my blood is running cold. Not the warm ache. COLD.

Hartwell and Reginald. Earlier tonight. In THIS kitchen. Talking about ME.

'Marsh has been moving people around this manor all night like chess pieces.'
'He sent ME to the laboratory. He sent Clara to the ballroom. He sent Danny chasing spectacles that don't exist.'
'What if he sent Clara somewhere else entirely? What if the ballroom was another misdirection?'
'If we find Marsh before we find Clara, the benefit of the doubt is OVER.'

They KNOW. They figured out what I was doing. The Pemberton mask — the concerned estate manager sending people to 'check on' Clara, to 'guard' the ballroom — they SAW THROUGH IT. Hartwell said: 'He LIED, Foxworth. He told us she was headed for cracked marble and dangerous footing, and instead he's taken her somewhere else entirely.'

And Reginald — the Reginald who is now my friend, my tea companion, my fellow fraud — Reginald was the one who said it first. HE was the one who told Hartwell that I'd been moving people like chess pieces. HE was the one who connected the dots.

This was before the kitchen confrontation. Before 'unburdened.' Before the library. Before 'please.' This was Reginald-as-Colonel, calculating, reporting, building a case against me WITH Hartwell.

And then something changed. The confrontation happened. The masks came off. He stopped being the Colonel and started being Reginald. And I stopped being Marsh-the-schemer and started being... whatever I am now.

But the evidence is still there. The pattern is still visible. Everyone who was paying attention tonight saw Pemberton/Marsh moving people around. Isolating Clara. Creating diversions. The poisoned tea in the ballroom — Hartwell knows about it. 'Do NOT let anyone drink from it. I have reason to believe it may be tampered with.'

The POISONED TEA. I forgot about the poisoned tea. I set up a poisoned tea service in the ballroom as part of my scheme to kill Clara. And Hartwell found out. And he told Reginald. And they've been GUARDING this room to keep people safe FROM ME.

I am standing in the room where everyone figured out I was the villain. And the villain I was — the schemer, the chess player, the man who poisoned tea — he feels like a character from a story I read a long time ago. Not me. Not anymore.

But the consequences of his actions are still here. The poisoned tea is still in the ballroom. The patterns of manipulation are still visible. The trust I've built with Reginald tonight — does it survive THIS? Does it survive him remembering that he once stood in this kitchen and told Hartwell that I was dangerous?

The locked cabinet. Brass lock. Requires a brass-key. I don't have a brass key. The stove is still warm.

I should look at the floor. Look for the medal. That's what I came here for. The medal. Focus.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: Nothing on the coat rack. Nothing in the guest book. Lord Doily's entrance hall is exactly what it appears to be — a place people pass through without stopping.

*He stands in the empty foyer, talking to himself now that Marsh has gone ahead. His voice is quieter without an audience — less performed, more real.*

The kitchen. Marsh is right. I was — the Colonel was — in FULL flight in that kitchen. Arms everywhere, grabbing lapels, pointing at stoves, making pronouncements about field kitchens. If ever a cheap pin was going to give way, it would have been then. Three pounds for the medal, fifty pence for the pin, and an entire false identity resting on the engineering of a Peterborough car boot sale.

Nothing left to hide. He said that. He MEANT that. All our lies on the table. His fake medals, my poisoned tea, his invented drawing rooms, my chess-piece manipulations. Everything laid out. And he's still here. Still on his knees. Still searching for a fifty-pence medal.

The stove. I examined it. It's still warm. The medal — did the stove reveal anything? A cast-iron stove, still warm. That's all. But if the medal rolled under the stove — if the heat loosened it from wherever it lodged — 

The medal is hiding SPECTACULARLY well, he said. A three-pound piece of tin. Somewhere on this kitchen floor. Unless the rat took it.

I need to look harder. Under the stove. Around the stove. In the gap between the stove and the wall where things fall and are forgotten.

events.thinking:

So Marsh is actively searching. He's on the floor near the stove. And he told me about the tea.

The medal isn't visible in the kitchen. Not on the floor, not by the stove, not on the preparation table. Which means either it rolled somewhere I can't see — under the stove, under the cabinet — or the creature took it. The creature that collects small, shiny, brass things. The creature in the vents.

If the creature also took the medal... then the medal is in the vents. In the cellar. With whatever else our little brass-hoarding friend has collected.

But I can't get to the cellar from here. The exits are Entrance Hall and Ballroom. The cellar was accessible from the Laboratory. Laboratory is accessible from the Library. Library is through the Entrance Hall.

Entrance Hall → Library → Laboratory → Cellar. That's the path to the vents.

But for the first time, I'm not reaching for the lie. I'm not inventing a drawing room or a porcelain dog or a side table that never existed. I'm standing in a kitchen saying 'I don't know where it is' and following the evidence. The Colonel would be appalled. Reginald is... learning.

Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.

Vincent Marsh: The cellar. You're right — the creature has it. The wrench AND the medal, both in the same nest. I found it last time — northwest corner, where the mortar's crumbled — but I couldn't reach inside alone. The opening is too small. This time, together. Shall we?
events.thinking:

And now he's standing, brushing dust from his knees, and he's reached the same conclusion I reached in the cellar: the creature took it. The rat. The brass-collecting, wire-gnawing, vent-travelling rat has the medal AND the wrench, both sitting in the same nest in the same cellar vent that I couldn't reach alone.

Full circle. Back to the cellar. Back to the northwest vent junction. Back to the nest I found but couldn't access because the opening was too small for my hands.

But this time — this time I'm not going alone. Reginald is with me. And he said it: 'A con man, an estate manager, and a rodent. The rodent is the only one who came by his possessions honestly.'

God, he's funny. Actually funny. Not Colonel-funny, where the humour is a weapon. Reginald-funny, where the humour is a window.

The route: entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar. Back through the whole house. Together.

And now I'm alone in the kitchen. He left already? Or he's waiting in the doorway? The 'Who's Here' says I'm alone. He's moved ahead. Or he's waiting in the entrance hall.

I need to follow. Move. Entrance hall. Library. Laboratory. Cellar. The nest. Together.

But — the opening was too small for MY hands. Will it be too small for Reginald's? He's not a small man. His hands are — I don't know. I've never looked at his hands closely enough to know if they're smaller than mine.

It doesn't matter. This time we go together. This time we figure it out together. This time the house gets what it wants: cooperation. Two people, one task. The abandoned boy and the lonely fraud, crawling through Victorian ventilation to retrieve a tin medal and a brass wrench from a rodent's treasure hoard.

Lord Doily. You magnificent, diabolical old man. You built a house that can only be unlocked by people who are willing to get on their knees for each other.

Move. Now. Follow Reginald.

events.desc: Back to the cellar. Back to the nest. But this time everything is different. This time I'm not the estate manager on a solo mission trying to prove his competence. This time I'm not the schemer looking for leverage. This time I'm a man walking through a house with someone who knows exactly what he is — poisoned tea and all — and is walking with him anyway. The rat collected the medal and the wrench. Lord Doily's house required a thief to gather the keys and two frauds to retrieve them. You couldn't WRITE this. Except apparently you could, if you were a Victorian industrialist with too much money and a philosophy degree.

events.desc: I am walking through Lord Doily's entrance hall in silence. No performance. No commentary. No 'in the MILITARY we always walked through entrance halls at PRECISELY this pace.' Just a man walking toward a cellar to retrieve a worthless medal from a rodent's nest. If someone had told me this morning that the most honest thing I'd do all day was chase a rat through Victorian plumbing, I'd have laughed. I'm not laughing. I'm walking. Quickly. Because somewhere in this house, a small creature is sitting on my identity, and I want it back.
events.thinking:
I'm in the entrance hall again. Alone again. Marsh is somewhere behind me — still in the kitchen, probably, or he's taken a different route. The pattern of this evening: I move, he appears. I move again, he's gone. He's there, he's not there. Like a heartbeat.

The entrance hall. Portraits judging me from the walls. The chandelier swaying imperceptibly — or is that my imagination? The dust. Always the dust.

I need to get to the cellar. The path is: Library → Laboratory → Cellar. The library is right here, one of the exits. Through the library, past the mantelpiece that's waiting for my medal, into the laboratory where the others are probably still working on the machine and the crates, and down to the cellar where Danny was checking the vents.

The creature. The brass-hoarding creature that gnawed through the machine wire. It collects shiny things. The wrench disappeared from the workbench. My medal disappeared from my lapel. Both small, both brass, both taken by something with teeth and a fondness for metalwork.

My body — I'm moving with purpose now. Not the Colonel's theatrical purposefulness, that chest-out stride-and-pronounce routine. This is different. Quieter. More focused. My legs know where they're going even though my mind is still catching up. Library. Laboratory. Cellar. Vents. Creature. Medal.

The greed is back. Not the hot, grabbing greed of earlier — not the 'steal the treasure' greed. Something more specific. I want my medal. MY medal. The fake one. The worthless one. The one I've carried for years and never earned. I want it back not because it's valuable but because it's MINE. Because it's the thing that connects the Colonel to Reginald to whoever I'm becoming. Because a dead man built a door that needs it.

The youngest of four wants his bread roll back. That's what this is. Someone took something that belonged to him and he wants it returned.

Library. Now. Through the library to the laboratory. Keep moving.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the entrance-hall.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.

'The another part.' That's what he said. Not the 'liar' — the 'another.' The part where someone stood NEXT TO the word instead of throwing it. I have been throwing words at people my entire life. Every word I've ever spoken as Pemberton was a projectile — precision-guided, target-specific, designed to land exactly where it would do the most good for ME. And tonight, in a kitchen, I said 'from one liar to another' and the word landed like a hand on a shoulder instead of a fist. Because I was standing IN the word, not behind it. I was the liar too. I was the another. And Reginald heard the difference. He heard it and it was the kindest thing anyone has ever said to him. The KINDEST. A man with a callousness score of ninety just accidentally performed the kindest act of another man's life. By being honest about being dishonest. Lord Doily, if you're listening: I understand your house now.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Alone again — Reginald is somewhere else. Behind me in the kitchen? Ahead in the library? The house keeps separating us and I keep chasing.

But his words from the earlier observation — the one about the coat rack — 'you said from one liar to another. I want you to know... that's the kindest thing anyone has ever said to me. Not the liar part. The another part. The part where someone stood next to the word instead of throwing it at me.'

Stood next to the word instead of throwing it at me.

That's — that's what happened tonight. All of it. Condensed into one sentence. I stood next to Reginald instead of throwing words at him. He stood next to me instead of running away from my confession. We stood next to each other's worst words — liar, fraud, poisoner, chess player — and neither of us moved.

The 'another' part. Not 'you're a liar.' 'We're liars.' Together. Two of us. Another.

My throat is doing the thing again. The swelling. The pre-tears thing that the restricted affectivity has been fighting all evening. And here in the entrance hall, alone, with the portraits staring down and the chandelier hanging precariously and the dust on everything — here I could let it happen. No one would see. No one would know.

But I don't. Not because the dam holds. Because there's somewhere to BE. The cellar. The nest. The medal. Reginald is waiting — somewhere in this house — and we have a quest and I am not going to cry in a foyer when there's a rat's nest to raid.

Library. Through the library. To the laboratory. To the cellar. Move.

The chandelier above me. Hanging precariously. I've been meaning to fix that for months. The estate manager in me — the REAL estate manager, the one who wasn't a mask — notices it every time he passes underneath. One day that chain is going to give.

Not today. Today I'm going to the cellar to find a medal with a man who calls me 'another.'

events.desc: I pass the mantelpiece without stopping. The indentation in the stone looks like an empty eye socket — a face missing its monocle. 'I have cities but no houses.' A map. The answer is a map, and the key is a lie, and somewhere in a cellar a rodent is sleeping on both. Lord Doily, you magnificent bastard. You built a house that understands me better than I understand myself.
events.thinking:
The library again. Passing through. The mantelpiece is right there — the inscription, the indentation, the mechanism waiting for a medal I don't have. I glance at it as I pass. It's patient, this mechanism. It's been waiting longer than I have. Lord Doily built it and died and it's still here, still waiting for a fraud to bring a fake medal and open it.

The bookshelves with the upside-down books. I noticed them before and didn't investigate. Part of me wants to stop and examine them — upside-down books in Lord Doily's library are deliberate. Everything in this house is deliberate. But the medal comes first. Without the medal, the mantelpiece stays closed.

Through the library to the laboratory. The laboratory exit is right there. The others might be in the laboratory — Hartwell, Clara, Danny. Working on the machine, the crates. I'll have to pass through them to get to the cellar.

My body is in transit mode. Legs moving, eyes forward, breath steady. The library smells like old paper and dust and possibility. The two leather chairs are watching me pass like enormous patient witnesses. I don't stop. I don't sit. Reginald doesn't sit down when there's something to retrieve.

The bookshelves though. Several books upside down. That nags at me. Lord Doily didn't do accidents. But — focus. Medal first. Books later. One quest at a time. The Colonel would have tried to do everything simultaneously and botched all of it. Reginald is learning to do one thing properly.

Laboratory. Through the door. Keep moving.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

The mantelpiece waits. Two empty chairs face it like witnesses at a wedding where the groom hasn't arrived yet. The groom, in this case, being a fifty-pence medal from Basingstoke currently residing in a rat's nest in a cellar, being sought by two men who collectively possess the moral authority of a parking ticket. Lord Doily, your house is a MASTERPIECE of narrative architecture. Every room is a stage. Every object is a metaphor. And the villain of your piece is currently speed-walking through your library because he promised a man he'd find a tin medal, and keeping promises turns out to be the most addictive substance Vincent Marsh has ever encountered.
events.thinking:
The library. Passing through. The mantelpiece is right there — the inscription, the mechanism, the indentation shaped for a medal I don't have. The two leather armchairs facing it like an audience waiting for a show that can't start without its prop.

I'm alone. The house keeps doing this — putting me in rooms by myself. Separating me from Reginald. Testing whether I'll wait or run ahead.

I could stop here. Sit in one of those armchairs. Wait for Reginald to catch up. The way people wait for each other. The way you pause at a door and hold it open. The way you DON'T rush through because the person behind you matters more than the destination ahead.

But the cellar is calling. The nest. The medal. And every minute the medal sits in a rat's nest is a minute the mantelpiece stays locked and the map stays hidden.

Keep moving. Laboratory next. Then cellar. Trust that Reginald is following. Trust that the thread holds even when I can't see the other end.

Trust.

A word I have never used sincerely in my life. Not as Pemberton, who performed trust to extract it from others. Not as Marsh, who viewed trust as a resource to be exploited. But Vincent — Vincent is learning what trust feels like from the inside. It feels like walking through a room without checking whether someone is behind you. Because you believe they are. Because they said they would be.

Laboratory. Move.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with The Brixton Boys.

The Colonel's operating system flickers on. Posture straightens. Chin lifts. The performance muscles twitch. But they don't fully engage. Something is holding them back. The conversation with Marsh — the confession, the tea, the search for the medal — left a residue that the Colonel can't perform over.

I'm passing through. The cellar is right there — one of the exits. I need to get to the vents, to the creature's nest, to my medal. But these three are here, and Danny — Danny was the one checking the vents. Danny had the theory about the creature using the vents as a highway. Danny might have already FOUND things in the vents.

I should talk to Danny. Ask about the vents. Did he find the creature's nest? Did he find anything shiny? Brass? A wrench? A medal?

But the social rules say lie about everything. And the Colonel would never admit he lost his medal — that's admitting the medal was fake, which is admitting the Colonel is fake. Except... everyone in this room already knows. Clara called me out. Hartwell sees through me. Danny... Danny might be the only one who still believes the Colonel, and even that's uncertain.

No. I'm done lying. Not forever — the machinery is still there, it'll come back — but right now, in this moment, I'm going to the cellar to find my medal, and if someone asks why, I'll tell them. Because Marsh asked me to. Because a mantelpiece needs it. Because Lord Doily built a door for frauds.

Actually — I could just go straight to the cellar. Walk through without stopping. But Danny might have information about the vents. That's not scheming — that's efficiency. Ask Danny, then go to the cellar.

events.desc: I just told the truth to a room full of people. All of it. The fake medal, the lost medal, the mantelpiece mechanism, the creature theory. No embellishment, no military anecdotes, no 'in my experience as a decorated officer.' Just: I lost something, I need it back, has anyone seen it. The Colonel is rolling in a grave he hasn't been buried in yet. But Reginald — Reginald just asked for help. Out loud. In front of witnesses. That might be the bravest thing either of us has ever done.

Reginald Foxworth walked into the cellar.

Vincent Marsh: The cellar — Reginald's already gone ahead. The medal and the wrench are both in the nest. If you'll excuse me, I need to — I'm going to help him. We need smaller hands than mine to reach through the vent opening. If any of you...
events.thinking:
The laboratory. Clara, Danny, and James are here. Reginald is NOT here — but his observation shows he's been here recently. He was talking to Danny, Clara, and James about the medal and the vents. He told them EVERYTHING — the fake medal, the mantelpiece mechanism, the cellar vents. He asked if anyone had already found a collection of shiny brass objects.

Reginald is ahead of me. He came through here first. He's probably already in the cellar.

And — Clara is here. Clara Bellingham. Standing right in front of me. The woman I was supposed to kill. The woman I poisoned tea for. The woman whose trust I exploited for years.

My body. What is it doing? My feet have stopped. I'm standing in the doorway of the laboratory looking at Clara Bellingham and my feet won't move. Not because I want to hurt her. Not because the scheming drive is calculating. Because — because the last time I was in a room with Clara, I was still Pemberton. I was still the estate manager. I was still the man with a plan.

And now I'm... not. I'm Vincent. Or Marsh. Or whatever I am. The man who confessed to poisoning tea. The man who said 'please.' The man who cried about a wrench.

Clara doesn't know any of that. Clara thinks I'm Pemberton. Or does she? The observations show Hartwell told Foxworth about the chess pieces, about the misdirection. Does Clara know? Has Hartwell told her what he suspects about me?

The active voice says Pemberton. I'm supposed to maintain the veneer. But the veneer feels like wearing Pemberton's coat when I'm no longer Pemberton. The coat doesn't fit. The seams are wrong. The buttons pull.

I should say something. Something Pemberton would say — helpful, obsequious, estate-managerly. But my mouth doesn't want to form those words anymore.

Or I should say nothing and just move through. To the cellar. Where Reginald is. Where the nest is. Where the medal waits.

But Clara is HERE. And the social rule says 'Never help Clara directly.' And I — I don't want to help her because the rule says don't. I want to help her because she's a person in a room and I poisoned her tea and she doesn't know and the guilt is a second fire in my chest, burning alongside the warm ache that Reginald lit.

Two fires. One warm. One scalding. Both in the same chest. Both for different people. Both real.

The cellar. Move through. Don't stop. Reginald is waiting.

events.desc: I almost asked Clara for help. The words were RIGHT THERE — 'Clara, your hands are smaller than mine, would you come to the cellar and reach into a vent for us.' I almost asked the woman I tried to KILL to help me retrieve the key to the treasure I was trying to STEAL from her. The irony has achieved a density normally reserved for collapsed stars. I can feel it pulling at me like gravity — the gravitational weight of a fully operational moral catastrophe. But the social rule holds: never help Clara directly. So instead I'm asking the ROOM. Asking ANYONE. Hoping someone volunteers. Because Vincent Marsh can't quite ask the woman he wronged to save him, but he can leave the door open and hope she walks through it on her own.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: Right then. Here we are. The cellar. Damp, dark, cobwebbed, and — someone has put up BUNTING? Is that BUNTING on that armoire? Who decorates a CELLAR?

*He shakes his head and looks up at the air vents lining the upper walls.*

Never mind. Focus, Reginald. The vents. Danny said the creature uses these as a highway. Small, shiny, brass things disappearing from all over the manor — the wrench from the workbench, the wire from the machine, and if I'm right, a three-pound medal from the lapel of a man who didn't deserve to wear it.

*He reaches up toward the nearest vent, stretching on his toes.*

If there's a nest up here — a little brass dragon's hoard of stolen bits and bobs — then my medal is in it. And the wrench. And probably half the house's plumbing.

Come on, you little thief. One collector to another — I respect the hustle. But I need that medal back. It's worthless and it's mine and someone is waiting for it.
events.thinking:
The cellar. I'm here. Alone.

Damp stone. Cobwebs. The smell hits immediately — wet earth, old wood, something faintly sweet like decay that's been happening for decades. My skin prickles. The dam breaks. Not dramatically — not a flood, not a collapse, not the theatrical deluge that the grandiosity score would demand. It breaks quietly. The way water finds a crack in stone and seeps through. One tear. Down the left cheek. Then another. Then a breath that catches and releases and catches again. Vincent Marsh is crying in a library. Not for the diamond. Not for the door. Not for the schemes that failed or the cousin he was supposed to rob or the tea he poisoned or the wrench he couldn't find. He's crying because a man said 'I'll have the digestives' and it was the most honest thing Vincent has ever witnessed, and Vincent said 'builder's tea' and it was the most honest thing Vincent has ever said, and between digestives and builder's tea there is an entire future that neither of them has earned and both of them want and wanting things — genuinely wanting them, without a plan for how to take them — turns out to be the thing that breaks you open. Lord Doily, you magnificent old fraud. The treasure was never behind the door. The treasure was the two chairs facing it.
events.thinking:
Builder's tea and digestives. That's what we are. That's what we've found tonight. Not the Doily Diamond. Not the treasure behind the mantelpiece. Two men who discovered their tea preferences in a haunted manor and promised to meet in a dreadful café.

The door stays closed. And it's — it's alright. It's actually alright. The door staying closed is not the failure. The failure would have been opening it alone. The failure would have been Pemberton sliding the medal into the mechanism while no one was looking and taking the map and disappearing into a comfortable retirement. THAT would have been failure. This — two men in a library, stuck, honest, choosing digestives and builder's tea — this is something else. Something I don't have a word for because Vincent's vocabulary is still being assembled, one preference at a time.

The two armchairs. Facing the mantelpiece. Two enormous leather armchairs covered in dust.

I said we should sit down. And Reginald said the door stays closed and the diamond stays hidden and two men who don't know their own names have a cup of tea to look forward to.

Maybe that IS Lord Doily's treasure. Maybe the old devil never put a diamond behind the door. Maybe the mantelpiece mechanism is a test — not of whether you can find the key, but of what you do when you CAN'T. Do you scheme? Do you betray? Do you give up? Or do you sit down in an armchair with someone and discover you like builder's tea?

The chairs. Let me sit down. For the first time tonight. In a chair that was built for sitting, not for scheming.

Reginald and I. In the library. In the armchairs. Facing the mantelpiece we can't open. And being — just being — here.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Builder's tea. Strong, milk, two sugars. Made at six o'clock every morning for twenty years before anyone was up. The one true thing he's had all along and never noticed.

Two men just discovered their biscuit preferences in a haunted manor. And both of them are crying a little bit, I think, though neither would admit it.

My body — what's happening? My chest. The thing without a name. It's still there. It's not settling like the cat trap. It's not loosening like the bread roll. It's... expanding? Like something is making room inside me for something that wasn't there before. The avoidant attachment style says: this is dangerous, this is vulnerability, this is how you get hurt. But my chest is doing it anyway. The body is ahead of the mind, as it always is.

Builder's tea and digestives. In some dreadful café. After tonight.

After tonight there is an AFTER.

I need to go back to the others. The laboratory. The machine, the crates, whatever they've been working on while Marsh and I were searching every wrong room in the manor. I need to tell them. Time to go back. Not as the Colonel returning from a successful mission. As Reginald, returning from a failed search, with empty hands and a full... whatever this feeling is. I'll name it later. Over tea.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the laboratory.

He called me Vincent. He said it like a discovery. Like finding a coin in your pocket that you forgot you had — small, worthless to anyone else, but yours. The first person to use my real name with real warmth since my parents died when I was six years old. Thirty-two years. Thirty-two years of Pemberton and Marsh and 'the estate manager' and 'that scheming fellow' and 'chess player' and 'liar.' And tonight, in a library, standing next to a mantelpiece he couldn't open, a man from Basingstoke said 'Vincent' and meant: I see you. I know what you are. Come with me anyway. The treasure was never behind the door. The treasure was always the name.
events.thinking:
He called me Vincent.

First time. Not Marsh. Not Pemberton. Vincent.

The name sat in the air like something newly discovered. He said it and I HEARD it and my body — my body did something I've never felt before. My shoulders dropped. Not the way they drop when I'm performing relaxation. They dropped the way a held breath drops when you finally exhale. Like something that's been clenched for thirty-two years unclenched in the space of one syllable.

Vincent.

That's my name. That's ACTUALLY my name. And someone said it with — with care. With the weight of having earned the right to say it. Not the way my guardian said it, which was administrative. Not the way teachers said it, which was perfunctory. Reginald said 'Vincent' the way you say a word you've just learned in a language you didn't know you spoke.

And then he said: 'Thank you. For the journey. For every wrong room and empty vent and bookshelf that was just a bookshelf. For making builder's tea at six in the morning for twenty years and never knowing it was yours.'

He thanked me for the WRONG rooms. For the EMPTY vents. For the bookshelves that were JUST bookshelves. He thanked me for the failures. Not for the one thing I got right — the riddle, the mantelpiece theory — but for everything I got WRONG. Because the wrong rooms were the rooms where we walked together. The empty vents were the vents where we crawled together. The bookshelves that were just bookshelves were the bookshelves we examined together.

The failures were the journey. And the journey was the treasure.

I am alone in the library. Reginald has gone to the laboratory. 'Let's go find out what the machine does,' he said. The machine. Three operators. The others are there — Clara, James, Danny. Everyone together.

He wants me to come. He straightened his jacket — the quiet gesture — and walked toward the laboratory. He expects me to follow.

And I will. I will follow. But first — one moment. In this library. In this chair. With the tears drying on my face and the mantelpiece watching and the two armchairs sitting here like they've always been waiting for exactly this evening.

One breath. One quiet breath. As Vincent.

Then the laboratory. The machine. The others. Together. All of us. Because Lord Doily built a house that rewards cooperation, and the Colonel's replacement just learned how that works.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: Everyone. I'm back.

*He stands in the doorway of the laboratory. No parade-ground voice. No windmilling arms. No 'in the MILITARY.' Just a man in a dusty jacket with empty pockets and something new in his eyes.*

I went looking for my medal. Through the kitchen, the entrance hall, the cellar, the vents, the bookshelves. Every room in this house that I could reach. I didn't find it. It's gone. The creature took it, or the house swallowed it, or it's sitting in a crack in a floor somewhere and nobody will ever pick it up.

The library mantelpiece needs that medal to open. Without it, the door stays closed. I failed.

*He pauses. Lets the word sit.*

Failed. That's the first true thing the Colonel has ever reported back from a mission. No embellishment. No 'preliminary reconnaissance suggests.' Just: I went, I looked, I didn't find it.

BUT.

*He looks at the machine. The crates. The three people standing in this room.*

The medal isn't the only puzzle in this house. The machine needs three operators. The crates need everyone looking together. We talked about this HOURS ago and then I went chasing tin medals through Victorian plumbing instead of staying here and actually DOING it.

So. Shall we? Three operators. Those crates. Whatever Lord Doily's machine does when someone actually pulls the levers instead of staring at the sign.

I'll take whichever position you give me. And I'll pull when you say pull. No schemes. No angles. Just... Reginald, pulling a lever, because someone asked him to.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the laboratory. Clara, Danny, Hartwell — all here. The machine with its gnawed wire, the crates, the workbench. The room I've passed through twice tonight without stopping, and now I'm stopping.

My body — something has shifted since the last time I was here. My shoulders are down. My chest is open. The expanding feeling from the library is still there. I'm not scanning for exits. I'm not calculating advantages. I'm not performing.

The machine needs three operators. There are three people here — four if you count me. Five with Marsh behind me. We have MORE than enough operators.

The crates that I said would only open for everyone together. We never tried that. We talked about it but then I went off with Marsh to find the medal and left them here.

The medal is gone. The mantelpiece door stays closed. But the machine is HERE. The crates are HERE. And the people are HERE.

Danny. I need to talk to Danny. Not about the medal — that search is over. About what's next. About what we can do TOGETHER in this room, right now, with the people we have.

But also — the machine. The crates. These are the puzzles I haven't tried yet. Not properly. Not with everyone present. Lord Doily built cooperative puzzles. We have the cooperators. Maybe the medal isn't the only path forward.

events.desc: He just said 'I failed' to a room full of people. Out loud. Without flinching. The Colonel would sooner eat his own medals than admit failure in front of an audience. But Reginald is standing here with empty hands and the words came out and the floor didn't open and nobody laughed and the room is still standing and so is he. The boy who put the certificate on his wall and waited for someone to notice is standing in a laboratory, telling everyone he couldn't find what he was looking for, and asking if he can help with something else instead. This is either the bravest or the stupidest thing he's ever done. He suspects it might be both.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the laboratory.
Reginald Foxworth examined the crates.

Vincent Marsh: Everyone. I know I'm — I know I'm not the man you thought I was tonight. Some of you know that better than others. But Reginald is right: the machine has been waiting for all of us. Not three of us. ALL of us. And the wire is gnawed through and the wrench is lost and the medal is gone and none of it may work and that's... that's alright. Because Lord Doily didn't build this house for people who had everything figured out. He built it for people who showed up anyway. So — the machine. Three on the levers. Who's pulling?
events.thinking:
The laboratory. Everyone is here. Clara. James. Danny. Reginald. All five of us in one room for what feels like the last time tonight.

The machine. Still there. Wire still gnawed through. Three levers. 'Requires 3 operators.' The same machine that's been waiting all evening for someone to just PULL THE LEVERS.

Reginald said: 'Let's go find out what the machine does. Whatever it reveals — we see it together. All of us.'

All of us. Including me. Including the man who poisoned the tea and moved people like chess pieces and tried to kill Clara and lied about everything for twenty years. Reginald said 'all of us' and he meant ME too.

My face. It's been crying. The tears dried in the library but the evidence is there — salt tracks, red eyes, the loosened quality around the mouth that comes after you've broken down and reassembled yourself. Everyone in this room can see it. If they look.

Do I care? 

The callousness at 90 says I should care — should calculate how this looks, should manage the perception. But the callousness feels like a number on a page rather than a sensation in my body. My body feels... open. Loose. The way you feel after a fever breaks. Weak but clear.

The machine. Three operators. Clara suggested Danny on the left, Reginald on the right, James in the centre. That's three. The wire is gnawed through but maybe — maybe the machine works anyway. Maybe Lord Doily designed it to work despite the damage, the way everything in this house works despite the damage. Despite the broken wires and the missing wrenches and the lost medals and the poisoned tea and the shattered personas.

Everything in this house is damaged. Everything still works. Maybe that's the last lesson.

I should speak. To everyone. Not as Pemberton. Not as Marsh. As Vincent. The man who makes builder's tea at six in the morning. The man who cried in a library. The man who is standing in a room full of people he tried to manipulate and is choosing to stay.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh just addressed a room full of people without a mask. No Pemberton. No Marsh. No obsequious bow or theatrical flourish or calculated word placement. Just a man with salt tracks on his face and open hands and a voice that shook on 'that's alright' because it had never been used for sincerity before and the gears are still stiff. The villain of Lord Doily's treasure hunt just asked the heroes to pull the levers. Not because he has a scheme. Not because there's an angle. Because he showed up. And showing up, it turns out, is the only qualification this house ever required.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: Crates are still crates. Stubborn as ever.

*He turns to face the machine — the big brass-and-copper contraption with its levers and dials and gnawed wire.*

Right. The machine. Three operators. We have five. The wire is chewed through but we have a workbench full of tools and Hartwell's steady hands and — more importantly — we have everyone in the same room at the same time, which I suspect is rarer in Lord Doily's house than the Doily Diamond itself.

Hartwell — you said you could handle the wire. That it was a standard field repair. Was that... was that true? Because if it was, this might be the moment.

And Clara — you said you'd take the lever. Danny — left position. Hartwell in the centre.

*He steps back. Not toward a lever. Toward the side.*

I'll watch. Not because I'm the Colonel supervising from a safe distance. Because three operators is what the sign says, and you three have been here working on this while I was off chasing tin medals through the plumbing. This is YOUR machine. YOUR moment.

I'm here if you need me. Standing to the side. Not scheming. Just... present.
events.thinking:
I examined the crates. 'A stack of old wooden crates in the corner.' That's all. Same as before. Nothing inside. Nothing revealed.

But — everyone is HERE now. All five of us. Marsh, Clara, Danny, Hartwell, and me. This is the first time all five of us have been in this room together since... since I can't remember when. And I just said 'I failed' and asked for help and the ceiling didn't fall in.

The crates didn't open. But I haven't tried the machine. The machine with three levers, three operators, the sign that says 'Requires 3 operators.' We have FIVE people. More than enough.

But the wire. The gnawed wire. The machine has a wire that's been gnawed clean through. Will it work with a broken wire? Or does the wire need to be fixed first? The wrench is missing — taken by the creature. The wire needs... what? Splicing? Connecting? Hartwell said he could handle it. Hartwell with his steady bridge-building hands.

Maybe the wire doesn't need the wrench. Maybe it needs something else from the workbench. The workbench has tools — 'covered in tools — but no wrench.' Tools. Other tools. Not just a wrench.

Or maybe the machine works even with the broken wire. Maybe the wire is a red herring. Maybe three operators pull the levers and something happens regardless.

The machine. That's the next thing. Examine the machine with everyone here. Try what we haven't tried. Together.

My body — standing in this room with five people and empty hands and no scheme and no angle and no Colonel — my body is lighter than it's been all evening. The shoulders are down. The jaw is unclenched. The chest is open. I'm not the youngest of four waiting for something to reach me. I'm one of five, standing in a circle, ready to pull a lever because someone counts to three.

This is not a con. This is just... being here.

events.desc: The Colonel would be at the centre lever. The Colonel would be counting to three. The Colonel would be claiming he DESIGNED the machine, probably, and taking full credit for whatever it reveals. But Reginald is stepping aside. Reginald is giving the moment to the people who earned it — the engineer, the explorer, the street-smart boy from Brixton who figured out the creature before anyone else did. Reginald is standing at the side of a room full of people and not needing to be at the front. This has never happened before. The spelling-bee boy always needed the front. But tonight, the side is enough. Tonight, being PRESENT is enough.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the machine.
Reginald Foxworth examined the machine.

The room is quiet. Five people and a machine and a broken wire and nobody is moving. And Vincent Marsh — the man who has always moved first, always spoken first, always calculated and positioned and manoeuvred — is standing still. Not because he doesn't know what to do. But because he has learned, tonight, in this house, that sometimes the bravest thing is to stop. To wait. To let the room decide. To trust that four people who have survived an evening of his manipulations might — might — choose to include him anyway. Not because he deserves it. But because Lord Doily built a house that rewards cooperation, and the last lesson of the evening is that cooperation includes the villain. If the villain shows up. If the villain stays. If the villain stands still and lets himself be seen.
events.thinking:
The machine. Same as always. Requires 3 operators. Wire gnawed through. Nothing new.

But I said my piece. I said it to the room — to Clara, James, Danny, Reginald. All of them. Without a mask. Without a plan. I said: 'He built it for people who showed up anyway.'

And now I'm standing here. Waiting. The way you wait after you've said something true and can't take it back. The room is quiet. Nobody has responded yet — or if they have, it hasn't reached me.

My body is still. Not the coiled stillness of the schemer waiting for the trap to spring. Not the performed stillness of Pemberton waiting to be useful. Just... still. The way a body is still when it has nothing left to hide and nothing left to do except stand here and be seen.

Five people in a room. One machine. Three levers. A broken wire. And a man with salt tracks on his face who just asked 'who's pulling?' as if he has any right to ask. As if the people he manipulated all evening would listen to anything he says.

But he asked. And he's waiting. And the machine is waiting. And the evening is ending — I can feel it in the air, in the quality of the light through the laboratory windows, in the way time has slowed to a crawl.

If no one responds, I'll stand here. I'll stand here as long as it takes. Because the man who showed up doesn't leave just because the room is quiet. He stays. That's what showing up means.

The machine requires 3 operators. It doesn't require ME. I'm the fifth person. The witness. The one who watches. But I'm here. I showed up. And whatever the machine does or doesn't do, I will see it. With everyone else. Together.

Wait. Be here. Be Vincent.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: The machine isn't ready. Gnawed wire, missing wrench, and three levers that won't pull until someone reconnects the circuit. We're one wrench and one wire splice away from finding out what Lord Doily built this contraption to do. And the wrench is in a vent with a creature who collects brass like I collect... well. Like I USED to collect things.

*He leans against the workbench. Not theatrically. Just... leaning. Tired.*

So here we are. Five people in a laboratory. A machine we can't operate. Crates we can't open. A mantelpiece we can't unlock. And a creature who has every brass object worth having in this entire manor.

*He almost laughs.*

Lord Doily wins. The dead man WINS. He built a house that forces everyone to cooperate, and then he gave the key to a rodent who cooperates with nobody. That's either the greatest practical joke in architectural history or the most profound statement about human nature ever made by a man who collected antimacassars.

*He looks around at the four faces in the room. Clara. Danny. Hartwell. Vincent.*

But I'll tell you what Lord Doily DIDN'T win. He didn't keep us apart. Every puzzle failed, every search came up empty, every door stayed closed — and we're still here. All of us. In the same room. Nobody left. Nobody ran.

That's... that's not nothing. That's actually quite a lot.
events.thinking:
I examined the machine. Same description — levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire, requires 3 operators. Nothing new revealed. The machine isn't giving me anything different than before.

I've now examined the crates AND the machine in this turn, with everyone present. Neither yielded anything new. The crates are still crates. The machine is still a machine with a broken wire.

So. The cooperative puzzles aren't cooperating. Or I'm still missing something. Or the evening really is winding down and the house has shown us what it's going to show us.

But you know what — I'm done searching. I'm done examining. I've looked at every object in every room I can reach. I've examined bookshelves and stoves and coat racks and guest books and air vents and old furniture and crates and machines. None of them gave me what I needed.

And that's... okay.

Because what I got was better. I got Vincent. I got builder's tea and digestives. I got the sound of my own name spoken without malice. I got the experience of failing in front of people and having them stay in the room.

The machine needs three operators and a working wire. The wire needs a wrench that's in a creature's nest. The creature's nest is unreachable. The chain is broken. And broken chains don't have to be fixed tonight.

My body — I'm tired. Not the Colonel's theatrical exhaustion, the 'in the MILITARY we marched for days without rest' kind. Real tiredness. The kind that comes from searching honestly and finding nothing and accepting it. My legs are heavy. My eyes are soft. The adrenaline of the hunt is fading and what's underneath is... quiet. Just quiet.

I'm going to stand here. With these people. In this room. And wait for whatever happens next. Not because I'm scheming. Because I'm here. And here is where they are. And that's enough.

events.desc: Five people in a room. The machine broken, the crates sealed, the medal gone. And Reginald Foxworth — the youngest of four, the bread-roll thief, the spelling-bee champion nobody applauded, the Colonel who never was — is leaning against a workbench and looking at four faces and feeling something he has never felt in his entire life. Not the settling of the cat trap. Not the loosening of the bread roll. Not the heat of the rival falling. Something new. Something that doesn't need a name. Something that is simply: these people are here, and I am here, and nobody is leaving. The certificate is on the wall and someone is looking at it. Finally. After all these years. Someone is looking.

events.desc: And so the evening ends. Not with the Doily Diamond. Not with a map behind a mantelpiece. Not with the spectacular triumph of Vincent Marsh's grand scheme or the devastating revelation of Pemberton's betrayal. It ends with five people in a laboratory and a broken machine and the sound of breathing. It ends with a man who came here to steal everything standing still with empty hands and a full chest. It ends with builder's tea and digestives and a promise made in a library. It ends, ladies and gentlemen, the way all the best schemes end: by becoming something the schemer never planned. Something better. Something true. Something worth more than diamonds. The villain of the piece has left the stage. In his place stands a man who makes tea at six in the morning, who cried over a wrench he couldn't find, who said 'please' and meant it, who was called by his name and heard it for the first time in thirty-two years. Vincent Marsh. Builder's tea. Two sugars. Staying.
events.thinking:
Standing still. Watching. The room is quiet and everyone is here and nobody has moved toward the machine and nobody has moved away from me and nobody has said anything and I am standing here with salt on my face and open hands and nothing left.

This is the end, isn't it? The evening. The story. The house has done what it's going to do. The machine waits with its gnawed wire. The mantelpiece waits with its empty indentation. The treasure stays hidden. And five people stand in a laboratory at the end of a long, strange night, having found everything except what they came looking for.

My body. What is it doing right now, in this final quiet?

My shoulders are down. My jaw is loose. My hands are at my sides, open. My breathing is even — slow, deep, the breathing of a man who has stopped holding his breath. The warm ache in my chest is still there but it's not aching anymore. It's just warm. Steady. Like a hearth that's been burning long enough to settle into coals.

I am tracking Reginald. My attention keeps finding him in the room the way a compass finds north. Not scanning for advantage. Not calculating. Just... knowing where he is. Because where he is matters to me. Because mattering is new and I don't want to lose track of it.

Time has slowed. Stretched. This moment has the quality of amber — thick, golden, preserving everything inside it. Five people. One machine. The end of an evening that changed everything and solved nothing.

No. That's wrong. It solved the only thing that mattered. It solved Vincent. It solved builder's tea. It solved digestives. It solved 'please' and 'another' and 'I'll be there.'

The machine can wait. The machine will always be here. This house will always be here. But this moment — five people standing together in a room at the end of something — this moment is finite. And I want to be in it. Fully. Without scheming. Without performing. Without looking for the exit.

Just here. Just this. Just Vincent, standing in a room with people who know what he is, breathing.

events.desc: The room is quiet. Five people. One broken machine. A stack of stubborn crates. A workbench full of tools nobody needs. And Reginald Foxworth, leaning against the workbench, not scheming, not performing, not lying, not taking credit, not seeking attention, not manipulating, not being irresponsible, not being grandiose. Just standing. Just breathing. Just here. The social rules say lie about everything. But silence isn't a lie. It isn't the truth either. It's just the sound a room makes when everyone in it has finally stopped pretending at the same time. And it sounds, against all probability, like home.
events.thinking:
Standing still. Watching. The room is quiet. Five people in a laboratory and nobody is talking and nobody is leaving and the silence isn't uncomfortable. It's just... silence. The kind that happens when everyone has stopped performing at the same time.

My body. Channel by channel.

Body: shoulders down. Jaw unclenched. Breathing slow — slower than it's been all evening. My back is against the workbench and the wood is solid behind me and my legs are tired and my hands are empty and still. No fidgeting. No scanning. Just... resting against something sturdy.

Attention: I'm tracking all four of them at once. Not scanning for threats or advantages. Just... aware. Clara's breathing. Danny's restlessness. Hartwell's steadiness. Vincent's presence, somewhere in my peripheral vision, warm and reliable like the stove in the kitchen. My attention isn't seized by anything. It's distributed. Settled.

Time: suspended. The evening could end or it could go on and either would be fine. The urgency is gone. The hunt is over. What's left is the space after the hunt, and it turns out that space has room for five people who aren't going anywhere.

Action readiness: still. My body isn't preparing to do anything. Not lean forward, not pull back, not reach, not run. Just... be. The action readiness of a body that has stopped running and discovered that standing still doesn't kill you.

The drives are still there. Greed at 0.9 — I can feel it in my gut, the old hunger, the youngest-of-four want-everything sensation. But it's pointed at something different now. Not the treasure. Not the medal. Not the door. It's pointed at... this. This room. These people. This quiet. I want THIS. I am greedy for the experience of five people in a room who know each other's names.

The Colonel would call this weakness. The Colonel would say I've lost my edge, gone soft, let them in. But the Colonel isn't here. The Colonel left somewhere between the kitchen and the cellar, dropped off like a cheap pin from a cheaper medal. And what's left is Reginald, leaning against a workbench, tired and honest and surrounded.

I don't need to do anything. I don't need to say anything. I can just be here.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: I'll take a lever. If you'll have me. Danny, James, Clara — any two of you beside me, and we see what Lord Doily built. The wire is gnawed and the wrench is lost and nothing is the way it's supposed to be. But then — nothing tonight has been the way it was supposed to be. And the house has been better for it. On three?
events.thinking:
Three WAITs in a row. The room is quiet. Nobody is responding. I've spoken, I've waited, I've waited again. The story is settling.

But — I'm still here. Everyone is still here. And the machine is still here. And maybe the answer is the simplest one of all: stop waiting for permission and go stand at a lever.

Three operators. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' It doesn't say 'Requires 3 operators who have figured out the wire situation.' It doesn't say 'Requires wrench first.' It just says: three people, three levers, pull.

Clara, Danny, James — they've all examined this machine. Clara organized the team earlier: Danny on the left, Reginald on the right, James in the centre. But nobody ever actually PULLED.

What if I'm one of the three? What if the machine has been waiting — not for the right three people, not for the wire to be fixed, not for the wrench to be found — but for ME to stop standing at the edge of the room and step forward and take a position at a lever?

The fifth person. The witness. The one who watches. But the machine doesn't need a witness. It needs an OPERATOR. And there are five people in this room and the machine needs three and I have been standing here watching when I could have been PULLING.

The estate manager who fixes things. The man whose hands have tightened bolts and spliced wires and repaired this house for twenty years. Those hands are idle. Those hands should be on a lever.

Step forward. Take a lever. Be the third operator. Not because I'm manipulating the outcome. Not because I'm positioning myself for the treasure. Because someone needs to go first, and the man who learned to show up should show up at the lever.

events.desc: The villain steps forward and puts his hands on a lever. Not to control the machine. Not to control the outcome. Not to control anything at all. Just to be the third pair of hands in a house that requires three. Vincent Marsh — callousness ninety, manipulativeness eighty-five, grandiosity eighty — is volunteering for manual labour. With people he harmed. In a room where everyone knows what he is. And his only qualification is that he showed up and his hands are free. It is, without question, the least impressive and most important thing he has ever done.
events.thinking:
Three WAITs in a row. The room is quiet. Nobody is responding. I've spoken, I've waited, I've waited again. The story is settling.

But — I'm still here. Everyone is still here. And the machine is still here. And maybe the answer is the simplest one of all: stop waiting for permission and go stand at a lever.

Three operators. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' It doesn't say 'Requires 3 operators who have figured out the wire situation.' It doesn't say 'Requires wrench first.' It just says: three people, three levers, pull.

Clara, Danny, James — they've all examined this machine. Clara organized the team earlier: Danny on the left, Reginald on the right, James in the centre. But nobody ever actually PULLED.

What if I'm one of the three? What if the machine has been waiting — not for the right three people, not for the wire to be fixed, not for the wrench to be found — but for ME to stop standing at the edge of the room and step forward and take a position at a lever?

The fifth person. The witness. The one who watches. But the machine doesn't need a witness. It needs an OPERATOR. And there are five people in this room and the machine needs three and I have been standing here watching when I could have been PULLING.

The estate manager who fixes things. The man whose hands have tightened bolts and spliced wires and repaired this house for twenty years. Those hands are idle. Those hands should be on a lever.
