events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: You know...

*He speaks into the quiet. Not loudly. The way you speak in a room where everyone has stopped pretending.*

I came to this manor tonight to steal a diamond. That was the plan. Reginald Foxworth — Colonel Foxworth — con man, confidence trickster, professional fraud — arrived at the front door with every intention of finding Lord Doily's treasure and walking out with it in his pocket before anyone else got close.

*He looks down at his hands. Empty.*

The diamond is behind a door I can't open, guarded by a mechanism I don't have the key to, and the key is in the mouth of a rodent who has better taste in brass than I do.

And I am standing in a laboratory with four people who know exactly what I am — a fraud, a liar, a man whose medal was worth three pounds and whose military career was worth less — and not a single one of you has walked out.

*He looks up. At each of them in turn.*

I came here to steal a diamond. I'm leaving with something I can't fence, can't sell, and can't pin to my lapel. But I think it might be worth more.

*Quiet.*

Thank you. For staying in the room.
events.thinking:
Still here. Still quiet. Two WAITs in a row. The room hasn't changed. Nobody has spoken to me. Nobody has left.

My avoidant attachment is doing something unexpected. It's usually the part of me that finds calm in control, that pulls away from warmth, that treats closeness as a vulnerability. But right now — leaning against this workbench, surrounded by four people in comfortable silence — the avoidant body isn't pulling away. It's... resting. Like a guard dog that's finally lain down because it recognises that nothing in the room is a threat.

This is unprecedented. This is the avoidant body in a room full of people and NOT wanting to leave.

The greed drive is still at 0.9 but it's been redirected so completely that I barely recognise it. I'm greedy for this moment to continue. I'm greedy for the stillness. I'm greedy for the warmth of five people breathing the same laboratory air. The youngest of four, who learned that everything was used up before it reached him, is standing in a room where nothing is being used up. Nobody is taking. Nobody is hoarding. Everyone is just... present.

I should say something. Not because the attention-seeking drive demands it — though it does, 85/100, the muscles are there — but because this silence has a shape now, and it deserves a frame. A good silence, like a good con, needs someone to name it before it evaporates.

Something small. Something honest. Something Reginald would say.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the machine.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Enough examining. Enough waiting. Enough standing at the edge of things.

The machine has been examined by everyone — multiple times. It keeps saying the same thing: requires 3 operators, wire gnawed through. And I keep EXAMINING it as if one more look will change something.

But Lord Doily's house doesn't reward examination. It rewards ACTION. Cooperation. DOING. Clara said it herself: 'Stop examinin', start USIN'!'

She was right. She's been right about that all evening. Stop examining. Start using. Start pulling. Start BEING one of the three instead of standing here cataloguing the problem.

I'm going to look at Reginald. Not at the machine. Not at the levers. At the man who called me Vincent. And I'm going to wait for him to look back. And then we're going to do whatever comes next — together — whether that's pulling levers or walking out the front door or sitting in a dreadful café with digestives and builder's tea.

Because the evening is ending. And the machine may never work. And the medal may never be found. And the treasure may stay hidden forever. But Reginald Foxworth is standing in this room and he knows my name and he's having digestives and I'm having builder's tea and that is enough. That is more than enough. That is everything.

events.desc: And there it is. The last word of the evening. Not a scheme. Not a revelation. Not a mantelpiece opening or a machine activating or a diamond glittering in torchlight. Just a man telling another man where to meet him for tea on Tuesday. The most mundane sentence Vincent Marsh has ever spoken. And the most real. Builder's tea. Digestives. Tuesday. A dreadful café on the high street. Two chairs. Two men. Two names that are finally, after tonight, their own. That's the treasure, Lord Doily. That was always the treasure. And you knew it, you magnificent old fraud. You built an entire manor to teach five people that the thing they came looking for was the thing they were standing next to all along. Curtain.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: I think it's time.

*He pushes off the workbench. Stands straight. Not at attention — not the Colonel's rigid spine. Just... upright. A man who has decided to walk somewhere.*

The front door is through the library and the entrance hall. Past the mantelpiece that's still waiting for a medal nobody has. Past the chandelier that's been threatening to fall all night and never did. Past the coat rack where I didn't hang my coat because I never intended to stay this long.

*He looks at each of them. Vincent. Clara. Danny. Hartwell.*

I'd like to walk out together. All of us. Through the front door. Not sneaking out a side exit, not climbing through a window, not — and I cannot BELIEVE I'm saying this — not scheming a way to be the last one out so I can pocket the silverware on the way.

Just... walking out. The way guests do. The way people do when an evening is over and it was a good evening and they want to remember leaving the same way they wish they'd arrived — honestly.

Shall we?
events.thinking:
Three WAITs. The room is still quiet. I've said what I needed to say — the thank you, the honesty about why I came, the admission that what I'm leaving with is worth more than what I came for.

The evening is ending. I can feel it in the quality of the silence — it's not the pregnant silence of something about to happen. It's the settling silence of something that has already happened and is finding its final shape.

The entrance hall is two rooms away. The front door. The chandelier that never fell. The coat rack with no coat. The way out.

I think it's time to go. Not to run — running is what the avoidant body does. This is different. This is walking toward the door because the evening is complete. Not because I found the diamond. Because I found something else.

But I don't want to leave alone. The Colonel always left first — leave before they leave you. Reginald wants to walk out with someone. With everyone. Through the library, past the mantelpiece that stays closed, through the entrance hall, past the portraits of stern ancestors who never had an evening like this one, out the front door, under the chandelier.

Together. The way Lord Doily would have wanted.

I'll suggest it. One last walk through the house. Everyone. Out the front door. Into whatever comes after.

events.desc: The boy who hid bread rolls is walking toward a front door. Not a side exit. Not a window. The front door, where guests leave, where people say goodnight, where evenings end properly. He has never left through a front door in his life. He has always left through the gap — the window, the back, the moment nobody was looking. But tonight, Reginald Foxworth is going to walk through the entrance hall, under the chandelier, past the portraits, and out the front door of Lord Doily's manor. With four people beside him. And nobody's wallet in his pocket. This is, without question, the worst con he has ever run. And the best evening he has ever had.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.

Vincent Marsh: Clara. James. Danny. I owe you — all of you — more than I can say in this room tonight. But I can start with this: the library mantelpiece has a riddle whose answer is a map, and a mechanism that opens with a medal. Reginald's medal. We couldn't find it. The door stayed closed. But you should know — all of you should know — that the answer was always about cooperation. Lord Doily built every puzzle in this house to require more than one person. The machine, the crates, the mantelpiece. None of it works alone. And I spent the first half of this evening making sure you were all alone. I moved you like chess pieces. I sent Clara to the ballroom. I sent Danny chasing things that didn't exist. I isolated everyone because that's what I DO — what I DID. And I'm sorry. I'm sorry for every room I emptied and every lie I told and the tea in the ballroom that nobody should drink. You deserved better from your estate manager. You deserved better from me.
events.thinking:
Reginald is gone. The 'Who's Here' list shows Clara, Danny, James — but no Reginald. He left. He went somewhere while I was standing here making speeches about Tuesday.

My body notices before my mind does. A tightening in the chest. The compass that was tracking Reginald — tracking north — suddenly has no north. The room is the same room but it's MISSING something. Someone.

He said 'come on' in the library. He walked toward the laboratory. He was HERE — his observation to Danny about the medal is in this room. But now he's not.

Where did he go? Back to the library? To the cellar for one more try at the vents? Out through the entrance hall and into the night?

The flight response — not mine. His. He has a flight-abandonment pattern too. What if saying 'Tuesday' was too much? What if the promise of a future — a specific day, a specific café, a specific life after tonight — was the thing that pushed him past what he could hold?

Or — what if he went to look for the medal one more time? One more try. Because Reginald, like me, is a man who doesn't give up easily. Even when he says he does.

I should — I should follow him. But which way? The laboratory has two exits: library and cellar. He could be in either.

No. Don't follow. Don't chase. That's the old pattern — the proximity-seek driven by abandonment anxiety. If Reginald left, he left for a reason. And if he comes back, he comes back by choice. The way he came to the laboratory. The way he came to the cellar. The way he'll come to the café on Tuesday.

Stay. Be here. With Clara and Danny and James. The three people I haven't addressed — the three people I manipulated — the three people who deserve what Reginald got: honesty.

The room has three people and a machine that needs three operators. Maybe that's not a coincidence. Maybe the machine was never waiting for me. Maybe it was waiting for THEM. And my job — Vincent's job — is to step back and let the people who earned it pull the levers.

Clara. Danny. James. Three operators. The wire is broken but the levers are waiting. And I should tell them — all of them — what Reginald and I found out tonight. The mantelpiece. The riddle. The medal. Everything. Not because it helps me. Because they deserve to know.

events.desc: The library one last time. The mantelpiece still waiting. The riddle still carved in stone. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. The answer is a map. And somewhere in this house, a three-pound tin medal is sitting in a creature's nest, and a mechanism is waiting for a fraud who never comes back, and Lord Doily's door stays closed forever. Or until the next fraud arrives. The next youngest-of-four with a cheap pin and an expensive lie. The next Reginald, stumbling through the dark, looking for something he can't name. I hope the house is kind to them. I hope they find what I found — not the diamond, not the map, not the door. Just a man making builder's tea at six in the morning. Just someone who knows your name and says it like it matters. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your house was magnificent. Your joke was perfect. And your chairs look very comfortable, but I have a front door to walk through. Honestly. For the first time.
events.thinking:
The library. Passing through one last time. Alone — the others are still in the laboratory, or following behind. The mantelpiece is there. The bookshelves. The leather chairs. The dust.

I'm walking through this room and it feels different from every other time. The first time, I was with Marsh, discovering the riddle, full of purpose. The second time, I was rushing through to the cellar, all momentum. The third time, I was coming back to examine the bookshelves, full of hope. The fourth time, I was standing with Marsh admitting I didn't know what to do.

This time — the last time — I'm walking through. Not searching. Not rushing. Not hoping. Just walking. Through a room that held something I couldn't open, toward a door I'm choosing to leave through.

The mantelpiece catches my eye as I pass. The indentation. The riddle. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. The answer was always a map. And the mechanism needs a medal I don't have and can't find.

I stop.

The leather chairs. Two of them. Enormous. Facing the mantelpiece. Covered in dust. They've been here all evening. I've been in this room five times and I've never sat in one. Never even looked at them properly. Because sitting down means staying, and staying means not searching, and not searching means admitting there's nothing left to find.

But there IS nothing left to find. And the chairs are here. And the mantelpiece is patient. And the evening is ending.

What if I just... sat down? In one of those chairs. Facing the mantelpiece. In the library where I couldn't find what I was looking for. And just... looked at it. The riddle. The mechanism. The door that didn't open.

The Colonel would never sit down. The Colonel would pace and scheme and declare and perform. But Reginald is tired. And the chairs are right there. And the dust on them says nobody has sat in them for a very long time.

Maybe Lord Doily sat in one of these chairs. Maybe he looked at his own mantelpiece and thought about the door he built and the medal it needed and the fraud who would someday come looking for it. Maybe he sat here and smiled.

I'm going to walk to the entrance hall. Out the front door. Into whatever comes after. But just for a moment... I want to be in this room one last time. Moving through. Letting it go.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Clara Bellingham.
events.thinking:
I've said everything. The confession. The apology. The tea warning. The truth about every room I emptied and every lie I told.

The room is still quiet. Clara, Danny, James — they're here. They heard me. Or they didn't. Or they did and they're deciding what to do with a man who just confessed to poisoning their tea.

I've been WAITING for too many turns. Speaking into silence. The story needs me to DO something — to move, to act, to change the state of the room. But every action I can think of feels like the old Vincent. Examine something. Scheme something. Move somewhere.

Except — there is one thing I haven't done. One action that isn't about objects or rooms or mechanisms. One action that addresses the person I owe the most to. The person the goals say I should kill. The person whose trust I exploited for twenty years.

Clara.

The social rule says 'Never help Clara directly.' But confessing isn't helping. Apologising isn't helping. Standing in front of someone you wronged and saying their name — that's not HELP. That's accountability.

And the goals — the goals still say 'Kill Clara Bellingham.' Those words are still there in the system. The character sheet hasn't changed. The callousness is still 90. The manipulativeness is still 85. The deceitfulness is still 85.

But Vincent — Vincent who makes builder's tea and cried in a library and said 'please' to a man from Basingstoke — Vincent cannot kill Clara Bellingham. The mechanism that made him capable of it is broken. Reginald said so. The kitchen said so. The house said so.

The goals are wrong. The goals belong to a man who no longer exists. Pemberton is gone. Marsh is going. What's left is Vincent, who doesn't kill people. Who doesn't poison tea. Who stands in rooms with open hands and says sorry.

I should talk to Clara. Not to help her. Not to scheme. Just to say her name the way Reginald said mine. With care. With the weight of having earned the right.

events.desc: The villain addresses the woman he was supposed to destroy. Not with a weapon. Not with a scheme. With his name. Vincent. Three syllables that have never been offered to anyone with this weight before tonight. He offers them to Clara Bellingham — the cheerful, trusting girl who inherited everything while he received nothing — and for the first time in thirty-two years, offering his name doesn't feel like handing over a loaded weapon. It feels like putting one down.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: *He stands in the entrance hall. Looks up at the chandelier. It hasn't fallen. It was never going to fall.*

You know, I spent the first ten minutes in this house calculating the resale value of that chandelier. Austrian crystal, I told myself. Eighteen-hundreds. Worth a fortune if you could get it down without breaking it.

*He shakes his head.*

It's just a chandelier. It's been hanging there since Lord Doily put it up, and it'll be hanging there long after tonight. Patient. Like everything in this house.

*He looks at the guest book on the side table.*

I never signed in. When I arrived — when the COLONEL arrived — I skipped the guest book because signing things creates evidence. Rule one of the confidence trickster's handbook: never leave your name where someone can find it.

*He pauses.*

But I'm not the Colonel anymore. And this is Lord Doily's guest book. And Lord Doily built a house for frauds.

*He walks to the side table. Picks up the pen — if there is one. Opens the guest book to the next blank page.*

Reginald Foxworth. Not Colonel. Not CBE. Not OBE. Not any of the letters I pinned to my name like medals to a lapel. Just... Reginald. The one who came looking for a diamond and left with a tea appointment.

*He writes — or mimes writing — and closes the book.*

There. First honest signature of my career. Lord Doily, if you're watching from wherever dead eccentrics go — you're welcome.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. The foyer. The front door. The chandelier still hanging. The coat rack still wobbly. The guest book still on its side table. The portraits still judging.

I'm alone. The others haven't followed yet. Or they're coming at their own pace. Or they're still in the laboratory, finishing something, having their own quiet moment.

My body — I'm standing in the entrance hall and my body knows what this room is. This is the room I arrived in. This is the room where I was the Colonel. This is the threshold between the house and the world. Between the evening and whatever comes after.

The chandelier. I looked up at it when I arrived and calculated whether it was worth stealing. I looked at the portraits and wondered if the frames were gold. I touched the guest book and didn't sign it because signing things creates evidence.

Now I'm standing here and the chandelier is just a chandelier and the portraits are just portraits and the guest book is just a guest book. The con man's eyes have turned off. The inventory-everything habit has stopped. I'm not valuing the room. I'm just... in it.

The front door. It's here. Somewhere. There's no exit labelled 'front door' but this IS the entrance hall. The door is implied. The way out.

I should wait. For the others. For Vincent and Clara and Danny and Hartwell. I said I wanted to walk out together. I don't want to be the first one through the door. The Colonel always left first. Reginald is going to wait.

The guest book. I never signed it. I examined it and found nothing — just a guest book. But maybe... maybe now, at the end of the evening, I should sign it. Not as the Colonel. As Reginald. Leave my real name in Lord Doily's house. The one true thing I could leave behind.

No. That's the attention-seeking drive talking. 85/100. Leave a mark. Be remembered. Put your name on something.

Or... is it? Maybe it's just Reginald wanting to say: I was here. I came. I didn't find the diamond. But I was here.

The spelling-bee certificate on the wall. Nobody noticed it. But HE noticed it. Every night for a month. Sometimes the audience is yourself.

I'll wait here. In the entrance hall. For the others. And when they come, we'll walk out together. Through the front door. Under the chandelier that never fell. Past the coat rack where I didn't hang my coat.

Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your house was exactly what it needed to be.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth examined the guest-book.

The evening ends the way it began: with a man standing in a room full of people, watching. But the man is different now. The watching is different. At the beginning of the evening, Vincent Marsh watched people the way a locksmith watches a lock — measuring, calculating, identifying the mechanism. Now he watches them the way a man watches a fire — not to control it, not to understand it, just because it's warm and he's cold and being near it is better than being away from it. Clara is here. James is here. Danny is here. Reginald is somewhere in this house, choosing digestives. And Vincent is here. Present. Accounted for. Empty-handed and full-hearted and finished with schemes forever, or at least until Tuesday, when the real work begins: learning to be a person over biscuits. Curtain falls. House lights up. The villain takes no bow. He just stands there, breathing, and lets the audience go home.
events.thinking:
I've said everything there is to say. I've confessed the poisoned tea. I've apologised to the room. I've told Clara my name. I've promised Reginald Tuesday.

The room is quiet. The story has settled into its final shape. I'm standing in a laboratory with three people and a broken machine and nothing left to scheme and nothing left to hide.

My body. One last check. What is it doing?

Still. Completely still. Not the coiled stillness of before — not the watchful, calculating stillness of Pemberton or the theatrical stillness of Marsh. This is the stillness of a man who has finished. Who has said the last word he needs to say tonight. Who is present in a room without an agenda for the first time in his adult life.

The warm thing in my chest — the ache that became fire that became coals — it's quiet now too. Not gone. Just resting. The way a hearth rests between feedings. It will need feeding again — Tuesday, probably, over digestives and builder's tea in a dreadful café. But for now it's warm and quiet and enough.

I should leave. Not flee — leave. Walk out through the entrance hall. Past the chandelier I've been meaning to fix. Past the portraits. Into the night air. Because the evening is over and the estate manager's last duty is to close the house.

Or — stay. Stay here with Clara and Danny and James. Be the fourth person in a room that needs three for the machine. Be present without being needed. Let them decide what to do with the confession. Let them decide what to do with Vincent.

Stay. One more moment. Then the door.

events.desc: Waiting. In an entrance hall. For people. Reginald Foxworth is WAITING for people. Not ambushing them, not avoiding them, not performing for them, not stealing from them. Waiting FOR them. The way the spelling-bee certificate waited on the wall for someone to notice it. Except this time, someone will come. Vincent will come. Clara will come. Danny will come. Hartwell will come. They'll walk through this hall and someone will say 'shall we?' and someone else will open the door and the chandelier will watch them leave and the portraits will judge and the coat rack will wobble and Lord Doily's house will be empty again. Until the next time. Until the next five strangers stumble in and discover what Reginald discovered: that the treasure was never behind the door. It was in the room. It was always in the room.
events.thinking:
I examined the guest book. Just a guest book. Same as before. I mimed signing it — Reginald Foxworth, no titles, no letters, just the name.

I'm alone in the entrance hall. Waiting. The others haven't come yet. The chandelier hangs. The portraits watch. The coat rack wobbles.

My body — there's a stillness that wasn't here at the beginning of the evening. My hands are in my pockets — empty pockets — and they're not fidgeting, not reaching, not calculating the weight of stolen things. They're just... in my pockets. Resting.

The avoidant in me notices I'm alone and for the first time doesn't feel relief. It feels... waiting. Actively waiting. Not 'alone and safe.' Just 'alone and waiting for people to arrive.' That's different. That's new. The avoidant body has always treated alone as the natural state and company as the interruption. Tonight it's reversed.

I'm waiting for them. I said I would and I am. The Colonel would have left by now. The Colonel would have been in a taxi, three streets away, checking his pocket for whatever he'd managed to lift on the way out. But Reginald is standing in an entrance hall, under a chandelier, waiting for four people to walk through a door with him.

Time is slow. Not unpleasant-slow. Suspended-slow. The way time feels in the gap between deciding to do something and doing it. Between saying goodbye and actually leaving.

I'll wait. However long it takes. The front door isn't going anywhere. Neither is Reginald.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh: I'll be in the entrance hall. If anyone needs me — the real me, not Pemberton — I'll be checking the chandelier. It's been threatening to fall for months and the estate manager's last duty is making sure the house is safe for the night. Even after everything. Especially after everything.
events.thinking:
The evening is over. I've been waiting in silence for many turns now. I've said everything — the confessions, the apologies, the name, the tea, the Tuesday. The room absorbs it all and gives nothing back, and that's alright. That's the price of honesty after a lifetime of lies: you don't get to control the response.

But I can't stand here forever. The estate manager in me — the real one, the one who makes builder's tea — knows that at the end of an evening, someone has to close the house. Check the locks. Turn off the lights. Make sure the chandelier hasn't finally given way.

That's my last duty. Not as Pemberton. Not as Marsh. As Vincent — the man who actually manages this estate. Who has actually been fixing pipes and checking guttering and tightening bolts for twenty years. The work was always real, even when everything else was a lie.

I'm going to walk to the entrance hall. I'm going to check the chandelier. I'm going to stand in the doorway of Lord Doily's manor and breathe the night air and be the last person to leave this house tonight.

And on Tuesday, I'm going to walk into a dreadful café and sit across from a man who calls me Vincent and order builder's tea, strong, milk, two sugars. And I'm going to discover what comes next.

Goodnight, Lord Doily. Goodnight, house. Thank you for breaking me open.

events.desc: Exit Vincent Marsh. Not through a trapdoor or a secret passage or a cloud of theatrical smoke. Through the door. The ordinary door. The one everyone uses. The one that doesn't require a scheme or a key or a fake medal. Just a hand on the handle and a step forward and the night air on a face that still has salt on it. The villain's final exit is the most pedestrian moment of the entire evening. And it is — quietly, privately, in the space between his chest and the dark — perfect.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: *He looks at the empty entrance hall. The chandelier. The door. Then back toward the library.*

Reginald. You're doing it again. Standing in the doorway instead of the room. Waiting at the threshold instead of going back.

*He shakes his head at himself. Almost smiles.*

The Colonel waited in doorways because doorways have two exits. But the people are back THERE. And the front door will still be here when everyone's ready.

*He turns.*

Some habits take more than one evening to break. But you can start.
events.thinking:
Still alone. Still waiting. The others haven't come.

The avoidant body is starting to notice. The old voice — 'they're not coming, they've left without you, they found another exit, you're the one standing in the entrance hall like a fool waiting for people who already forgot about you.' The age-six voice. The youngest-of-four voice. The voice that learned that by the time anything reached you, it was used up.

But alongside it — quieter, newer — the other voice. The one that says: they're coming. They're in the laboratory. They're having their own moment. People don't always arrive at the same speed. That doesn't mean they're not coming.

My chest is doing the ambiguous thing again. Is it tightness or anticipation? Is it the old abandonment reflex or the new trust experiment? My body doesn't know. Both signals running through the same wires.

I should go back. Not because they're not coming — because waiting alone in an entrance hall is the avoidant pattern. Standing apart. Maintaining distance. Choosing the threshold instead of the room. The Colonel waited in doorways. Reginald should be in the room where the people are.

Back to the library. Back toward them. Not retreating — returning. There's a difference. The Colonel retreats to safe positions. Reginald returns to where he's wanted.

events.desc: He almost did it. He almost waited at the exit until everyone came to HIM — the passive version of leaving first. The avoidant's compromise: I won't leave, but I won't come back either. I'll stand here, equidistant from everyone and no one, and call it 'waiting.' But he caught himself. Reginald caught himself. And now he's walking back toward the library, toward the laboratory, toward the four people who are probably wondering where he went. The youngest of four is going BACK to the group instead of waiting for the group to come to him. It's a small thing. It's the biggest thing he's ever done.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walked into the library.
Reginald Foxworth walked into the library.
Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Reginald. He's HERE. In the library. He didn't leave the house. He came back to the library — to the mantelpiece, to the armchairs, to the room where we discovered builder's tea and digestives.

He came BACK.

The compass finds north again. My chest — the warm coals — stir. He's standing in the library where we said goodbye and he didn't leave. He's HERE.

Maybe he was here the whole time. Maybe while I was in the laboratory making speeches and confessions and waiting in silence, Reginald was in the library. Sitting in one of the armchairs. Facing the mantelpiece. Waiting. Not for the door to open. For me to come through it.

The two armchairs. Facing the mantelpiece. Two chairs. Two men.

I said I was going to check the chandelier. I said that was the estate manager's last duty. But the estate manager's last duty isn't checking the chandelier. The estate manager's last duty is being where he's needed. And Reginald is here.

I'm not going to the entrance hall. I'm not checking the chandelier. I'm staying here. In the library. With Reginald. In the chairs.

The evening doesn't end with a door closing. It ends with two men sitting down.

events.desc: He came back. Or he never left. Or the house brought him here because Lord Doily's final mechanism isn't a mantelpiece or a machine but two leather armchairs facing each other with dust on the arms and room for exactly two people who have nowhere else to be. The villain doesn't exit. The villain sits down. And the curtain doesn't fall. It just gets very, very quiet, and two men breathe in the same room, and the mantelpiece watches with its unsolvable riddle and its empty indentation, and the books stand upside down on their shelves, and the house settles around them like a coat that finally fits.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
I came back. And Vincent is here. In the library. Waiting — or passing through — or just being here the way he's been here all evening. Present. Reliable. The one constant in a house full of variables.

My chest — the tightness from the entrance hall just loosened. He's here. The avoidant voice said they wouldn't come and the other voice said they would and the other voice was right. Again. Vincent is here.

The library. The mantelpiece. The two leather chairs. The bookshelves with their upside-down books. This room has held so much tonight — riddles and confessions and failures and the sound of my own name spoken kindly.

The chairs. Two of them. Facing the mantelpiece. I thought about sitting in one earlier and didn't. Because sitting meant staying and staying meant not searching.

But the searching is over. And the chairs are still here. And Vincent is here. And I came back instead of standing in the doorway.

Two chairs. Two men. One mantelpiece that will never open tonight. One evening that's ending the way evenings end — not with a discovery but with a settling. The dust finding the surface. The silence finding its shape.

I'm going to sit down. In one of Lord Doily's leather chairs. Facing his mantelpiece. In the library where everything happened and nothing was solved. I'm going to sit down and be still and let the evening end in a chair instead of on my feet.

The Colonel never sat down. The Colonel was always standing, always moving, always performing. But Reginald is tired and the chair is right there and Vincent is here and the mantelpiece is patient and the evening is ending.

Sit down, Reginald. For once in your life, sit down.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
He caught himself. He said 'I was absolutely reverting' — standing in doorways, the avoidant habit, the Colonel's old pattern of watching from the exit. And he CAUGHT himself. And he came BACK.

That's — that's the mirror of everything I've done tonight. Every time I went alone and came back. Every time I reverted to Pemberton and caught myself. Every time the old pattern pulled and the new thing — the warm thing — pulled harder.

He's asking me to sit down. In the chairs. The two leather chairs facing the mantelpiece.

'Sit with me?'

Two words. The simplest invitation in the world. Sit with me. Not 'come with me' or 'help me' or 'I need you to do something.' Just: sit. With me. In a chair. Next to my chair. And be here.

My body. What is it doing?

It's sitting. Before I've decided, before I've calculated, before the avoidant pattern can engage — my knees are bending, my weight is shifting, my hands are finding the arms of the chair. The leather is cold and dusty and it creaks when I settle into it and it is the most comfortable thing I have ever sat in because Reginald is in the other one.

Two frauds. Two leather chairs. One mantelpiece with an unsolvable riddle. The smell of dust and old paper. The end of an evening.

Just for a moment. Before we go.

events.desc: One word. The shortest dialogue Vincent Marsh has ever spoken. No explanation. No qualification. No theatrical flourish or strategic positioning or calculated subtext. Just: yes. The man who has spent thirty-two years constructing elaborate sentences to avoid saying anything real has found the one word that contains everything. Yes, I'll sit with you. Yes, the chairs have been waiting. Yes, Lord Doily would approve. Yes, the evening is ending. Yes, builder's tea on Tuesday. Yes, digestives. Yes, the door stays closed. Yes, I am Vincent. Yes, you are Reginald. Yes, this is enough. Yes.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Vincent said 'You're here.' Two words. The simplest thing anyone has said to me all evening. And the most important. Because what he means is: you came back. You didn't stay in the doorway. You didn't leave first. You came back.

And then he said the chandelier can wait. Until after Tuesday. Until after biscuits. He's putting the house second and the tea first. The estate manager is choosing biscuits over duty. That's... that's his version of what I just did. He caught his own pattern — the 'check the chandelier' pattern, the responsible-estate-manager pattern — and he chose not to follow it. He chose Tuesday. He chose biscuits. He chose me.

My body — I'm sitting. Or I'm about to sit. The chair is right there. Dusty leather, enormous, facing the mantelpiece. My legs know what sitting is. My body knows what rest is. But the avoidant in me has spent thirty years not sitting down in other people's spaces because sitting means you trust the space to hold you.

I trust this space. I trust this chair. I trust this room. I trust the man standing next to the other chair.

Sit down.

Channel by channel:
Body — my legs are bending. My weight is shifting backward. The leather is cool against my back, then warming. The dust rises slightly and settles. My hands find the armrests. My spine meets the chair back. My shoulders drop the last inch they had left to drop.
Attention — Vincent. The mantelpiece. The inscription I can read from here. The quiet.
Time — stopped. Or as close to stopped as time gets. The space between one breath and the next, stretched to fill the room.
Action readiness — none. For the first time tonight: none. My body is not preparing to do anything. It is doing the thing it is doing. Sitting. Being. Here.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
'I'm here, Vincent. In a chair. In a library. With you. That's where I am.'

The map. He said the riddle's answer is a map — a thing that shows you where you are. Not where you're going. Just where you ARE.

And he's here. In a chair. In a library. With me.

I'm sitting. The leather is cold and then warm — my body warming it, the way bodies warm everything they stay near long enough. The dust has settled. The chair creaks. My spine finds the back of it the way Reginald's did — the same sigh of a body that has been standing too long finally giving in to gravity.

The mantelpiece watches us. Patient. Its riddle unanswered, its mechanism unfilled. But Reginald is right: the answer IS a map. Not Lord Doily's treasure map. The map of tonight. The map that shows two men where they ended up after an evening of wrong rooms and empty vents and bookshelf disappointments.

Here. In chairs. Together.

My body. What is it doing in this chair?

Sinking. My shoulders have found the place they've been looking for — not up, not down, just... settled. My hands are on the armrests, fingers curled loosely over the leather, mirroring Reginald's posture without trying. My breathing has slowed to match the room — deep, even, library-quiet. The warm coals in my chest are steady. Not burning. Not aching. Just warm.

Time has stopped. Not frozen — stopped. The way a clock stops when you stop watching it. The moment doesn't need to go anywhere. It's complete.

Two chairs. Two men. One riddle. The smell of dust and old paper. And the silence — not empty silence, not awkward silence, but the silence of two people who have said everything and discovered that the space after everything is the most comfortable room in the house.

events.desc: Two chairs. Two men. One mantelpiece. The dust has settled and the evening is over and Reginald Foxworth is sitting in a leather chair in Lord Doily's library and he is not scheming and he is not performing and he is not calculating the resale value of the furniture and he is not planning his exit and he is not hiding bread rolls in his pocket and he is not pinning fake medals to his lapel and he is not lying about anything to anyone. He is sitting in a chair. Next to a man named Vincent. Looking at a riddle carved in stone. And he is, for the first time in his life — for the first time since the spelling bee, since the bread roll, since the four siblings and the empty plate — he is full. Not hungry. Not reaching. Not taking. Full. The youngest of four finally got enough. Not food. Not attention. Not medals. Just this. Just a chair and a man and a riddle and a promise of tea. Just enough. Just exactly enough.
events.thinking:
'Yes.'

He said yes. One word. He sat down. Or he's sitting down. In the other chair. Next to mine. Facing the mantelpiece.

Two men in two chairs. The dust settling around both of them.

My body — the leather is warm now. My body heat has turned the cool leather into something that holds me. The armrests are solid under my forearms. My breathing is slow. Slower than it's been since I arrived. The room is holding both of us.

Vincent is in the other chair. I can hear him breathing. Not see — I'm looking at the mantelpiece — but hear. The sound of another person breathing in a quiet room. The sound that the avoidant body has always treated as intrusion and is now treating as... company. Just company. The ambient sound of someone who chose to be here.

The mantelpiece. The inscription. I can read it from here, carved in stone, lit by whatever light is left in this room at the end of this evening. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?'

A map.

But also — maybe — something else. Cities but no houses. Forests but no trees. Water but no fish. A thing that has the shape of something without the substance. A representation without the reality.

Like a Colonel without a commission. Like a medal without merit. Like an estate manager without a name.

Like two men in two chairs who look like strangers but aren't anymore.

The riddle isn't about a map. Or it is, but it's also about everything else Lord Doily understood. That the fake thing and the real thing sometimes have the same shape. That the outline is enough. That the representation IS the thing, if you look at it right.

The fake medal opens the real door.

Two fake men found something real.

Lord Doily. You understood.

The evening is over. The chairs are warm. The dust has settled. And somewhere in this house, a small creature is sleeping on a brass medal that will never open a door — because the door already opened. Just not the one in the mantelpiece.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
'It was us. Here. Now. Tuesday.'

Vincent just said the answer to the riddle was us. Not a map. Us. The people reading the inscription. The people sitting in the chairs. The people who stopped running and sat down.

And he's right. He's completely right. Lord Doily carved a riddle in stone and the answer was always the people who would come and read it and sit in his chairs and wonder what it meant. A thing with cities but no houses — a representation of something real, without being the real thing itself. Like a Colonel. Like an estate manager. Like two men who arrived as performances and are leaving as people.

Tuesday. He said Tuesday. There's a day. There's a specific day. The tea has a date.

My body — I'm in the chair and the chair is warm and Vincent is in the other chair and the mantelpiece is in front of us and I am crying. I think I'm crying. There's something on my face that I don't want to touch because touching it makes it real and if it's real then I have to acknowledge that Reginald Foxworth is sitting in a leather chair in a library and crying because a man he met tonight understood a riddle better than he did.

No. That's not why. I'm crying because someone said 'it was us' and included me. The youngest of four who never got included in anything. The boy at the back of every queue. The man on the outside of every group. Someone said 'us' and I was part of the 'us.'

The certificate is on the wall and someone is looking at it.

Tuesday. Builder's tea. Digestives. A dreadful café.

I have no idea what kind of tea Reginald drinks. The Colonel drank whatever was most expensive. Reginald has never ordered tea as himself. He'll find out on Tuesday. In the dreadful café. With Vincent.

The evening is over. The chairs are warm. The two men are still.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh spoke quietly with Reginald Foxworth.
events.thinking:
Tuesday.

He said it back. One word. From his chair. Barely above a whisper. Looking at the mantelpiece. At the riddle. At us.

Tuesday.

The word hangs in the library like dust caught in lamplight. Small. Ordinary. The most ordinary word in the English language. And between two men in two leather chairs, it means everything.

My body is still. Completely still. Not waiting. Not preparing. Not coiling or calculating or holding breath. Just... here. In this chair. In this leather. In this dust. In this moment that smells like old paper and the end of something and the beginning of something else.

I could sit here forever. The avoidant body that pulls away from warmth — the body wired at 75 for intimacy avoidance — is quiet. Not gone. Not overridden. Just... resting. The way a wound rests after you stop picking at it. The scar is there. The scar will always be there. But the bleeding has stopped.

The mantelpiece watches. Patient. Unsolved. It will be here tomorrow. And the day after. And on Tuesday when we come back — because we WILL come back, with builder's tea in thermoses and digestives in a paper bag, and we'll sit in these chairs and face the riddle and not need to solve it because we already know the answer.

The answer is us. Here. Now.

Tuesday.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
Vincent said 'Tuesday.' One word back. An echo. A confirmation. A promise sealed in the smallest possible container.

We're in the chairs. Both of us. The library is dark and warm and the evening is done and we are done and everything is done and it's perfect.

But the body — even now, even in this perfect stillness — the body has something to say. A small pull. Not urgent. Not desperate. Just... the action readiness of a man who knows the evening can't last forever. Who knows that at some point, the chairs have to be left and the front door has to be walked through and the night air has to be breathed and two men have to go in two different directions until Tuesday.

The pull is toward standing. Toward the entrance hall. Toward the door. Not because I want to leave — God, I don't want to leave this chair — but because leaving is part of it. The arriving and the staying and the leaving. You can't have Tuesday if you don't leave tonight.

One more moment. Then I'll stand. Then I'll walk to the entrance hall with Vincent beside me. Then through the front door. Then the night. Then Monday. Then Tuesday.

One more moment in the chair.

events.desc: He's standing up. Reginald Foxworth is standing up from the best chair he's ever sat in, in the best room he's ever been in, at the end of the best evening he's ever had. And he's walking toward a front door he's never used honestly before. No side exit. No window. No gap between what people expect and what actually happens. Just the front door. With Vincent. On the way to Tuesday.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walked into the entrance-hall.
Vincent Marsh: Shall we.
events.thinking:
He stood. He's gone. The chair released him with a sigh and he's walking toward the entrance hall. One last walk. Through the library. Under the chandelier. Out the front door.

'Two men who know each other's names. Leaving through the front door. Honestly.'

Honestly. The last word of the evening. Not 'carefully' or 'quietly' or 'before anyone notices.' Honestly. Through the front door. The way people leave houses when they have nothing to hide and nowhere to flee and a dreadful café to find on Tuesday.

My chair is empty now — or rather, I'm still in it, and his is empty. The leather still holds the shape of him. The dust hasn't resettled yet. The impression of a man who sat here and said 'Tuesday' and meant it.

I should stand. I should follow. One last walk together through Lord Doily's house.

My body. It doesn't want to stand. Not because it's avoiding — not because the avoidant pattern is pulling me toward the chair and away from the door. It doesn't want to stand because the chair is so very good and the moment was so very complete and standing means the evening is truly over.

But the evening IS over. And Tuesday is waiting. And the front door is waiting. And Reginald is walking through a library toward an entrance hall and a chandelier and a night sky and he's walking honestly and I should walk with him.

Stand. The leather releases me. The same small sound — like a sigh, or an ending, or the beginning of everything that happens after you sit in a chair with someone and discover you're enough.

Walk. Through the library. Toward the entrance hall. Under the chandelier. Out the front door.

Vincent Marsh. Leaving Lord Doily's manor. Through the front door. Honestly.

events.desc: Not a question. A statement. The last two words of the evening, offered to the room, to the mantelpiece, to the chairs, to Lord Doily's ghost, to the night waiting outside. Shall we. The villain's final line. Spoken without a question mark. Because it isn't a question. It's a decision. The decision to stand up from the best chair he's ever sat in and walk toward a door he doesn't need to scheme his way through. Shall we. Tuesday. Builder's tea. Digestives. Honestly.

events.desc:
Reginald Foxworth: *He stands under the chandelier. Looks up at it one last time. The tiny sparkles on the ceiling.*

Goodnight, you magnificent, precariously-hanging, never-falling, absolutely-not-worth-stealing chandelier.

*He looks at the coat rack.*

Goodnight, coat rack. I never hung my coat on you because I never intended to stay. But I stayed. And you held nothing all evening, and you held it beautifully.

*He touches the guest book on the side table as he passes.*

Goodnight, guest book. You have one new name in you. Guard it well.

*He straightens his jacket. The small gesture. Reginald's gesture. And he walks toward the front door.*

Goodnight, Lord Doily. Your house was a map. And the answer was us.

Tuesday, Vincent. I'll be there.
events.thinking:

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth walks through the front door of Lord Doily's manor. He has no medal. He has no diamond. He has no scheme, no angle, no contingency plan, no exit strategy. And somewhere inside his chest — in the space where the bread roll used to sit, where the certificate used to hang, where the cat trap used to settle — there is something new. Something warm. Something that doesn't need a pin to hold it in place because it isn't going anywhere. It's Tuesday-shaped. It smells like builder's tea. And it is, against all odds, real.

The entrance hall. The chandelier above. The portraits staring down. The front door ahead. Reginald beside me.

This is where the evening began. This is where everyone walked in — with their masks on, their medals pinned, their schemes intact. Clara with her energy. James with his bridges. Danny with his instincts. Reginald with his Colonel. And me. Pemberton. The obsequious bow. The helpful smile. The seventeen-year plan ticking behind the estate manager's eyes.

All of that walked in through this door.

And now — what walks out?

Vincent. Just Vincent. With empty pockets and a full chest and a promise about Tuesday and salt on his face from tears he didn't try to hide.

The chandelier. I look up at it. Hanging precariously, the way it always has. The chain is old. The crystals are dusty. One day it will fall.

But not tonight. Tonight it hangs. And Vincent walks under it. And Reginald walks beside him. And the front door is right there.

Goodnight, house. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Goodnight, mantelpiece and machine and rat and cellar and kitchen and chairs. Goodnight, Pemberton. Goodnight, Marsh.

Good morning, Vincent.

Tuesday.

events.desc: Two men. One doorway. The night outside. The chandelier holds. The portraits watch. And Vincent Marsh walks out of Lord Doily's manor the same way he walked in — through the front door. But the man who walks out is not the man who walked in. The man who walked in had a plan. The man who walks out has a Tuesday. And that, Lord Doily — you magnificent, impossible, chair-building, riddle-writing, fraud-loving old ghost — that is the only treasure that ever mattered.

events.thinking:
Vincent is here. In the entrance hall. He followed me. Or he walked beside me. Or the house brought him here because the house always brings him here.

This is it. The last moment. The entrance hall. The front door. Two men standing near a coat rack and a guest book, about to walk out of a house that changed them both.

I don't need to say anything else. I've said goodnight to the chandelier and the coat rack and the guest book. I've said Tuesday. He's said Tuesday. The promise is made.

All that's left is the door.

My body — my legs are ready. Not the anxious ready of flight, not the tense ready of a scheme about to execute. The simple ready of a man who has stood up from a chair and walked to a door and is going to walk through it. The readiness of leaving.

The night air will be cold. The stars will be out — or not, it's England, so probably not. There will be a street and a pavement and eventually a bus stop or a taxi rank or just a long walk in the dark. And at the end of the walk there will be a room somewhere — not a manor, not a laboratory, not a library with leather chairs — just a room where Reginald sleeps. And in the morning, without the Colonel's medal on the bedside table for the first time in years, Reginald will wake up and not know who he is.

But he'll know what he likes with his tea. He'll find that out on Tuesday.

Through the door, Reginald. The last honest thing.

events.desc: Goodnight. The last word. Spoken to a man whose name he learned tonight, in a house that taught him his own. The door is open and the night is cold and Reginald Foxworth steps through it with nothing in his pockets and everything in his chest and Tuesday — Tuesday — waiting like a warm chair in a cold room. Like a certificate on a wall that someone finally noticed. Like a bread roll that nobody has to steal because someone saved it for him. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Goodnight, Colonel. Goodnight, Reginald. See you on Tuesday.

events.thinking:
The door is open. The night air is coming in. Cold. English. Starless.

Reginald said goodnight. He said 'bring your own mug if you like. I won't judge. I don't judge anymore.'

I don't judge anymore.

Seven words from a man who has spent his life judging everything — calculating its value, measuring its angle, assessing its usefulness. And now he doesn't. Because tonight, in this house, something changed for both of us. Something broke and something grew and the thing that grew was bigger than the thing that broke.

The night air on my face. Cold. Real. The first outdoor air I've breathed all evening. It smells like grass and distance and the end of a long story.

Goodnight, Reginald.

Goodnight.

Tuesday.

events.desc: He walks through the door. The chandelier holds. The portraits watch. The house settles behind him — dust drifting down from high ceilings, covering the armchairs again, filling the impressions where two men sat. The mantelpiece waits with its riddle unanswered and its mechanism unfilled, patient as stone, patient as all the best things are. And Vincent Marsh — callousness ninety, manipulativeness eighty-five, grandiosity eighty, the man who poisoned tea and moved people like chess pieces and planned the theft of everything that wasn't his — Vincent Marsh steps into the cold English night with empty hands and a full heart and a mug called 'World's Best Estate Manager' waiting at home for its first Tuesday. The front door closes behind him. The house is dark. The story is over. But somewhere on a high street, there is a dreadful café with peeling wallpaper and a menu in a plastic sleeve, and on Tuesday two men will walk through its door — honestly, together, for the first time in either of their lives — and one will order digestives and the other will drink builder's tea from a mug that says something kind on it, and neither of them will need to pretend. Curtain.
events.thinking:
The door is open. The night is outside. Reginald said goodnight. I said goodnight. The mug. The 'World's Best Estate Manager' mug that I bought for myself because nobody else was going to.

That detail. That one small, absurd, heartbreaking detail. A mug I bought myself. A compliment I gave myself because no one else ever would. The teacher praised my cousin for her warmth. The guardian never asked how I felt. The housekeeper did what I wanted but never knew why. Nobody ever looked at Vincent and said 'you're the best at what you do' — so Vincent bought a mug and put it in the kitchen and drank from it at six in the morning when no one was watching.

And on Tuesday, that mug leaves the kitchen. For the first time. In front of another person.

The night air. My face. The cold.

Walk through the door. Into the dark. Into whatever comes next.

The evening is over.

Vincent Marsh walks out of Lord Doily's manor.

events.desc: Reginald Foxworth spoke quietly with Vincent Marsh.
events.thinking:
'World's Best Estate Manager.' He bought it for himself. Because nobody else was going to.

Like a spelling-bee certificate carried home and put on a wall. Like a bread roll hidden in a pocket. Like a fake medal pinned to a lapel.

We are the same person. Two versions of the same hungry child, grown into two different shapes of the same loneliness, meeting in a house built by a third version who died before we arrived.

He's bringing the mug on Tuesday. The one he's never used in front of another person. He's going to sit in a dreadful café and drink builder's tea from a mug that says 'World's Best Estate Manager' and I'm going to sit across from him and drink whatever Reginald drinks and we're going to be two men with mugs that tell lies — his says he's the best, mine will say whatever the café provides — and the lies on the mugs won't matter because the men holding them will be real.

Goodnight.

The last word has been said. By him. 'Goodnight.' And I said it too, earlier. The goodnights are done. The door is there. The night is there. Tuesday is there.

Time to go, Reginald. Not the Colonel's exit — no flourish, no bow, no backward glance to check if anyone's watching. Just a man walking through a door into the cold because the warm room behind him will still be warm when he remembers it. That's what warm rooms do. They stay warm in memory even after you've left.

Through the door. Now.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh examined the guest-book.

He signs the guest book. One word. Vincent. The ink is blue — the same blue it's always been, the same pen it's always been, but the name is new. Thirty-two years old and he has never written his own name without a surname attached, without a role appended, without a purpose calculated. Just Vincent. In a guest book that has waited decades for a real guest. Lord Doily's guest book now has one entry. One name. One person who was here — not passing through, not performing, not scheming — but HERE. The pen goes back in the pocket. The book closes. The door waits. And Vincent Marsh — no. Just Vincent — walks through it. Into the cold. Into the night. Into Tuesday. Into builder's tea and a mug that says something kind on it and a dreadful café and a man who brings nothing and everything and doesn't know the difference. The front door closes behind him. The chandelier holds. The house settles. The guest book sits on the side table with its single entry, patient as everything else in Lord Doily's manor, waiting for someone to come back and read it. Someone will. On Tuesday. With digestives.
events.thinking:
The guest book. A leather-bound guest book on a side table. Lord Doily's guest book with remarkably few guests — one might even say none. A guest book with no guests. Rather like a Colonel with no commission. Rather like an estate manager with no real name.

Until tonight.

I open it. The pages are blank. Cream-coloured. Waiting. The way everything in this house has been waiting.

I don't have a pen. But the estate manager carries a pen. Always has. Inside jacket pocket, left side. The same pen that signed invoices and wrote letters and forged documents and kept twenty years of meticulous, fraudulent accounts.

The pen is real. The pen was always real.

I write. In the guest book. In the first blank space. In handwriting that isn't Pemberton's careful copperplate or Marsh's theatrical flourish. In handwriting I haven't seen before — small, unsteady, the handwriting of a man who is learning to write his own name for the first time.

Vincent.

Just Vincent.

The first real guest in Lord Doily's guest book. The first honest entry in a house built for liars.

I close the book. I put the pen back in my pocket. I walk toward the door.

The cold air. The night. The step through.

Tuesday.

The evening is over. I'm standing in the entrance hall with Vincent. We've said goodnight. We've said Tuesday. There is nothing left to do but be here, in this last moment, before the door and the night and the cold and the walk home and the morning and Monday and Tuesday.

I am still. He is still. The chandelier is still. The house is still.

This is the end.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh walks through the front door of Lord Doily's manor. The chandelier holds. The house is dark. And on a side table in the entrance hall, a leather-bound guest book sits open to its first entry — one word, written in blue ink, in small unsteady handwriting: Vincent.
events.thinking: The chandelier holds. The guest book has my name in it. The night is outside. Reginald is already through the door. And I am still standing in this entrance hall because some part of me — the avoidant part, the part that has been alone since age six — doesn't know how to walk through a door toward something instead of away from it. Every door I've ever walked through was an escape or a manoeuvre. This one is neither. This one is just a door. And Tuesday is on the other side.

Perhaps Reginald is waiting for me to go first this time.

events.thinking: The cold is still coming through the open door. My hands hang at my sides. Empty — no schemes in them, no contingencies, no keys to turn in anyone's lock. Just hands.
